hiragana-chart.intro_tr: The hiragana chart, traditionally called the gojūon (五十音[ごじゅうおん], "fifty sounds"), is the foundational phonetic syllabary of Japanese and the very first thing every learner memorizes. It consists of 46 basic characters arranged in a 5×9 grid by vowel (a/i/u/e/o) and consonant row, plus the single nasal character ん. From these 46 base characters, adding dakuten (゛) or handakuten (゜) marks produces 25 more voiced/semi-voiced sounds, and combining certain い-row characters with small や/ゆ/よ produces 33 additional "yōon" glide sounds. Hiragana is used for native Japanese grammar elements (particles, verb/adjective endings) and native words without kanji, so fluent recognition of this chart is a hard prerequisite for reading anything in Japanese. A handful of characters have special pronunciation rules when used as grammatical particles, and several character pairs are frequently confused by beginners due to visual similarity.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Hiragana (Gojūon) Chart; 46 base characters
footnotes_tr: The い and う columns of や行 and わ行 are empty because those sounds already exist in あ行/や行 and are not written separately.
し is 'shi' (not 'si'), ち is 'chi' (not 'ti'), つ is 'tsu' (not 'tu'), ふ is 'fu' (not 'hu'); these four are the classic Romanization exceptions in the gojūon.

tables.caption_tr: Dakuten (゛) and Handakuten (゜); Voiced and Semi-Voiced Sounds
rows: が行 (g); dakuten on か行
ざ行 (z); dakuten on さ行
だ行 (d); dakuten on た行
ば行 (b); dakuten on は行
ぱ行 (p); handakuten on は行
footnotes_tr: じ and ぢ are pronounced identically ('ji') in standard modern Japanese; ず and づ are both 'zu'. ぢ/づ appear almost only in specific words like 鼻血[はなぢ] or 続く[つづく], mostly due to sequential voicing (rendaku) of ち/つ.
は行 is the only row that can take both dakuten (ば行) and handakuten (ぱ行).

tables.caption_tr: Yōon; Combination Sounds (small ゃ/ゅ/ょ)
footnotes_tr: The small ゃ/ゅ/ょ must be written noticeably smaller than a regular や/ゆ/よ; at full size they would form two separate syllables (e.g. きや = 'ki-ya', two beats, vs きゃ = 'kya', one beat).
Yōon syllables always count as a single mora (beat) in Japanese rhythm, just like any other single kana.

rows: Pronounced 'wa' when functioning as the topic particle
わたしは学生[がくせい]です → 'watashi wa'

学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きます → 'gakkou e'
Pronounced 'o' in modern Japanese; used only as the object particle, never in regular words

あ/い/う/え/お after same-row vowel

おかあさん (okaa-san), おにいさん (onii-san), すうがく (suugaku)

Long-vowel bar; standard in katakana, rare/informal in hiragana

katakana-chart.intro_tr: Katakana (カタカナ) is one of the two Japanese phonetic syllabaries, covering the exact same 46 basic sounds as hiragana but written with more angular, straight-edged shapes. It is used mainly for loanwords (gairaigo) borrowed from other languages, foreign personal and place names, onomatopoeia, scientific/technical terms, and for stylistic emphasis (similar to italics in English). Because Japanese has a limited native sound inventory, katakana developed a set of extended combinations (like ファ, ティ, ヴァ) to approximate foreign sounds such as f, v, ti, and w-glides that don't exist in the native syllable set. Two marks are essentially exclusive to katakana usage: the long vowel bar ー (chōonpu) and the middle dot ・ (nakaguro) used to separate foreign name elements. Mastering this chart is a prerequisite for reading any menu, ad, brand name, or piece of modern Japanese text.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Katakana Chart; Gojūon (46 core sounds)
footnotes_tr: シ is pronounced 'shi', チ is 'chi', ツ is 'tsu', フ is 'fu'; these do not follow the plain consonant+vowel pattern.
ヲ is almost never used in katakana text; it survives mainly as a historical/stylistic curiosity (the hiragana を is the real object-marker particle).
ン never starts a word and has no vowel of its own; it represents a syllabic 'n' sound.

tables.caption_tr: Voiced (゛ dakuten) and Semi-voiced (゜ handakuten) Katakana
footnotes_tr: ヂ and ヅ are extremely rare in katakana loanwords; ジ and ズ are used instead in almost all cases.
The handakuten (゜) only ever attaches to the h-row (ハヒフヘホ → パピプペポ).

tables.caption_tr: Contracted Sounds; Yōon (small ャ/ュ/ョ combinations)
footnotes_tr: The small ャュョ are written at reduced size and never pronounced as a separate syllable; they fuse with the preceding consonant to form one mora.

tables.caption_tr: Extended Katakana for Foreign Sounds (used only in loanwords)
rows: トゥ (rare, e.g. in some transliterations)
footnotes_tr: These combinations were created after WWII specifically to write foreign sounds more accurately (e.g. 'v' via ヴ, since native Japanese has no 'v').
In casual writing ヴ is often replaced with the simpler ブ (e.g. バイオリン instead of ヴァイオリン).

tables.caption_tr: Special Marks Unique or Central to Katakana

コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), ケーキ (kēki, cake)
Doubles the following consonant, creating a brief stop
ベッド (beddo, bed), サッカー (sakkā, soccer)
Separates elements of foreign names or items in a list

By far the most common use of katakana

Can also be written in hiragana; katakana adds punch/emphasis
Common in advertising, manga, and casual text

dakuten-handakuten.intro_tr: Dakuten (゛) and handakuten (゜) are small diacritical marks placed in the upper-right corner of certain hiragana and katakana characters to change how they are pronounced. Dakuten turns an unvoiced consonant into its voiced counterpart (k→g, s→z, t→d, h→b), while handakuten is used exclusively with the は-row to produce a p-sound. These marks are not optional decorations; they can completely change the meaning of a word, so reading and writing them correctly is essential from the very beginning. The same rules apply identically to hiragana and katakana, and modern keyboards/IMEs add the marks automatically when you type the voiced sound (e.g., typing "ga" produces が).

tables.caption_tr: Dakuten Conversion Chart; Hiragana (か/さ/た/は rows)
footnotes_tr: Only the か, さ, た and は rows can take dakuten. あ, な, ま, ら, や, わ rows never take dakuten.

tables.caption_tr: Dakuten Conversion Chart; Katakana (カ/サ/タ/ハ rows)
footnotes_tr: Katakana follows exactly the same dakuten rules as hiragana; only カ, サ, タ, ハ rows are affected.

tables.caption_tr: Handakuten Conversion; は/ハ Row Only (Hiragana & Katakana)
footnotes_tr: Handakuten (゜) exists ONLY for the は-row. No other row (か, さ, た, or any other) can ever take a handakuten.

tables.caption_tr: Sound Change Overview: Why Dakuten and Handakuten Change Pronunciation
footnotes_tr: The は-row is historically special: in Old Japanese it was pronounced with a /p/ sound. That original /p/ survives today only when handakuten is added, while dakuten instead gives the row a /b/ sound.

tables.caption_tr: Minimal Pairs: How Dakuten Changes Meaning
footnotes_tr: Always check for dakuten carefully when reading; missing a small mark can turn one word into a completely unrelated one.

tables.caption_tr: Special Case: じ/ぢ and ず/づ (Yotsugana; 'the four kana')
column_headers: When the rare spelling is used
rows: Only when ぢ comes from rendaku of a word starting with ち, or in words with a repeated ち sound
鼻血[はなぢ] (nosebleed = 鼻[はな] + 血[ち])
Only when づ comes from rendaku of a word starting with つ, or in words with a repeated つ sound
手作[てづく]り (handmade = 手[て] + 作[つく]り)
footnotes_tr: In modern standard Japanese orthography, じ and ず are used for almost all words. ぢ and づ survive only in specific rendaku compounds and a handful of words such as ちぢむ (to shrink) and つづく (to continue).

tables.caption_tr: Writing and Typing Rules
rows: Dakuten (゛) and handakuten (゜) are always written in the upper-right corner of the kana character, slightly smaller than the character itself
Dakuten: か・さ・た・は rows only. Handakuten: は row only; no other row can ever take handakuten
Type the voiced consonant directly; 'ga' → が, 'pa' → ぱ; the IME attaches the correct mark automatically
Most dakuten/handakuten kana exist as single pre-composed characters, but combining marks (U+3099 dakuten, U+309A handakuten) also exist for special cases
Voiced and semi-voiced kana are alphabetized immediately after their unvoiced base: か, が, き, ぎ, く, ぐ...

small-kana-combos.title_tr: Small Kana Combinations (きゃ, しゅ...)
small-kana-combos.intro_tr: Small kana combinations, called 拗音[ようおん] (yōon), are formed by pairing a consonant + i kana (き・し・ち・に・ひ・み・り and their voiced forms ぎ・じ・ぢ・び・ぴ) with a tiny ゃ, ゅ, or ょ. The small kana removes the "i" sound of the base kana and fuses with it into a single mora; きゃ is pronounced "kya", not "ki-ya". This applies identically to hiragana (used for native/Sino-Japanese words) and katakana (used for loanwords), and katakana further extends the system with combinations like ファ, ティ, ヴィ to represent sounds foreign to native Japanese. Even though yōon combinations use two written characters, they always count as exactly ONE mora/beat in pronunciation and pitch accent; this is the single most important rule to remember.

tables.caption_tr: Hiragana Yōon; Full Combination Chart
footnotes_tr: *ぢゃ/ぢゅ/ぢょ are extremely rare, appearing only in a handful of compound words (e.g. 縮[ちぢ]む‑related forms); for almost all purposes use じゃ/じゅ/じょ instead.
There is no ya/yu/yo row for す, ず, つ, づ, ぬ, ふ, ぶ, ぷ, ゆ, る; these consonant groups do not form yōon combinations in standard Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Katakana Yōon; Full Combination Chart (for loanwords & foreign names)
footnotes_tr: Example words: 東京[とうきょう] Tokyo, 写真[しゃしん] photo, 兄弟[きょうだい] siblings, 病院[びょういん] hospital, 旅行[りょこう] trip.

tables.caption_tr: Extended Katakana Combinations; Modern Sounds for Loanwords (not taught with hiragana)
footnotes_tr: These combinations exist ONLY in katakana. They were created after WWII to more accurately represent foreign loanword sounds that don't fit the native Japanese mora system.
In casual or older writing, ヴ-series is sometimes replaced with バ行 (バ/ビ/ブ/ベ/ボ), e.g. ヴァイオリン → バイオリン.

tables.caption_tr: Writing & Size Rules for Small Kana
rows: Small ゃ/ゅ/ょ are written at roughly half the size (or slightly less) of a normal kana, and printed/typed fonts render them visibly smaller.

In horizontal writing, the small kana sits slightly lower and to the left within its character box, tucked against the bottom-left of the preceding kana. In vertical writing, it sits in the upper-right of its box.
A small ゃ/ゅ/ょ never starts a word or sentence on its own; it always follows a base consonant+i kana (き, し, ち, に, ひ, み, り, ぎ, じ, び, ぴ, or their katakana equivalents).
A yōon pair (e.g. きょ) = 1 mora, NOT 2. This matters for pitch accent counting and for poetic mora counting (e.g. haiku).
Type the base consonant + 'ya/yu/yo', e.g. kya→きゃ, sha/sya→しゃ, cha/tya→ちゃ, ja/zya/dya→じゃ.
きや (2 morae: 'ki-ya') is different from きゃ (1 mora: 'kya'); compare 気[き]や (and...) vs 客[きゃく] (customer).

tables.caption_tr: Common Confusions & Quick Contrast Table
rows: じゃ is one syllable; じや would be two separate kana, rarely occurring together this way in real words.
社[しゃ] 'company/shrine' vs a hypothetical しや sequence; pronunciation and mora count differ.
お茶[ちゃ] 'tea' (1 mora ちゃ) vs 乳母[ちゃや]-type sequences read as two morae.
利用[りよう] 'usage' is spelled with big よ (2+1 morae: り-よ-う); NOT りょ. Common beginner misspelling trap!
footnotes_tr: Always double-check dictionary spelling: some words that SOUND like they might contain a yōon actually use full-size や/ゆ/よ as a separate mora, e.g. 利用[りよう] (riyō) vs a similar-sounding but different りょう (ryō).

long-vowels-sokuon.intro_tr: Japanese has two features that beginners frequently mishear, mispronounce, or mistype: long vowels (chōonpu, 長音[ちょうおん]) and the small っ (sokuon, 促音[そくおん]). A long vowel simply holds a vowel sound for one extra beat (mora); it is not a different vowel, just a longer one; and changing vowel length can completely change a word's meaning (おばさん 'aunt' vs おばあさん 'grandmother'). The small っ represents a short, silent pause of exactly one mora before certain consonants, which doubles the following consonant sound in romanization (きて 'come' vs きって 'stamp'). Both features are written differently depending on script: hiragana uses extra vowel kana (or occasionally an irregular お), katakana always uses the dash-like mark ー, and both scripts use a small っ/ッ for the pause. Getting these two features right is essential from day one, since mixing them up changes real words into other real words.

tables.caption_tr: Long vowels in hiragana; how each vowel row is lengthened
rows: あ row (か/さ/た/な/は/ま/や/ら/わ + あ)
え row (…+ い, the normal pattern)
え row (rare exception, written with え)
お row (…+ う, the normal pattern)

tables.caption_tr: Irregular お-row long vowels written with お instead of う (must be memorized)
footnotes_tr: Most お-row long vowels use う (e.g. 学校 がっこう, 空港 くうこう). Only a small closed set of common words use お; these must simply be memorized individually.

tables.caption_tr: Long vowels in katakana; always marked with ー (chōonpu bar)
rows: ー lengthens both お and い sounds here
two ー marks in one word
ー after け lengthens the え sound
ー lengthens the え sound
footnotes_tr: Unlike hiragana, katakana never spells out the extra vowel kana; it always uses the single dash-like mark ー, regardless of which vowel is being lengthened.
In vertical writing, ー is rotated 90° to appear as a vertical bar.

tables.caption_tr: Small っ (sokuon); formation and pronunciation rules
rows: Only directly before か/さ/た/ぱ row consonants (k, s, sh, t, ch, ts, p)
Silent pause worth exactly one mora/beat, then the following consonant is pronounced longer/doubled
あ/な/は/ま/や/ら/わ rows, or が/ざ/だ/ば rows (voiced consonants)
not possible: っが, っな, etc.
っ counts as one full mora on its own, same length as any kana
切手 = き・っ・て = 3 morae

tables.caption_tr: Minimal pairs distinguished only by vowel length
Minimal pairs distinguished only by presence/absence of small っ

kanji-basics.title_tr: Kanji Basics: On'yomi and Kun'yomi Readings
kanji-basics.intro_tr: Every kanji brought into Japanese from Chinese usually carries at least two kinds of reading: the on'yomi[音読み] (音読み), an approximation of the original Chinese pronunciation, and the kun'yomi[訓読み] (訓読み), a native Japanese word that was matched to the character's meaning. As a rough rule, kanji standing alone (often with hiragana okurigana[送り仮名] attached) use kun'yomi, while kanji strung together into two-or-more-character compounds (熟語[じゅくご]) use on'yomi. Many kanji have several on and several kun readings, and a handful of common words (熟字訓[じゅくじくん]) ignore the individual kanji readings entirely and must be memorized as whole units. This page collects the core patterns, common multi-reading kanji, and the irregular exceptions you'll hit constantly at N5.

tables.caption_tr: On'yomi vs. Kun'yomi at a Glance
rows: Borrowed approximation of the original Chinese pronunciation
Native Japanese word matched to the kanji's meaning
Inside kanji compounds (熟語[じゅくご]) of 2+ characters
Single kanji standing alone, often with okurigana[送り仮名]
Short, 1–2 morae, often ends in ん/っ or a long vowel
Can be longer, follows native Japanese word shapes
さん; 富士山[ふじさん] (Mt. Fuji)
すい; 水曜日[すいようび] (Wednesday)
じん/にん; 日本人[にほんじん] (Japanese person)

tables.caption_tr: Common Kanji with Both On and Kun Readings
rows: い(きる) / う(まれる) / なま
うえ / あ(げる) / のぼ(る)
した / さ(げる) / くだ(さい)

tables.caption_tr: Irregular Word-Level Readings (熟字訓[じゅくじくん])
footnotes_tr: These words cannot be sounded out kanji-by-kanji; the reading applies to the whole written word and must simply be memorized.

tables.caption_tr: Quick Rules: How to Guess Which Reading Applies
rows: Single kanji + hiragana okurigana forming a verb/adjective
食[た]べる (to eat), 高[たか]い (tall)
Two or more kanji joined with no okurigana in between
食事[しょくじ] (meal), 天気[てんき] (weather)
Single kanji used alone as a plain noun
Days of the week (曜日[ようび] compounds)
一[ひと]つ, 二[ふた]つ
一人[ひとり], 二人[ふたり], 三人[さんにん]
Often kun'yomi, but highly irregular; must check each name
山田[やまだ], 田中[たなか]

tables.caption_tr: The Three Historical Layers of On'yomi (Good to Recognize)
rows: Earliest layer, via the Wu region of China (~5th–6th century), common in Buddhist terms
ぎょう; 行事[ぎょうじ] (event)
Tang dynasty standard (~7th–9th century); the most common on'yomi today
こう; 旅行[りょこう] (travel)
Later Song/Ming era borrowings; rare, appears in a small set of words
あん; 行灯[あんどん] (paper lantern)
footnotes_tr: Most kanji only keep one of these three on'yomi in everyday use, but a few high-frequency characters like 行 preserve all three in different words; this is why some kanji seem to have unexpectedly many on'yomi listed in dictionaries.

examples.target: 山[やま]に登[のぼ]ります。
examples.reading: やまにのぼります。
examples.translation_tr: I climb the mountain.
examples.note_tr: 山 is read with its kun'yomi やま because it stands alone as a plain noun.

examples.target: 富士山[ふじさん]はとても高[たか]いです。
examples.reading: ふじさんはとてもたかいです。
examples.translation_tr: Mt. Fuji is very tall.
examples.note_tr: Inside the compound word 富士山[ふじさん], 山 switches to its on'yomi さん.

examples.target: 火[ひ]を消[け]してください。
examples.reading: ひをけしてください。
examples.translation_tr: Please put out the fire.
examples.note_tr: 火 alone as a noun uses the kun'yomi ひ.

examples.target: 火曜日[かようび]に会[あ]いましょう。
examples.reading: かようびにあいましょう。
examples.translation_tr: Let's meet on Tuesday.
examples.note_tr: In the compound 火曜日[かようび], 火 uses the on'yomi か.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は毎日[まいにち]水[みず]を飲[の]みます。
examples.reading: わたしはまいにちみずをのみます。
examples.translation_tr: I drink water every day.
examples.note_tr: 水 as a standalone noun uses the kun'yomi みず.

examples.target: 水曜日[すいようび]はプールに行[い]きます。
examples.reading: すいようびはプールにいきます。
examples.translation_tr: I go to the pool on Wednesdays.
examples.note_tr: 水 inside 水曜日[すいようび] switches to the on'yomi すい.

examples.target: 今日[きょう]は一人[ひとり]で映画[えいが]を見[み]ます。
examples.reading: きょうはひとりでえいがをみます。
examples.translation_tr: Today I'll watch a movie alone.
examples.note_tr: 今日[きょう] and 一人[ひとり] are both irregular jukujikun readings; the whole word must be memorized, not built kanji-by-kanji.

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]は毎朝[まいあさ]早[はや]く起[お]きます。
examples.reading: せんせいはまいあさはやくおきます。
examples.translation_tr: The teacher wakes up early every morning.
examples.note_tr: 先生[せんせい] is read entirely with on'yomi, while 起[お]きる uses the kun'yomi verb stem お + okurigana きる.

wa-topic-particle.intro_tr: The particle は (pronounced "wa" when used as a particle, even though written with the hiragana for "ha") marks the TOPIC of a sentence; what the sentence is about; rather than strictly identifying the grammatical subject. It sets up a "as for X..." frame, and everything after it is a comment about that topic. は is one of the very first and most important particles learners meet, and it is frequently confused with が (the subject particle) because both can translate as "is/are" in English. Understanding the topic-vs-subject distinction, how は interacts with negation, contrast, and other particles, and when NOT to use は, is essential for natural Japanese from the very beginning.

tables.caption_tr: Core facts about は as the topic particle
rows: Written with hiragana は (normally 'ha'), but pronounced わ [wa] ONLY when used as this grammatical particle
わたし[は] → read as 'watashi WA', not 'watashi HA'
Marks the TOPIC of the sentence: 'as for X, ...'
わたし[は]がくせいです。(As for me, I'm a student.)
Attaches directly after the noun/pronoun it marks; comes first in the sentence in most simple statements
When a noun marked by が (subject) or を (object) becomes the topic, が/を is DROPPED and replaced by は
ねこ[が]すき[です] → ねこ[は]すき[です]。
Does NOT replace に/で/と/へ
With other particles, は is added AFTER them, it does not remove them
とうきょう[に]は いきません。(As for going to Tokyo, I won't.)
A sentence can have multiple は, especially in contrastive statements
コーヒー[は]すき[です]が、おちゃ[は]すき[じゃ]ない[です]。
Sentences with negative predicates almost always use は for the item being negated, not が
わたし[は]がくせいでは[ありません]。

tables.caption_tr: は vs が: the core contrast (both often translate as 'is/are' in English)
rows: Introducing or re-mentioning a known/established topic
わたし[は]たなかです。(I'm Tanaka; topic: me)
だれ[が]きましたか。田中[さん][が]きました。(Who came? Tanaka came.)
Making a general statement about the topic
ぞうは はな[が]ながい[です]。(As for elephants, [their] noses are long.)
Marking the grammatical subject inside a description clause
ぞうは はな[が]ながい[です]。(が marks 'nose' as subject of 'long')
にく[は]たべます[が]、さかな[は]たべません。(I eat meat, but not fish.)
Emphasizing/selecting one specific item among possibilities
これ[が]いい[です]。(THIS one is good; pointing it out)
The topic is already clear from context (often omitted, but は still implied)
(わたしは) げんきです。(I'm fine.)
After question words like 何/誰/どこ used as the grammatical subject

tables.caption_tr: Common sentence patterns using は
rows: これ[は]ペン[です]。(This is a pen.)
この[へや][は]ひろい[です]。(This room is spacious.)
Xは Yがあります/います
X has Y / there is Y (topic + existence, note が for the thing that exists)
わたし[は]じかん[が]ありません。(I don't have time.)
Xは Yが好き[すき]です/上手[じょうず]です
X likes/is good at Y (double-particle pattern: は for topic, が for the target)
わたし[は]にほんご[が]じょうず[です]。(I'm good at Japanese.)
Xは Yではありません/じゃないです
X is not Y (negation always pairs with は)
これ[は]ほん[では]ありません。(This is not a book.)
Adding contrast/emphasis on a location, time, or method already marked by another particle
きょう[に]は いきません。(As for today [specifically], I won't go.)

tables.caption_tr: When NOT to use は (common beginner mistakes)
rows: The answer is NEW information, not the established topic; use が
だれ[が]すき[です]か。→ たなかさん[が]すき[です]。(NOT たなかさんは)
Inside a relative/subordinate clause describing a noun
は cannot normally mark the subject of a clause that modifies another noun; use が
わたし[が]かいた[ほん] (the book [that] I wrote); NOT わたしは かいた本
Marking existence of an indefinite/unknown thing (there is a cat)
New/unspecified existence uses が, not は
にわに ねこ[が]います。(There is a cat in the garden.) NOT ねこは
Double-marking a particle that already shows relation (に, で, と)
は is added in addition to, never instead of, these particles
がっこう[に][は]いきません, not がっこうはいきません for 'to school'

examples.target: わたし[が]がくせいです。 → わたし[は]がくせいです。
examples.reading: watashi wa gakusei desu
examples.translation_tr: As for me, I am a student. (topic: わたし)

examples.target: これ[は]ほん[です]。
examples.reading: kore wa hon desu
examples.translation_tr: As for this, it is a book. / This is a book.

examples.target: きょう[は]あつい[です]。
examples.reading: kyō wa atsui desu
examples.translation_tr: As for today, it's hot. / Today is hot.

examples.target: わたし[は]にほんじん[では]ありません。
examples.reading: watashi wa nihonjin dewa arimasen
examples.translation_tr: As for me, I am not Japanese.

examples.target: コーヒー[は]すき[です]が、おちゃ[は]すき[じゃ]ない[です]。
examples.reading: kōhī wa suki desu ga, ocha wa suki janai desu
examples.translation_tr: I like coffee, but I don't like tea. (contrastive は on both nouns)

examples.target: パンダ[は]かわいい[です]。
examples.reading: panda wa kawaii desu
examples.translation_tr: Pandas are cute. (generic statement about the topic)

examples.target: きのう[は]あめ[でした]が、きょう[は]はれ[です]。
examples.reading: kinō wa ame deshita ga, kyō wa hare desu
examples.translation_tr: It rained yesterday, but today is sunny. (comparing two topics)

examples.target: この[ほん][は]わたし[が]かいました。
examples.reading: kono hon wa watashi ga kaimashita
examples.translation_tr: As for this book, I bought it. (は marks topic, が marks the doer within the comment)

ga-subject-particle.intro_tr: が marks the grammatical subject of a sentence, while は marks the topic; what the sentence is about. This is one of the trickiest distinctions for English speakers, because both particles can translate as the English subject 'is/are', yet they work very differently in Japanese. が tends to introduce new, unknown, or specifically-identified information and directly answers 'who/what' questions, whereas は presents already-known information, states general facts, or sets up an implicit contrast. Certain verbs and adjectives; ある/いる, 好き, わかる, できる, ほしい, 上手/下手; grammatically require が to mark their logical object rather than を or は. Mastering は vs が is mostly about context and information structure, not just sentence position.

tables.caption_tr: Core Function Comparison: は vs が
rows: Topic; what the sentence is about
Can extend over the whole sentence, even multiple clauses
Limited to the clause it appears in
De-emphasizes the marked noun (it's just the frame)
Often implies an unstated contrast ("as for A... but...")
Usually neutral description, or exclusive identification ("A, and only A")
Often omitted once topic is established in context
Rarely omitted; it marks exactly who/what does the action

tables.caption_tr: When が Is Required
rows: 誰[だれ]が来[き]ますか → 田中[たなか]さんが来[き]ます
The new information supplied as the answer takes が, never は
Introducing a character/thing for the first time
昔々[むかしむかし]、おじいさんがいました
First mention in a story uses が; later mentions of the same character switch to は
Existence verbs ある / いる
The subject of existence always takes が
日本語[にほんご]ができます
できる marks what one is able to do with が, not を
The desired object is marked with が
Preference/liking 好[す]き・嫌[きら]い
The liked/disliked object takes が, not を
Perception わかる・見[み]える・聞[き]こえる
意味[いみ]がわかりません
The thing perceived/understood is marked with が
Subject inside a relative or subordinate clause
これは私[わたし]が作[つく]ったケーキです
Embedded-clause subjects use が; は is reserved for the outer topic
彼[かれ]が犯人[はんにん]です
"He (and only he) is the culprit"; が singles out the one correct answer

tables.caption_tr: Verbs & Adjectives That Take が for Their Logical Object
rows: コーヒーが好[す]きです
納豆[なっとう]が嫌[きら]いです
新[あたら]しい車[くるま]がほしいです
日本語[にほんご]がわかります
料理[りょうり]ができます
音楽[おんがく]が聞[き]こえます
英語[えいご]が上手[じょうず]です
時間[じかん]がありません
footnotes_tr: Learners often mistakenly mark these objects with を because of the English 'like/want/understand + object' pattern; remember these are grammatically subject-like in Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Side-by-Side Comparison Sentences
rows: 私[わたし]は学生[がくせい]です。
As for me, I am a student (neutral self-introduction)
私[わたし]が学生[がくせい]です。
I am the student (the specific one being asked about)
象[ぞう]は鼻[はな]が長[なが]い。
As for elephants, their trunk is long (general fact about elephants)
The trunk is long (simple statement about a specific trunk)
田中[たなか]さんは来[き]ません。
Mr. Tanaka is not coming (implies contrast: maybe others are)
田中[たなか]さんが来[き]ません。
It's Mr. Tanaka (specifically) who isn't coming
ケーキは私[わたし]が作[つく]りました。
As for the cake, I made it (topic = cake, focus on who made it)
私[わたし]がケーキを作[つく]りました。
I made the cake (neutral statement, answers "who made the cake")

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: これは私[わたし]は作[つく]ったケーキです。
Two competing topics with は in one sentence; the embedded clause subject needs が
これは私[わたし]が作[つく]ったケーキです。
私[わたし]は水[みず]をほしいです。
ほしい takes が for its object, not を
私[わたし]は水[みず]がほしいです。
私[わたし]が日本人[にほんじん]です。（out of context, self-introduction）
が sounds like exclusive identification ("I am THE Japanese person here"), too strong for a plain introduction
私[わたし]は日本人[にほんじん]です。
昔々[むかしむかし]、おじいさんはいました。
は implies the character is already known; new characters in narration need が
昔々[むかしむかし]、おじいさんがいました。
Marking every noun in a sentence with は
Creates multiple competing topics and sounds unnatural
Keep only one は (the topic) per sentence; use が for other subjects

examples.target: 誰[だれ]が来[き]ますか。
examples.reading: だれがきますか。
examples.translation_tr: Who is coming?
examples.note_tr: が follows question words like 誰 (who) and 何 (what) because the answer will be new information.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんが来[き]ます。
examples.reading: たなかさんがきます。
examples.translation_tr: Mr. Tanaka is coming.
examples.note_tr: A direct answer to a 'who' question always uses が, never は.

examples.target: 庭[にわ]に猫[ねこ]がいます。
examples.reading: にわにねこがいます。
examples.translation_tr: There is a cat in the garden.
examples.note_tr: いる/ある (existence) always take が for the thing that exists.

examples.target: 私[わたし]はコーヒーが好[す]きです。
examples.reading: わたしはコーヒーがすきです。
examples.translation_tr: I like coffee.
examples.note_tr: は marks the topic (me), while が marks the object of the emotion/preference (coffee).

examples.target: これは私[わたし]が作[つく]ったケーキです。
examples.reading: これはわたしがつくったケーキです。
examples.translation_tr: This is the cake that I made.
examples.note_tr: Inside the relative clause '私が作った', が marks the subject; は cannot be used there.

examples.target: 象[ぞう]は鼻[はな]が長[なが]い。
examples.reading: ぞうははながながい。
examples.translation_tr: Elephants have long trunks.
examples.note_tr: Classic double-subject sentence: は sets the overall topic (elephants), が marks the specific subject of the description (the trunk).

examples.target: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。
examples.reading: あめがふっています。
examples.translation_tr: It's raining.
examples.note_tr: が is used because this is a fresh observation, not a statement about a known topic.

examples.target: 山田[やまだ]さんが日本語[にほんご]の先生[せんせい]です。
examples.reading: やまださんがにほんごのせんせいです。
examples.translation_tr: Mr. Yamada is the Japanese teacher.
examples.note_tr: が gives an exclusive/identifying nuance; 'he, specifically, is the teacher' (compare with 山田さんは先生です, a neutral topic statement).

o-object-particle.intro_tr: The particle を (pronounced exactly like お, "o") is the direct object marker in Japanese; it attaches to the noun that directly receives the action of a transitive verb, roughly equivalent to the object in "I eat bread" (English "bread"). Beyond marking plain objects, を has two other important N5 uses: marking the space or path a movement verb travels through (公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]く "walk through the park"), and marking the point of departure or separation from which someone leaves (家[いえ]を出[で]る "leave the house"). を never marks a destination; that job belongs to に or へ. In casual spoken Japanese を is very frequently dropped after the noun, but it must always be included in formal/written Japanese and on tests.

tables.caption_tr: Core Functions of を
rows: Direct object of a transitive verb
Path / space traversed by a movement verb
公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]く
Place Noun + を + Verb of leaving
Object of a たい (want to) desire form
to want to read a book
Object made to act, in causative sentences (intransitive verb base)
子供[こども]を歩[ある]かせる

tables.caption_tr: Verbs of Traversal that Take を (marks the space passed through, NOT the destination)
rows: 道[みち]を歩[ある]く; to walk along the street
公園[こうえん]を走[はし]る; to run through the park
橋[はし]を渡[わた]る; to cross the bridge
トンネルを通[とお]る; to pass through the tunnel
空[そら]を飛[と]ぶ; to fly through the sky
公園[こうえん]を散歩[さんぽ]する; to stroll through the park
川[かわ]を泳[およ]ぐ; to swim across the river

tables.caption_tr: Verbs of Departure / Separation that Take を (marks the point left FROM)
rows: 家[いえ]を出[で]る; to leave home
バスを降[お]りる; to get off the bus
大学[だいがく]を卒業[そつぎょう]する; to graduate from university
故郷[こきょう]を離[はな]れる; to leave one's hometown
空港[くうこう]を飛[と]び立[た]つ; to take off from the airport

tables.caption_tr: を vs に vs で; Avoiding Confusion with Movement and Location
rows: 公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]く
公園[こうえん]に行[い]く
the location where an action takes place
公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]ぶ
the direct object of a transitive verb
indirect object / target of a directional verb
先生[せんせい]に聞[き]く

tables.caption_tr: Writing & Pronunciation Notes
rows: を is pronounced identically to お, i.e. [o]; NOT "wo" in modern spoken Japanese.
The hiragana を is used only as this grammatical particle; it never appears inside ordinary words (unlike お, which appears in many words: 多[おお]い, お茶[ちゃ], etc.).
In classical/old orthography を represented a distinct sound [wo]; in modern Japanese the two sounds merged into [o], but the spelling で 区別[くべつ] (distinction) was kept for this particle.
Typed by pressing "wo" on a Japanese IME, even though it is pronounced "o".
In casual conversation を is very often dropped: 水[みず]飲[の]む? instead of 水[みず]を飲[の]む?; but it must be kept in writing and formal speech.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with を
rows: Using に for a plain direct object
❌りんごに食べる → ✅りんごを食[た]べる
に marks direction/target, not the thing directly acted upon.
Using を for a destination with 行く/来る
❌学校[がっこう]を行[い]く → ✅学校[がっこう]に行[い]く
Destination of 行く/来る/帰る takes に (or へ), not を.
Confusing を (path) with で (place of action)
公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]く (walking THROUGH the park) vs 公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]ぶ (playing AT the park)
を = space traversed by movement; で = static location where an action occurs.
Forgetting を marks departure point, not destination
❌大学[だいがく]に卒業[そつぎょう]する → ✅大学[だいがく]を卒業[そつぎょう]する
卒業する, 出る, 降りる all take を for the place being left.
Casual: 水[みず]飲[の]む？ / Written: 水[みず]を飲[の]みますか。
Particle omission is a spoken-casual feature only; keep を in formal writing/tests.

examples.target: 私[わたし]はパンを食[た]べます。
examples.reading: わたしはパンをたべます。
examples.translation_tr: I eat bread.

examples.target: 公園[こうえん]を散歩[さんぽ]します。
examples.reading: こうえんをさんぽします。
examples.translation_tr: I take a walk through the park. (movement across a space)

examples.target: 電車[でんしゃ]を降[お]ります。
examples.reading: でんしゃをおります。
examples.translation_tr: I get off the train. (point of departure/separation)

examples.target: 毎朝[まいあさ]家[いえ]を出[で]ます。
examples.reading: まいあさいえをでます。
examples.translation_tr: I leave the house every morning.

examples.target: 橋[はし]を渡[わた]ります。
examples.reading: はしをわたります。
examples.translation_tr: I cross the bridge.

examples.target: 大学[だいがく]を卒業[そつぎょう]しました。
examples.reading: だいがくをそつぎょうしました。
examples.translation_tr: I graduated from university.

examples.target: 本[ほん]を読[よ]みたいです。
examples.reading: ほんをよみたいです。
examples.translation_tr: I want to read a book.

examples.target: 空[そら]を飛[と]ぶ鳥[とり]を見[み]ました。
examples.reading: そらをとぶとりをみました。
examples.translation_tr: I saw a bird flying through the sky.

ni-particle.intro_tr: に is one of the busiest particles in Japanese, and that is exactly why beginners mix it up with で, へ, and を. At its core, に always points to a fixed point; a point in time, a point in space (destination or location of existence), or a point that an action is directed toward (a target, a recipient, or a result). Once you see all of its jobs side by side, the pattern becomes much easier to remember: に marks "the specific point something is anchored to," whether that point is 7時, 学校, 友達, or 医者. This page collects every core N5 use of に in one place so you can check it whenever a sentence feels ambiguous.

tables.caption_tr: Core functions of に (overview)
rows: 七時[しちじ]に寝[ね]ます
公園[こうえん]に猫[ねこ]がいます
There is a cat in the park
東京[とうきょう]に行[い]きます
母[はは]に電話[でんわ]します
友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]をあげます
I give a book to my friend
買[か]い物[もの]に行[い]きます
先生[せんせい]になります
一日[いちにち]に二回[にかい]
先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められました
I was praised by the teacher
電車[でんしゃ]に乗[の]ります

tables.caption_tr: Time expressions: does に attach or not?
rows: 三時[さんじ]に会[あ]います
月曜日[げつようび]に休[やす]みます
八月[はちがつ]七日[なのか]に行[い]きます
二〇二六年[にせんにじゅうろくねん]に生[う]まれました
今日[きょう]/明日[あした]/昨日[きのう]
今日[きょう]働[はたら]きます
Relative day words normally drop に
毎日[まいにち]勉強[べんきょう]します
毎朝/毎晩/毎週 etc. do not take に
夏[なつ](に)旅行[りょこう]します
に is optional, often dropped in casual speech
今週[こんしゅう]/来月[らいげつ]/去年[きょねん]
来月[らいげつ]会[あ]います
footnotes_tr: General rule: if the time word can be pinpointed on a calendar/clock (a fixed, countable point), it takes に. If the time word is relative to 'now' (today, this week, every day), に is dropped.

tables.caption_tr: に vs へ vs で vs を; common confusion
rows: 学校[がっこう]に着[つ]きます
学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きます
Emphasizes the direction, softer/more literary than に; interchangeable with に for 行く/来る/帰る
学校[がっこう]で勉強[べんきょう]します
The action takes place at/in this location, not toward it
公園[こうえん]を歩[ある]きます
Used with movement verbs over a space (歩く, 渡る, 通る)
footnotes_tr: に and へ are interchangeable for simple direction verbs (行く/来る/帰る), but only に can mark existence location (います/あります) and indirect objects; へ cannot.

tables.caption_tr: Verbs that require に for their target
rows: 友達[ともだち]に会[あ]う
電車[でんしゃ]に乗[の]る
空港[くうこう]に着[つ]く
東京[とうきょう]に住[す]む
会社[かいしゃ]に勤[つと]める
友達[ともだち]に電話[でんわ]する
footnotes_tr: These verbs treat に as fixed and idiomatic; using で or へ instead is a common beginner mistake.

tables.caption_tr: に for purpose of movement (verb-stem + に + 行く/来る/帰る)
rows: 映画[えいが]を見[み]に行[い]きます
I go to watch a movie
手伝[てつだ]いに来[き]ました
買[か]い物[もの]に行[い]きます
昼寝[ひるね]に帰[かえ]ります
footnotes_tr: Only works with movement verbs (行く/来る/帰る); the に here marks 'in order to,' the purpose of the trip.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は七時[しちじ]に起[お]きます。
examples.reading: わたしはしちじにおきます。
examples.translation_tr: I get up at seven o'clock. (に marks the specific point in time)

examples.target: 毎朝[まいあさ]、学校[がっこう]に行[い]きます。
examples.reading: まいあさ、がっこうにいきます。
examples.translation_tr: I go to school every morning. (に marks the destination)

examples.target: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に本[ほん]があります。
examples.reading: つくえのうえにほんがあります。
examples.translation_tr: There is a book on the desk. (に marks the location where something exists)

examples.target: 友達[ともだち]に会[あ]います。
examples.reading: ともだちにあいます。
examples.translation_tr: I meet a friend. (に marks the target of the verb 会う)

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]に日本語[にほんご]を教[おし]えます。
examples.reading: せんせいはわたしににほんごをおしえます。
examples.translation_tr: The teacher teaches me Japanese. (に marks the indirect object; the receiver)

examples.target: バスに乗[の]ります。
examples.reading: バスにのります。
examples.translation_tr: I get on the bus. (に marks the point of contact with the verb 乗る)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は医者[いしゃ]になりました。
examples.reading: かれはいしゃになりました。
examples.translation_tr: He became a doctor. (に marks the result of a change, used with なる)

examples.target: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]に三回[さんかい]、ジムに行[い]きます。
examples.reading: いっしゅうかんにさんかい、ジムにいきます。
examples.translation_tr: I go to the gym three times a week. (に marks the rate/frequency; 'per' week)

de-particle.intro_tr: The particle で is one of the most versatile particles in Japanese, but all of its uses share a common thread: it marks the "field" or "framework" within which an action takes place; whether that is a physical place, a tool, a method, a cause, a material, a quantity, or a condition. Unlike に, which marks a fixed point (existence, destination, specific time), で marks the surrounding circumstance that makes the action possible. Because so many unrelated-looking meanings (place, tool, cause, material, scope, deadline, state) are expressed by the same single particle, で is one of the first grammar points where beginners get confused; this page lays out every core function side by side so you can see the underlying logic and avoid the classic で/に mix-ups.

tables.caption_tr: Core functions of で at a glance
rows: 図書館[としょかん]で 勉強[べんきょう]します
ペンで 書[か]きます
日本語[にほんご]で 話[はな]します
電車[でんしゃ]で 行[い]きます
風邪[かぜ]で 休[やす]みました
I was absent DUE TO a cold
全部[ぜんぶ]で 三千円[さんぜんえん]です
Time needed / deadline (duration, not a point)
一時間[いちじかん]で 終[お]わります
一人[ひとり]で 行[い]きます
go ALONE (in the state of being one person)

tables.caption_tr: で vs に; the classic beginner confusion (location)
rows: The fixed location where something EXISTS (a state)
Existence verbs: いる, ある, 住[す]む
教室[きょうしつ]に 学生[がくせい]が います (Students ARE in the classroom)
The location where an ACTION takes place (an event)
Action verbs: 勉強する, 食べる, 読む, 遊ぶ, etc.
教室[きょうしつ]で 勉強[べんきょう]します (I study IN the classroom)
行く, 来る, 着く, 入る
家[いえ]に 帰[かえ]ります (I return TO my house; arrival point)
The place where movement/action itself unfolds (not the destination)
歩く, 走る, 泳ぐ, 遊ぶ
公園[こうえん]で 走[はし]ります (I run IN the park; the action happens there)

tables.caption_tr: で vs に for time expressions
rows: A specific point in time (clock time, day of week, date)
三時[さんじ]に 会[あ]います
A time span/limit needed to complete something (duration-as-deadline)
一週間[いっしゅうかん]で 終[お]わります
It will be finished WITHIN one week
The total time something took (retrospective duration)
三十分[さんじっぷん]で 着[つ]きました

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions built with で
rows: 一人[ひとり]で / 二人[ふたり]で
ひとりで / ふたりで
alone / as a group of two
in a hurry (て-form of 急ぐ, not the particle, but often confused visually)
with this, at this point (concluding a task)
病気[びょうき]で / 事故[じこ]で
びょうきで / じこで
due to illness / due to an accident

tables.caption_tr: で compared with related particles を and と (common mix-ups)
rows: 公園[こうえん]で 遊[あそ]ぶ (play IN the park)
Marks the setting/tool, not the direct object
Direct object of a transitive verb, or place passed through
公園[こうえん]を 歩[ある]く (walk THROUGH the park)
を with movement verbs marks the space traversed, not the location of a static action
友達[ともだち]と 遊[あそ]ぶ (play WITH a friend)
と marks a person you do something together with; で never marks a person as a companion

examples.target: 図書館[としょかん]で 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みます。
examples.reading: としょかんで ほんを よみます。
examples.translation_tr: I read a book at the library. (で marks the place where the action happens)

examples.target: バスで 学校[がっこう]へ 行[い]きます。
examples.reading: ばすで がっこうへ いきます。
examples.translation_tr: I go to school by bus. (で marks the means of transport)

examples.target: 箸[はし]で ご飯[はん]を 食[た]べます。
examples.reading: はしで はんを たべます。
examples.translation_tr: I eat rice with chopsticks. (で marks the tool/instrument used)

examples.target: 日本語[にほんご]で 手紙[てがみ]を 書[か]きます。
examples.reading: にほんごで てがみを かきます。
examples.translation_tr: I write a letter in Japanese. (で marks the language/method)

examples.target: 病気[びょうき]で 学校[がっこう]を 休[やす]みました。
examples.reading: びょうきで がっこうを やすみました。
examples.translation_tr: I was absent from school due to illness. (で marks the cause/reason)

examples.target: 全部[ぜんぶ]で 五千円[ごせんえん]でした。
examples.reading: ぜんぶで ごせんえんでした。
examples.translation_tr: It was 5000 yen in total. (で marks the total scope of a sum)

examples.target: この 橋[はし]は 石[いし]で できています。
examples.reading: このはしは いしで できています。
examples.translation_tr: This bridge is made of stone. (で marks the raw material)

examples.target: 一人[ひとり]で 旅行[りょこう]します。
examples.reading: ひとりで りょこうします。
examples.translation_tr: I travel alone. (で marks the state/condition under which the action is done)

e-direction-particle.intro_tr: The particle へ marks the direction or general destination of movement, roughly translating to "toward" or "to." It attaches after a place (and sometimes a person) and pairs most naturally with motion verbs like 行く[いく] (to go), 来る[くる] (to come), and 帰る[かえる] (to return). Although written with the hiragana へ, as a particle it is always pronounced "e," never "he." In everyday motion sentences へ and に are often interchangeable, but へ highlights the direction of travel while に pins down the exact arrival point; and only に can mark time, the indirect object of giving verbs, or the location of existence with あります/います.

tables.caption_tr: Core Function of へ; Marking Direction/Destination
rows: 場所[ばしょ] + へ + 行[い]く／来[く]る／帰[かえ]る
Emphasizes the direction of movement, not necessarily final arrival
Common with letters, messages, gifts sent to someone
Never pronounced 'he' when functioning as a particle, even though the kana is へ
footnotes_tr: へ historically comes from the noun 方[へ] meaning 'direction,' which is why it feels less precise than に about the exact endpoint.

tables.caption_tr: へ vs. に; Choosing the Right Direction Particle
rows: General direction / orientation toward a place
Yes, in most cases (行く・来る・帰る etc.)
Yes, but stresses the precise destination
Standard (友達[ともだち]に あげる)
Marking location of existence (あります/います)
Possible (東京[とうきょう]にいます)
Slightly more literary/formal; common in addresses, titles, letters

tables.caption_tr: Common Verbs Paired with へ
rows: 学校[がっこう]へ行[い]く
手紙[てがみ]を彼[かれ]へ送[おく]る
新[あたら]しい部屋[へや]へ移[うつ]る

tables.caption_tr: Set Expressions and Address Usage with へ
rows: Toward the future (used in titles, dedications)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with へ
rows: 東京[とうきょう]へいます
へ cannot mark the location of existence
東京[とうきょう]にいます
へ cannot mark a point in time
友達[ともだち]へ本[ほん]をあげる
へ is not the standard particle for the recipient of giving verbs
友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]をあげる

examples.target: 学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きます。
examples.reading: がっこうへいきます。
examples.translation_tr: I'm going to school.

examples.target: 日本[にほん]へようこそ！
examples.reading: にほんへようこそ！
examples.translation_tr: Welcome to Japan!

examples.target: 母[はは]へ手紙[てがみ]を書[か]きました。
examples.reading: ははへてがみをかきました。
examples.translation_tr: I wrote a letter to my mother.
examples.note_tr: へ marks the person as the direction/recipient of the letter, common in written correspondence.

examples.target: 駅[えき]へ向[む]かっています。
examples.reading: えきへむかっています。
examples.translation_tr: I'm heading toward the station.

examples.target: どこへ行[い]くのですか。
examples.reading: どこへいくのですか。
examples.translation_tr: Where are you going?

examples.target: 明日[あした]、国[くに]へ帰[かえ]ります。
examples.reading: あした、くにへかえります。
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow I'm going back to my home country.

examples.target: 右[みぎ]へ曲[ま]がってください。
examples.reading: みぎへまがってください。
examples.translation_tr: Please turn to the right.

examples.target: これは未来[みらい]への手紙[てがみ]です。
examples.reading: これはみらいへのてがみです。
examples.translation_tr: This is a letter to the future.
examples.note_tr: へ + の turns the directional phrase into a noun modifier: 'a letter [directed] toward the future'.

no-possessive.intro_tr: The particle の is one of the most frequently used words in Japanese and has several distinct jobs: linking two nouns to show possession, description, material, or category (Noun A の Noun B); turning a verb or clause into a noun-like phrase (nominalizer); replacing an already-mentioned noun so you don't have to repeat it ("the ... one"); and softening or explaining a statement/question at the end of a sentence (especially in casual speech, where it also appears as んです in polite speech). Even though it looks like a single tiny word, understanding which "job" の is doing in a sentence is essential for reading comprehension from the very first weeks of study. This page organizes all of these uses into tables so you can quickly check which pattern applies.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Possessive/Descriptive Use: Noun A の Noun B
rows: 田中[たなか]さんの車[くるま]
日本[にほん]の首都[しゅと]
大学[だいがく]の先生[せんせい]
日本語[にほんご]の本[ほん]

tables.caption_tr: Overview: The Five Main Functions of の
rows: 友達[ともだち]の田中[たなか]さん
Plain form + の / んです

tables.caption_tr: の as Nominalizer: Turning Verbs/Clauses into Noun Phrases
rows: 音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]くのが好[す]きです
ongaku o kiku no ga suki desu
写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]るのを手伝[てつだ]ってください
shashin o toru no o tetsudatte kudasai
Please help me take the photo
Clause + の + を + 知る/見る/聞く
彼[かれ]が来[く]るのを知[し]らなかった
kare ga kuru no o shiranakatta
I didn't know he was coming
毎日[まいにち]勉強[べんきょう]するのは大変[たいへん]です
mainichi benkyou suru no wa taihen desu
footnotes_tr: With verbs of reporting/thinking such as 思う, 言う, the nominalizer こと is required instead of の (e.g., 彼が来ると思う, not 来るのと思う). See the こと/の nominalization topic for the full contrast.

tables.caption_tr: の Replacing a Noun ('the one')
rows: 赤[あか]いのをください
Please give me the red one
新[あたら]しいのが欲[ほ]しい
この本[ほん]は私[わたし]のです
kono hon wa watashi no desu
どれが田中[たなか]さんのですか
dore ga Tanaka-san no desu ka
footnotes_tr: Here の stands in for a noun already mentioned or understood from context, avoiding repetition; similar to English 'one' or possessive pronouns (mine, yours).

tables.caption_tr: の in Questions and Sentence-Final Position (Explanatory/Softening Tone)
rows: Plain form + んです / んですか
どうして遅[おく]れたんですか
Why were you late? (asking for an explanation)
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いんです
The thing is, I have a headache
footnotes_tr: んです is the polite-speech contraction of の + です, used constantly in natural conversation to give background, reasons, or explanations; not just in questions.

tables.caption_tr: Chaining Multiple の (A の B の C)
rows: 私[わたし]の母[はは]の誕生日[たんじょうび]
日本語[にほんご]の先生[せんせい]の本[ほん]
会社[かいしゃ]の同僚[どうりょう]の田中[たなか]さん
footnotes_tr: の can be chained (each 'link' modifies the next noun), but more than 2–3 in a row becomes hard to parse and is best avoided in careful writing.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with の
rows: な-adjectives take な, not の, directly before a noun
の is required between two nouns to show possession; it cannot be dropped
い-adjectives modify nouns directly; の is not inserted
の never means 'is'; that role belongs to だ/です

examples.target: これは私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。
examples.reading: Kore wa watashi no hon desu.
examples.translation_tr: This is my book.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんの車[くるま]は赤[あか]いです。
examples.reading: Tanaka-san no kuruma wa akai desu.
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka's car is red.

examples.target: 日本[にほん]の首都[しゅと]は東京[とうきょう]です。
examples.reading: Nihon no shuto wa Toukyou desu.
examples.translation_tr: Japan's capital is Tokyo.

examples.target: これは木[き]の机[つくえ]です。
examples.reading: Kore wa ki no tsukue desu.
examples.translation_tr: This is a wooden desk.

examples.target: 音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]くのが好[す]きです。
examples.reading: Ongaku o kiku no ga suki desu.
examples.translation_tr: I like listening to music.

examples.target: 赤[あか]いのをください。
examples.reading: Akai no o kudasai.
examples.translation_tr: Please give me the red one.

examples.target: どこへ行[い]くの?
examples.reading: Doko e iku no?
examples.translation_tr: Where are you going? (casual, curious/soft tone)

examples.target: どうして遅[おく]れたんですか。
examples.reading: Doushite okuretan desu ka.
examples.translation_tr: Why were you late? (explanatory んです)

to-particle.intro_tr: The particle と is one of the most versatile function words in Japanese, but at N5 level it covers three core jobs: (1) joining nouns into a complete, exhaustive list meaning "and", (2) marking a person or thing you do something together WITH, and (3) marking a quotation; the exact words or thought that comes before verbs like 言う (say) or 思う (think). と also has a fourth, more advanced use as a conditional connector ("whenever/if"), which is treated fully under Conditional Forms. Unlike English "and", と can only connect NOUNS directly; to connect verbs or adjectives in a sentence you need the て-form instead. Keeping と's three beginner functions straight, and knowing how it differs from や and も, is essential for basic sentence building.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Core Functions of と (N5 level)
rows: Noun A と Noun B (と Noun C...)
dog and cat (this is the complete list; nothing else)
Person と 一緒[いっしょ]に + Verb
友達[ともだち]と 映画[えいが]を 見[み]る
watch a movie together with a friend
Person と + verb like 話[はな]す/会[あ]う/結婚[けっこん]する
兄[あに]と 話[はな]す
「...」/ plain form + と + 言[い]う・思[おも]う・書[か]く etc.
A は B と 違[ちが]う／同[おな]じだ
これは それと 違[ちが]う
春[はる]に なると 花[はな]が 咲[さ]く
footnotes_tr: と directly connects only nouns for the 'and' meaning. To connect verbs/adjectives ('and then', 'and also'), use the て-form instead; see て Form and Its Uses.

tables.caption_tr: Listing Particles Compared: と vs や vs も
rows: りんごと みかんを 買[か]った
I bought (only) an apple and a mikan
りんごや みかんを 買[か]った
I bought an apple, a mikan, and other things too
Each item individually marked as 'in addition'
りんごも みかんも 買[か]った
I bought both an apple AND a mikan (emphasis on both)
footnotes_tr: や is often paired with 〜など ('etc.') at the end: りんごやみかんなど. See や / とか Örnekleyerek Sayma for more.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verbs Used With Quotation と
rows: 「行[い]きます」と 言[い]った
無理[むり]だと 思[おも]う
手紙[てがみ]に「元気[げんき]です」と 書[か]いた
田中[たなか]さんが 来[く]ると 聞[き]いた
「わかりません」と 答[こた]えた
行[い]くべきだと 考[かんが]えている
これを 猫[ねこ]と 呼[よ]ぶ
footnotes_tr: Before と, verbs and adjectives normally appear in their PLAIN (dictionary/casual) form, even inside otherwise polite sentences: 難[むずか]しいと思います (NOT 難[むずか]しいですと思います).

tables.caption_tr: Direct vs Indirect Quotation with と
rows: 彼[かれ]は「もう 帰[かえ]ります」と 言[い]った
He said, "I'm going home now." (his exact words)
彼[かれ]は もう 帰[かえ]ると 言[い]った
He said (that) he was going home
plain-form clause + と 思[おも]う／考[かんが]える
明日[あした] 雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]ると 思[おも]う
I think it will rain tomorrow
plain-form clause + か + と + 聞[き]く／思う
彼[かれ]が 来[く]るかと 思[おも]った
I wondered whether he would come

tables.caption_tr: Common Set Expressions Built on と
rows: 寿司[すし]というのは 日本[にほん]の 食[た]べ物[もの]です
家族[かぞく]と一緒[いっしょ]に 住[す]む
兄[あに]と違[ちが]って 私[わたし]は 静[しず]かだ
去年[きょねん]と比[くら]べて 暑[あつ]い
5時[ごじ]に 会[あ]うとする

tables.caption_tr: Beginner Pitfalls: と vs Other Options
rows: Using と to connect verbs/adjectives for 'and'
と only joins nouns; it cannot chain predicates
Use て-form: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を 食[た]べて 学校[がっこう]へ 行[い]く
Putting だ/です before と with quotation verbs
The clause before quotation と must stay in plain form
難[むずか]しいと思う (not 難[むずか]しいですと思う)
Using と when the list is only partial/example-based
と implies the list is complete; unnatural if more items exist
Use や instead: りんごやみかんを買った
Forgetting 一緒[いっしょ]に in accompaniment sentences
と alone can mean 'with' but often sounds incomplete without 一緒に for activities
友達[ともだち]と一緒[いっしょ]に 遊[あそ]ぶ (more natural than 友達と遊ぶ alone, though both are grammatical)

examples.target: 私[わたし]と 田中[たなか]さんは 友達[ともだち]です。
examples.reading: わたしと たなかさんは ともだちです。
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka and I are friends.

examples.target: 犬[いぬ]と 猫[ねこ]を 飼[か]っています。
examples.reading: いぬと ねこを かっています。
examples.translation_tr: I have a dog and a cat.

examples.target: 友達[ともだち]と 一緒[いっしょ]に 買[か]い物[もの]に 行[い]きました。
examples.reading: ともだちと いっしょに かいものに いきました。
examples.translation_tr: I went shopping together with a friend.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は「明日[あした] 来[き]ます」と 言[い]いました。
examples.reading: かれは「あした きます」と いいました。
examples.translation_tr: He said, "I will come tomorrow."

examples.target: これは 難[むずか]しいと 思[おも]います。
examples.reading: これは むずかしいと おもいます。
examples.translation_tr: I think this is difficult.

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]と 相談[そうだん]しました。
examples.reading: せんせいと そうだんしました。
examples.translation_tr: I consulted with the teacher.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは 山田[やまだ]さんと 違[ちが]う 意見[いけん]を 持[も]っています。
examples.reading: たなかさんは やまださんと ちがう いけんを もっています。
examples.translation_tr: Mr. Tanaka holds an opinion different from Mr. Yamada's.

examples.target: 春[はる]に なると 桜[さくら]が 咲[さ]きます。
examples.reading: はるに なると さくらが さきます。
examples.translation_tr: When spring comes, cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.note_tr: This is the conditional use of と ("whenever X, then Y"); see the dedicated Conditional Forms topic for full details.

mo-also-particle.intro_tr: The particle も means "also," "too," or "even," and it marks a word as being included in addition to something else already mentioned. When も attaches to a noun, it typically REPLACES the particles は, が, and を entirely; you never see はも, がも, or をも. However, も can COMBINE with location/time/direction particles like に, で, から, and まで, simply adding も after them. も is also the building block for several very common expressions: question words + も (誰も, 何も, どこも) create "everyone/nothing/nowhere" meanings depending on affirmative or negative context, and numbers + も create emphasis on a surprisingly large quantity ("as many as..."). Mastering も early is essential because it appears constantly in everyday speech from the very first lessons.

tables.caption_tr: Core Function: も Replaces or Combines with Other Particles
rows: わたし[は]→わたし[も]学生[がくせい]です
猫[ねこ][が]→猫[ねこ][も]います
パン[を]→パン[も]食[た]べます
日曜日[にちようび]にも働[はたら]きます
図書館[としょかん]でも勉強[べんきょう]します
I study at the library too
先生[せんせい]からも聞[き]きました
I heard it from the teacher too
駅[えき]までも歩[ある]けます
I can even walk as far as the station
友達[ともだち]とも話[はな]しました
I talked with my friend too
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: only は, が, and を are fully replaced by も. All other particles keep their place and simply add も after them.
Never write はも, がも, or をも; these combinations do not exist in Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Question Word + も: Universal (Affirmative) vs. None (Negative)
rows: 何[なに]でも食[た]べます
何[なに]も食[た]べません
どこにも行[い]きません
いつも忙[いそが]しいです
いつも忙[いそが]しくないです
どれも美味[おい]しいです
every one (of a set) is delicious
どれも好[す]きじゃないです
I don't like any of them
どちら/どっち (which of two)
どちらも好[す]きじゃないです
footnotes_tr: For affirmative 'anything/everyone' meaning, question word + でも (何でも, どこでも,誰でも) is far more natural than word + も.
For negative 'nothing/nobody/nowhere' meaning, question word + に + も + negative verb is the standard pattern (どこにも, 誰にも).
いつも in the affirmative simply means 'always'; it does not need でも.

tables.caption_tr: も with Numbers and Quantities: Emphasizing a Surprising Amount
rows: 三[さん]時間[じかん]も待[ま]ちました
I waited as long as three hours! (emphasizes it felt long)
Amount + も + する/かかる
一万円[いちまんえん]もかかりました
It cost as much as 10,000 yen!
Number + counter + も + いる/ある
学生[がくせい]が百人[ひゃくにん]もいます
There are as many as 100 students!
一つ[ひとつ]も残[のこ]っていません
一度[いちど]も行[い]ったことがありません
I have never even once been there
footnotes_tr: This use of も conveys the speaker's surprise, emphasis, or feeling that the quantity is greater/smaller than expected; contrast with くらい/だけ which are neutral.
With small numbers (一つも, 一度も) + negative, も means 'not even a single...'; a very common emphatic negation pattern.

tables.caption_tr: も in Parallel Listing: A も B も (Both...and...)
rows: Noun A も Noun B も + affirmative
犬[いぬ]も猫[ねこ]も好[す]きです
I like both dogs and cats
Noun A も Noun B も + negative
肉[にく]も魚[さかな]も食[た]べません
I eat neither meat nor fish
安[やす]いし、便利[べんり]でもある
It's cheap, and it's also convenient
footnotes_tr: This 'A も B も' structure is the standard way to say 'both A and B' or, in the negative, 'neither A nor B'; です/verb only appears once, after the final も.

examples.target: わたしも学生[がくせい]です。
examples.reading: Watashi mo gakusei desu.
examples.translation_tr: I am also a student.

examples.target: コーヒーも紅茶[こうちゃ]も好[す]きです。
examples.reading: Kōhī mo kōcha mo suki desu.
examples.translation_tr: I like both coffee and tea.

examples.target: 誰[だれ]も来[こ]ませんでした。
examples.reading: Dare mo kimasen deshita.
examples.translation_tr: Nobody came. (negative + universal question word)

examples.target: 何[なに]も食[た]べたくないです。
examples.reading: Nani mo tabetakunai desu.
examples.translation_tr: I don't want to eat anything.

examples.target: 教室[きょうしつ]にも学生[がくせい]がいます。
examples.reading: Kyōshitsu ni mo gakusei ga imasu.
examples.translation_tr: There are students in the classroom too. (に + も combine)

examples.target: 千円[せんえん]もしました。
examples.reading: Sen'en mo shimashita.
examples.translation_tr: It cost as much as 1000 yen! (surprise at a large amount)

examples.target: 三回[さんかい]もそこに行[い]ったことがあります。
examples.reading: San-kai mo soko ni itta koto ga arimasu.
examples.translation_tr: I've been there as many as three times.

examples.target: どこにも行[い]きたくないです。
examples.reading: Doko ni mo ikitakunai desu.
examples.translation_tr: I don't want to go anywhere. (どこ + に + も + negative)

ka-question.intro_tr: か is the core question particle of Japanese: attached to the very end of a sentence, it turns a plain statement into a question with no change to word order, since Japanese questions are formed purely by particles, not by inversion (SOV order is always preserved). か works after every sentence type; verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and the copula です/だ; though its politeness feel differs by register: だ+か is avoided, ですか/ますか is the neutral-polite default, and plain-form+か alone can sound blunt or masculine in casual speech (casual speakers often prefer rising intonation or の instead). Beyond simple yes/no questions, か also embeds questions inside larger sentences (〜かどうか 'whether or not', 疑問詞+か 'who/what/where...'), joins two options into an alternative question (AかB), and attaches directly after question words to build indefinite pronouns like 何か 'something' and 誰か 'someone'. This page gathers all of these uses into one reference.

tables.caption_tr: Forming yes/no questions with か across sentence types
rows: Do you eat? / Will you eat?
Are you going to eat? (blunt/casual, often male speech)
学生[がくせい]です (I'm a student)
学生[がくせい]だ (I'm a student, plain)
学生[がくせい]か。 (NOT 学生だか)
Is that a student? (だ is dropped before か)
footnotes_tr: The plain copula だ is always dropped directly before か: 学生だか is ungrammatical; the correct casual form is simply 学生か.

tables.caption_tr: か and question forms by register (from blunt to very formal)
rows: 行[い]かれるでしょうか。
Would you be going, by any chance?
I wonder if I should go. (talking to oneself)

tables.caption_tr: か for embedded questions and alternatives inside a sentence
rows: 疑問詞 + か + 動詞
誰[だれ]が 来[く]るか 知[し]りません。
I don't know who is coming.
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るかどうか 心配[しんぱい]です。
I'm worried about whether it will rain or not.
電車[でんしゃ]かバスで 行[い]きます。
I'll go by train or by bus.
〜か〜か (explicit either/or, often + 決[き]める/選[えら]ぶ)
行[い]くか 行[い]かないか 決[き]めてください。
Please decide whether to go or not.
疑問詞 + か + どちら/どれ
どちらがいいか 教[おし]えてください。
Please tell me which one is better.
footnotes_tr: In embedded questions, the verb before か stays in the plain form even if the overall sentence is polite: 誰が来るか知りません, not 誰が来ますか知りません.

tables.caption_tr: Question word + か → indefinite pronouns (different meaning from embedded か!)
rows: either one, one of the two
footnotes_tr: Be careful: 誰か来ましたか means 'Did someone come?' (indefinite pronoun), while 誰が来たか教えてください means 'Please tell me who came' (embedded question word). The particle after 誰 (か vs が) and the surrounding grammar disambiguate the two uses.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes with か
rows: だ cannot be followed directly by か
学生[がくせい]か。 or 学生[がくせい]ですか。
これは 何[なん]ですか？（with written 「？」）
In neutral/formal Japanese writing, か itself marks the question; adding 「？」 is redundant (acceptable only in very casual texting)
これは 何[なん]ですか。
誰[だれ]が 来[く]るか？と 聞[き]きました。
Using か for an embedded question with a question mark is stylistically odd in writing
誰[だれ]が 来[く]るか 聞[き]きました。
Confusing 何[なに]か (something) with 何[なに]が…か (embedded 'what')
何[なに]か食[た]べた (ate something) vs 何[なに]を食[た]べたか (what [they] ate)

examples.target: これは本[ほん]ですか。
examples.reading: Kore wa hon desu ka.
examples.translation_tr: Is this a book? (noun + です + か, polite yes/no question)

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは 学生[がくせい]ですか。
examples.reading: Tanaka-san wa gakusei desu ka.
examples.translation_tr: Is Mr./Ms. Tanaka a student?

examples.target: 何[なに]か 食[た]べますか。
examples.reading: Nanika tabemasu ka.
examples.translation_tr: Will you eat something? (何か = 'something' + か = polite question)

examples.target: コーヒーと 紅茶[こうちゃ]と、どちらがいいですか。
examples.reading: Kōhī to kōcha to, dochira ga ii desu ka.
examples.translation_tr: Coffee or tea; which would you like? (alternative question)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]が 来[く]るかどうか わかりません。
examples.reading: Kare ga kuru ka dō ka wakarimasen.
examples.translation_tr: I don't know whether he is coming or not. (embedded 〜かどうか)

examples.target: 明日[あした] 晴[は]れるかな。
examples.reading: Ashita hareru kana.
examples.translation_tr: I wonder if it will be sunny tomorrow. (self-directed かな, not asking someone else)

examples.target: 行[い]くか 行[い]かないか 決[き]めてください。
examples.reading: Iku ka ikanai ka kimete kudasai.
examples.translation_tr: Please decide whether you'll go or not. (question-word-less embedded alternative with か…か)

examples.target: 誰[だれ]が 来[く]るか 知[し]りません。
examples.reading: Dare ga kuru ka shirimasen.
examples.translation_tr: I don't know who is coming. (question word + か as an embedded question, not the indefinite 誰か)

kara-made.intro_tr: から and まで are two of the most basic Japanese particles, and they are usually taught as a pair because they mark the two ends of a range: から marks the starting point ("from…") and まで marks the ending point or limit ("…to/until"). They can be used with time, place, or even abstract ranges (like page numbers or amounts), and they are frequently combined in a single sentence as "A から B まで" ("from A to B"). Besides marking a range's start, から has an important second life as the particle meaning "because" (covered separately under から／ので), so context tells you which meaning is intended. まで also has an extended nuance of "even" or "as far as" when emphasizing an extreme degree.

tables.caption_tr: Core functions of から and まで
rows: Beginning of time, place, or action
End or limit of time, place, or action
A complete range with both start and end stated
月曜日[げつようび]から金曜日[きんようび]まで (from Monday to Friday)
Reason/cause clause, attaches to plain-form sentence + から
雨[あめ]だから、行[い]きません。(Because it's raining, I won't go.)
footnotes_tr: The reason-marking から is grammatically unrelated in function to the range-marking から, though the word is identical; see から／ので for that usage.

tables.caption_tr: から / まで with time expressions
rows: 九時[くじ]から会議[かいぎ]です。
五時[ごじ]まで仕事[しごと]をします。
Time A から Time B まで
九時[くじ]から五時[ごじ]まで働[はたら]きます。
来週[らいしゅう]から休[やす]みです。
土曜日[どようび]まで待[ま]ってください。
何時[なんじ]から / 何時[なんじ]まで
何時[なんじ]から何時[なんじ]までですか。
From what time to what time is it?

tables.caption_tr: から / まで with places and other ranges
rows: Place A から Place B まで
東京[とうきょう]から大阪[おおさか]まで
ここから駅[えき]まで十分[じゅっぷん]です。
It's 10 minutes from here to the station.
一[いち]ページから十[じゅっ]ページまで読[よ]んでください。
Please read from page 1 to page 10.
百円[ひゃくえん]から千円[せんえん]までです。
It ranges from 100 yen to 1000 yen.
駅[えき]からバスに乗[の]ります。
I take the bus from the station (no end point mentioned).
空港[くうこう]まで送[おく]ります。
I'll take you (as far as) to the airport.

tables.caption_tr: まで vs までに; continuous range vs one-time deadline
rows: The action/state continues without stopping until that point
五時[ごじ]まで待[ま]ちます。(I will wait until 5; waiting continues the whole time.)
The action happens once, at any point no later than X
五時[ごじ]までに来[き]てください。(Please come by 5; arrival happens once, before or at 5.)
footnotes_tr: A common beginner mistake is using まで where までに is needed for deadlines: 宿題[しゅくだい]を明日[あした]までにしてください (Please do the homework by tomorrow); not まで, because the act of finishing is a single point-in-time event, not an ongoing state.

tables.caption_tr: Extended and idiomatic uses of まで and から
rows: 子供[こども]まで知[し]っています。
宿題[しゅくだい]をしてから、遊[あそ]びます。
I'll play after doing my homework.
このお酒[さけ]は米[こめ]から作[つく]られます。
This sake is made from rice.
日本[にほん]に来[き]てから三年[さんねん]です。
It's been 3 years since I came to Japan.
どこからどこまで行[い]きますか。
From where to where are you going?

examples.target: 学校[がっこう]は九時[くじ]から始[はじ]まります。
examples.translation_tr: School starts from 9 o'clock.

examples.target: 会議[かいぎ]は三時[さんじ]まで続[つづ]きます。
examples.translation_tr: The meeting continues until 3 o'clock.

examples.target: 東京[とうきょう]から大阪[おおさか]まで新幹線[しんかんせん]で行[い]きます。
examples.translation_tr: I'll go from Tokyo to Osaka by bullet train.

examples.target: 月曜日[げつようび]から金曜日[きんようび]まで働[はたら]きます。
examples.translation_tr: I work from Monday to Friday.

examples.target: ここから駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いて十分[じゅっぷん]です。
examples.translation_tr: It's a 10-minute walk from here to the station.

examples.target: 今日[きょう]から日本語[にほんご]の勉強[べんきょう]を始[はじ]めます。
examples.translation_tr: Starting today, I'll begin studying Japanese.

examples.target: 何時[なんじ]から何時[なんじ]まで働[はたら]きますか。
examples.translation_tr: From what time to what time do you work?

examples.target: 家[いえ]から会社[かいしゃ]まで一時間[いちじかん]かかります。
examples.translation_tr: It takes one hour from home to the office.

sentence-ending-particles.intro_tr: Japanese sentences frequently end with small particles that add emotional color rather than grammatical meaning. ね (ne) invites agreement or shares a feeling with the listener, much like an English tag question ("isn't it?"). よ (yo) asserts information the listener doesn't already know, similar to "I'm telling you" or an exclamation point. な (na) does double duty: as a casual, often male-leaning cousin of ね it softens statements or expresses exclamation, but placed directly after a verb's dictionary form it becomes a blunt prohibition ("don't ~!"). Getting these particles right; and knowing when to leave them out; is essential for sounding natural, since misuse can come across as either pushy, distant, or unintentionally rude.

tables.caption_tr: Core Functions of ね, よ, and な
rows: Seeks agreement or confirmation from the listener
Softens the statement, invites empathy, like 'isn't it?'
Gives information the listener doesn't already know
Casual equivalent of ね; agreement-seeking or self-directed exclamation
Attaches to a verb's dictionary form to forbid an action

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Patterns and Examples
Common Combinations Built on ね and よ
rows: Asserts and seeks confirmation at the same time ('right?')
これでいいですよね。 (Kore de ii desu yo ne.); 'This is fine, right?'
素敵[すてき]だわね。 (Suteki da wa ne.); 'How lovely, isn't it.'
どうしようかしら。; 'I wonder what to do.'
Polite register with ね attached for agreement or filler
そうですね。; 'That's right...' / 'Let me see...'
Casual, blunt filler, often male-leaning, close cousin of よ/な
だからさ、無理[むり]だって。; 'Like I said, it's impossible.'

tables.caption_tr: Common Learner Mistakes
rows: Using よ when the listener already knows the information
よ signals new information; using it for known facts sounds pushy or condescending
Use ね instead to show shared feeling: 天気[てんき]がいいですね (not よ)
Using softener な in polite or formal contexts
な is casual and often male-associated; it sounds too familiar with strangers or superiors
Use ね or ですね in polite speech instead
Confusing softener な with prohibition な
Same sound, different grammar: the softener attaches loosely after casual/polite predicates, while prohibition attaches directly to a verb's plain dictionary form
行[い]くな! = 'Don't go!' (prohibition) vs 疲[つか]れたな = 'I'm tired...' (softener)
Overusing よ in nearly every sentence
Repeated よ makes speech sound aggressive, bossy, or overly insistent
Reserve よ for genuinely new or important information; use ね more often for rapport

examples.target: 今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いですね。
examples.reading: Kyou wa atsui desu ne.
examples.translation_tr: It's hot today, isn't it?
examples.note_tr: ね seeks agreement; it expects the listener to share the same feeling.

examples.target: これ、おいしいですよ。
examples.reading: Kore, oishii desu yo.
examples.translation_tr: This is delicious, you know.
examples.note_tr: よ shares new information the listener didn't have yet.

examples.target: 明日[あした]、テストがありますよね?
examples.reading: Ashita, tesuto ga arimasu yo ne?
examples.translation_tr: There's a test tomorrow, right?
examples.note_tr: よね combines assertion (よ) with a request for confirmation (ね).

examples.target: 危[あぶ]ない!行[い]くな!
examples.reading: Abunai! Iku na!
examples.translation_tr: Watch out! Don't go!
examples.note_tr: な right after the dictionary form of a verb is a blunt prohibition; a completely different function from the softener な.

examples.target: きれいだなあ。
examples.reading: Kirei da naa.
examples.translation_tr: How beautiful...
examples.note_tr: な(あ), drawn out, is an emotive exclamation typical of casual/male-leaning speech.

examples.target: そうですね、考[かんが]えておきます。
examples.reading: Sou desu ne, kangaete okimasu.
examples.translation_tr: Well... let me think about it.
examples.note_tr: ね also works as a hesitation filler while the speaker is thinking.

examples.target: 早[はや]く帰[かえ]ろうよ。
examples.reading: Hayaku kaerou yo.
examples.translation_tr: Let's go home already!
examples.note_tr: よ after a volitional form (〜よう) adds urging or insistence.

examples.target: わかったよ。
examples.reading: Wakatta yo.
examples.translation_tr: Alright, I got it.
examples.note_tr: よ here gives a mildly assertive, 'I'm telling you' nuance.

personal-pronouns.title_tr: Personal Pronouns (わたし, あなた, and more)
personal-pronouns.intro_tr: Japanese personal pronouns work very differently from their English counterparts: they are used far less often, since a subject can simply be dropped once it is clear from context, and repeating a pronoun in every sentence can sound unnatural or even childish. Instead of a single fixed word for "I" or "you," speakers choose among several options depending on gender, formality, regional background, and personal style. For "you" in particular, Japanese strongly prefers using the listener's name + さん rather than a pronoun at all. This page organizes the main first-, second-, and third-person pronouns by register and gender association, shows how to pluralize them, and flags the most common mistakes beginners make when using them.

tables.caption_tr: First-Person Pronouns (I / Me)
rows: The safest default choice; appropriate in both casual and polite speech
Business settings, formal speeches, service industry staff
Common among boys and men; softer and more modest-sounding than おれ
Used among close friends/family; sounds blunt; avoid with superiors or strangers
Softer, feminine-sounding variant of わたし, common in casual speech
Literally 'oneself'; also used reflexively; common in sports/military contexts
Common in Kansai dialect and among young women; also means 'my home/family'

tables.caption_tr: Second-Person Pronouns (You)
rows: Textbook word for 'you'; in real speech it can sound cold or overly formal; wives sometimes use it for husbands; avoid it with superiors
Used by men toward juniors, students, or romantic partners; can sound condescending to superiors
Used among close friends/family; can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone
Casual contraction of あなた; can sound confrontational or overly familiar
The natural, most common way to say 'you'; use the listener's name instead of a pronoun

tables.caption_tr: Third-Person Pronouns and Natural Alternatives
rows: A common, natural alternative to 彼/彼女 for a person present or previously mentioned
Respectful version of あの人, used for people of higher status
Most natural: refer to a third person by name + さん rather than a pronoun

tables.caption_tr: Making Pronouns Plural
Common Mistakes and Better Practices
rows: Use the person's name + さん
あなた can sound distant or even rude toward someone you know; Japanese strongly prefers names
Talking about a known third person
Using 彼/彼女 for any man/woman
彼/彼女 outside romantic context can sound overly casual or imply a romantic relationship
Adding 私 to nearly every sentence
Omit the subject once it is clear from context
Japanese drops pronouns very often; overusing them sounds unnatural or foreign
Using おれ in polite or business settings
Use 私/わたくし in formal contexts
おれ is too casual/rough for polite or professional speech

examples.target: 私[わたし]は学生[がくせい]です。
examples.reading: わたしはがくせいです。
examples.translation_tr: I am a student.
examples.note_tr: わたし is the safest, most neutral first-person pronoun for any gender or situation.

examples.target: あなたの名前[なまえ]は何[なん]ですか。
examples.reading: あなたのなまえはなんですか。
examples.translation_tr: What is your name?
examples.note_tr: Grammatically correct, but in real conversation Japanese speakers usually drop あなた and just say お名前は? instead.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は先生[せんせい]です。
examples.reading: かれはせんせいです。
examples.translation_tr: He is a teacher.
examples.note_tr: 彼 can also mean 'boyfriend' depending on context.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は日本人[にほんじん]です。
examples.reading: かのじょはにほんじんです。
examples.translation_tr: She is Japanese.
examples.note_tr: 彼女 can also mean 'girlfriend' depending on context.

examples.target: 僕[ぼく]たちは友達[ともだち]です。
examples.reading: ぼくたちはともだちです。
examples.translation_tr: We are friends.
examples.note_tr: たち turns 僕 into a plural 'we', typically used by male speakers.

examples.target: お名前[なまえ]は何[なん]ですか。
examples.reading: おなまえはなんですか。
examples.translation_tr: What is your name?
examples.note_tr: The most natural way to ask this, no pronoun ('you') is needed at all.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは医者[いしゃ]です。
examples.reading: たなかさんはいしゃです。
examples.translation_tr: Mr./Ms. Tanaka is a doctor.
examples.note_tr: Using the person's name + さん instead of 'he/she' is the natural, polite default in Japanese.

examples.target: これは私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。
examples.reading: これはわたしのほんです。
examples.translation_tr: This is my book.
examples.note_tr: の attaches to a pronoun to form the possessive, e.g. 私の = 'my'.

kosoado.title_tr: The こそあど System (これ/それ/あれ/どれ)
kosoado.intro_tr: The こそあど system is a set of demonstrative words built from four fixed prefixes: こ- (near the speaker), そ- (near the listener), あ- (far from both, or shared knowledge), and ど- (the question form, "which/what"). Each prefix generates a whole family of words; pronouns for things, adjective forms for modifying nouns, place words, direction/people words, and manner/degree words; so learning the pattern once unlocks dozens of vocabulary items. Beyond simply pointing at physical objects, これ/それ/あれ are also used in conversation to refer back to things already mentioned (それ) or to shared memories/experiences both speaker and listener know (あれ). Getting the こ/そ/あ distinction right is essential for natural-sounding Japanese, and mixing up the pronoun forms (これ) with the noun-modifying forms (この) is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: The Five こそあど Word Families (full overview)
footnotes_tr: All eight rows follow the exact same こ/そ/あ/ど prefix logic; memorize the pattern once, not eight separate vocabulary lists.

tables.caption_tr: Physical Distance Usage (pointing at real objects; exophoric use)
rows: これ / この / ここ
Close to the speaker, far from the listener
You are holding the object, or it is right beside you
それ / その / そこ
Close to the listener, far from the speaker
The object is near the person you are talking to
あれ / あの / あそこ
Far from both speaker and listener
The object is visible but distant from both people
どれ / どの / どこ
Asking which one / where among several options

tables.caption_tr: Discourse (Textual) Usage; Referring to Things Already Mentioned (anaphoric use)
rows: Refers to something the LISTENER just mentioned, or something known to the listener but not yet directly experienced by the speaker
A: 新[あたら]しいカフェができたよ。 B: それ、行[い]きたい！ ("That, I want to go!")
Refers to something BOTH speaker and listener already know or remember together; a shared past experience or common knowledge
あの時[とき]のこと、覚[おぼ]えてる？ ("Do you remember that time (we both experienced)?")
Introduces something the SPEAKER is about to say or present; points forward, not backward
これから話[はな]すことをよく聞[き]いてください。 ("Please listen carefully to what I'm about to say.")
footnotes_tr: This textual usage is independent of physical distance; it depends on whose 'territory of knowledge' the information belongs to.

tables.caption_tr: Pronoun Forms vs. Noun-Modifying Forms; a key beginner trap
rows: Stand ALONE as a noun/pronoun; cannot be placed directly before another noun
これは 私[わたし]のペンです。
Must ALWAYS be followed by a noun; cannot stand alone as a subject or object
この ペンは 私[わたし]のです。
footnotes_tr: Rule of thumb: これ = "this (thing)"; この = "this ___" and always needs a noun right after it.

tables.caption_tr: こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら; Directions, People, and Polite Substitutes
rows: polite way to introduce "this person" (yourself or someone near you); polite substitute for これ in business speech
こちらは 田中[たなか]さんです。 ("This is Mr. Tanaka.")
polite way to say "you/your side", e.g. on the phone
そちらのご都合[つごう]はいかがですか。 ("How does that work for you?")
polite way to refer to a person or place far from both parties
あちらの 方[かた]が 部長[ぶちょう]です。 ("That person over there is the department head.")
polite substitute for どこ/どれ; also used to politely ask someone's home country or name
お国[くに]はどちらですか。 ("Where are you from?")

tables.caption_tr: こう/そう/ああ/どう; Referring to Manner or Way of Doing Something
rows: like this (the way I'm about to show/describe)
こうやってください。 ("Please do it like this.")
like that (agreeing with / referring to what was just said)
そうですね。 ("That's right, I agree.")
like that (a fixed, well-known way, often distant)
彼[かれ]はいつもああだ。 ("He's always like that.")
これはどうやって 使[つか]いますか。 ("How do you use this?")
footnotes_tr: そう is extremely common as a standalone reaction word meaning "I see / that's right"; see also そう/よう/らしい for its role expressing appearance and hearsay.

tables.caption_tr: こんな/そんな/あんな/どんな; Describing Kind or Type (behave like な-adjectives)
rows: this kind of N / N like this
こんな 服[ふく]が 欲[ほ]しいです。 ("I want clothes like this.")
that kind of N (near listener / just mentioned)
そんな 話[はなし]は 聞[き]きたくない。 ("I don't want to hear that kind of story.")
that kind of N (distant / well-known example)
あんな 人[ひと]にはなりたくない。 ("I don't want to become a person like that.")
どんな 仕事[しごと]をしていますか。 ("What kind of work do you do?")
footnotes_tr: Note the な that appears before the noun; こんな, そんな, あんな, どんな always need な, unlike この/その/あの/どの which attach directly.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with こそあど
rows: これ本 / それ人 (pronoun + noun directly)
これ/それ/あれ/どれ are pronouns and cannot modify a noun directly
Use この本 / その人 instead
Using どこ to ask about a person
どこ only refers to places, not people
Use どなた (polite) or だれ (plain) for people
あんな/こんな/そんな/どんな + noun without な
These words require な before the noun, like a な-adjective
どんな音楽 (not どん音楽)
Using それ when both speaker and listener share the memory
それ implies the info belongs mainly to the listener's side
