Use あれ for things both people already know/remember together
Confusing こちら (polite) with こっち (casual) in formal speech
こっち is casual and can sound rude in business or formal contexts
Use こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら in polite or business settings

examples.target: これは 本[ほん]です。
examples.reading: これは ほんです。
examples.translation_tr: This is a book. (the book is near the speaker)

examples.target: それを 取[と]ってください。
examples.reading: それを とってください。
examples.translation_tr: Please take/hand me that. (the object is near the listener)

examples.target: あれは 富士山[ふじさん]です。
examples.reading: あれは ふじさんです。
examples.translation_tr: That (over there) is Mt. Fuji. (far from both speaker and listener)

examples.target: どれがあなたのカバンですか。
examples.reading: どれがあなたのカバンですか。
examples.translation_tr: Which one is your bag?

examples.target: この 本[ほん]はとても 面白[おもしろ]いです。
examples.reading: このほんはとてもおもしろいです。
examples.translation_tr: This book (right here) is very interesting.; note: この must be followed by a noun, unlike これ.

examples.target: そちらの 方[かた]はどなたですか。
examples.reading: そちらのかたはどなたですか。
examples.translation_tr: Who is that person (near you)?; polite/formal register.

examples.target: あの 映画[えいが]、もう 見[み]た?
examples.reading: あのえいが、もうみた?
examples.translation_tr: Did you already watch that movie (the one we both know about)?

examples.target: どんな 音楽[おんがく]が 好[す]きですか。
examples.reading: どんなおんがくがすきですか。
examples.translation_tr: What kind of music do you like?

family-terms.title_tr: Family Terms (your own family vs. someone else's family)
family-terms.intro_tr: Japanese has two separate vocabularies for family members: a plain/humble set used when you talk ABOUT your own family to an outside listener, and an honorific set (usually built with お〜/ご〜 + さん) used to talk about SOMEONE ELSE'S family; or to directly address/call your own family members. Mixing these up is one of the most common beginner mistakes: saying お父さん about your own father to an outsider sounds like you're bragging or being overly polite, while calling ご両親 about your own parents is simply wrong. The core logic mirrors the uchi/soto (in-group/out-group) principle that runs through all of Japanese politeness: lower your own group, raise the other person's group. Note that within the home, even your own family members are usually addressed with the honorific-looking forms (お母さん, お兄さん, etc.); the plain forms (母, 兄) are reserved for third-person reference to outsiders.

tables.caption_tr: Immediate family: your own family (humble) vs. someone else's family (honorific)
rows: 夫[おっと] / 主人[しゅじん]
妻[つま] / 家内[かない]
お嬢[じょう]さん / 娘[むすめ]さん
footnotes_tr: 主人/家内 are traditional, slightly gendered-role terms (husband as 'master', wife as 'inside the house'); 夫/妻 are the more neutral, modern default choices in speaking or writing.
弟 and 妹 do not take お〜 in the honorific form; they simply add さん (弟さん, 妹さん), unlike 兄 and 姉.

tables.caption_tr: Extended family: own vs. someone else's
rows: おじ (伯父[おじ]/叔父[おじ])
おば (伯母[おば]/叔母[おば])
甥[おい]御[ご]さん (rare; name is usually used instead)
姪[めい]御[ご]さん (rare; name is usually used instead)
footnotes_tr: 伯父/伯母 (older than your parent) vs 叔父/叔母 (younger than your parent) is a formal written distinction; in casual speech おじ/おば cover both.
For nephew/niece, honorific forms are rarely used in speech; Japanese speakers usually just say the child's name plus さん/ちゃん instead.

tables.caption_tr: Direct address (vocative): what you call family members to their face
column_headers: Referring to them (talking about, to an outsider)
rows: お父[とう]さん / パパ (casual)
お母[かあ]さん / ママ (casual)
お兄[にい]さん / にいちゃん (casual)
お姉[ねえ]さん / ねえちゃん (casual)
おじいさん / じいじ (casual)
おばあさん / ばあば (casual)
弟[おとうと]/妹[いもうと] (to outsiders)
usually called by first name, not a kinship term
footnotes_tr: This is the point beginners get wrong most: you almost never call your own father 父 to his face; that plain form is strictly for third-person reference when speaking with someone outside the family.
Younger siblings and children are normally addressed by their given name (+ ちゃん/くん), not by the kinship word itself.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and register notes
rows: Talking to a coworker about your own mother
私[わたし]のお母[かあ]さんは…
Asking a friend about their father
あなたの父[ちち]は…ですか
〜さんのお父[とう]さんは…ですか
Calling your dad at the dinner table
お父[とう]さん、ご飯[はん]だよ
Referring to a friend's whole family
あなたの家族[かぞく]は…
Saying how many people are in your own family
何人[なんにん]家族[かぞく]ですか → answer with ご家族
家族[かぞく]は◯人[にん]です (no ご for your own)
footnotes_tr: General rule of thumb: お〜/ご〜 + さん = raise (used for others, or for your own family members when addressing them directly); plain form = lower (used only in third-person reference to your own family, spoken to an outsider).

examples.target: 私[わたし]の父[ちち]は医者[いしゃ]です。
examples.reading: わたしのちちはいしゃです。
examples.translation_tr: My father is a doctor. (talking to an outsider about your own father; humble form 父)

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんのお父[とう]さんは先生[せんせい]です。
examples.reading: たなかさんのおとうさんはせんせいです。
examples.translation_tr: Mr. Tanaka's father is a teacher. (someone else's father; honorific form お父さん)

examples.target: お母[かあ]さん、ただいま!
examples.reading: おかあさん、ただいま!
examples.translation_tr: Mom, I'm home! (directly addressing your own mother; use お母さん, not 母)

examples.target: 兄[あに]は大学生[だいがくせい]です。
examples.reading: あにはだいがくせいです。
examples.translation_tr: My older brother is a university student. (own family, humble 兄)

examples.target: お兄[にい]さんは何歳[なんさい]ですか。
examples.reading: おにいさんはなんさいですか。
examples.translation_tr: How old is your older brother? (asking about someone else's brother)

examples.target: ご家族[かぞく]は何人[なんにん]ですか。
examples.reading: ごかぞくはなんにんですか。
examples.translation_tr: How many people are in your family? (someone else's family; ご家族)

examples.target: 私[わたし]の家族[かぞく]は四人[よにん]です。
examples.reading: わたしのかぞくはよにんです。
examples.translation_tr: There are four people in my family. (own family; no ご prefix)

examples.target: ご両親[りょうしん]によろしくお伝[つた]えください。
examples.reading: ごりょうしんによろしくおつたえください。
examples.translation_tr: Please give my regards to your parents. (someone else's parents; ご両親)

counters.intro_tr: In Japanese, you cannot simply put a number directly before a noun the way you do in English; you must attach a counter (助数詞) that matches the category of the thing being counted, roughly like saying "three sheets of paper" or "two head of cattle" in English, but for almost everything. Different counters exist for people, long thin objects, flat objects, small animals, bound books, cups of liquid, floors of a building, and more. Many counters also trigger sound changes (gemination っ or rendaku voicing) when combined with certain numbers, especially 1, 3, 6, 8, and 10; these irregular readings simply have to be memorized. The native Japanese counter 〜つ (ひとつ, ふたつ...) is the most general, all-purpose counter and is a safe fallback for small, uncategorized objects up to ten. Below is a reference covering the most essential N5 counters, their full readings 1–10, sound-change patterns, and the matching question words (何人, 何本, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Overview: Which Counter to Use for What
rows: general objects / abstract things with no specific counter (fallback, 1–10 only)
学生[がくせい]が三人[さんにん] (three students)
long, thin objects: pens, bottles, trees, umbrellas
ペンが二本[にほん] (two pens)
flat, thin objects: paper, plates, shirts, tickets
紙[かみ]が三枚[さんまい] (three sheets of paper)
small, compact objects: apples, boxes, eggs
りんごが二個[にこ] (two apples)
small animals: cats, dogs, fish, insects
猫[ねこ]が二匹[にひき] (two cats)
牛[うし]が三頭[さんとう] (three cows)
鳥[とり]が二羽[にわ] (two birds)
本[ほん]が三冊[さんさつ] (three books)
車[くるま]が二台[にだい] (two cars)
コーヒーが一杯[いっぱい] (one cup of coffee)
三階[さんがい]に住[す]んでいます (I live on the 3rd floor)
二十歳[はたち] (20 years old)
三回[さんかい]見[み]ました (I saw it 3 times)

tables.caption_tr: Native Japanese Counter 〜つ (General Objects, 1–10)
rows: ten; irregular, no つ suffix, and note the long おお reading
how many? (question word, also used to casually ask age)

tables.caption_tr: Counter 〜人 for People (1–10)
rows: regular from here on: number + にん
not よんにん or しにん

tables.caption_tr: Counter 〜本 for Long, Thin Objects (1–10)
rows: also read じっぽん; っ + ぽん
footnotes_tr: Pattern: ほん stays plain after ご/に/な; becomes っぽん after いち/ろく/はち/じゅう (which end in a stop sound); becomes ぼん after さん (voicing).

tables.caption_tr: Counter 〜枚 for Flat, Thin Objects (1–10, No Sound Changes)
footnotes_tr: 枚 is one of the few common counters that never changes sound; a good one to lean on when unsure of the pattern for other counters.

tables.caption_tr: Sound-Change Comparison Across Counters (個・匹・冊・杯・階)
rows: 八階[はちかい / はっかい]
footnotes_tr: General rule of thumb: counters starting with a k-, s-, h-, or p- sound tend to double the following consonant (sokuon っ) after いち, ろく, はち, and じゅう.
Counters starting with an h-sound (本, 匹, 杯) additionally shift to a voiced b-sound after さん (三) and often after なん (何).
八階 has two accepted readings, はちかい and はっかい, both commonly heard.

tables.caption_tr: Question Words: Asking "How Many?" for Each Counter
rows: general つ-counter items; also casually asks someone's age
何歳[なんさい] / おいくつ
age (おいくつ is the polite form)

examples.target: りんごを三[みっ]つください。
examples.reading: りんごをみっつください。
examples.translation_tr: Three apples, please. (using the native counter 〜つ, since 'apple' has no special counter in casual speech)

examples.target: 教室[きょうしつ]に学生[がくせい]が二十人[にじゅうにん]います。
examples.reading: きょうしつにがくせいがにじゅうにんいます。
examples.translation_tr: There are twenty students in the classroom.

examples.target: ビールを一本[いっぽん]ください。
examples.reading: びーるをいっぽんください。
examples.translation_tr: One bottle of beer, please.
examples.note_tr: 本 counts long, thin objects like bottles, pens, and trees. Note the sound change: いち+ほん → いっぽん.

examples.target: 紙[かみ]を五枚[ごまい]もらいました。
examples.reading: かみをごまいもらいました。
examples.translation_tr: I received five sheets of paper.

examples.target: 庭[にわ]に猫[ねこ]が三匹[さんびき]います。
examples.reading: にわにねこがさんびきいます。
examples.translation_tr: There are three cats in the garden.
examples.note_tr: 匹 counts small animals; after さん it becomes びき (dakuten change).

examples.target: この本[ほん]は三冊[さんさつ]あります。
examples.reading: このほんはさんさつあります。
examples.translation_tr: There are three copies of this book.

examples.target: コーヒーをもう一杯[いっぱい]ください。
examples.reading: こーひーをもういっぱいください。
examples.translation_tr: One more cup of coffee, please.

examples.target: 「何歳[なんさい]ですか。」「二十歳[はたち]です。」
examples.reading: 「なんさいですか。」「はたちです。」
examples.translation_tr: "How old are you?" "I'm twenty."
examples.note_tr: 20 years old has the special irregular reading はたち instead of the expected にじゅっさい.

numbers-dates-time.intro_tr: Japanese numbers, dates, and time expressions are essential N5 building blocks, but they are full of irregular readings that simply must be memorized rather than derived from rules. There are two full sets of numbers; the Sino-Japanese set (ichi, ni, san...) used for counting years, minutes, and most counters, and the native Japanese set (hitotsu, futatsu, mittsu...) used for counting generic objects up to ten. Days of the month, months, hours, and minutes each have their own cluster of "irregular" readings (4, 7, 9, and 10 are the most common troublemakers) that appear constantly in daily conversation. This page collects every core number, date, and time reading into reference tables so you can look them up quickly instead of re-deriving them each time. For counting specific objects (people, flat things, long things, etc.) see the dedicated Counters (〜つ, 〜人, 〜本, 〜枚...) page.

tables.caption_tr: Basic numbers 0–10: Sino-Japanese vs. Native Japanese
column_headers: Sino-Japanese (used for math, time, most counting)
footnotes_tr: Native Japanese numbers (hitotsu, futatsu...) only go up to 10 (とお); from 11 onward only the Sino-Japanese set is used.
Where two Sino-Japanese readings exist (4, 7, 9), the choice depends on the word; see the Days, Months, Hours, and Minutes tables below for which one is used where.

tables.caption_tr: Numbers 11 and above: tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands
rows: 三十[さんじゅう] / 四十[よんじゅう] / 五十[ごじゅう]
六十[ろくじゅう] / 七十[ななじゅう] / 八十[はちじゅう] / 九十[きゅうじゅう]
footnotes_tr: Japanese groups large numbers by units of 10,000 (万), not 1,000 as in English; this is the single biggest source of confusion for beginners doing math or reading prices.
The irregular sound changes (byaku→pyaku, sen→zen/ssen) happen only at 3, 6, 8 for hundreds and 3, 8 for thousands; other digits stay regular.

tables.caption_tr: Days of the month (〜日); irregular readings for 1–10, 14, 20, 24
rows: 十一日[じゅういちにち]
二十四日[にじゅうよっか]
十七日[じゅうしちにち] / 十九日[じゅうくにち] / 二十七日[にじゅうしちにち] / 二十九日[にじゅうくにち]
use しち and く, not なな/きゅう
footnotes_tr: Days 1–10 must simply be memorized as a set; they do not follow the regular 'number + にち' pattern at all.
All other days follow 'number + 日[にち]' except 14, 20, and 24, which reuse the irregular よっか/はつか readings.

tables.caption_tr: Days of the week (曜日[ようび])
footnotes_tr: The kanji for each day (月火水木金土日) come from the sun, moon, and five classical elements; the same order appears in many East Asian calendars.

tables.caption_tr: Months (〜月); irregular readings for 4, 7, 9
rows: April; irregular: し, not よん
July; irregular: しち, not なな
September; irregular: く, not きゅう
十一月[じゅういちがつ]
footnotes_tr: Only 4, 7, and 9 are irregular in month names; every other month uses the plain Sino-Japanese number + がつ.

tables.caption_tr: Hours (〜時); irregular readings for 4, 7, 9
rows: irregular: よじ, not よんじ
irregular: しちじ, not ななじ
irregular: くじ, not きゅうじ
footnotes_tr: The irregular hours (4, 7, 9) exactly mirror the irregular months; memorizing one set helps with the other.

tables.caption_tr: Minutes (〜分); irregular sound changes are common
rows: 十分[じゅっぷん] / 十分[じっぷん]
三十分[さんじゅっぷん] / 半[はん]
footnotes_tr: ふん becomes ぷん after digits ending in a small っ sound (1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10); this is a regular sound-euphony (renjou) pattern, not random.
半[はん] ('half') is added directly after the hour, e.g. 3時半[さんじはん] = '3:30', and never needs 分.

tables.caption_tr: Relative time words (today, this week, next month, etc.)
rows: 毎年[まいとし] / [まいねん]
footnotes_tr: Notice 今日/明日/昨日/明後日/一昨日 have irregular, non-obvious readings that must be memorized as whole words.

examples.target: 今日[きょう]は8月[はちがつ]7日[なのか]です。
examples.reading: きょうは はちがつ なのかです。
examples.translation_tr: Today is August 7th.

examples.target: 今[いま]、何時[なんじ]ですか。
examples.reading: いま、なんじですか。

examples.target: 毎朝[まいあさ]7時[しちじ]に起[お]きます。
examples.reading: まいあさ しちじに おきます。
examples.translation_tr: I wake up at 7 o'clock every morning.

examples.target: 会議[かいぎ]は3時[さんじ]半[はん]から4時[よじ]まで です。
examples.reading: かいぎは さんじはんから よじまでです。
examples.translation_tr: The meeting is from 3:30 to 4:00.

examples.target: 誕生日[たんじょうび]は4月[しがつ]14日[じゅうよっか]です。
examples.reading: たんじょうびは しがつ じゅうよっかです。
examples.translation_tr: My birthday is April 14th.

examples.target: りんごを二[ふた]つ買[か]いました。
examples.reading: りんごを ふたつ かいました。
examples.translation_tr: I bought two apples.

examples.target: 来年[らいねん]は2027年[にせんにじゅうななねん]です。
examples.reading: らいねんは にせんにじゅうななねんです。

desu-copula.title_tr: です Copula; Affirmative / Negative / Past
desu-copula.intro_tr: The copula です (polite) and だ (plain/casual) attach to nouns and な-adjectives to form the English "is/am/are" and their negative and past equivalents. Unlike verbs, です itself has only a limited conjugation: it changes for tense and polarity, but it has no true stem-based conjugation system like verbs or い-adjectives. です is the polite register form used in everyday polite speech (丁寧語), while だ is its plain/casual counterpart used with friends, family, or in casual/written contexts. Note that です attached directly to an い-adjective (e.g. 高いです) is only a politeness marker; the adjective itself, not です, carries tense and negation. Mastering these four basic forms (present affirmative, present negative, past affirmative, past negative) in both registers is one of the very first and most essential steps in Japanese grammar.

basic-word-order.intro_tr: Japanese follows a Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) pattern, which is the mirror image of English's Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) order: the verb (or adjective/copula acting as the predicate) always comes at the very end of the sentence or clause. Unlike English, grammatical roles in Japanese are not defined by word position but by particles (は, が, を, に, で, へ, と, etc.) attached directly after each element, which is why word order is far more flexible than in English; elements can often be reshuffled for emphasis as long as the verb stays last and each particle stays glued to its noun. Modifiers (adjectives, relative clauses, possessives) always precede the noun they describe, and subordinate/dependent clauses precede the main clause. Subjects and even objects are frequently omitted entirely when they are clear from context, since Japanese is a pro-drop, topic-prominent language. Mastering this skeleton; Topic/Subject → (Time) → (Place) → (Object/Indirect object) → Verb; is the foundation for building every longer, more complex Japanese sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Word order flexibility: scrambling is possible because particles carry the grammar, but the verb must stay last
rows: 私[わたし]は 昨日[きのう] 図書館[としょかん]で 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みました。
Default, neutral order: Topic → Time → Place → Object → Verb
本[ほん]を 私[わたし]は 昨日[きのう] 図書館[としょかん]で 読[よ]みました。
Fronting the object adds emphasis/contrast on 本 ('the book, specifically')
昨日[きのう]、私[わたし]は 図書館[としょかん]で 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みました。
Very common; time expressions are often moved to the very front
私[わたし]は 読[よ]みました 本[ほん]を 図書館[としょかん]で。
Ungrammatical; the predicate (verb/adjective/copula) can never leave the final position
In casual spoken Japanese, particles like を and は are often omitted, but the verb-final rule still holds

tables.caption_tr: Common word-order mistakes made by English-speaking beginners
rows: 私[わたし]は 食[た]べます 寿司[すし]を。
私[わたし]は 寿司[すし]を 食[た]べます。
The verb must be moved to the very end, mirroring the reverse of English SVO order.
本[ほん] 面白[おもしろ]い
面白[おもしろ]い 本[ほん]
Descriptive modifiers (adjectives, relative clauses) always precede the noun, just like in English, but this is easy to reverse by mistake when translating literally.
Forgetting the particle after a fronted element
本[ほん] 私[わたし]は 買[か]いました。
本[ほん]を 私[わたし]は 買[か]いました。
Even when scrambled to the front for emphasis, the noun keeps its particle (を) so its grammatical role stays clear.
私[わたし]は 学生[がくせい]で そして 彼[かれ]は 先生[せんせい]です。
私[わたし]は 学生[がくせい]で、彼[かれ]は 先生[せんせい]です。
Japanese usually links clauses with the て-form or a comma rather than a separate word for 'and' between full clauses.
私[わたし]は 私[わたし]の 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みます。
(私[わたし]は) 本[ほん]を 読[よ]みます。
Japanese frequently drops the subject/topic once it's clear from context; repeating it sounds unnatural.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は 学生[がくせい]です。
examples.reading: わたしは がくせいです。
examples.translation_tr: I am a student. (Topic + Noun + copula; the simplest SOV-style pattern with no explicit verb-object.)

examples.reading: わたしは まいにち にほんごを べんきょうします。
examples.translation_tr: I study Japanese every day. (Topic → Time → Object → Verb: the verb 勉強します sits at the very end.)

examples.reading: たなかさんは としょかんで ほんを よみます。

examples.reading: きのう、ともだちと えいがを みました。
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday I watched a movie with a friend. (Time → Companion[と] → Object[を] → Verb; the subject 'I' is omitted because it's obvious from context.)

examples.target: 猫[ねこ]が 魚[さかな]を 食[た]べました。
examples.reading: ねこが さかなを たべました。
examples.translation_tr: The cat ate the fish. (Subject[が] → Object[を] → Verb; a clean textbook SOV sentence.)

examples.reading: ほんを わたしは きのう かいました。

arimasu-imasu.title_tr: あります / います (Expressing Existence: "there is / there are")
arimasu-imasu.intro_tr: あります and います are the two Japanese "existence verbs," both roughly meaning "there is / there are," but they are never interchangeable: あります is used for inanimate things (objects, plants, buildings, abstract items), while います is used for animate beings (people, animals, insects). Both verbs also double as "have" verbs when talking about possessions, relatives, or abilities. They follow the same basic sentence pattern, [Place]に[Thing/Person]が あります/います, and both have full polite and plain conjugation paradigms covering present, past, and negative forms. Choosing the right verb depends purely on whether the subject is alive and capable of independent movement, not on politeness or formality.

本[ほん] (book), 木[き] (tree), 建物[たてもの] (building), 会議[かいぎ] (meeting), お金[かね] (money)
人[ひと] (person), 猫[ねこ] (cat), 犬[いぬ] (dog), 虫[むし] (insect), 学生[がくせい] (student)

there was not / there were not

verb-groups.intro_tr: Every Japanese verb belongs to one of three conjugation groups, and knowing which group a verb is in tells you exactly how it changes for tense, politeness, negation, and every other grammatical form. Godan verbs (五段動詞[ごだんどうし], "u-verbs") shift their final syllable through all five vowel rows (a-i-u-e-o) depending on the ending attached. Ichidan verbs (一段動詞[いちだんどうし], "ru-verbs") are simpler: you just drop the final る and attach the ending, with no stem change. The two irregular verbs, する (to do) and 来る[くる] (to come), follow their own unique patterns and must be memorized individually. The trickiest part for learners is a group of verbs that end in -いる/-える like ichidan verbs but are actually godan; these "fake ichidan" verbs need to be memorized by heart.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Verb Groups at a Glance
rows: 五段動詞[ごだんどうし]
Ends in an u-sound: く・ぐ・す・つ・ぬ・ぶ・む・う・る
書く[かく] (write), 話す[はなす] (speak), 飲む[のむ] (drink), 買う[かう] (buy), 待つ[まつ] (wait)
Stem vowel shifts through all five a-i-u-e-o rows when conjugating
一段動詞[いちだんどうし]
Ends in -iる or -eる, stem never changes
食べる[たべる] (eat), 見る[みる] (see), 起きる[おきる] (wake up), 寝る[ねる] (sleep)
Just drop る and add the ending; no stem-vowel shift
不規則動詞[ふきそくどうし]
Only two verbs in the entire language
Each conjugates in its own unique way; must be memorized separately

footnotes_tr: These are informally called "fake ichidan" or "exception" verbs; since they visually match the ichidan pattern but conjugate like godan verbs (e.g. 帰る → 帰ります, not 帰えます), they must be memorized individually rather than by rule.

It's irregular; memorize its unique forms.
Does the dictionary form end in a syllable other than る (く/ぐ/す/つ/ぬ/ぶ/む/う)?
Does it end in る, with an -aる/-uる/-oる sound right before る (e.g. 分[わ]かる, 作[つく]る, 乗[の]る)?

masu-form.intro_tr: The ます form is the polite (teineigo) conjugation used for present/future and, with additional endings, past tense of Japanese verbs. It is built by attaching ます to the "stem" (連用形[れんようけい]) of a verb, and this stem is exactly what changes depending on whether the verb is godan, ichidan, or irregular. Because ます is the first conjugation pattern most learners memorize, it also functions as the default polite register for speaking to strangers, teachers, coworkers, and anyone outside your inner circle. Note that ます itself is a suffix, not a verb; it conjugates in only four practical forms (nonpast affirmative/negative, past affirmative/negative) plus the volitional ましょう. Getting the stem formation right for each verb group is the single most important skill this page drills.

tables.caption_tr: How to Form the ます-stem by Verb Group
footnotes_tr: Ichidan verbs simply drop る and attach ます; no sound change occurs.
Godan verbs change the final u-row kana to the corresponding i-row kana, then attach ます.

tables.caption_tr: Full ます Conjugation Paradigm (all 5 practical forms)
footnotes_tr: Past negative is always the present negative + でした; never a separate irregular form.
ましょう is the polite equivalent of the plain volitional 〜よう and is commonly used for invitations and suggestions.

tables.caption_tr: Godan Stem Formation: Every Final Kana Pattern
footnotes_tr: This is the same u-row → i-row shift used for other godan conjugations (て-form uses different sound changes, so don't confuse them).
す verbs are the only group whose stem ends in し; this is the same し that appears in irregular します, which can cause confusion for beginners.

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: Plain Form vs ます Form
rows: casual = friends/family; polite = strangers, work, teachers
casual = suggestion among close friends; polite = general invitation
footnotes_tr: The ます form is the safe default for beginners: it is understood and appropriate almost everywhere, even if slightly more formal than needed among close friends.
Mixing plain and ます forms within the same sentence for the same verb is a common learner mistake; pick one register and stay consistent within a clause.

tables.caption_tr: Trap Verbs: る-ending Verbs That Are Actually Godan
footnotes_tr: These verbs end in いる/える like ichidan verbs but conjugate as godan; the ます-stem drops る and shifts to the い-row (り), not simply dropping る.
There is no fully reliable shortcut for spotting these; they must be memorized individually as vocabulary is learned.

tables.caption_tr: Special Case: ある (to exist, inanimate); Irregular Negative
footnotes_tr: ある is grammatically godan, so its affirmative forms are fully regular (あ+り+ます). Its plain negative, however, is the irregular suppletive ない (not あらない), while the polite negative ありません IS regular; a common point of confusion.

examples.reading: まいあさ コーヒーを のみます。

examples.reading: あした ともだちに あいます。
examples.translation_tr: I will meet a friend tomorrow. (future, ます-form affirmative)

examples.target: 昨日[きのう]は勉強[べんきょう]しませんでした。
examples.reading: きのうは べんきょう しませんでした。
examples.translation_tr: I didn't study yesterday. (ます-form, past negative of する)

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは来[き]ません。
examples.reading: たなかさんは きません。
examples.translation_tr: Mr./Ms. Tanaka isn't coming. (ます-form, present negative of 来る[くる])

examples.target: 一緒[いっしょ]に映画[えいが]を見[み]ましょう。
examples.reading: いっしょに えいがを みましょう。
examples.translation_tr: Let's watch a movie together. (ます-form volitional, an invitation)

past-tense.intro_tr: The past tense in Japanese is expressed by changing the ending of verbs, adjectives, and the copula; there is no separate "did" or "was" word as in English. In polite speech (丁寧語), verbs take 〜ました (affirmative) and 〜ませんでした (negative). In plain/casual speech, verbs take the た-form (affirmative) and 〜なかった (negative), which follows the same sound-change rules as the て-form. い-adjectives and the copula だ/です have their own past patterns that do not follow verb rules. Mastering this topic means knowing the て/た-form sound changes (音便) for godan verbs by heart, since these are the most irregular-looking part of N5 grammar.

tables.caption_tr: Polite Past Tense: ます → ました / ませんでした
Plain Past (た-form): Godan Verb Sound Changes (音便)
rows: 買[か]う / 待[ま]つ / 乗[の]る
買[か]った / 待[ま]った / 乗[の]った
死[し]ぬ / 遊[あそ]ぶ / 飲[の]む
死[し]んだ / 遊[あそ]んだ / 飲[の]んだ
footnotes_tr: These are the exact same sound-change groups used for the て-form (て-form = た-form with て/で instead of た/だ).
行く is the single most important exception: it does NOT become 行いた, it becomes 行った.

tables.caption_tr: Plain Past: Ichidan and Irregular Verbs
footnotes_tr: Ichidan verbs are the easiest group: just drop る and add た, with no sound changes at all.

tables.caption_tr: Negative Past Tense: Plain vs Polite
rows: ません → ませんでした
ません → ませんでした
footnotes_tr: The plain negative past always ends in 〜なかった regardless of verb group; this rule has zero exceptions.
です can be optionally added after a plain negative past (食べなかったです) for a softer, slightly casual-polite tone, though 〜ませんでした is the standard polite form.

tables.caption_tr: Past Tense of Adjectives and the Copula (だ / です)
rows: 高[たか]くなかったです / 高[たか]くありませんでした
静[しず]かではなかった
静[しず]かではありませんでした
学生[がくせい]だ / です (is a student)
学生[がくせい]ではなかった
学生[がくせい]ではありませんでした
footnotes_tr: い-adjectives never use だった/でした; that pattern belongs only to な-adjectives and the copula.
じゃ is a casual spoken contraction of では, so じゃなかった / じゃありませんでした are extremely common in speech.
いい (good) is the one irregular い-adjective: all conjugation happens on the old form よい, giving よかった, never いかった.

examples.reading: せんしゅう きょうとに いきました。

examples.reading: きのうは いそがしかったです。

examples.target: 昨日[きのう]は忙[いそが]しかった。

examples.target: パーティーは楽[たの]しくなかったです。
examples.reading: パーティーは たのしくなかったです。

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は学生[がくせい]でした。
examples.reading: かれは がくせいでした。

negative-form.intro_tr: The negative form is one of the most essential conjugations in Japanese, used to state that an action does not happen, did not happen, or that something is not the case. There are two main registers: the polite ます-form negative (〜ません), used in formal or polite speech, and the plain/dictionary-form negative (〜ない), used in casual speech and as the base for many other grammar patterns. Verb negation depends on the verb group; godan verbs shift the final -u sound to -a before adding ない, ichidan verbs simply drop る and add ない, and the irregular verbs する and 来る have their own special negative forms (しない and 来[こ]ない). Adjectives and the copula です/だ follow entirely separate negative patterns that must be memorized on their own. Mastering these forms is critical because ない itself conjugates like an い-adjective and serves as the building block for dozens of other grammar points (〜ないで, 〜なければならない, 〜なくてもいい, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Polite Negative; ます Form (present/future & past)
rows: 食[た]べませんでした (tabemasen deshita)
footnotes_tr: The polite negative is formed simply by replacing ます with ません (present) or ませんでした (past).

tables.caption_tr: Plain Negative Formation by Verb Group (overview)
rows: Change final -u sound to -a sound, add ない
footnotes_tr: ある is the only verb whose negative is a completely separate word (ない) rather than a regular conjugation.
いる (to exist; people/animals) is ichidan, so it conjugates regularly: いる → いない.

tables.caption_tr: Godan Verb Negative Conjugation; Full Ending Chart (u-column → a-column + ない)
footnotes_tr: Watch out for 'fake ichidan' verbs that end in -iru/-eru but are actually godan, e.g. 帰[かえ]る (kaeru), 入[はい]る (hairu), 走[はし]る (hashiru), 要[い]る (iru, to need); these follow this godan table, not the ichidan pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Present vs. Past Negative; Plain and Polite Side by Side
footnotes_tr: The plain past negative is formed by conjugating ない as an い-adjective: ない → なかった (just like 高[たか]い → 高[たか]かった).

tables.caption_tr: Negative Forms of Adjectives and the Copula です/だ
rows: 高[たか]くないです / 高[たか]くありません
よくないです / よくありません
静[しず]かではない (静[しず]かじゃない)
静[しず]かではありません (静[しず]かじゃありません)
学生[がくせい]です (is a student)
学生[がくせい]ではない (学生[がくせい]じゃない)
学生[がくせい]ではありません (学生[がくせい]じゃありません)
footnotes_tr: い-adjectives negate by dropping the final い and adding くない; never confuse this with verb ない conjugation.
な-adjectives and nouns share the same negative pattern via では/じゃ + ない, since both use the copula です/だ.

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: When to Use Each Negative Form
rows: Talking to strangers, teachers, business, formal writing
Talking to friends/family, diaries, casual writing, embedded clauses before だろう/と思う etc.
footnotes_tr: じゃ is the contracted, more casual form of では; both mean the same thing.

te-form.intro_tr: The て-form (te-form) is one of the most essential verb forms in Japanese because it acts as a connector; linking actions, softening commands into requests, and combining with a huge number of auxiliary expressions (〜ている, 〜てください, 〜てしまう, etc.) to build complex, natural sentences. Unlike the polite ます-form, the て-form itself carries no tense; its meaning depends entirely on what follows it or the context of the sentence. Learning the sound-based conversion rules for Godan verbs (う/つ/る→って, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, く→いて, ぐ→いで, す→して) is the biggest hurdle, but Ichidan and irregular verbs are simple. Adjectives and the copula だ also have their own て-form equivalents used for listing qualities or giving reasons.

tables.caption_tr: Te-Form Formation: Godan (u-verbs); sound-based conversion rules
rows: う, つ, る → って
買[か]う, 待[ま]つ, 乗[の]る
買[か]って, 待[ま]って, 乗[の]って
買[か]う → 買[か]って (to buy)
む, ぶ, ぬ → んで
飲[の]む, 遊[あそ]ぶ, 死[し]ぬ
飲[の]んで, 遊[あそ]んで, 死[し]んで
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで (to drink)
書[か]く → 書[か]いて (to write)
泳[およ]ぐ → 泳[およ]いで (to swim)
話[はな]す → 話[はな]して (to speak)
Irregular exception: 行[い]く → って
行[い]く → 行[い]って (to go); NOT 行いて

tables.caption_tr: Te-Form Formation: Ichidan verbs, する, and 来[く]る
rows: Simply drop る and add て
Same rule for all Ichidan verbs

tables.caption_tr: Te-Form for Adjectives and the Copula だ
rows: このカバンは高[たか]くて、買[か]えません。 (It's expensive, so I can't buy it.)
天気[てんき]がよくて、うれしいです。 (The weather is good, so I'm happy.)
この部屋[へや]は静[しず]かで、快適[かいてき]です。 (This room is quiet and comfortable.)
学生[がくせい]だ (is a student)
彼[かれ]は学生[がくせい]で、まだ働[はたら]いていません。 (He is a student and doesn't work yet.)

tables.caption_tr: Negative Te-Form: 〜なくて vs 〜ないで
rows: ない-form stem + くて (e.g. 食[た]べない→食[た]べなくて)
States a reason/cause for a negative situation, or lists negative qualities
お金[かね]がなくて、困[こま]っています。 (I have no money, so I'm in trouble.)
ない-form stem + で (e.g. 食[た]べない→食[た]べないで)
Means 'without doing X'; the main action happens instead of / without X
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べないで、学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きました。 (I went to school without eating breakfast.)
Same as 〜ないで, more formal/written style
何[なに]も言[い]わずに、部屋[へや]を出[で]た。 (He left the room without saying anything.)

tables.caption_tr: Major Grammar Patterns Built on the Te-Form
rows: 朝[あさ]起[お]きて、シャワーを浴[あ]びて、出[で]かけます。 (I get up, shower, and go out.)
Ongoing action / continuous state / result state
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。 (It is raining.)
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてください。 (Please open the window.)
入[はい]ってもいいですか。 (May I come in?)
〜てはいけません / 〜てはだめです
ここに車[くるま]を止[と]めてはいけません。 (You must not park here.)
Completion, often with regret or finality
財布[さいふ]をなくしてしまいました。 (I ended up losing my wallet.)
Doing something in advance / leaving as-is for later benefit
飲[の]み物[もの]を買[か]っておきます。 (I'll buy drinks in advance.)
Resulting state from someone's deliberate action (transitive verb)
窓[まど]が開[あ]けてあります。 (The window has been left open.)
Trying an action to see the result
このケーキを食[た]べてみてください。 (Please try eating this cake.)
'After doing X'; sequencing with emphasis on the first action
宿題[しゅくだい]をしてから、遊[あそ]びます。 (I'll play after doing my homework.)
先生[せんせい]が説明[せつめい]してくれました。 (The teacher explained it for me.)
Direction of change or movement in time/space
日本語[にほんご]が上手[じょうず]になってきました。 (My Japanese has been getting better.)
Gives a reason or lists qualities (like 'and')
この店[みせ]は安[やす]くて、おいしいです。 (This shop is cheap and delicious.)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with the Te-Form
rows: 行く is the one く-ending Godan verb that is irregular and follows the う/つ/る pattern instead.
Treating て-form as having its own tense
Te-form has no tense by itself
Tense comes from what follows (e.g. 〜てください is a request regardless of past/present); memorize meaning from the attached pattern, not the て-form alone.
Use 〜なくて for reason/cause, 〜ないで for 'without doing'
お金[かね]がなくて (because I have no money) vs 何[なに]も食[た]べないで寝[ね]た (went to sleep without eating anything).
Using ない-form + て directly (食[た]べないて)
食[た]べなくて or 食[た]べないで
There is no 'ないて' form; negative te-forms always use なくて or ないで, never ないて.

examples.reading: あさおきて、かおをあらいます。
examples.translation_tr: I wake up in the morning and wash my face. (te-form connecting two sequential actions)

examples.target: 今[いま]、テレビを見[み]ています。
examples.reading: いま、テレビをみています。

examples.reading: すみません、ちょっとまってください。
examples.translation_tr: Excuse me, please wait a moment. (〜てください: polite request)

examples.target: ここで写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: ここでしゃしんをとってもいいですか。
examples.translation_tr: Is it okay to take photos here? (〜てもいいですか: asking permission)

examples.target: ここでたばこを吸[す]ってはいけません。
examples.reading: ここでたばこをすってはいけません。
examples.translation_tr: You must not smoke here. (〜てはいけません: prohibition)

te-iru.intro_tr: 〜ている is one of the most important N5 grammar points: it attaches to the て-form of a verb and adds the auxiliary いる (or the polite います). Depending on the type of verb, it expresses either an action currently in progress ("is doing") or the resulting state after a change has happened ("is [in the state of having done]"). It is also used for habitual/repeated actions and for a small set of verbs (知る, 住む, 結婚する, 似る, etc.) that can ONLY be used in the ている form to describe a present state. Mastering which meaning applies to which verb type is the key challenge of this grammar point.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: て-form + いる / います
Full conjugation paradigm of 〜ている / 〜ています
rows: 食[た]べていませんでした

tables.caption_tr: The two core meanings, by verb type
rows: Continuative / durative verb (継続動詞); action that takes time to complete
食[た]べる, 読[よ]む, 書[か]く, 見[み]る, 勉強[べんきょう]する
本[ほん]を読[よ]んでいます (is reading a book)
Instantaneous verb (瞬間動詞); action completed in a single instant
結婚[けっこん]する, 死[し]ぬ, 落[お]ちる, 開[あ]く, 閉[し]まる, 来[く]る
Resulting state after the change happened ('is [in the state of having] ~ed')
窓[まど]が閉[し]まっています (the window is closed)
Stative-only verb; no plain non-past 'action' meaning in daily use
知[し]っている, 住[す]んでいる, 似[に]ている, 持[も]っている, そびえている
Permanent/ongoing state; NEVER used as a bare present-tense verb for this meaning
大阪[おおさか]に住[す]んでいます (I live in Osaka)
走[はし]る, 通[かよ]う, 吸[す]う
Habit or repeated occurrence over a period of time
毎日[まいにち]ジョギングをしています (I jog every day)

tables.caption_tr: State-only verbs: common trap for beginners
rows: 知[し]ります ✗ (means 'will come to know', not 'know')
住[す]みます ✗ (sounds like a future/one-time act)
結婚[けっこん]します ✗ (means 'will get married')
結婚[けっこん]しています

tables.caption_tr: Negative form: two nuances depending on verb type
rows: まだ宿題[しゅくだい]をしていません
haven't done the homework yet (action not started/finished)
窓[まど]が開[あ]いていません
the window is not open (i.e., it is closed; negative of a state)

I (habitually/will) eat bread every morning; general statement, not necessarily happening now
今[いま]パンを食[た]べています

I ate bread (the eating is finished, no focus on current state)
もう食[た]べ終[お]わっています／もう食[た]べています
I have already eaten (result: I am now in the 'having eaten' state)

te-kudasai.intro_tr: 〜てください is the standard N5 pattern for making a polite request or giving an instruction to someone. It is built by attaching ください; the polite imperative form of the honorific verb くださる ('to give'); to the te-form of any verb, so the same rule applies uniformly across all verb groups. Because ください literally means 'please give (me the favor of doing X)', the pattern reads as 'please do ~'. Its negative counterpart, 〜ないでください, is used to ask someone NOT to do something. 〜てください is polite enough for teachers, coworkers, service staff, and classroom instructions, but it is still a fairly direct request, so it is normally avoided when addressing social superiors or customers, where お〜ください or 〜ていただけますか are preferred instead.

dictionary-form.title_tr: Dictionary Form and Casual Speech (辞書形[じしょけい])
dictionary-form.intro_tr: The dictionary form (辞書形[じしょけい]), also called the plain present/future form, is the base form of a verb; the form you'd look up in a dictionary. It is the foundation for every other verb conjugation and is the standard form used in casual conversation among friends and family, replacing the polite ます-form. Beyond casual speech, the dictionary form is essential grammar: it's required before nouns (relative clauses), before nominalizers like こと/の, before つもり, と思う, and many other grammar patterns throughout this course. Mastering how to derive it from the ます-form for each verb group; and knowing when casual speech drops particles or adds sentence-final particles; is a core N5 skill.

tables.caption_tr: Forming the Dictionary Form: Ichidan (る-verbs) and Irregular Verbs
footnotes_tr: Ichidan verbs are the easy group: the ます-stem always ends in an い or え sound (い-row or え-row), and you simply attach る.
する and 来[く]る are the only two truly irregular verbs in Japanese and must be memorized separately.

tables.caption_tr: Forming the Dictionary Form: Godan (う-verbs); All Nine Sound-Row Endings
footnotes_tr: For godan verbs, take the ます-stem's final い-row kana and shift it to the corresponding う-row kana within the same consonant column (五十音[ごじゅうおん] chart logic).
Warning: some godan verbs look like ichidan verbs because their ます-stem also ends in い/え (e.g. 帰[かえ]ります). Always check a dictionary; 帰[かえ]る is godan, not 帰[かえ]る→帰[かえ]える.

tables.caption_tr: Full Plain Form Paradigm (Present / Past, Affirmative / Negative)
footnotes_tr: 行[い]く is the one godan verb that irregularly takes った instead of いた in the past tense.
These four plain forms are what get used directly in casual conversation instead of the polite ます/ません/ました/ませんでした set.

tables.caption_tr: Key Grammar Patterns That Require the Dictionary Form
rows: turning a verb into a noun
走[はし]ることが好[す]き

tables.caption_tr: Formal → Casual Sentence-Ending Conversions
rows: 学生[がくせい]だ / 学生[がくせい]
は・が・を often dropped in speech

rows: asserting new info to the listener
I'm leaving now, (just so you know).
明日[あした]、休[やす]みだっけ?

nai-form.title_tr: ない Form and Its Derivatives
nai-form.intro_tr: The ない form is the plain (casual) negative form of Japanese verbs, and it is also the foundation for a huge family of essential grammar patterns (obligation, prohibition, permission-to-omit, conditionals, and more). Because ない itself behaves exactly like an い-adjective, it conjugates for past tense (なかった) and te-form (なくて / ないで) the same way an adjective does. Mastering how to build the ない form correctly for each verb group; and knowing the handful of irregular exceptions; unlocks dozens of downstream patterns (〜なければならない, 〜ないでください, 〜なくてもいい, 〜ずに, etc.), so this is one of the highest-leverage forms in all of Japanese grammar. Below you'll find the formation rules, a full godan ending reference, the complete conjugation paradigm, and the most common ない-based grammar patterns side by side.

rows: Change the final -u sound to the -a sound of the same consonant row, then add ない (Note: う endings become わ, not あ)

Full Conjugation Paradigm (ない as an い-adjective-like auxiliary)

tai-form.intro_tr: 〜たい is the basic N5 pattern used to express that the SPEAKER wants to do something. It is formed by dropping ます from the polite ます-form of a verb and attaching たい, and the resulting word conjugates exactly like an い-adjective (たい/たくない/たかった/たくなかった). Because it expresses a personal desire, plain 〜たい is normally used only for the speaker's own wish (1st person) or, in questions, to ask about the listener's wish (2nd person); for third parties, 〜たがる or 〜たがっている is used instead. A key grammar point beginners often miss is that the direct object particle を is frequently replaced by が when using 〜たい with a transitive verb.

Destination with 行きたい/来たい
Normal directional particles stay the same

i-adjectives.intro_tr: い-adjectives (also called keiyōshi) are one of the two adjective classes in Japanese, and they are unique because they conjugate on their own, without needing a copula like だ/です to show tense or negation. Every plain-form い-adjective ends in the syllable い (e.g., 高[たか]い, 安[やす]い, 面白[おもしろ]い), and all of their conjugations are built by dropping this final い and attaching different endings. This makes them behave more like verbs than like English adjectives: they have their own present, past, affirmative, and negative forms. The one true irregular is いい/よい ("good"), which uses いい only in the plain present affirmative and reverts to the stem よ- for every other conjugation. Be careful: a handful of common words that end in い (きれい, きらい, ゆうめい, etc.) are actually な-adjectives in disguise and conjugate completely differently.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation Paradigm (example: 高[たか]い, "expensive/tall")
rows: 高[たか]くなかったです
footnotes_tr: A more formal/written-style negative also exists: 高[たか]くありません (present) and 高[たか]くありませんでした (past). These are common in news, announcements, and business writing.
Never attach だ or です directly onto the negative stem to form a compound copula; 高[たか]くないだ is ungrammatical; だ is simply dropped after i-adjective negatives.

tables.caption_tr: General Formation Rule (drop the final い, then attach the ending)
rows: 安[やす]ければ買[か]います
安[やす]くする ("make it cheap")

〜がる (a third person appears to feel X) is used mainly with feeling/desire adjectives like 欲[ほ]しい → 欲[ほ]しがる, 痛[いた]い → 痛[いた]がる.

いい天気[てんき] / よい天気[てんき]

悪[わる]い ("bad") is fully regular and does NOT follow this irregular pattern: 悪[わる]くない, 悪[わる]かった, etc.

Negative is きらいではない/じゃない, NOT きらくない
ゆうめい(な) / 有名[ゆうめい](な)
Conjugates with な/だ/です like a noun, not with く/かった

na-adjectives.title_tr: な-Adjectives (な形容詞) and Their Conjugation
na-adjectives.intro_tr: な-adjectives (な形容詞[けいようし], also called 形容動詞[けいようどうし]) are one of the two adjective classes in Japanese, alongside い-adjectives. Unlike い-adjectives, な-adjectives behave grammatically like nouns: they cannot conjugate on their own and instead rely on the copula だ/です for tense and politeness, and they take な (not the adjective itself) when placed directly before a noun. Most な-adjectives are written with kanji and do not end in い, but a small handful of tricky exceptions (きれい, きらい, ゆうめい, etc.) end in い yet still conjugate as な-adjectives, not い-adjectives. Mastering な-adjectives means memorizing the copula conjugation pattern (だ/です system) rather than an adjective-specific conjugation, and knowing exactly when to insert な, に, or で depending on the grammatical role the adjective plays in the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation of a な-adjective (example: 静か[しずか] 'quiet')

'is not quiet'; casual (じゃない is more spoken, ではない more written)

adjective-adverbs.intro_tr: In Japanese, adjectives cannot directly modify verbs the way English adverbs (quickly, quietly, well) do; they first need to be converted into an adverbial form. For い-adjectives, drop the final い and add く (早い → 早く "early/quickly"). For な-adjectives, simply add に after the stem (静か → 静かに "quietly"). This く/に form is used to modify verbs ("do something quickly"), to modify other adjectives ("early-becoming"), and; very commonly; before なる (become) and する (make/do) to express a change of state, e.g. 大きくなる "to become big" or きれいにする "to make clean". A handful of い-adjectives are irregular, the most important being いい/よい, whose adverb form is よく, not いく.

drop final い, add く
drop final い, add く

同[おな]じく (formal) / 同[おな]じように (common)

kara-node-reason.title_tr: から / ので (Because / Since; Expressing Reason)
kara-node-reason.intro_tr: から and ので both correspond to English "because" / "since" and introduce the reason for the statement that follows, always in the pattern [Reason clause] + から/ので、[Result clause]。 から attaches straight onto the plain (or polite) form of a verb, adjective, or noun+だ, and tends to sound more subjective, direct, and personal; it is the natural choice for warnings, commands, invitations, opinions, and for answering a "why?" question with the fixed pattern 〜からです. ので also attaches after the plain form, but nouns and な-adjectives change だ to な before it (静[しず]かだ → 静[しず]かなので); it sounds softer, more objective, and more polite, so it is preferred in formal explanations, polite requests, and apologies. In everyday casual conversation the two are often interchangeable, but swapping them can shift the nuance from blunt/assertive (から) to considerate/indirect (ので). Mastering the connection rules (especially the だ→な shift before ので) and the register differences is essential at N5 and keeps mattering at every level above it.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Rules: How から and ので Attach to Each Word Type
rows: 行かない[いかない]から
行かない[いかない]ので
footnotes_tr: With な-adjectives and nouns, だ changes to な before ので (静か[しずか]だ → 静か[しずか]なので), but だ is kept before から (静か[しずか]だから).
Any tense/polarity (present, past, negative) can be used before から or ので; the tense belongs to the reason clause itself, not to the particle.

tables.caption_tr: から vs ので: Nuance and Usage Comparison
rows: Casual to neutral; can feel blunt or forceful
Yes; 〜からです is the fixed answer pattern
Rarely used alone to close an answer
Followed by imperative/request/volitional (〜てください/〜ましょう/命令形)
Very natural, common with warnings and commands
だ is kept: 学生[がくせい]だから
だ becomes な: 学生[がくせい]なので
Possible, but can sound a bit abrupt
Less preferred, can sound too casual

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Patterns by Register and Context
rows: 忙[いそが]しいから、行[い]けない。
Direct and blunt; typical between friends
忙[いそが]しいので、行[い]けません。
Same reason, but softer and more considerate
どうして？ ― 疲[つか]れたからです。
〜からです is the standard, expected reply pattern
危[あぶ]ないから、触[さわ]らないで。
から pairs naturally with imperatives and warnings
時間[じかん]が ないので、失礼[しつれい]します。
ので softens an excuse for leaving/declining
電車[でんしゃ]が 遅[おく]れましたので、遅刻[ちこく]しました。
ので (or 〜ため) is preferred over から in formal writing

だ cannot be dropped before から with nouns/な-adjectives
✕ 疲[つか]れたので。(as a complete answer)

ga-kedo-contrast.intro_tr: が and けど both translate as "but / however" and connect two clauses with a contrasting or simply additional relationship: [Clause 1] + が/けど + [Clause 2]. が is neutral-to-formal and works in both spoken and written Japanese, while けど (and its more polite siblings けれど/けれども) is primarily spoken/casual. Crucially, neither word always signals a strong contrast; both are extremely common as a soft cushion before requests, questions, or opinions, and sentences are often left trailing off after が/けど to sound less blunt. Attachment is simple: just add が/けど directly after a plain or polite predicate, though な-adjectives and nouns need だ in the plain style (静かだが, 学生だけど).

tables.caption_tr: The が / けど family: register differences
rows: Written Japanese, business speech, textbooks, polite conversation
Spoken and light written style, a bit more polished than けど
Formal speech, essays, news, polite writing
footnotes_tr: All four words are interchangeable in basic meaning ('but'); the difference is purely one of politeness/formality level, not grammar.

tables.caption_tr: How to attach が/けど to each predicate type
footnotes_tr: な-adjectives and nouns require だ before が/けど in the plain style, but です already covers this role in the polite style, so です/だ is not doubled.

tables.caption_tr: Functions of が/けど beyond simple 'but'
rows: Joins two clauses with opposite or unexpected meanings
日本語[にほんご]は難[むずか]しいですが、面白[おもしろ]いです。
Used before a request, question, or opinion to sound less abrupt; often no real contrast is intended
すみませんが、道[みち]を教[おし]えてください。
Sets up context or a preceding fact before the main point
明日[あした]パーティーがありますが、来[こ]られますか。
The sentence is left deliberately unfinished; very common to soften refusals or hesitant opinions
ちょっと用事[ようじ]があるんですが…。

tables.caption_tr: が/けど vs similar 'but/however' expressions; quick comparison
rows: Neutral connector; formal-safe; often just a soft link, not strong contrast
忙[いそが]しいですが、手伝[てつだ]います。
Casual spoken version of が; very frequent in daily conversation
忙[いそが]しいけど、手伝[てつだ]うよ。
Stronger contrast; often carries surprise, frustration, or disappointment
頑張[がんば]ったのに、失敗[しっぱい]した。
Standalone 'but/however'; conversational, cannot join clauses directly
忙[いそが]しいです。でも、手伝[てつだ]います。
footnotes_tr: A common beginner mistake is using でも in the middle of one sentence like が/けど; でも must start a new sentence instead.

examples.target: 静[しず]かだが、少[すこ]し寂[さび]しい。

examples.target: 肉[にく]は好[す]きだけど、魚[さかな]はちょっと…。

temo-ii-dame.title_tr: 〜てもいい / 〜てはだめ; Asking Permission and Expressing Prohibition
temo-ii-dame.intro_tr: The pattern 〜てもいい expresses permission; "it's fine to ~," "you may ~"; while 〜てはだめ, 〜てはいけない, and 〜てはならない express prohibition; "you must not ~." Both attach to the te-form of a verb: literally, 〜てもいい means "even if you do X, it's good/fine," and 〜てはだめ means "if you do X, it's no good," so the word that follows て (いい "good" vs. だめ "no good") flips the meaning between permission and prohibition. These are the everyday N5 patterns for asking, granting, and denying permission, and they range in formality from very casual (ちゃだめ) to formal/written (てはならない). A very common beginner trap is confusing 〜てもいい (permission) with the similar-looking but unrelated 〜なくてもいい ("you don't have to," no obligation); the tables below separate these clearly.

tables.caption_tr: Forming 〜てもいい (permission) from the te-form, by verb type
rows: 買ってもいい[かってもいい]
書いてもいい[かいてもいい]
泳いでもいい[およいでもいい]
話してもいい[はなしてもいい]

Very casual, contracted spoken form (て+は→ちゃ)

食べてはならない[たべてはならない]
One shall not eat that. (formal rule, signage, law)
Soft prohibition; 'it would cause trouble if...'
遅刻[ちこく]しては困ります[こまります]
Please don't be late (it would be a problem).

tables.caption_tr: Variants of the permission pattern, by nuance and politeness
rows: 行ってもいい[いってもいい]?
Is it OK if I go?
行ってもいいですか[いってもいいですか]
'I don't mind if...'; slightly more formal/indifferent nuance
行ってもかまいません[いってもかまいません]
I don't mind if you go. / It's fine if you go.
Very polite; used with superiors, customers, in business
お先に失礼[しつれい]してもよろしいですか
Would it be alright if I excused myself first?
〜ても大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です
触[さわ]っても大丈夫です
It's totally fine if you touch it.

帰ってはいけない[かえってはいけない]
帰らなくてもいい[かえらなくてもいい]
You don't have to go home.
帰らなければならない[かえらなければならない]

tables.caption_tr: Asking for and responding to permission
rows: Asking permission (very polite, e.g. to a superior)
お邪魔[じゃま]してもよろしいですか。
Would it be alright if I came in / intruded?

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes
rows: The は after て is required to mark contrast/prohibition; without it, the sentence is ungrammatical
食べてはだめ[たべてはだめ]
食[た]べますてもいい (attaching て to the ます-stem)
〜てもいい must attach to the plain te-form of the verb, not the polite ます-stem
食べてもいい[たべてもいい]
だめかった (treating だめ like an い-adjective)
だめ is a な-adjective; it conjugates with だ/です, not like an い-adjective
だめだった[だめだった] (was no good)

自転車に乗れません[じてんしゃにのれません] (I can't ride a bike)

honorific-titles.title_tr: Honorific Titles: さん, くん, ちゃん, 様
honorific-titles.intro_tr: In Japanese, you almost never say a person's name completely bare; a title (敬称[けいしょう]) is attached after the name to show the right level of respect and social distance. The four core titles さん, くん, ちゃん, and 様[さま] form a scale from casual/affectionate to highly formal, and choosing the wrong one can sound rude, childish, or oddly stiff. These titles replace English "Mr./Ms./Mrs." but work very differently: they combine with first OR last names, are used far more often than English titles, and must never be attached to your own name. Beyond the basic four, professional and written Japanese also uses titles like 先生[せんせい], 様[さま] in letters, 殿[どの], 氏[し], and 御中[おんちゅう] for organizations. This page covers the full system so you always pick the right title for the right person.

greetings-expressions.title_tr: Greetings and Set Expressions (挨拶[あいさつ])
greetings-expressions.intro_tr: Japanese daily life runs on a set of fixed, almost ritual phrases (挨拶[あいさつ], "greetings") that native speakers use automatically in specific situations; greeting someone, leaving the house, starting a meal, thanking, apologizing, or introducing yourself. Unlike free grammar constructions, these are largely fixed expressions: you memorize the whole phrase and the situation it belongs to, rather than building it from grammar rules. Many phrases come in matched pairs (one person says A, the other replies with B), and almost every phrase has a casual and a polite/formal version. Mastering this list is essential for sounding natural from your very first lesson, since these phrases appear constantly in daily conversation, anime, and textbooks.

tables.caption_tr: Time-of-Day Greetings
rows: おはよう / おはようございます
おはよう / おはようございます
Casual / polite. Used roughly until 10–11 a.m.; also used at the start of a shift regardless of actual time (e.g., in workplaces, broadcasting).
Used from late morning through the afternoon/early evening. Note the particle は is pronounced 'wa', not 'ha'.
Used after dark. Same は→wa pronunciation note applies.
おやすみ / おやすみなさい
おやすみ / おやすみなさい
Said only when parting for the night or before sleep, never as a daytime greeting.

Reply from the person already home
Said when entering someone else's home

kanji-radicals.intro_tr: A kanji radical (部首, bushu) is the core graphical component used to classify and look up a kanji in a dictionary, and it often (though not always) hints at the kanji's meaning or, less often, its pronunciation. Every kanji has exactly one "official" radical, even though it may contain several recognizable parts. Radicals appear in different positions within a kanji; left, right, top, bottom, wrapping, or enclosing; and each position type has its own Japanese name (hen, tsukuri, kanmuri, ashi, tare, nyou, kamae). Many common radicals also have a special "simplified" shape they take only when used as a radical (e.g., 水 becomes 氵 when placed on the left), which beginners must memorize separately from the standalone kanji. Learning the most frequent ~20 radicals dramatically speeds up both kanji memorization and dictionary lookup.

tables.caption_tr: The Seven Position Types of Radicals (部首の位置)

Bottom of the kanji, like legs

yori-comparison.intro_tr: The particle より marks the standard against which something is compared, corresponding to English "than." The basic pattern is X は Y より [adjective], meaning "X is more [adjective] than Y." Word order around より is flexible; the compared item (Y より) can move to the front of the sentence for emphasis, and adding のほうが to the item being praised makes the comparison sharper and more natural-sounding. Besides comparison, より has a completely separate, formal/written meaning equivalent to から ("from," as in "starting from"), which beginners often confuse with the comparative use. This page also covers how より interacts with degree adverbs (もっと, ずっと), how negative comparison works with ほど, and how to form superlatives with 一番/最も.

tables.caption_tr: Basic comparative sentence patterns with より
rows: X は Y より Adj
私[わたし]は兄[あに]より背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
I am taller than my brother.
Y より X のほうが Adj
兄[あに]より私[わたし]のほうが背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
Compared to my brother, I am the taller one (I emphasized).
X のほうが Y より Adj
私[わたし]のほうが兄[あに]より背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
I am the taller one, more than my brother.
X は Y ほど Adj-ない
私[わたし]は兄[あに]ほど背[せ]が高[たか]くないです。
I am not as tall as my brother (negative comparison, uses ほど not より).
footnotes_tr: Japanese word order is flexible: the 'Y より' phrase can appear anywhere before the predicate without changing the core meaning, but placing it right before のほうが emphasizes the contrast most clearly.
Adding のほうが to the compared-favorably item is optional but very common and sounds more natural than より alone in conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Intensifying or softening the comparison with degree adverbs
rows: もっと安[やす]い店[みせ]がありますよ。(There's an even cheaper shop.)
今日[きょう]は昨日[きのう]よりずっと暑[あつ]いです。(Today is far hotter than yesterday.)
新[あたら]しい方法[ほうほう]ははるかに効率的[こうりつてき]です。(The new method is far more efficient.)
これはあれより少[すこ]し高[たか]いです。(This is a little more expensive than that.)
彼[かれ]は前[まえ]よりだいぶ上手[じょうず]になりました。(He has become considerably better than before.)
footnotes_tr: These adverbs are placed directly before the adjective, after the より phrase: [Y より] + [adverb] + [adjective].

tables.caption_tr: より vs ほど vs 一番／最も; the three comparison systems
rows: これはそれより高[たか]いです。
This is more expensive than that.
これはそれほど高[たか]くないです。
This is not as expensive as that.
一番[いちばん] / 最[もっと]も Adj
これが一番[いちばん]高[たか]いです。
Xの中[なか]で一番[いちばん] Adj
Superlative within a group: 'the most ~ among X'
果物[くだもの]の中[なか]でりんごが一番[いちばん]好[す]きです。
Among fruits, I like apples the most.
footnotes_tr: 最[もっと]も is more formal/written than 一番[いちばん], which is the everyday spoken choice.
ほど always requires a negative predicate; より never does in the basic comparative pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Asking and answering comparison questions
rows: A と B と どちらが Adj ですか
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]とどちらが好[す]きですか。
Which do you like more, dogs or cats?
A と B(と)どちらのほうが Adj ですか
電車[でんしゃ]とバスとどちらのほうが速[はや]いですか。
Which is faster, the train or the bus?
Answer: A のほうが B より Adj です
犬[いぬ]のほうが猫[ねこ]より好[す]きです。
I like dogs more than cats.
Answer: A のほうが Adj です (Y より omitted)
犬[いぬ]のほうが好[す]きです。
I like dogs more (than the other one, understood from context).
footnotes_tr: どちら is used for exactly two choices; for three or more choices use どれ/どの with 一番.

tables.caption_tr: より used as a formal/written equivalent of から ('from'); not a comparison
rows: 本日[ほんじつ]午後[ごご]3時[さんじ]より開始[かいし]いたします。
We will begin from 3:00 p.m. today. (formal)
会場[かいじょう]より徒歩[とほ]5分[ふん]です。
It is a 5-minute walk from the venue.
footnotes_tr: This より is grammatically unrelated to the comparative より, though it comes from the same historical root; context (no adjective following, formal register) distinguishes it.
In casual speech, から is used instead of this formal より.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions built on より
rows: more/less than expected, than I thought
思[おも]ったより安[やす]かったです。(It was cheaper than I thought.)
予想[よそう]より人[ひと]が多[おお]かったです。(There were more people than predicted.)
いつもより早[はや]く起[お]きました。(I woke up earlier than usual.)
前[まえ]より元気[げんき]になりました。(I've become more energetic than before.)
more than that / by the way (topic shift)
それより、今日[きょう]の予定[よてい]は?(By the way, what's the plan for today?)
even more, all the more (written/formal intensifier)
より一層[いっそう]努力[どりょく]します。(I will make even greater effort.)
footnotes_tr: それより as a discourse marker means 'more importantly / setting that aside, ...' and is common in casual conversation to change the subject.

examples.reading: わたしは あにより せがたかいです。
