examples.target: 兄[あに]より私[わたし]のほうが背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
examples.reading: あにより わたしのほうが せがたかいです。
examples.translation_tr: Compared to my older brother, I am the taller one.

examples.target: 犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]とどちらが好[す]きですか。
examples.reading: いぬと ねこと どちらが すきですか。
examples.translation_tr: Which do you like more, dogs or cats?

examples.target: この試験[しけん]は思[おも]ったより難[むずか]しかったです。
examples.reading: このしけんは おもったより むずかしかったです。
examples.translation_tr: This exam was harder than I expected.
examples.note_tr: 思ったより is a fixed expression meaning "more than I thought / than expected".

examples.target: 彼[かれ]はいつもより早[はや]く来[き]ました。
examples.reading: かれは いつもより はやく きました。
examples.translation_tr: He came earlier than usual.

examples.target: 会議[かいぎ]は3時[さんじ]より始[はじ]まります。
examples.reading: かいぎは さんじより はじまります。
examples.translation_tr: The meeting will start from 3 o'clock.
examples.note_tr: Here より functions like formal/written から ("from"), a separate, unrelated use of より often seen in announcements, invitations, and schedules; not a comparison.

ya-toka-listing.title_tr: や / とか; Listing Examples (Non-Exhaustive Listing)
ya-toka-listing.intro_tr: や and とか are both particles used to list a few representative examples out of a larger, unspecified group; unlike と, which lists a complete and exhaustive set of items. や is neutral in register and works in both speech and writing, but it can only connect nouns. とか is casual and mainly spoken; unlike や, it can attach not just to nouns but also to plain-form verbs, adjectives, and even whole quoted phrases, giving it a loose "things like..." or "stuff like..." nuance. Both particles are frequently reinforced with など ("etc.") after や, or by repeating とか after the final item, to make the "and so on, non-exhaustive" meaning explicit. Because neither や nor とか claims to be a complete list, they are the natural choice whenever you want to mention a couple of illustrative examples rather than every single item.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: listing/enumeration particles compared
rows: Lists a few representative examples from a larger set
Neutral; used in both speech and writing
Lists every item in the set
footnotes_tr: と is covered separately under 'と Edatı'; use it only when the list is complete.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence patterns with や and とか
rows: Noun1 + や + Noun2 (+ が/は/を...)
本[ほん]や雑誌[ざっし]があります
Implies other, unmentioned items also exist
など makes the 'among others' meaning explicit
コーヒーとか紅茶[こうちゃ]とか
Casual; とか is often repeated after the last item too
X + とか + Y + とか
宿題[しゅくだい]とか掃除[そうじ]とか
Trailing とか is optional but very common in speech
疲[つか]れたとか眠[ねむ]いとか
とか attaches to plain-form verbs and adjectives; や cannot
Phrase + とか + 言う/思う
忙[いそが]しいとか言[い]ってた
Functions like a soft, uncertain quotative, 'said something like...'

tables.caption_tr: What や and とか can grammatically connect to
footnotes_tr: This is the single biggest grammatical difference between the two particles: とか is far more flexible than や.

tables.caption_tr: や vs とか; stylistic and usage differences
rows: Neutral; fine in both speech and writing
Casual; mostly spoken, avoid in formal writing
Common; とか often follows even the final item
Casual conversation, vague or approximate listing
服[ふく]や靴[くつ]を買[か]いました
服[ふく]とか靴[くつ]とか買[か]った

examples.target: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]に本[ほん]や雑誌[ざっし]があります。
examples.reading: つくえのうえにほんやざっしがあります。
examples.translation_tr: There are things like books and magazines (among other things) on the desk.

examples.target: コーヒーとか紅茶[こうちゃ]とか、何[なに]か飲[の]み物[もの]はいかがですか。
examples.reading: コーヒーとかこうちゃとか、なにかのみものはいかがですか。
examples.translation_tr: Would you like something to drink; coffee, tea, or something like that?

examples.target: 果物[くだもの]はりんごやみかんなどが好[す]きです。
examples.reading: くだものはりんごやみかんなどがすきです。
examples.translation_tr: As for fruit, I like things like apples and mandarins.

examples.target: 疲[つか]れたとか眠[ねむ]いとか、言[い]い訳[わけ]ばかりだ。
examples.reading: つかれたとかねむいとか、いいわけばかりだ。
examples.translation_tr: "I'm tired," "I'm sleepy"; nothing but excuses.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんや佐藤[さとう]さんが来[き]ました。
examples.reading: たなかさんやさとうさんがきました。
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka, Sato, and others came.

examples.target: 宿題[しゅくだい]とか掃除[そうじ]とか、やることがたくさんある。
examples.reading: しゅくだいとかそうじとか、やることがたくさんある。
examples.translation_tr: There's a lot to do; homework, cleaning, and so on.

examples.target: パーティーには友達[ともだち]や家族[かぞく]を招待[しょうたい]するつもりです。
examples.reading: パーティーにはともだちやかぞくをしょうたいするつもりです。
examples.translation_tr: I plan to invite friends, family, and others to the party.

examples.target: 「明日[あした]忙[いそが]しいとか言[い]ってたよね。」
examples.reading: 「あしたいそがしいとかいってたよね。」
examples.translation_tr: You said something like "I'm busy tomorrow," right?

dake-shika-bakari.title_tr: だけ / しか / ばかり (Only / Nothing But)
dake-shika-bakari.intro_tr: だけ, しか, and ばかり all correspond roughly to English "only," but they are not interchangeable; each has its own grammatical restrictions and emotional flavor. だけ is the neutral, all-purpose choice that works in both affirmative and negative sentences and simply states a limit or amount. しか is grammatically locked to negative predicates (しか...ない) and adds a subjective feeling of insufficiency, disappointment, or "that's really all there is." ばかり normally pairs with affirmative predicates and expresses excess, one-sidedness, or repetition; "nothing but," "always doing X"; often with a critical or exasperated tone, and it has two extra verb-based patterns (〜てばかりいる and 〜たばかり) beyond the basic noun usage. Mastering the differences means paying attention not just to meaning but to sentence polarity (affirmative vs. negative) and to the emotional coloring each particle brings.

tables.caption_tr: Core Overview: Meaning, Polarity, and Nuance
rows: Neutral, objective; simply states a fact
Negative ONLY; verb/predicate must be negative
Subjective; implies insufficiency, dissatisfaction, or surprise at how little there is
Critical, exasperated, or emphasizes one-sided excess/repetition

tables.caption_tr: Grammatical Connection Patterns
rows: 水[みず]しかない (there's only water)
待[ま]つしかない (nothing to do but wait)
ゲームばかり (nothing but games)
遊[あそ]んでばかりいる (does nothing but goof off)

tables.caption_tr: Interaction with Case Particles (が / を / に / で / と)
column_headers: With other particles に・で・と・から
rows: が/を are optional after だけ (だけが / だけを, or dropped)
Noun + だけ + に/で/と (だけ comes first)
ここだけで話[はな]す (talk only here)
が and を are always dropped (never しかが / しかを)
Particle attaches BEFORE しか (に+しか, で+しか, と+しか)
ここでしか買[か]えない (can only buy here)
が/を optional (ばかりが / ばかりを, or dropped), similar to だけ
Noun + ばかり + に/で/と, though に+ばかり is also used for emphasis
甘[あま]い物[もの]ばかり食[た]べる (eats nothing but sweets)
footnotes_tr: The one rule to memorize: しか always removes が/を, and other particles must come BEFORE しか; this is the opposite order from だけ and ばかり.

tables.caption_tr: だけ vs しか Side-by-Side: Same Fact, Different Feeling
rows: 五百円[ごひゃくえん]だけあります。 (I have just 500 yen.)
五百円[ごひゃくえん]しかありません。 (I only have 500 yen.)
だけ simply reports the amount; しか implies that 500 yen is not enough / disappointing
漢字[かんじ]を十[じゅう]だけ覚[おぼ]えました。 (I memorized just 10 kanji.)
漢字[かんじ]を十[じゅう]しか覚[おぼ]えていません。 (I've only memorized 10 kanji.)
だけ is a plain count; しか suggests the speaker feels it's too few
一人[ひとり]だけ来[き]ました。 (Only one person came.)
一人[ひとり]しか来[き]ませんでした。 (Only one person came [and that was disappointing].)
しか + negative past stresses how few/lacking it was

tables.caption_tr: Three Special Uses of ばかり
rows: "nothing but N, only N"; often with a critical undertone about imbalance
お菓子[かし]ばかり食[た]べないで。 (Don't eat nothing but sweets.)
"does nothing but keep doing V"; criticizes a repeated/habitual action
テレビを見[み]てばかりいる。 (He does nothing but watch TV.)
"just did V"; emphasizes that the action happened very recently
今[いま]起[お]きたばかりです。 (I just woke up.)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes to Avoid
rows: コーヒーしか飲[の]みます。
しか requires a NEGATIVE predicate; it can never end in an affirmative verb
コーヒーしか飲[の]みません。
が/を must be dropped when しか is used; they never appear together
東京[とうきょう]しかに行[い]ったことがない。
With しか, other particles (に/で/と) must come BEFORE しか, not after
東京[とうきょう]にしか行[い]ったことがない。
Using しか where だけ is meant, in a purely neutral/positive context
しか always adds a negative-feeling nuance of insufficiency, even when the fact itself sounds neutral in English
Use だけ if you simply want to state an amount without implying it's too little

examples.target: わたしはコーヒーだけ飲[の]みます。
examples.reading: わたしはコーヒーだけのみます。
examples.translation_tr: I only drink coffee. (Neutral statement of fact; no emotional coloring.)

examples.target: わたしはコーヒーしか飲[の]みません。
examples.reading: わたしはコーヒーしかのみません。
examples.translation_tr: I only drink coffee (and nothing else); carries a subtle nuance of limitation, as if that's all there is.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]はゲームばかりしています。
examples.reading: かれはゲームばかりしています。
examples.translation_tr: He does nothing but play games (all the time); critical, exasperated tone.

examples.target: 財布[さいふ]には千円[せんえん]しかありません。
examples.reading: さいふにはせんえんしかありません。
examples.translation_tr: I only have 1,000 yen in my wallet; implies this is a problem, not enough.

examples.target: 学生[がくせい]だけが教室[きょうしつ]に残[のこ]りました。
examples.reading: がくせいだけがきょうしつにのこりました。
examples.translation_tr: Only the students remained in the classroom. (Objective fact.)

examples.target: 昨日[きのう]買[か]ったばかりです。
examples.reading: きのうかったばかりです。
examples.translation_tr: I just bought it yesterday. (Recency; ばかり after ta-form.)

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は泣[な]いてばかりいる。
examples.reading: かのじょはないてばかりいる。
examples.translation_tr: She does nothing but cry (all the time); criticism of a repeated action.

examples.target: あと三日[みっか]だけ待[ま]ってください。
examples.reading: あとみっかだけまってください。
examples.translation_tr: Please just wait three more days. (だけ softening a request, neutral limit.)

potential-form.intro_tr: The potential form (可能形, kanōkei) expresses the ability to do something or the possibility that something can happen; the equivalent of English "can" verbs. It is formed differently depending on the verb group (Godan, Ichidan, or Irregular), and once formed, the resulting potential verb always conjugates like an Ichidan verb, regardless of its original group. A key grammatical shift is that the direct object particle を is usually replaced by が with potential verbs. Be careful not to confuse potential verbs with the separate spontaneous-perception verbs 見える/聞こえる, and watch for the common casual contraction known as ら抜き言葉 (ra-nuki kotoba).

tables.caption_tr: Potential Form Formation Overview
rows: Change the final -u sound to the corresponding -e sound, then add る
Drop the final る, add られる
食[た]べる → 食[た]べられる
Suppletive form; becomes できる entirely
勉強[べんきょう]する → 勉強[べんきょう]できる
Reading changes to 来[こ]られる
来[く]る → 来[こ]られる
footnotes_tr: Once formed, all potential verbs (regardless of original group) conjugate exactly like Ichidan verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Godan Verb Potential Form by Final Kana
Full Conjugation Paradigm (example: 書[か]ける, from 書[か]く)
footnotes_tr: Since potential verbs behave as Ichidan verbs, they never take another potential/passive ending on top of themselves (e.g., 書けられる is incorrect).

tables.caption_tr: Particle Usage with the Potential Form
rows: 漢字[かんじ]を読[よ]む → 漢字[かんじ]が読[よ]める
が highlights that the object itself is the thing that 'can be done'
私[わたし]は泳[およ]げる
東京[とうきょう]に行[い]ける
図書館[としょかん]で勉強[べんきょう]できる
footnotes_tr: In casual speech を is sometimes kept instead of が, especially in longer or emphatic sentences, but が is the standard textbook choice.

tables.caption_tr: Special Cases and Common Confusions
rows: Colloquial dropping of ら from Ichidan potential forms; common in casual speech, avoided in formal writing
食[た]べられる → 食[た]べれる
見[み]える / 聞[き]こえる
NOT the potential forms of 見る/聞く; separate verbs describing spontaneous, unintentional perception ('naturally visible/audible')
星[ほし]が見[み]える (stars are visible) vs 星[ほし]が見[み]られる (I get the chance to see stars)
Already an intransitive stative verb meaning 'to understand/be comprehensible'; has no separate potential form
日本語[にほんご]がわかる (I understand Japanese)
The suppletive potential of する; also used independently to mean 'to be completed' or 'to be good at'
料理[りょうり]ができる (can cook / good at cooking)

tables.caption_tr: Potential Form (可能形) vs 〜ことができる
rows: Casual to neutral, very common in speech
Slightly more formal, common in writing
Change the verb ending itself (e.g., 書ける)
Dictionary form + ことができる (e.g., 書くことができる)
勉強[べんきょう]できる
勉強[べんきょう]することができる

examples.target: 私[わたし]は漢字[かんじ]が読[よ]めます。
examples.translation_tr: I can read kanji.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは辛[から]い物[もの]が食[た]べられません。
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka-san can't eat spicy food.

examples.target: 今晩[こんばん]は忙[いそが]しくて来[こ]られません。
examples.translation_tr: I'm busy tonight, so I can't come.

examples.target: 昔[むかし]は速[はや]く泳[およ]げましたが、今[いま]は泳[およ]げません。
examples.translation_tr: I used to be able to swim fast, but I can't anymore.

examples.target: この漢字[かんじ]、読[よ]める?
examples.translation_tr: Can you read this kanji? (casual)

examples.target: 富士山[ふじさん]の頂上[ちょうじょう]からは海[うみ]が見[み]えます。
examples.translation_tr: From the summit of Mt. Fuji, you can see the ocean.
examples.note_tr: 見える is NOT the potential form of 見る; it's a separate spontaneous-perception verb meaning 'to naturally be visible.'

examples.target: 一人[ひとり]で日本[にほん]に行[い]けますか。
examples.translation_tr: Can you go to Japan alone?

examples.target: その料理[りょうり]、食[た]べれる?
examples.translation_tr: Can you eat that dish? (casual, ら抜き言葉)
examples.note_tr: 食べれる drops the ら from 食べられる; very common in casual speech but avoided in formal writing.

volitional-form.title_tr: Volitional Form (〜よう / 〜ましょう); Let's.../Shall we...?
volitional-form.intro_tr: The volitional form (意向形[いこうけい]) is used to say "let's do ~" or "I shall do ~", expressing a suggestion, invitation, or the speaker's own resolve/intention. It has two registers: the plain form (よう) used casually with friends and family or in one's own inner thoughts, and the polite form (ましょう) used in formal or polite contexts such as invitations to acquaintances, customer service, or business. The volitional form is also the base for several very common patterns like 〜ようと思う (intend to) and 〜ようとする (try to/about to). Formation differs by verb group, so mastering the conjugation table below is essential before combining it with other grammar points.

tables.caption_tr: Plain Volitional Form (〜よう); Formation by Verb Group
rows: drop final る, add よう
drop final る, add よう

tables.caption_tr: Polite Volitional Form (〜ましょう); Formation
footnotes_tr: Formation is regular for every verb: simply replace ます with ましょう on the polite stem; no exceptions.

tables.caption_tr: 〜よう vs 〜ましょう; Register & Usage Comparison
rows: Polite; acquaintances, strangers, business, customer service
〜ましょうか = "shall I/we...?" (polite invitation or offer of help)
Can stand alone as full sentence?
Yes, common in speech and writing (novels, thoughts)
Yes, very common in polite conversation and announcements
食[た]べよう (I'll eat / Let's eat; casual)
食[た]べましょう (Let's eat; polite)

tables.caption_tr: Common Grammar Patterns Built on the Volitional Form
rows: to intend to do something (stating one's own plan)
勉強[べんきょう]しようと思[おも]います (I intend to study)
to try to do / to be about to do (often interrupted)
出[で]ようとしたとき (just as I was about to leave)
volitional + ではないか / じゃないか
頑張[がんば]ろうではないか (Let us do our best!)
polite "shall I/we...?"; often an offer to help
手伝[てつだ]いましょうか (Shall I help you?)
ませんか = softer, asks if the other wants to; ましょう = more direct, assumes agreement
行[い]きませんか (Won't you go?) vs 行[い]きましょう (Let's go)

tables.caption_tr: Ways to Say "Let's..." in Japanese; Politeness Scale
rows: Direct suggestion/resolve, used with close people
"Should we...?" said informally, sometimes to oneself
Polite offer or suggestion, softer than ましょう
Asks about the listener's wish, most indirect/humble invitation

examples.target: 一緒[いっしょ]に映画[えいが]を見[み]ましょう。
examples.reading: Issho ni eiga o mimashou.
examples.translation_tr: Let's watch a movie together. (polite invitation)

examples.target: さあ、始[はじ]めよう。
examples.reading: Saa, hajimeyou.
examples.translation_tr: Alright, let's begin. (casual, among friends)

examples.target: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]よう。
examples.reading: Kyou wa hayaku neyou.
examples.translation_tr: I'll go to bed early today. (self-directed decision, said/thought to oneself)

examples.target: 来週[らいしゅう]、旅行[りょこう]に行[い]きましょうか。
examples.reading: Raishuu, ryokou ni ikimashou ka.
examples.translation_tr: Shall we go on a trip next week? (polite suggestion/question)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は新[あたら]しい仕事[しごと]を始[はじ]めようとしている。
examples.reading: Kare wa atarashii shigoto o hajimeyou to shite iru.
examples.translation_tr: He is about to start (trying to start) a new job.

examples.target: 日本語[にほんご]を勉強[べんきょう]しようと思[おも]います。
examples.reading: Nihongo o benkyou shiyou to omoimasu.
examples.translation_tr: I intend to study Japanese.

examples.target: お荷物[にもつ]をお持[も]ちしましょうか。
examples.reading: Onimotsu o omochi shimashou ka.
examples.translation_tr: Shall I carry your luggage? (polite offer to help)

examples.target: みんなで頑張[がんば]ろう!
examples.reading: Minna de ganbarou!
examples.translation_tr: Let's all do our best! (casual group encouragement)

passive-form.intro_tr: The passive form (受身形[うけみけい]) turns a sentence around so that the person or thing affected by an action becomes the grammatical subject, similar to English "was/were + past participle." In Japanese it is formed by adding られる (Ichidan/irregular) or れる (Godan) to the verb stem, and the resulting word then conjugates exactly like an Ichidan verb (られる/れる, られない/れない, られた/れた, etc.). Besides the ordinary "direct passive" (things translatable with English passive), Japanese also has a distinctive "suffering/adversative passive" (迷惑[めいわく]の受身[うけみ]) that expresses that the speaker was inconvenienced by someone else's action; this can even be built from intransitive verbs like 降る (rain), which is impossible in English. The agent of the action is usually marked with に, though によって is preferred in formal/written contexts describing creation (books, buildings, laws, etc.). Note that for Ichidan verbs the passive form is identical in shape to the potential form (見られる = "is seen" or "can see"), so context or the presence of an agent marked with に is what tells them apart.

tables.caption_tr: Formation rule by verb group
rows: Change final -u to -a, add れる (う→わ instead of あ)
Drop final る, add られる
勉強[べんきょう]される
来[く]る → 来[こ]られる (reading of 来 changes to こ)
footnotes_tr: The resulting れる/られる form always conjugates like a regular Ichidan verb: negative られない/れない, past られた/れた, te-form られて/れて, etc.

tables.caption_tr: Godan verb passive conjugation examples (u → a + れる)
footnotes_tr: Note: verbs ending in う take わ, not あ, before れる (買う → 買われる, never 買あれる).

tables.caption_tr: Ichidan verb passive conjugation examples (drop る + られる)
Types of passive sentences and their meaning
rows: Object of active sentence becomes subject, agent marked with に
私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められた。
Translates naturally into English passive: "I was praised by the teacher."
A body part or belonging of the subject is affected
私[わたし]は犬[いぬ]に手[て]を噛[か]まれた。
Literally "I was bitten (as to) hand by the dog"; the whole person, not just the hand, is emotionally affected.
Suffering / adversative passive (迷惑[めいわく]の受身[うけみ])
Can even be formed from intransitive verbs; expresses that the speaker was inconvenienced
私[わたし]は雨[あめ]に降[ふ]られた。
No direct English passive equivalent; closest translation is "it rained on me (and I was bothered by it)".
Used for facts, historical events, books, laws, buildings; agent often omitted or marked with によって
この寺[てら]は8世紀[はっせいき]に建[た]てられた。
によって is preferred over に when naming the creator/author explicitly, especially in writing.

tables.caption_tr: Passive vs. potential form: telling them apart for Ichidan verbs
rows: この番組[ばんぐみ]は見[み]られる。
This program can be watched / is available to watch.
Passive usually needs an agent with に or describes something being done to the subject; potential describes ability/possibility.
This can be eaten (it's edible / I am able to eat it).
Context and the presence of a に-marked agent are the main clues; the edible/ability reading is far more common in everyday speech.
パーティーに来[こ]られる。
(rare) someone is 'come upon'; essentially never used this way.
I/you/they can come to the party.
For 来る, the potential reading is overwhelmingly more common than the passive reading.
footnotes_tr: In casual speech, many Ichidan verbs use a shortened potential form (ら抜き言葉[らぬきことば], e.g. 食べれる instead of 食べられる) precisely to avoid this ambiguity; but this shortened form is potential-only and considered non-standard in formal writing.

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められました。
examples.reading: せんせいに ほめられました。
examples.translation_tr: I was praised by the teacher.
examples.note_tr: Direct passive: the subject (I) directly receives the teacher's action.

examples.target: この本[ほん]は多[おお]くの人[ひと]に読[よ]まれています。
examples.reading: このほんは おおくのひとに よまれています。
examples.translation_tr: This book is read by many people.
examples.note_tr: Direct passive describing a general fact; agent marked with に.

examples.target: 弟[おとうと]に財布[さいふ]を盗[ぬす]まれました。
examples.reading: おとうとに さいふを ぬすまれました。
examples.translation_tr: I had my wallet stolen by my little brother.
examples.note_tr: Possessive/direct passive: the object (財布) belongs to the speaker, who is affected.

examples.target: 雨[あめ]に降[ふ]られて、濡[ぬ]れてしまいました。
examples.reading: あめに ふられて、ぬれてしまいました。
examples.translation_tr: I got rained on and ended up soaked.
examples.note_tr: Suffering (adversative) passive made from the intransitive verb 降る; expresses inconvenience, has no direct English passive equivalent.

examples.target: 電車[でんしゃ]の中[なか]で足[あし]を踏[ふ]まれました。
examples.reading: でんしゃのなかで あしを ふまれました。
examples.translation_tr: My foot got stepped on inside the train.
examples.note_tr: Adversative passive: something unpleasant happened to a part of the speaker's body.

examples.target: このビルは1990年[せん きゅうひゃく きゅうじゅう ねん]に建[た]てられました。
examples.reading: このビルは せんきゅうひゃくきゅうじゅうねんに たてられました。
examples.translation_tr: This building was built in 1990.
examples.note_tr: Passive used for factual/historical description; agent often omitted or marked with によって for creative works.

examples.target: この歌[うた]は若[わか]い人[ひと]に愛[あい]されている。
examples.reading: このうたは わかいひとに あいされている。
examples.translation_tr: This song is loved by young people.
examples.note_tr: する-verb 愛する becomes 愛される in the passive.

examples.target: 犬[いぬ]に手[て]を噛[か]まれた。
examples.reading: いぬに てを かまれた。
examples.translation_tr: I got bitten on the hand by a dog.
examples.note_tr: Direct passive with a body-part object; the whole person is emotionally affected, not just the hand.

causative-form.intro_tr: The causative form (〜させる) expresses that someone makes or lets another person do an action; corresponding to English "make ~ do" (force) or "let ~ do" (permit), with the exact nuance decided by context and verb type rather than by the form itself. It is built by changing the verb's dictionary form to its -a stem (or adding させる to ichidan/する/来る) and conjugates afterward exactly like an ichidan verb (させます, させない, させた, させて...). A key beginner stumbling block is particle choice for the "causee" (the person being made/let to act): intransitive verbs mark the causee with を, while transitive verbs mark the causee with に and keep を for the original object. The causative also combines very productively with てください, てあげる/くれる/もらう, and ていただく to form polite requests and permission-giving expressions.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rules by Verb Group
rows: Change final -u sound to -a sound, then add せる
う → わ (not あ) before せる
Drop る, add させる
Drop る, add させる
勉強[べんきょう]させる
来[く]る → 来[こ]させる
footnotes_tr: In casual speech, godan causatives are often contracted: 待[ま]たせる → 待[ま]たす, 読[よ]ませる → 読[よ]ます. This 〜す contraction is colloquial and not used in writing or polite contexts.
Ichidan causatives are also sometimes contracted colloquially: 食[た]べさせる → 食[た]べさす, but 〜させる is the standard/textbook form and safer for beginners.

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation Paradigm (example: 食[た]べさせる, 'make/let eat')
rows: 食べさせませんでした
たべさせませんでした
make/let eat, and... / please let (someone) eat
be made to eat (see causative-passive topic)
footnotes_tr: Because させる itself ends in -eru, it conjugates exactly like a regular ichidan verb; all standard ichidan endings apply directly.

tables.caption_tr: Particle Pattern: Marking the Causee (person being made/let to act)
rows: 子供[こども]を歩[ある]かせる
子供[こども]に泣[な]かせておく
let the child cry (leave them be)
Causee + に, Object + を + causative
子供[こども]に野菜[やさい]を食[た]べさせる
Causee + に, Object + を + causative
学生[がくせい]に作文[さくぶん]を書[か]かせる
make/let the student write an essay
footnotes_tr: General rule: if を is already needed for the direct object, the causee must take に instead (を cannot mark two things in one clause).
With intransitive verbs, using に instead of を often softens the nuance toward 'allowing' rather than 'forcing', though both are commonly seen and context usually decides the meaning either way.

tables.caption_tr: Disambiguating 'Make' (force) vs 'Let' (permit)
rows: Verb describes something unpleasant/effortful + no permissive marker
毎日[まいにち]漢字[かんじ]を書[か]かせる; make (someone) write kanji every day
Causative + てあげる / てくれる
好[す]きなことをやらせてあげる; let them do what they like
好[す]きなだけ話[はな]させておく; let them talk as much as they want
Causative + てください / てほしい
帰[かえ]らせてください; please let me go home
Verb is inherently about emotion (喜ぶ, 驚く, 困る)
彼[かれ]を困[こま]らせる; cause him trouble / put him in a bind
footnotes_tr: The causative form itself is neutral between 'make' and 'let'; English speakers must rely on context, the verb's meaning, and any attached auxiliary (てあげる/てください/ておく) to pick the right translation.

tables.caption_tr: Common 'Emotion-Causative' Verbs (fixed idiomatic pairs)
rows: to trouble, to put (someone) in a bind
to relieve, to put (someone) at ease
footnotes_tr: These pairs behave like transitive English verbs ('surprise', 'disappoint') even though grammatically they are causative forms of intransitive Japanese verbs; very common in both speech and writing.

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]は学生[がくせい]に本[ほん]を読[よ]ませました。
examples.translation_tr: The teacher made/had the students read the book.
examples.note_tr: Transitive verb 読む → causee marked with に, object 本 keeps を.

examples.target: 母[はは]は妹[いもうと]を買[か]い物[もの]に行[い]かせた。
examples.translation_tr: Mom made (or let) my little sister go shopping.
examples.note_tr: Intransitive verb 行く → causee marked with を.

examples.target: 子供[こども]を自由[じゆう]に遊[あそ]ばせてあげたい。
examples.translation_tr: I want to let the child play freely.
examples.note_tr: Causative + てあげる softens it into a permissive, benefactive nuance ('let them for their sake').

examples.target: すみません、少[すこ]し考[かんが]えさせてください。
examples.translation_tr: Excuse me, please let me think about it a little.
examples.note_tr: Causative + てください = polite request for permission to do something yourself.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は冗談[じょうだん]でみんなを笑[わら]わせた。
examples.translation_tr: He made everyone laugh with a joke.
examples.note_tr: う-ending godan verb 笑う → 笑わせる (う→わ+せる).

examples.target: 息子[むすこ]に部屋[へや]を掃除[そうじ]させます。
examples.translation_tr: I make/have my son clean his room.
examples.note_tr: する-verb 掃除する → 掃除させる; transitive, so son is marked に.

examples.target: そのニュースは私[わたし]を驚[おどろ]かせた。
examples.translation_tr: That news surprised me.
examples.note_tr: Idiomatic 'emotion-causative'; 驚かせる functions like the English verb 'to surprise'.

examples.target: 部長[ぶちょう]は新人[しんじん]に来週[らいしゅう]プレゼンをさせるつもりだ。
examples.translation_tr: The manager intends to have the new employee do the presentation next week.
examples.note_tr: する itself becomes させる; new employee marked に since プレゼン is the direct object.

conditional-forms.title_tr: Conditional Forms (〜たら / 〜ば / 〜と / なら)
conditional-forms.intro_tr: Japanese has four main ways to express "if/when" conditions; と, ば, たら, and なら; and each carries a distinct nuance plus its own restrictions on what can follow in the main clause. と expresses automatic, mechanical, or habitual results and generally cannot be followed by a command, request, or invitation. ば expresses general hypothetical conditions, logical relationships, and proverbs, but is restricted when the main clause is a request or command tied to a controllable same-subject action. たら is the most flexible and by far the most common in everyday conversation, covering both hypothetical and definite future/sequential events, and it can be followed by any type of clause (command, request, volitional, etc.). なら responds to a premise already mentioned or implied by the listener; often used to give advice; and is unique in that the main-clause action can occur even before the condition itself is realized.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rules by Word Type
rows: godan: final -u → -e sound + ば; ichidan: drop る + れば; irregular: すれば / 来[く]れば
stem + であれば (or stem + なら)
noun + であれば (or noun + なら)
dictionary form (or any plain form) + なら

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation Across Word Types (Affirmative)
rows: 学生[がくせい]であれば
学生[がくせい]だったら

tables.caption_tr: Negative Conditional Forms (model: 行[い]く)
rows: 静[しず]かではない (not quiet)
静[しず]かではなかったら
静[しず]かではないなら
footnotes_tr: 〜なければ is also the base of the obligation pattern 〜なければならない ('must ~').

tables.caption_tr: Usage & Nuance Comparison
column_headers: Works for a one-time future event?
rows: automatic / natural consequence, mechanism, habitual result
general hypothetical condition, logical relationship, proverbs
limited; mainly with adjectives/states or differing subjects
restricted; not with a controllable same-subject verb that must finish first
proverbs, general truths, degree comparison 〜ば〜ほど
yes; the most natural everyday choice
everyday conversation, one-time future events, discovery, requests
responds to a premise/topic already mentioned; condition assumed true
yes; the main clause can even precede the condition in time
giving advice, contrastive topics, reacting to what was just said

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes & Restrictions
rows: ✕ 日本[にほん]へ行[い]けば、写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]ってください。
ば + request is unnatural when the if-clause is a controllable action by the same subject that must finish before the main clause
○ 日本[にほん]へ行[い]ったら、写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]ってください。
✕ 春[はる]になると、花見[はなみ]に行[い]きましょう。
と cannot be followed by a volitional/invitation in the main clause
○ 春[はる]になったら、花見[はなみ]に行[い]きましょう。
✕ 明日[あした]晴[は]れると、出[で]かけます。 (as a single uncertain plan)
と implies a near-automatic/habitual result, not one uncertain future event
○ 明日[あした]晴[は]れたら、出[で]かけます。
△ 分[わ]からなければ、聞[き]けば？
stacking ば with a volitional-like suggestion sounds unnatural
○ 分[わ]からなかったら、聞[き]いてください。

tables.caption_tr: Quick Decision Guide: Which Form to Use
rows: 水[みず]は100度[ど]になると沸騰[ふっとう]します。
朝[あさ]起[お]きると、まず水[みず]を飲[の]みます。
宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たったら、家[いえ]を買[か]います。
Advice about a topic just mentioned
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いなら、薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ方[ほう]がいいですよ。
終[お]わり良[よ]ければ全[すべ]て良[よ]し。
駅[えき]に着[つ]いたら、電話[でんわ]してください。
ドアを開[あ]けると、猫[ねこ]がいました。
勉強[べんきょう]すればするほど、上手[じょうず]になります。

examples.target: 春[はる]になると、桜[さくら]が咲[さ]きます。
examples.reading: はるになると、さくらがさきます。
examples.translation_tr: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.note_tr: と; natural, automatic seasonal result; cannot end in a volitional clause.

examples.target: お金[かね]があれば、旅行[りょこう]に行[い]きたいです。
examples.reading: おかねがあれば、りょこうにいきたいです。
examples.translation_tr: If I had money, I'd want to travel.
examples.note_tr: ば; general hypothetical condition.

examples.target: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ったら、すぐシャワーを浴[あ]びます。
examples.reading: いえにかえったら、すぐシャワーをあびます。
examples.translation_tr: When I get home, I take a shower right away.
examples.note_tr: たら; sequential 'when/after', works for a personal habit too.

examples.target: 京都[きょうと]へ行[い]くなら、新幹線[しんかんせん]が便利[べんり]ですよ。
examples.reading: きょうとへいくなら、しんかんせんがべんりですよ。
examples.translation_tr: If you're going to Kyoto, the shinkansen is convenient.
examples.note_tr: なら; advice responding to a plan the listener just mentioned; the recommendation applies before the trip happens.

examples.target: このボタンを押[お]すと、電気[でんき]がつきます。
examples.reading: このボタンをおすと、でんきがつきます。
examples.translation_tr: If you press this button, the light turns on.
examples.note_tr: と; mechanical, automatic cause and effect.

examples.target: 安[やす]ければ、買[か]います。
examples.reading: やすければ、かいます。
examples.translation_tr: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.note_tr: ば with an i-adjective is perfectly natural even with a volitional main clause.

examples.target: 明日[あした]雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]です。
examples.reading: あしたあめがふったら、しあいはちゅうしです。
examples.translation_tr: If it rains tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.
examples.note_tr: たら; uncertain, one-time future event; the most flexible and common everyday choice.

examples.target: 分[わ]からないことがあれば、聞[き]いてください。
examples.reading: わからないことがあれば、きいてください。
examples.translation_tr: If there's anything you don't understand, please ask.
examples.note_tr: ば + request is fine here because the if-clause is a state (あれば), not a controllable same-subject action.

giving-receiving.title_tr: あげる / くれる / もらう (Giving and Receiving)
giving-receiving.intro_tr: The verbs あげる, くれる, and もらう all express the act of giving and receiving, but the choice among them depends entirely on the "direction" of the action relative to the speaker (or the speaker's in-group), not just on who is grammatically the subject. あげる is used when someone (often the speaker) gives something to another person who is not the speaker. くれる is used when someone else gives something to the speaker or to a person in the speaker's in-group; it is the mirror image of あげる. もらう is used when the subject receives something, with the giver marked by に or から. Each of these three verbs also has plain, humble, and respectful (keigo) variants used depending on the relative social status of the giver and receiver. Getting the direction and the politeness level right is the key challenge for learners, since English "give" does not encode this directionality.

tables.caption_tr: The three basic verbs: direction and meaning
rows: Speaker / third party → someone else (not the speaker)
Someone else → speaker or speaker's in-group

tables.caption_tr: Perspective rules: who can be the giver and who can be the receiver
rows: Cannot say あげる when something is given TO the speaker; use くれる instead
Cannot say くれる when the speaker is the giver; use あげる instead
The subject is always the one who receives, regardless of who the giver is

tables.caption_tr: Politeness levels: give-away verbs (あげる family)
rows: Giving to plants, animals, or condescendingly to much lower-status people
Giving to equals or people not of lower status (most common everyday form)
Speaker gives to a social superior (customer, boss, teacher)

tables.caption_tr: Politeness levels: give-to-me verbs (くれる family)
rows: Someone gives to the speaker or the speaker's in-group
A social superior gives to the speaker or in-group

tables.caption_tr: Politeness levels: receiving verbs (もらう family)
rows: Speaker receives from a social superior

tables.caption_tr: Common direction mistakes
rows: 私[わたし]は友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]をくれました。
くれる cannot have the speaker as the giver
私[わたし]は友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]をあげました。
友達[ともだち]は私[わたし]に本[ほん]をあげました。
あげる cannot have the speaker as the receiver
友達[ともだち]は私[わたし]に本[ほん]をくれました。
先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]に本[ほん]をあげました。
Using plain あげる toward the speaker ignores both direction and politeness
先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]に本[ほん]をくださいました。

examples.target: 私[わたし]は友達[ともだち]にプレゼントをあげました。
examples.reading: わたしはともだちにプレゼントをあげました。
examples.translation_tr: I gave a present to my friend.
examples.note_tr: あげる: subject (giver) is 'I', receiver is someone else. Cannot use あげる if the receiver is 'me'.

examples.target: 友達[ともだち]は私[わたし]にプレゼントをくれました。
examples.reading: ともだちはわたしにプレゼントをくれました。
examples.translation_tr: My friend gave me a present.
examples.note_tr: くれる: subject (giver) is someone else, receiver is 'me' or my in-group. This is the mirror image of あげる.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は友達[ともだち]にプレゼントをもらいました。
examples.reading: わたしはともだちにプレゼントをもらいました。
examples.translation_tr: I received a present from my friend.
examples.note_tr: もらう: subject is the receiver ('I'), and the giver is marked with に or から.

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]に本[ほん]をくださいました。
examples.reading: せんせいはわたしにほんをくださいました。
examples.translation_tr: My teacher kindly gave me a book.
examples.note_tr: くださる is the respectful (尊敬語) version of くれる, used when the giver is a social superior.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]に本[ほん]をいただきました。
examples.reading: わたしはせんせいにほんをいただきました。
examples.translation_tr: I humbly received a book from my teacher.
examples.note_tr: いただく is the humble (謙譲語) version of もらう, lowering the speaker relative to the giver.

examples.target: 父[ちち]は花[はな]に水[みず]をやります。
examples.reading: ちちははなにみずをやります。
examples.translation_tr: My father waters the flowers.
examples.note_tr: やる is a plain/rough version of あげる, typically used for plants, animals, or condescendingly toward much lower-status people.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は社長[しゃちょう]にお土産[おみやげ]を差し上げました。
examples.reading: わたしはしゃちょうにおみやげをさしあげました。
examples.translation_tr: I gave a souvenir to the company president.
examples.note_tr: 差し上げる is the humble version of あげる, used when giving to a social superior.

examples.target: 弟[おとうと]は妹[いもうと]におもちゃをあげました。
examples.reading: おとうとはいもうとにおもちゃをあげました。
examples.translation_tr: My younger brother gave a toy to my younger sister.
examples.note_tr: Third-party-to-third-party giving (neither side is 'me') normally uses あげる, not くれる.

transitive-intransitive.title_tr: Transitive / Intransitive Verb Pairs (自動詞・他動詞)
transitive-intransitive.intro_tr: Japanese verbs often come in matched pairs called intransitive verbs (自動詞[じどうし]) and transitive verbs (他動詞[たどうし]) that describe the same physical event from two different angles. The intransitive member says something happened by itself; no one is mentioned as causing it; and its subject is marked with が. The transitive member says someone deliberately performed the action, and the thing affected is marked with を. Many pairs follow predictable sound patterns (like -aru/-eru or -eru/-su), which makes them easier to memorize as sets rather than individually. Getting the particle and the verb right together is essential, especially once you combine these verbs with 〜ている (natural resulting state) versus 〜てある (a state someone deliberately arranged).

tables.caption_tr: Core Differences: Intransitive (自動詞) vs Transitive (他動詞)
rows: The action/change happens by itself, naturally, or the cause is unknown/unimportant
Someone deliberately performs the action on something
(人が) ドアを (a person acts on the door)
What happened? What is the state?
What did someone do to it?
ドアが開[あ]く; the door opens
ドアを開[あ]ける; (someone) opens the door
footnotes_tr: Some verbs are intransitive-only or transitive-only and have no pair at all (e.g., 行く[いく] to go, 食べる[たべる] to eat).

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns: How Pairs Are Built by Sound
rows: 見つかる[みつかる] mitsukaru
見つける[みつける] mitsukeru
wake up, happen / wake someone, cause
footnotes_tr: These patterns are helpful memory aids, but there are exceptions; always confirm a new pair in a dictionary rather than guessing purely from the sound shape.

tables.caption_tr: More Essential N4 Transitive/Intransitive Pairs
rows: turn on, light up (itself) / turn on (something)
生まれる[うまれる] umareru

tables.caption_tr: 〜ている vs 〜てある: Which Resultant State to Use
rows: A natural resultant state; no agent is implied
窓[まど]が開[あ]いている; The window is open.
A resultant state someone deliberately arranged, often for a purpose
窓[まど]が開[あ]けてある; The window has been left open (on purpose).
An action currently in progress (not a resultant state)
彼[かれ]がドアを開[あ]けている; He is opening the door (right now).
footnotes_tr: With 〜てある the object is normally marked with が, not を, because the sentence focuses on the resulting state rather than the actor.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: Mixing Up Particle and Verb Type
rows: ドアが開[あ]いた / ドアを開[あ]けた
開[あ]く is intransitive and cannot take を; use が. To say someone opened it, use the transitive 開[あ]ける with を.
火[ひ]が消[き]えた / 火[ひ]を消[け]した
消[き]える is intransitive (が); 消[け]す is transitive (を); they are not interchangeable forms of the same verb.
授業[じゅぎょう]を始[はじ]まる
授業[じゅぎょう]が始[はじ]まる / 授業[じゅぎょう]を始[はじ]める
始[はじ]まる is intransitive (が); 始[はじ]める is transitive (を).
エアコンを消[き]えている
エアコンが消[き]えている / エアコンを消[け]してある
Match ている/てある to the correct verb: intransitive+ている for a natural state, transitive+てある for a deliberately arranged state.

examples.target: ドアが開きました。
examples.reading: ドアがあきました。
examples.translation_tr: The door opened (by itself).

examples.target: 彼がドアを開けました。
examples.reading: かれがドアをあけました。
examples.translation_tr: He opened the door.

examples.target: 電気が消えています。
examples.reading: でんきがきえています。
examples.translation_tr: The light is off (has gone out).

examples.target: 電気を消してください。
examples.reading: でんきをけしてください。
examples.translation_tr: Please turn off the light.

examples.target: 会議は9時に始まります。
examples.reading: かいぎはくじにはじまります。
examples.translation_tr: The meeting starts at 9 o'clock.

examples.target: 先生が会議を始めました。
examples.reading: せんせいがかいぎをはじめました。
examples.translation_tr: The teacher started the meeting.

examples.target: 窓が開けてあります。
examples.reading: まどがあけてあります。
examples.translation_tr: The window has been left open (someone opened it on purpose).

examples.target: 財布が見つかりました。
examples.reading: さいふがみつかりました。
examples.translation_tr: My wallet was found.

comparatives-superlatives.intro_tr: Unlike English, Japanese adjectives have no special comparative (-er) or superlative (-est) form; the adjective itself never changes. Instead, comparison is expressed through particles: より marks the thing being compared against ("than"), で or の中で marks the group for superlatives ("among/in"), and ほど or くらい/ぐらい express "as much as" or rough equality. The word 一番[いちばん] (colloquial) or 最[もっと]も (formal) means "the most" and is placed before the adjective. Because the adjective form stays constant, mastering comparison in Japanese is really about mastering which particle to use and where to place it in the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Comparative Sentence Patterns (A vs B)
rows: 私[わたし]は兄[あに]より背[せ]が高[たか]い。
I am taller than my brother.
A は B より もっと [adjective]

Today is even colder than yesterday.
B より A のほうが [adjective]
兄[あに]より私[わたし]のほうが背[せ]が高[たか]い。

A と B と どちらが [adjective] ですか
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]とどちらが好[す]きですか。

A のほうが [adjective] です
犬[いぬ]のほうが好[す]きです。

rows: クラスで田中[たなか]さんが一番[いちばん]頭[あたま]がいい。

Group marked with の中[なか]で

Which sport do you like the most?

tables.caption_tr: Equal Comparison and Negative Comparison
rows: A は B と 同[おな]じくらい/ぐらい [adjective]
このかばんはあのかばんと同[おな]じくらい高[たか]い。

この問題[もんだい]はあの問題[もんだい]ほど難[むずか]しくない。

どちらもおいしいです。
A も B も 同[おな]じだ

tables.caption_tr: Core Particles Used in Comparison
rows: marks the item being compared against ('than')
夏[なつ]は冬[ふゆ]より暑[あつ]い。
Always attaches to the noun, not the adjective.
'as much as'; almost always used with a negative predicate
彼[かれ]は私[わたし]ほど忙[いそが]しくない。
Positive use (〜ほど〜はない) means 'nothing is as ~ as X'.
妹[いもうと]は私[わたし]と同[おな]じくらいの背[せ]だ。
くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable; ぐらい is slightly more casual.
marks the scope/group for a superlative
日本[にほん]で一番[いちばん]大[おお]きい都市[とし]は東京[とうきょう]だ。
Used when the group is a place, category, or set.
'among ~'; marks the group for a superlative, more explicit than で
家族[かぞく]の中[なか]で父[ちち]が一番[いちばん]背[せ]が高[たか]い。
Preferred when で alone would be ambiguous.
marks the comparison partner in どちら/同じ constructions
コーヒーと紅茶[こうちゃ]とどちらが好[す]きですか。
Pairs with どちら, 同[おな]じ, 違[ちが]う.

tables.caption_tr: Question Words for Comparison
rows: choosing between exactly two items (more polite than どっち)
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]とどちらが好[す]きですか。
choosing among three or more specific items
この中[なか]でどれが一番[いちばん]安[やす]いですか。
何[なに]/だれ/どこ + 一番[いちばん]
open-ended superlative question (no fixed item list)
日本[にほん]でどこが一番[いちばん]有名[ゆうめい]ですか。

tables.caption_tr: How Adjective Type Behaves in Comparative Sentences
rows: no change to the adjective itself; only particles change

no change; だ/です attaches normally, no な needed before です
この街[まち]はあの街[まち]より静[しず]かです。
same pattern; noun acts as the compared quality
この店[みせ]のほうが人気[にんき]がある。
adjective takes its normal negative form (〜くない / 〜じゃない)
今日[きょう]は昨日[きのう]ほど寒[さむ]くない。

relative-clauses.intro_tr: In Japanese, a relative clause (also called a noun-modifying clause) always comes BEFORE the noun it describes, and there is no separate relative pronoun like "who," "which," or "that." Instead, you take a verb, adjective, or noun+copula phrase, put it into its plain (dictionary-style) form, and place it directly in front of the noun; the whole clause acts like one giant adjective. Crucially, the subject inside the embedded clause is marked with が, never は, even if the whole phrase later becomes the topic of the main sentence. Any tense/polarity (non-past, past, negative) can appear inside the clause, so a single noun can be modified by present, past, affirmative, or negative information. This structure is used constantly in everyday Japanese, so mastering the plain-form conjugations below is essential.

tables.caption_tr: Verb Forms Used to Modify a Noun (always plain form, never ます-form)
rows: 食[た]べなかった人[ひと]

tables.caption_tr: Adjectives Modifying a Noun
rows: 高[たか]くなかった山[やま]
静[しず]かではない町[まち]
静[しず]かだった町[まち]
静[しず]かではなかった町[まち]

tables.caption_tr: Noun + Copula (だ) Modifying a Noun
rows: noun + の + noun (だ is replaced by の)
the person who is a doctor
noun + じゃない/ではない + noun
医者[いしゃ]じゃない人[ひと]
the person who isn't a doctor
医者[いしゃ]だった人[ひと]
the person who was a doctor
noun + じゃなかった/ではなかった + noun
医者[いしゃ]じゃなかった人[ひと]
the person who wasn't a doctor

tables.caption_tr: Subject Marking Inside the Clause: が, not は
rows: The subject of the embedded clause is marked with が, even though は is used for the main sentence topic
[私[わたし]が作[つく]った]料理[りょうり]はおいしいです。
'I' takes が because it is the subject of the inner clause 'that I made'; は marks the whole phrase 料理 as the topic of the main sentence
は cannot mark the embedded subject
✗ 私[わたし]は書[か]いた手紙[てがみ] → ✓ 私[わたし]が書[か]いた手紙[てがみ]
は would incorrectly try to make '私' the topic of the entire sentence instead of just the subject inside the clause
If the clause has no separate subject (subject = the modified noun itself), が is simply omitted
昨日[きのう]買[か]った本[ほん]
the implied subject '私が' is dropped because it's understood from context

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with Relative Clauses
rows: Verbs must be in PLAIN form before a noun, never ます-form
だれ食[た]べる人[ひと] (adding a word for 'who')
Japanese needs NO relative pronoun at all; the clause itself does the modifying
な-adjectives use な (not だ) when directly modifying a noun
私[わたし]は書[か]いた手紙[てがみ]
は cannot mark the subject of an embedded clause; use が instead
私[わたし]が書[か]いた手紙[てがみ]
本[ほん]、私[わたし]が読[よ]んだ (clause placed after noun, like English 'the book that I read')
Japanese relative clauses ALWAYS precede the noun; there is no post-noun clause order
私[わたし]が読[よ]んだ本[ほん]

toki-when.intro_tr: とき (時) literally means "time," and attached to a clause it works like the English conjunction "when"; it links a time-setting clause to a main clause: [clause] + とき, [main clause]. Unlike English, the tense you choose for the verb right before とき does NOT describe absolute past/present/future; instead it shows whether the とき-clause's action is completed or not YET completed relative to the main-clause action. This relative-tense rule (dictionary form vs た form) is the single trickiest point of とき for beginners, and it's covered in detail below. とき can follow verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns, each with its own connecting form, all summarized in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Connecting Forms Before とき (by word type)
rows: while eating / in the middle of eating
忙[いそが]しくないとき
学生[がくせい]だったとき

tables.caption_tr: The Key Rule: Dictionary Form vs た Form Before とき (relative tense, not absolute tense)
rows: The とき-clause action has NOT finished yet at the moment of the main-clause action (it may even never finish before the main action)
日本[にほん]へ行[い]くとき、カメラを買[か]いました。
I bought a camera before going to Japan (I hadn't left yet; still preparing to go).
The とき-clause action is already completed/underway by the time of the main-clause action
日本[にほん]へ行[い]ったとき、写真[しゃしん]をたくさん撮[と]りました。
I took a lot of photos after arriving in Japan (I had already gone/arrived).
The とき-clause action is in progress at the exact same moment as the main-clause action
電話[でんわ]しているとき、地震[じしん]が起[お]きました。
While I was on the phone, an earthquake happened.
No completion issue; the state simply holds true at that time, so only one form is natural
若[わか]いとき、よく旅行[りょこう]しました。
When I was young, I traveled often.

tables.caption_tr: とき vs Similar Time/Condition Expressions (quick disambiguation)
rows: Neutral "when"; simply sets the time frame, works with any tense combination
出[で]かけるとき、傘[かさ]を持[も]っていきます。
The default, most versatile time-setting word; safe default choice for beginners
Conditional/sequential trigger; "once X happens, then Y"; stronger cause-and-effect or one-time-event feel
家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ったら、電話[でんわ]します。
Often interchangeable with 〜たとき in casual speech, but たら emphasizes the trigger-result link
Formal equivalent of とき, used in business/written Japanese
ご利用[りよう]の際[さい]に、会員証[かいいんしょう]をご提示[ていじ]ください。
More polite/formal register than とき; rarely used in casual conversation
"While/within the time that...", implying the window closes/changes soon
若[わか]いうちに、いろいろ挑戦[ちょうせん]したほうがいい。
Adds a nuance of "before it's too late" that plain とき does not have
Same subject doing two actions simultaneously
音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]きながら、勉強[べんきょう]します。
Only for one single subject doing two actions at once; とき has no such subject restriction

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions Using とき
rows: in case of emergency / when it really comes down to it

examples.target: 子供[こども]のとき、よく公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]びました。
examples.reading: こどものとき、よくこうえんであそびました。

examples.reading: いえにかえるとき、コンビニによりました。

examples.reading: いえにかえったとき、だれもいませんでした。
examples.translation_tr: When I got home (after arriving), no one was there. (た form → the とき-action is already complete)

examples.reading: いそがしいときは、でんわしないでください。
examples.translation_tr: When I'm busy, please don't call me. (い-adjective plain form + とき)

examples.target: 日本[にほん]にいたとき、寿司[すし]をたくさん食[た]べました。
examples.reading: にほんにいたとき、すしをたくさんたべました。
examples.translation_tr: When I was in Japan, I ate a lot of sushi. (past state + とき)

examples.target: わからないときは、先生[せんせい]に聞[き]いてください。
examples.reading: わからないときは、せんせいにきいてください。
examples.translation_tr: When you don't understand (something), please ask the teacher. (ない form + とき)

examples.target: 電話[でんわ]しているとき、友達[ともだち]が来[き]ました。
examples.reading: でんわしているとき、ともだちがきました。
examples.translation_tr: While I was on the phone, my friend came. (ている form + とき, simultaneous action)

examples.target: 暇[ひま]なとき、映画[えいが]を見[み]ます。
examples.reading: ひまなとき、えいがをみます。
examples.translation_tr: When I'm free, I watch movies. (な-adjective + な + とき)

mae-ato-nagara.title_tr: まえに / あとで / ながら; Time Connectors: "Before", "After", and "While"
mae-ato-nagara.intro_tr: まえに ("before doing"), あとで ("after doing"), and ながら ("while doing") are three essential time connectors that link two actions or events performed by (usually) the same person. まえに always pairs with the dictionary (non-past) form of the verb, no matter what tense the main clause is in, because it marks a point that is still "in the future" relative to the moment described. あとで always pairs with the た-form because the action it attaches to has already been completed. ながら is different in kind: it attaches to the ます-stem and describes two actions happening at the same time by the same subject, with the action after ながら being the main, focused action. Getting the tense of the verb before まえに/あとで right, and remembering the same-subject rule for ながら, are the two most common trouble spots for learners.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation patterns
rows: 食事[しょくじ]のまえに (before the meal)
食事[しょくじ]のあとで (after the meal)
三年前[さんねんまえ]に (three years ago)

tables.caption_tr: Meaning and usage comparison
rows: Always dictionary form, regardless of main-clause tense
Subject of the まえに-clause can differ from the main clause
Main action comes after まえに-clause
Subject can differ from the main clause
Main action comes after あとで-clause
ます-stem only, no tense marking (tense shown only on the final verb)
Must be the SAME subject for both actions
Main/focused action is the verb AFTER ながら

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation examples across verb types
Common mistakes and key points to remember
rows: Even when the whole sentence is in the past, the verb directly before まえに must stay in the dictionary (non-past) form, because まえ describes a point that is still 'before' relative to the following event.
寝[ね]るまえに、歯[は]をみがきました。 (NOT 寝[ね]たまえに)
ながら requires the same subject
Both actions linked by ながら must be performed by the same person. You cannot use ながら if the two actions have different subjects.
（私[わたし]が）音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]きながら（私[わたし]が）勉強[べんきょう]する; correct; mixing two different subjects is wrong.
The clause that comes after ながら is the main, emphasized action; the clause with ながら is the background/accompanying action.
テレビを見[み]ながらご飯[はん]を食[た]べる = 'eating' is the main action, 'watching TV' is the background action.
あとで vs てから

あとで simply states that one action follows another; てから (a different pattern) also shows sequence but more strongly emphasizes 'and then, as a deliberate next step,' often followed by an important resulting action.
食[た]べたあとで出[で]かけます (after eating, I'll go out) vs 手[て]を洗[あら]ってから食[た]べます (I wash my hands and then eat).
When まえに or あとで attaches directly to a noun (not a verb clause), you must insert の between the noun and まえに/あとで.
仕事[しごと]のまえに (before work) / 仕事[しごと]のあとで (after work); never 仕事[しごと]まえに without の.
When 前に follows a duration of time (not a verb), it means '... ago' rather than 'before doing something'; a completely separate usage from the clause-connecting まえに.
三年前[さんねんまえ]に日本[にほん]へ行[い]きました。 (I went to Japan three years ago.)

examples.target: 寝[ね]るまえに、歯[は]を みがきます。
examples.reading: ねるまえに、はをみがきます。
examples.translation_tr: Before going to bed, I brush my teeth. (Note: 寝る stays in dictionary form even though the overall action is habitual/future.)

examples.target: ご飯[はん]を 食[た]べたあとで、宿題[しゅくだい]を します。
examples.reading: ごはんをたべたあとで、しゅくだいをします。
examples.translation_tr: After eating, I do my homework. (食べる is in た-form because the eating already finished.)

examples.target: 音楽[おんがく]を 聞[き]きながら、勉強[べんきょう]します。
examples.reading: おんがくをききながら、べんきょうします。
examples.translation_tr: I study while listening to music. (Same subject does both actions; 勉強する is the main action.)

examples.target: 日本[にほん]へ 行[い]くまえに、日本語[にほんご]を 勉強[べんきょう]しました。
examples.reading: にほんへいくまえに、にほんごをべんきょうしました。
examples.translation_tr: Before going to Japan, I studied Japanese. (行く is dictionary form even though the whole sentence is past tense.)

examples.target: 授業[じゅぎょう]が 終[お]わったあとで、友達[ともだち]と 遊[あそ]びます。
examples.reading: じゅぎょうがおわったあとで、ともだちとあそびます。
examples.translation_tr: After class ends, I'll go play with friends.

examples.target: テレビを 見[み]ながら ご飯[はん]を 食[た]べないでください。
examples.reading: テレビをみながらごはんをたべないでください。
examples.translation_tr: Please don't eat while watching TV.

examples.target: 食事[しょくじ]の まえに、手[て]を 洗[あら]います。
examples.reading: しょくじのまえに、てをあらいます。
examples.translation_tr: I wash my hands before meals. (Noun + の + まえに pattern.)

examples.target: 三年前[さんねんまえ]に、日本[にほん]に 住[す]んでいました。
examples.reading: さんねんまえに、にほんにすんでいました。
examples.translation_tr: Three years ago, I was living in Japan. (Time-duration + 前に means '... ago', a separate usage from the clause connector.)

to-omoimasu.title_tr: と思います (I think, In my opinion)
to-omoimasu.intro_tr: と思います is the standard way to express personal opinion, belief, or supposition; "I think that..." It attaches directly after a plain-form (dictionary/casual) clause, never after the polite ます-form. The verb 思う ("to think") itself is conjugated to control politeness and tense, while the content of your thought stays in plain form. A key beginner trap is negation: in Japanese it is usually more natural to negate the *content* clause (〜ないと思います, "I think that... not") rather than saying 〜と思いません, even though English speakers instinctively want to negate "think."

tables.caption_tr: How to attach と思います to each word type (plain form required before と)
rows: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]る + と思います
面白[おもしろ]い + と思います
Add だ before と (do NOT drop だ)
簡単[かんたん]だ + と思います
Add だ before と (do NOT drop だ)
先生[せんせい]だ + と思います
Never use polite form before と
✗ 降[ふ]りますと思います

tables.caption_tr: Tense and aspect variants of 思う
rows: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ると思います (I think it will rain)
Opinion held at a specific past moment, may differ from now
忙[いそが]しいと思いました (I thought [then] he was busy)
A settled, continuing opinion; standard for describing someone ELSE's opinion
彼[かれ]はいいと思っています (He thinks/believes it's good)
plain + と思っていました
An opinion you held continuously over a past period
ずっとそうだと思っていました (I had always thought so)
Softens the opinion, often before a request or suggestion
無理[むり]だと思うんですが... (I think it might be hard, but...)

tables.caption_tr: Negation: where does 'not' go?
rows: 'I think that... is not...'; the normal, neutral way to disagree or doubt
来[こ]ないと思います (I don't think he'll come)

Inference, often about future/uncertain facts, softer certainty than 思う

quotation-to-iu.intro_tr: と言う literally means "to say that ~," and it is built from the quotation particle と (marking exactly what was said or thought) plus the verb 言う "to say." Right after a direct quote in「」brackets or after a plain-form clause, と marks the content, and 言う reports who said it. When という appears directly in front of a noun, its function shifts from "say" to "called/named," introducing an unfamiliar word, title, or name (Xという Y = "a Y called/named X"). という can also summarize hearsay ("I heard/it's said that ~") without a specific speaker, especially in news, rumors, or written reports. Because と itself is the real quotation marker, almost any verb of speech, thought, or perception (思う, 聞く, 書く, 考える, etc.) can replace 言う after と; this page focuses on the core と言う/という pattern that all of those build on.

tables.caption_tr: Core pattern: と + verb of speech/thought
rows: 〜と いう / 〜と いいます
彼は「はい」と言いました。
〜と おもう / 〜と おもいます
明日は晴れると思います。
〜と きく / 〜と ききました
彼は結婚すると聞きました。
本に「注意」と書いてあります。
この薬はよく効くと言われている。

tables.caption_tr: Direct quotation vs. indirect quotation
rows: 彼は「今日は忙しい」と言いました。
彼は今日は忙しいと言いました。
He said (that) he was busy today.
Plain past form + と + 言う
彼女は昨日雨が降ったと言いました。
She said (that) it had rained yesterday.
Plain negative form + と + 言う
彼は行かないと言いました。
Plain form + か + と + 聞く/言う
誰が来るかと聞きました。

tables.caption_tr: という for naming and introducing (X という Y)
rows: introduces an unfamiliar name/title before a noun
田中さんという人が来ました。
「もったいない」という言葉を知っていますか。
Place/thing name + という + category noun
names a specific place, book, shop, etc.
「東京」という町を知っていますか。
Do you know a town called "Tokyo"?
Clause (plain form) + という + うわさ/話/天気予報 etc.
reports hearsay attached to a noun
彼が辞めるといううわさを聞きました。
I heard a rumor that he is quitting.

tables.caption_tr: Quick conjugation reference for 言う (godan verb)
rows: dictionary form, used before という
used in と言っている (is saying)
used in と言われている (it is said)

tables.caption_tr: Common set expressions built on という
rows: as for the thing called ~ / the reason ~ is
日本語というのは面白い言語です。
I heard that ~ / it means that ~
彼は来ないということだ。
部長は明日休むとのことです。
忙しいというより疲れています。
彼は嘘をついているという気がする。

koto-nominalizer.title_tr: Nominalizing Verbs with こと and の
koto-nominalizer.intro_tr: こと and の are both particles that turn a verb (or an entire clause ending in a verb) into a noun, letting you use an action as the subject or object of a sentence; something English does with "-ing" or "to ~" (e.g., "swimming is fun," "I saw him leave"). こと nominalizes an action as an abstract fact, ability, decision, or general concept, and is locked into many fixed grammar patterns like 〜ことができる and 〜ことにする. の nominalizes an action as something concretely perceived in the moment; used above all with verbs of direct sensory perception (見る, 聞く, 感じる) and with helping/waiting verbs (手伝う, 待つ). In many everyday sentences (especially with 好き, 上手, 難しい) both are grammatically acceptable and the difference is a matter of nuance rather than correctness, but in the fixed patterns below only one of the two is ever allowed; mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

tables.caption_tr: こと vs. の at a Glance
rows: Nominalizes an action/clause as an abstract fact, ability, decision, or general concept
〜ことができる / 〜ことにする / 〜ことになる / 〜ことがある / 〜たことがある
Talking about abilities, decisions, results, general facts, past experience
Nominalizes an action as something directly seen, heard, felt, helped with, or waited for; also used to identify "the one who ~"
〜のを見る / 〜のを聞く / 〜のを手伝う / 〜のを待つ / 〜のは〜です
Direct sensory perception, pointing at a specific concrete act, casual/spoken register

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Expressions That MUST Use こと (の is Ungrammatical)
rows: 泳[およ]ぐことができる; can swim
雪[ゆき]が降[ふ]ることがある; it sometimes snows
京都[きょうと]に行[い]ったことがある; have been to Kyoto
毎日[まいにち]走[はし]ることにする; decide to run every day
it has been decided that ~ / it turns out that ~
引[ひ]っ越[こ]すことになった; it's been decided I'll move
高[たか]いことは高[たか]いですが…; it IS expensive, but...

tables.caption_tr: Patterns That MUST/Strongly Prefer の (こと is Wrong or Unnatural)
rows: 動詞+のを見[み]る/聞[き]く/感[かん]じる
子供[こども]が歌[うた]っているのを聞[き]いた; heard the child singing
動詞+のを手伝[てつだ]う
母[はは]が料理[りょうり]するのを手伝[てつだ]った; helped mom cook
バスが来[く]るのを待[ま]った; waited for the bus to come
窓[まど]を割[わ]ったのは弟[おとうと]です; it was my brother who broke the window

tables.caption_tr: Interchangeable Cases; Subtle Nuance Differences
rows: 好[す]きな活動[かつどう] (liked activity)
本[ほん]を読[よ]むことが好[す]きです
本[ほん]を読[よ]むのが好[す]きです
の sounds more natural/colloquial for a concrete activity; こと sounds slightly more formal/abstract
難[むずか]しい・大切[たいせつ]だ etc. (evaluative comment)
漢字[かんじ]を覚[おぼ]えることは難[むずか]しい
漢字[かんじ]を覚[おぼ]えるのは難[むずか]しい
Both are correct; こと leans toward a general statement, の toward the specific act just mentioned
大切[たいせつ]な行動[こうどう] (important action)
早寝早起[はやねはやお]きをすることが大切[たいせつ]だ
早寝早起[はやねはやお]きをするのが大切[たいせつ]だ
Fully interchangeable in most everyday speech and writing

tables.caption_tr: Common Beginner Mistakes
rows: 泳[およ]ぐのができます (✗)
泳[およ]ぐことができます (○)
Ability expressions always use こと, never の
子供[こども]が遊[あそ]んでいることを見[み]た (unnatural)
子供[こども]が遊[あそ]んでいるのを見[み]た (natural)
Direct perception verbs (見る/聞く/感じる) require の, not こと
京都[きょうと]に行[い]ったのがあります (✗)
京都[きょうと]に行[い]ったことがあります (○)
The experience pattern is fixed as 〜たことがある; の cannot replace こと here
彼[かれ]が来[く]ることを待[ま]った (unnatural)
彼[かれ]が来[く]るのを待[ま]った (natural)
待つ (wait for) takes の because it refers to a concretely anticipated event

examples.target: 泳[およ]ぐことができます。

examples.translation_tr: I can swim. (ability; こと is required here, not の)

examples.target: 京都[きょうと]に行[い]ったことがあります。
examples.reading: きょうとにいったことがあります。
examples.translation_tr: I have been to Kyoto. (past experience pattern 〜たことがある)

examples.target: 毎朝[まいあさ]、走[はし]ることにしました。

examples.reading: らいげつ、おおさかにてんきんすることになりました。
examples.translation_tr: It has been decided that I'll be transferred to Osaka next month.

examples.target: 子供[こども]が公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]んでいるのを見[み]ました。
examples.reading: こどもがこうえんであそんでいるのをみました。
examples.translation_tr: I saw the children playing in the park. (direct perception; の, not こと)

examples.target: 母[はは]が晩[ばん]ごはんを作[つく]るのを手伝[てつだ]いました。
examples.reading: ははがばんごはんをつくるのをてつだいました。
examples.translation_tr: I helped my mother cook dinner.

examples.target: 音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]くのが好[す]きです。
examples.reading: おんがくをきくのがすきです。
examples.translation_tr: I like listening to music. (の feels more natural for a concrete activity here)

examples.target: 漢字[かんじ]を覚[おぼ]えるのは難[むずか]しいです。
examples.reading: かんじをおぼえるのはむずかしいです。
examples.translation_tr: Memorizing kanji is difficult. (cleft-style の marking the specific act being discussed)

tsumori-yotei.title_tr: つもり / 予定 (Intention and Plan)
tsumori-yotei.intro_tr: つもり and 予定 both translate roughly as "plan/intention" but differ in nature: つもり expresses the speaker's own subjective will, determination, or belief about a future (or even past) action; it lives inside the speaker's head and can change. 予定, on the other hand, describes an objective, often already-arranged schedule item, something that exists on a calendar or itinerary regardless of the speaker's personal feelings about it. Both attach to the dictionary form of a verb (or a noun + の) and behave grammatically like the noun-modifying だ/です predicate. Mastering the difference; and the special past-tense nuance of 〜たつもりだ; is essential for sounding natural when talking about future actions in Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation patterns
rows: 行[い]くつもりだ; I intend to go
行[い]かないつもりだ; I intend not to go
I believed/thought I had done ~ (often contrasted with reality)
説明[せつめい]したつもりだ; I thought I had explained it
先生[せんせい]のつもりで話[はな]す; to speak as if one were the teacher
Verb (dictionary form) + 予定[よてい]だ
出発[しゅっぱつ]する予定[よてい]だ; scheduled to depart
Noun + の + 予定[よてい]だ
会議[かいぎ]の予定[よてい]だ; a meeting is scheduled
footnotes_tr: Both つもり and 予定 are na-adjective-like nouns: they take だ/です, な before another noun, and で before a clause continuation.

tables.caption_tr: Nuances and negative forms of つもり
rows: 働[はたら]くつもりだ; I intend to work
a deliberate intention to refrain from doing something
食[た]べないつもりだ; I intend not to eat
a firm, explicit denial of any intention (stronger/more direct than Vないつもりだ)
やめるつもりはない; I have no intention of quitting
I did it thinking/believing so (but it may not have worked out / reality differs)
覚[おぼ]えたつもりだ; I thought I had memorized it
Vる/Vた + つもりだった
had intended to ~ (often left unrealized, tinged with regret)
早[はや]く来[く]るつもりだったが、遅[おく]れた; I meant to come early, but I was late
to consider oneself as ~, to act under the (mistaken) belief that ~
若[わか]いつもりだ; I think of myself as (still) young

tables.caption_tr: Nuances and negative forms of 予定
rows: an arranged, scheduled event or plan
来週[らいしゅう]出張[しゅっちょう]する予定[よてい]だ; I am scheduled for a business trip next week
結婚式[けっこんしき]は来年[らいねん]の予定[よてい]だ; the wedding is planned for next year
Vる + 予定[よてい]はない
there is currently no such plan/schedule
海外[かいがい]に行[い]く予定[よてい]はない; there is no plan to go abroad
予定[よてい]が変[か]わる／決[き]まる
予定[よてい]が変[か]わりました; the schedule has changed
予定[よてい]通[どお]りに
予定[よてい]通[どお]りに進[すす]んでいる; it's proceeding as scheduled
footnotes_tr: 予定 emphasizes an item fixed on a schedule/calendar, often set by circumstances, other people, or institutions rather than pure personal will.

tables.caption_tr: つもり vs 予定 vs related expressions of future intention
rows: moderate–firm, but can still fall through
personal decisions, resolutions, plans not yet formally arranged
留学[りゅうがく]するつもりだ; I intend to study abroad
来月[らいげつ]帰国[きこく]する予定[よてい]だ; I'm scheduled to return home next month
weaker, can be a passing thought
旅行[りょこう]に行[い]こうと思[おも]う; I think I'll go on a trip
expectation based on logic/evidence, not intention
彼[かれ]はもう着[つ]いているはずだ; he should have already arrived
footnotes_tr: Use つもり for your own resolve, 予定 for something already on a schedule, 〜(よ)うと思う for a softer/more casual first-person intention, and はず for a logical expectation rather than a plan at all.

examples.target: 来年[らいねん]、日本[にほん]に行[い]くつもりです。
examples.reading: らいねん、にほんにいくつもりです。
examples.translation_tr: I intend to go to Japan next year. (personal decision/intention)

examples.target: 今日[きょう]はもう勉強[べんきょう]しないつもりです。
examples.reading: きょうはもうべんきょうしないつもりです。
examples.translation_tr: I don't intend to study anymore today.
examples.note_tr: Negative intention: dictionary-form-negative (ない-form) + つもりだ.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]と結婚[けっこん]するつもりはありません。
examples.reading: かれとけっこんするつもりはありません。
examples.translation_tr: I have no intention of marrying him.
examples.note_tr: 〜つもりはない is a stronger/more explicit denial than 〜ないつもりだ.

examples.target: ちゃんと説明[せつめい]したつもりですが、うまく伝[つた]わっていなかったようです。

examples.translation_tr: I thought I had explained it properly, but it seems it didn't get across well.
examples.note_tr: た-form + つもりだ = 'I believed/thought I had done X' (often contrasted with reality).

examples.target: 来週[らいしゅう]、会議[かいぎ]がある予定[よてい]です。
examples.reading: らいしゅう、かいぎがあるよていです。
examples.translation_tr: There is a scheduled meeting next week.
examples.note_tr: 予定 presents this as a fixed item on a schedule, not a personal decision.

examples.target: 明日[あした]は出張[しゅっちょう]の予定[よてい]です。
examples.reading: あしたはしゅっちょうのよていです。
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow I'm scheduled for a business trip.
examples.note_tr: Noun + の + 予定だ.

examples.target: 旅行[りょこう]に行[い]くつもりだったが、仕事[しごと]が入[はい]ってしまった。
examples.reading: りょこうにいくつもりだったが、しごとがはいってしまった。
examples.translation_tr: I had planned to go on a trip, but work came up (so it fell through).
examples.note_tr: つもりだった = a past intention that often ended up unfulfilled.

examples.target: 来月[らいげつ]引[ひ]っ越[こ]す予定[よてい]はまだ決[き]まっていません。
examples.reading: らいげつひっこすよていはまだきまっていません。
examples.translation_tr: The plan to move next month has not been decided yet.
examples.note_tr: 予定 can be negated with はない, similar to how a schedule item can be absent/undecided.

deshou-kamoshirenai.title_tr: でしょう / かもしれない (Expressing Probability)
deshou-kamoshirenai.intro_tr: でしょう and かもしれない are two essential N4 grammar points for expressing probability and conjecture in Japanese, but they express very different levels of confidence. でしょう (plain form: だろう) signals a fairly confident prediction or judgment made by the speaker, and with rising intonation it can also soften a statement into a "right?"-style confirmation question. かもしれない, on the other hand, expresses a weaker possibility; something like "might" or "perhaps" in English; and makes no strong claim either way. Both attach to the plain/short form of verbs and i-adjectives, but drop だ after na-adjectives and nouns. Mastering the difference between these two, along with related expressions like はず and と思う, is key to sounding natural when guessing, speculating, or hedging in Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Connection rules: 〜でしょう (probable / confirming judgment)
rows: 行く + でしょう → 行くでしょう
行った + でしょう → 行ったでしょう
行かない + でしょう → 行かないでしょう
いかない でしょう
plain form + でしょう (keep い)
高い + でしょう → 高いでしょう
静か + でしょう → 静かでしょう
学生 + でしょう → 学生でしょう
がくせい でしょう
footnotes_tr: でしょう is the polite form; だろう is the plain/casual equivalent used in casual speech or writing.
With rising intonation (でしょう？), it functions like a tag question: "right?" / "don't you think?"

tables.caption_tr: Connection rules: 〜かもしれない (possibility, "might")
rows: dictionary form + かもしれない
行く + かもしれない → 行くかもしれない
いく かもしれない
行った + かもしれない → 行ったかもしれない
いった かもしれない
ない-form + かもしれない
行かない + かもしれない → 行かないかもしれない
いかない かもしれない
plain form + かもしれない (keep い)
高い + かもしれない → 高いかもしれない
たかい かもしれない
stem (drop だ) + かもしれない
静か + かもしれない → 静かかもしれない
しずか かもしれない
noun (drop だ) + かもしれない
学生 + かもしれない → 学生かもしれない
がくせい かもしれない
footnotes_tr: Unlike でしょう, かもしれない never takes rising intonation to become a question; it is a statement of low-to-moderate possibility.

tables.caption_tr: Register / politeness variants
rows: conversation with friends, inner thoughts, casual writing
conversation with strangers, superiors, formal writing
footnotes_tr: だろう is often used by male speakers in casual speech as a blunt-sounding guess or tag question; でしょう is safer for learners in mixed company.
かもしれない has no informal/formal distinction in the stem itself; only ます↔plain endings change.

tables.caption_tr: Confidence scale: comparing conjecture expressions
rows: きっと〜でしょう / だろう
きっと 合格[ごうかく]するでしょう (I'm sure you'll pass)
もう 着[つ]いているはずです (they should have arrived by now)
たぶん〜でしょう / だろう
たぶん 雨[あめ]でしょう (it will probably rain)
彼[かれ]は 来[く]るでしょう (he will probably come)
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]ると 思[おも]います (I think it will rain)
possibility, weaker than でしょう
雨[あめ]が 降[ふ]るかもしれません (it might rain)
もしかしたら〜かもしれない
もしかしたら 遅[おく]れるかもしれません (I might possibly be late)
footnotes_tr: These percentages are rough intuitive guides for learners, not fixed statistics.
でしょう and かもしれない can combine with adverbs (たぶん, きっと, もしかしたら) to reinforce their respective confidence levels; see next table.

tables.caption_tr: Common adverb pairings
footnotes_tr: Using the matching adverb is optional but makes the sentence sound more natural and native-like.

examples.target: 明日[あした]は 雨[あめ]でしょう。
examples.translation_tr: It will probably rain tomorrow.

nakereba-narimasen.title_tr: 〜なければなりません (Expressing Obligation: 'Must ~ / Have to ~')
nakereba-narimasen.intro_tr: 〜なければなりません is the standard polite way to express obligation or necessity in Japanese; the equivalent of English "must ~" or "have to ~". It is built from the negative (ない) form of a verb: drop the final い of 〜ない and attach 〜ければなりません, literally meaning something like "if [it] does not happen, it will not do"; a double-negative construction that produces a strong positive obligation. Because it is a double negative, learners often confuse it with prohibition (〜てはいけません, "must not") or with the "no obligation" pattern (〜なくてもいいです, "don't have to"); all three are compared below. There are several interchangeable variants ranging from formal written Japanese down to very casual spoken contractions like 〜なきゃ, and the whole expression can be conjugated for tense and politeness just like a normal verb phrase (なります/なりません/なりませんでした, etc.).

ta-koto-ga-aru.intro_tr: 〜たことがある expresses life experience; whether the speaker has ever done something at some unspecified point in the past, regardless of when. It attaches to the plain past (た-form) of a verb and is followed by ある/ない, which conjugates for politeness and negation like a normal い-type predicate. Because it talks about accumulated experience "up to now," it is normally incompatible with specific recent-time expressions like 昨日 (yesterday); for a single definite past event, plain 〜た is used instead. Do not confuse this with the dictionary-form pattern 〜ことがある, which means "it sometimes happens" rather than "I have experienced."

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb (plain past, た-form) + ことがある
footnotes_tr: The た-form used here is exactly the plain past tense form of the verb, the same one used in casual past statements.

footnotes_tr: ある/ない conjugate exactly like ordinary い-type predicates: あります/ありません, ない/なかった, etc.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 昨日[きのう]、寿司[すし]を食[た]べたことがある。
たことがある is for general life experience, not a single recent event with a specific time marker.
昨日[きのう]、寿司[すし]を食[た]べた。 (I ate sushi yesterday.)
日本[にほん]に行[い]くことがあります。 (intending to mean 'I have been to Japan')
Using the dictionary form instead of the た-form changes the meaning to 'sometimes I go to Japan.'
日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがあります。 (I have been to Japan.)
彼[かれ]はよく学生[がくせい]だったことがある。
Mixing たことがある with よく is fine, but だった + ことがある is awkward for state-experience; usually plain だ + ことがある patterns need care with な/だ nouns.
彼[かれ]は昔[むかし]、学生[がくせい]だったことがある。 (He was once a student, long ago.); add a time-in-the-past marker like 昔 for clarity.

politeness-levels.title_tr: Politeness Levels: Casual Speech vs. Polite Speech (丁寧語[ていねいご]) Overview
politeness-levels.intro_tr: Japanese does not have a single neutral way to speak; the verb, adjective, and copula endings you choose signal your relationship with the listener. At the most basic level there are two everyday registers: casual/plain speech (普通体[ふつうたい], the だ-form) used with close friends, family, and in one's own thoughts or diary, and polite speech (丁寧体[ていねいたい], the です・ます form) used with strangers, coworkers, and in most textbook Japanese. A third, higher tier; 敬語[けいご] (honorific/humble speech); exists for superiors, customers, and formal business situations, but that is a separate, more advanced system covered on its own pages. Beginners should master です・ます first, since it is safe in almost any situation, and only switch to casual speech once a relationship is established or the other person uses it first. Mixing registers within the same sentence (e.g. a casual verb ending with です tacked on awkwardly) is a common learner mistake to avoid.

nara-baai.title_tr: なら / 場合[ばあい]; "If" / "In the Case That"
nara-baai.intro_tr: なら and 場合[ばあい] both translate roughly as "if / in the case that", but they work differently from たら/ば/と. なら presents a premise; often something the listener just mentioned or a hypothetical situation; and comments on it, with no implication of time sequence (the なら-clause can even happen *after* the main clause). 場合 is a noun meaning "case, occasion" and is used to describe what one should do or what happens under a stated circumstance; it feels more formal/objective and is common in instructions, rules, and manuals. Both are essential N3 conditionals that beginners must be able to distinguish from たら/ば/と.

ni-tsuite-kanshite.title_tr: について / に関して (about, regarding)
ni-tsuite-kanshite.intro_tr: について and に関して both mean "about" or "regarding," attaching to a noun to introduce the topic that a verb (talk, think, research, explain, write, etc.) is concerned with. について is the everyday, all-purpose choice used in both speech and writing, while に関して sounds slightly more formal and is common in written, academic, or business contexts. Both can be modified with の to describe a following noun (についての/に関しての), with は to make a contrastive topic (については/に関しては), or with も to mean "also regarding" (についても/に関しても). A stiffer, more bureaucratic cousin, につき, is often seen on notices and official documents. This grammar point is essential for stating the subject matter of a discussion, essay, report, or question.

Noun + に関[かん]する + Noun
Formal written form, used before a noun
Neutral form, used before a noun
footnotes_tr: に関して and について are interchangeable in most contexts; について is safer for everyday conversation.
につき's 'reason' meaning (= のため) only appears in formal/business notices, e.g. 台風[たいふう]につき休業[きゅうぎょう] 'closed due to typhoon'.
