examples.target: これは私[わたし]の一存[いちぞん]では決[き]められません。上司[じょうし]次第[しだい]です。
examples.reading: これは わたしの いちぞんでは きめられません。じょうし しだいです。
examples.translation_tr: I can't decide this on my own judgment; it's up to my boss.

examples.target: 電車[でんしゃ]が事故[じこ]で止[と]まり、遅刻[ちこく]した次第[しだい]です。
examples.reading: でんしゃが じこで とまり、ちこく した しだいです。
examples.translation_tr: The train stopped because of an accident, and that is the reason I was late.
examples.note_tr: Very formal register: 〜次第です at the end of a sentence explains the circumstances behind a situation, common in apologies and business reports.

you-ni-purpose.intro_tr: 〜ように is a versatile N2 pattern built on the noun よう ('way, manner') plus に, and it covers three closely related core functions: (1) PURPOSE; 'so that / in order that' a certain state or ability is achieved; (2) MANNER/SIMILARITY; 'in the way that' or 'like' something else, including quoting instructions; and (3) WISH/PRAYER; expressing a hope for a future state, typically standing alone at the very end of a sentence. Which meaning applies depends heavily on the verb form placed immediately before ように and on where in the sentence it appears. Because of this range, ように is frequently confused with the intention marker 〜ために (which requires a plain volitional verb and usually a single subject) and with the appearance marker よう(だ) (which describes how something 'seems', not a wish). Mastering ように means learning to recognize potential-form and negative-form verbs (purpose), plain/past-form verbs or の (manner), and bare sentence-final ように (wish).

tables.caption_tr: Table 1; The Three Core Functions of 〜ように
rows: Describes a goal, ability, or state to be brought about
早[はや]く治[なお]るように、薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ。 (I took medicine so that I would recover quickly.)
Manner / Similarity (as, like, per instructions of)
Describes doing something the same way as a model, or quoting an instruction
説明書[せつめいしょ]に書[か]いてあるように、組[く]み立[た]てた。 (I assembled it as written in the manual.)
Expresses a hope for a future state; nothing follows grammatically
早[はや]く元気[げんき]になりますように。 (I hope you get well soon.)
footnotes_tr: All three functions share the same core idea: 'toward a certain way/state (よう) + に'.

tables.caption_tr: Table 2; Purpose Usage: Which Verb Form Goes Before ように
rows: Potential-form verbs (見える, 聞こえる, できる, わかる, 話せる...)
早く走れるように毎日練習する。
早[はや]く走[はし]れるように毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]する。
I practice every day so that I can run fast.
Verbs of change/state (なる, 慣れる, 治る...)
上手になるように頑張ります。
上手[じょうず]になるように頑張[がんば]ります。
I'll do my best so that I become skilled.
風邪をひかないように気をつける。
風邪[かぜ]をひかないように気[き]をつける。
I'll be careful so as not to catch a cold.
Plain volitional action verbs (行く, 買う, 食べる for one's own intentional act)
✕ Not typical; use ために instead
家を買うために働く。(◯) / 家を買うように働く。(✕ unnatural)
家[いえ]を買[か]うために働[はたら]く。
I work in order to buy a house. (Use 〜ために here, not 〜ように.)
footnotes_tr: ように is naturally paired with verbs describing a state, capability, or change; not with a plain intentional action for one's own direct benefit.

tables.caption_tr: Table 3; 〜ように vs 〜ために (Purpose Comparison)
rows: Potential form, ない-form, or state/change verbs
Dictionary form of a volitional action verb
Can differ; the first clause often benefits someone/something else
Effort or adjustment made to reach a state or avoid a problem
A clear, deliberate intention or benefit-driven goal
皆[みな]に聞[き]こえるように話[はな]す (speak so that everyone can hear)
家[いえ]を買[か]うために働[はたら]く (work in order to buy a house)
〜ないように (so as not to...); very common and natural
〜ないために; rare and usually rephrased for naturalness
footnotes_tr: A quick test: if the sentence describes making something possible/impossible or reaching a state, use ように; if it describes a deliberate personal goal with a single actor, ために fits better.

tables.caption_tr: Table 4; Manner / Similarity Usage
rows: 鳥[とり]のように飛[と]ぶ
Verb (dictionary or past form) + ように
先生が言ったように書く
先生[せんせい]が言[い]ったように書[か]く
〜ように言う / 伝える / 頼む / 注意する
早[はや]く来[く]るように言[い]う

you-to-suru.title_tr: 〜ようとする / 〜ようとしない (Trying to / Refusing to Try)
you-to-suru.intro_tr: 〜ようとする attaches to the volitional (let's-do) form of a verb plus とする, and it describes the moment of attempting or being on the verge of an action; "to try to do," "to attempt to do," or, with events and involuntary verbs, "to be about to happen." The negative counterpart 〜ようとしない means "to refuse to even try" or "won't make an attempt," often carrying a nuance of stubbornness or resistance. Because とする itself is a full verb (する), the whole phrase conjugates like any する-verb: past 〜ようとした, progressive 〜ようとしている, negative 〜ようとしない, past negative 〜ようとしなかった. This grammar point is very common with contrastive but-clauses (〜が/〜のに) to show that an effort was made yet failed, and it frequently modifies a following clause as 〜(よ)うとした時/瞬間/矢先 ("just as X was about to..."). Do not confuse it with 〜たがる (visible desire) or 〜つもりだ (plan/intention); 〜ようとする specifically marks the active moment of attempting, not merely wanting or planning.

dake-ni.title_tr: 〜だけに / 〜だけあって (Precisely Because... / Just As You'd Expect)
dake-ni.intro_tr: 〜だけに and 〜だけあって are two closely related N2 causal expressions that both roughly mean "precisely because...". They mark that a result or state is a natural, fitting consequence of a reason, status, effort, or characteristic already known to speaker and listener. 〜だけあって is used almost exclusively to praise or express admiration; it means "no wonder, given that..." and is always followed by a positive result that matches expectations (often paired with さすが). 〜だけに is more flexible: it can lead either to a fitting positive result (like だけあって) or to a contrastive result, where precisely BECAUSE of the reason, a disappointing or ironic outcome feels even stronger. Both expressions attach to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives (+な), and nouns, and both function as mid-sentence connectors rather than sentence-final forms.

wari-ni.intro_tr: 〜わりに (also 〜わりには for stronger emphasis) expresses that the actual result Y does not match what you would normally expect based on a given standard or premise X; it is either better or worse than expected, in a mildly surprising way. It is often translated as "considering X..., surprisingly Y" or "for X, Y is...". Unlike 〜のに, which usually carries disappointment or complaint, 〜わりに is more neutral or even mildly complimentary, simply noting a gap between expectation and reality. It attaches directly after verbs and い-adjectives in the plain form, but requires な after な-adjectives and の after nouns. This is an N2-level pattern common in both spoken and written Japanese, frequently used to comment on food, prices, performance, and appearances.

hanmen.intro_tr: 〜反面 (はんめん, literally "the other side/aspect") means "while... on the other hand" or "although... at the same time." It is used to present two contrasting facets of the very same person, thing, or situation; typically one positive point and one negative point that coexist as facts, rather than a surprising contradiction. Because both clauses must describe the same subject, it differs from more general contrast markers that can link two separate subjects. It attaches to the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and requires な or である before it with な-adjectives and nouns. This is a common N2 written/formal-speech pattern, often translated as "while it is true that... it is also true that..."

stem + な / である + 反面
便利[べんり]な反面[はんめん] / 便利[べんり]である反面[はんめん]; while being convenient...
学生[がくせい]である反面[はんめん]; while being a student...
知[し]らない反面[はんめん]; while not knowing...

tables.caption_tr: Tense and aspect before 〜反面
rows: Two ongoing, general, or habitual contrasting traits
この機械[きかい]は速[はや]い反面[はんめん]、うるさい。; It's fast, but on the other hand it's loud.
Two contrasting results of a single completed event/change
給料[きゅうりょう]が上[あ]がった反面[はんめん]、仕事[しごと]が増[ふ]えた。; My salary went up, but on the other hand my workload increased.

tables.caption_tr: 〜反面 compared with similar contrastive grammar
rows: Two coexisting sides (usually good + bad) of the same subject
彼[かれ]は厳[きび]しい反面[はんめん]、優[やさ]しい。; He's strict, but on the other hand he's kind.
Surprise/disappointment at an unexpected, often single-event outcome
勉強[べんきょう]したのに、落[お]ちた。; Even though I studied, I failed.
Concession: 'even though X, the expected result did not fully follow'
合格[ごうかく]したものの、喜[よろこ]べなかった。; I passed, but I couldn't feel happy about it.
'While/meanwhile'; can link two contrasting sides of one subject OR two separate simultaneous actions/subjects
父[ちち]は働[はたら]く一方[いっぽう]で、母[はは]は家[いえ]にいた。; Father worked, while Mother stayed home.
Simple, casual contrast between two clauses, any relationship
高[たか]いけど、おいしい。; It's expensive, but it's delicious.

tables.caption_tr: Usage notes and common pitfalls
rows: Both halves must describe facets of ONE subject; 太郎[たろう]は忙[いそが]しい反面[はんめん]、花子[はなこ]は暇[ひま]だ is unnatural; use 一方[いっぽう]で instead for two different people.
Usually pairs a light and a shadow
The most natural use pairs one advantage with one disadvantage (or vice versa), e.g. convenient-but-expensive, strict-but-kind.
反面 does NOT mean 'then' or 'after that'; it only marks a logical/qualitative contrast, not a chronological sequence of unrelated actions.
Common in essays, news, and formal speech; slightly stiffer than casual けど/が, but not as literary as 〜ものの in casual conversation.
No volitional/command restriction, but stylistic mismatch
Because it states facts about a subject, pairing it with commands (〜てください) or invitations (〜ましょう) in the second clause sounds unnatural.

examples.target: この薬[くすり]はよく効[き]く反面[はんめん]、副作用[ふくさよう]もある。
examples.reading: この くすりは よく きく はんめん、ふくさようも ある。
examples.translation_tr: This medicine works well, but on the other hand it also has side effects.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]ができる反面[はんめん]、人[ひと]付[づ]き合[あ]いが苦手[にがて]だ。
examples.reading: かれは しごとが できる はんめん、ひとづきあいが にがてだ。
examples.translation_tr: He is capable at his job, but on the other hand he's bad at socializing.

examples.target: この町[まち]は静[しず]かな反面[はんめん]、交通[こうつう]が不便[ふべん]だ。
examples.reading: この まちは しずかな はんめん、こうつうが ふべんだ。
examples.translation_tr: This town is quiet, but on the other hand transportation is inconvenient.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は先生[せんせい]である反面[はんめん]、一人[ひとり]の母親[ははおや]でもある。
examples.reading: かのじょは せんせいである はんめん、ひとりの ははおやでも ある。
examples.translation_tr: She is a teacher, but at the same time she is also a mother.

examples.target: 新[あたら]しいシステムは便利[べんり]な反面[はんめん]、使[つか]い方[かた]が難[むずか]しい。
examples.reading: あたらしい システムは べんりな はんめん、つかいかたが むずかしい。
examples.translation_tr: The new system is convenient, but on the other hand it's hard to use.

examples.target: 都会[とかい]の生活[せいかつ]は便利[べんり]な反面[はんめん]、物価[ぶっか]が高[たか]い。
examples.reading: とかいの せいかつは べんりな はんめん、ぶっかが たかい。
examples.translation_tr: City life is convenient, but on the other hand the cost of living is high.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]はテストに合格[ごうかく]した反面[はんめん]、あまり嬉[うれ]しそうではなかった。
examples.reading: かれは テストに ごうかくした はんめん、あまり うれしそうでは なかった。
examples.translation_tr: He passed the test, but on the other hand he didn't seem very happy.

examples.target: 収入[しゅうにゅう]が増[ふ]えた反面[はんめん]、自由[じゆう]な時間[じかん]が減[へ]った。
examples.reading: しゅうにゅうが ふえた はんめん、じゆうな じかんが へった。
examples.translation_tr: My income increased, but on the other hand my free time decreased.

ippou-de.intro_tr: 〜一方(で) is a formal, written-leaning connector meaning "while, on the other hand, at the same time." It links two clauses that describe two different (often contrasting) facts, or two different aspects/activities of the very same subject that hold true at once. Unlike simple contrast markers like が or けど, 一方(で) has a slightly essay-like, explanatory tone and is common in news, reports, and formal writing, though it is also heard in careful spoken Japanese. It attaches to the plain/dictionary form of verbs and い-adjectives, to な-adjectives with な, and to nouns with である. Be careful not to confuse the connector 〜一方で with the unrelated pattern 〜一方だ ("only keeps ~ing"), which attaches directly to a verb of change and expresses one-directional progression, not contrast.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: how to attach 一方(で) to each word type
rows: 働[はたら]く一方で (while working)
働かない一方で (while not working)
高[たか]い一方で (while being expensive)
便利[べんり]な一方で (while being convenient)
学生[がくせい]である一方で (while being a student)
彼は厳しい。一方、優しい。

tables.caption_tr: The two core functions of 〜一方(で)
rows: Two separate, often opposing, situations are placed side by side; like English 'while / whereas'.
賛成[さんせい]する人がいる一方、反対[はんたい]する人もいる。(While some agree, others disagree.)
2. Two simultaneous aspects of the SAME subject
One subject has two things true about it at the same time; often one positive/one negative, or two different roles/activities.
彼女は歌手である一方で、女優としても活動している。(She is a singer while also working as an actress.)
Common in news/reports: as one thing changes, a related but different thing also changes.
人口が増える一方で、食料が不足している。(As population grows, food is running short.)

tables.caption_tr: 一方で vs. sentence-initial 一方 vs. the unrelated 一方だ; do not confuse these!
rows: 'while ~, on the other hand ~' (contrast/parallel, within one sentence)
忙[いそが]しい一方で、充実[じゅうじつ]している。
Start of a new sentence, after a full stop
Same meaning as 一方で, but functions as a stand-alone conjunction linking two sentences
忙しい。一方、充実している。
Directly after dictionary-form verb of change (増える, 悪化する, 減る, etc.), NO で
'only keeps ~ing, continues one-directionally'; NO contrast, just steady change
物価[ぶっか]は上[あ]がる一方だ。(Prices just keep rising.)

tables.caption_tr: 〜一方(で) compared with similar 'while / on the other hand' grammar
rows: Neutral connector for two contrasting or parallel facts
Formal, written/essay-like, also usable in careful speech
働く一方で勉強[べんきょう]もする。
Almost always contrasts a GOOD point with a BAD point (or vice versa) of the same thing
便利な反面、高い。(Convenient, but on the downside expensive.)
Same as 反面, slightly more literary spelling
楽[らく]な半面、退屈[たいくつ]だ。
Simultaneous action by the SAME subject, more literary; can also mean 'even though'
知[し]りつつ、黙[だま]っていた。(Knowing it, I stayed silent.)
Simultaneous action by the SAME subject, plain/everyday; can also mean 'while/though'
歩きながら話す。(Talk while walking.)
Strong, often subjective contrast between two things, sometimes critical tone
兄にひきかえ、弟は勤勉だ。(Unlike his brother, the younger one is diligent.)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]をする一方[いっぽう]で、家事[かじ]も手伝[てつだ]っている。
examples.reading: かれはしごとをするいっぽうで、かじもてつだっている。
examples.translation_tr: While he works, he also helps with the housework.

examples.target: 都会[とかい]は便利[べんり]な一方[いっぽう]で、生活費[せいかつひ]が高[たか]い。
examples.reading: とかいはべんりないっぽうで、せいかつひがたかい。
examples.translation_tr: The city is convenient, but on the other hand, the cost of living is high.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は歌手[かしゅ]である一方[いっぽう]で、女優[じょゆう]としても活動[かつどう]している。
examples.reading: かのじょはかしゅであるいっぽうで、じょゆうとしてもかつどうしている。
examples.translation_tr: She is a singer, and at the same time she is also active as an actress.

examples.target: 人口[じんこう]が増[ふ]える一方[いっぽう]で、食料[しょくりょう]が不足[ふそく]している。
examples.reading: じんこうがふえるいっぽうで、しょくりょうがふそくしている。
examples.translation_tr: While the population is increasing, food is becoming scarce.

examples.target: 景気[けいき]は悪化[あっか]する一方[いっぽう]だ。
examples.reading: けいきはあっかするいっぽうだ。
examples.translation_tr: The economy just keeps getting worse and worse.
examples.note_tr: This is the special ~一方だ pattern (no で, no comparison) attached directly to a dictionary-form verb of change. It means 'only ever ~, continuously ~'; see the note table below.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は厳[きび]しい。一方[いっぽう]、優[やさ]しいところもある。
examples.reading: かれはきびしい。いっぽう、やさしいところもある。
examples.translation_tr: He is strict. On the other hand, he also has a kind side.
examples.note_tr: Here 一方 stands alone at the start of a new sentence as a conjunction, equivalent to 'on the other hand'.

examples.target: 賛成[さんせい]する人[ひと]がいる一方[いっぽう]、反対[はんたい]する人[ひと]もいる。
examples.reading: さんせいするひとがいるいっぽう、はんたいするひとがいる。
examples.translation_tr: While there are people who agree, there are also people who disagree.

examples.target: 父[ちち]は無口[むくち]な一方[いっぽう]、母[はは]はとてもよくしゃべる。
examples.reading: ちちはむくちないっぽう、はははとてもよくしゃべる。
examples.translation_tr: My father is quiet, whereas my mother talks a lot.

to-tomo-ni.title_tr: 〜とともに (Together With / As... / Both X and Y)
to-tomo-ni.intro_tr: 〜とともに is an N2 written/formal pattern meaning "together with," "as...," or "along with." It attaches to nouns (N + とともに) to show physical or figurative accompaniment ("together with X"), and to dictionary-form verbs or nouns describing change (V/N + とともに) to show that two things happen or change simultaneously ("as A happens, B also happens"). A special pattern, であるとともに, connects two nouns/na-adjectives to say the subject has both qualities at once ("being both X and Y"). It is more formal than と一緒に and appears frequently in news reports, essays, and written Japanese rather than casual conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns
rows: together with N (physical or figurative accompaniment)
家族[かぞく]とともに (together with family)
as V happens, B happens simultaneously / correlated change
成長[せいちょう]するとともに (as [it] grows)
as N progresses/occurs, correlated change happens
時代[じだい]とともに (with the times)
the subject is both X and Y at the same time (dual role/quality)
医者[いしゃ]であるとともに (being a doctor as well as ...)
い-Adj → く + なるとともに
as [state] becomes more so, correlated change happens
暑[あつ]くなるとともに (as it gets hotter)

tables.caption_tr: Three Core Meanings of とともに
rows: 'together with' someone/something, physically or in spirit
友人[ゆうじん]とともに旅行[りょこう]した (traveled together with a friend)
'as A happens/changes, B happens/changes too'; a natural, parallel development
V(dict)/N + とともに + [change verb, often も]
年[とし]をとるとともに白髪[しらが]が増[ふ]える (as one ages, gray hair increases)
the subject 'is both X and Y'; combines two roles, states, or identities
N/Na + であるとともに + [second noun/adj]でもある
教師[きょうし]であるとともに研究者[けんきゅうしゃ]でもある (both a teacher and a researcher)

tables.caption_tr: とともに vs Similar Grammar Points
rows: formal 'together with' OR 'as A, so B' OR 'both X and Y'
'as A progresses, B gradually changes'; no sense of accompaniment
'in accordance with A's progress, B changes'; often rule-like progression
'accompanying event A, B occurs'; often a side-effect or consequence

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with とともに
rows: 成長[せいちょう]とともに
年齢[ねんれい]とともに
これをもって、みなさまとともに
これをもって、みなさまとともに
hereby, together with everyone (formal speech opener)

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes
rows: 彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しいとともに、疲[つか]れている。
とともに cannot directly follow an い-adjective's plain form in this way to mean 'and also'; it is not a simple 'and' connector for two states of the same subject like this.
彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しくて、疲[つか]れている。(use て-form for simple 'and')
友達[ともだち]とともに遊[あそ]ぼう！(casual chat)
とともに is formal/written; sounds stiff and unnatural in casual spoken conversation.
友達[ともだち]と一緒[いっしょ]に遊[あそ]ぼう！
食[た]べますとともに、話[はな]した。
とともに attaches to the dictionary (plain) form of verbs, not the ます-form.
食[た]べるとともに、話[はな]した。
医者[いしゃ]とともに作家[さっか]だ。
To express 'is both X and Y' (dual role of the same subject), である is required before とともに.
医者[いしゃ]であるとともに作家[さっか]でもある。

examples.target: 家族[かぞく]とともに東京[とうきょう]へ引[ひ]っ越[こ]しました。
examples.reading: かぞくとともにとうきょうへひっこしました。
examples.translation_tr: I moved to Tokyo together with my family.

examples.target: 年[とし]を取[と]るとともに、体力[たいりょく]が衰[おとろ]える。
examples.reading: としをとるとともに、たいりょくがおとろえる。
examples.translation_tr: As one grows older, physical strength declines.
examples.note_tr: Correlation meaning: dictionary-form verb + とともに = 'as A happens, B happens too'.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は医者[いしゃ]であるとともに、作家[さっか]でもある。
examples.reading: かれはいしゃであるとともに、さっかでもある。
examples.translation_tr: He is a doctor as well as a writer (he holds both roles).
examples.note_tr: N/Na-adj + であるとともに expresses that the subject has two qualities/roles simultaneously.

examples.target: 経済[けいざい]の成長[せいちょう]とともに、生活[せいかつ]水準[すいじゅん]も向上[こうじょう]した。
examples.reading: けいざいのせいちょうとともに、せいかつすいじゅんもこうじょうした。
examples.translation_tr: Along with economic growth, the standard of living also improved.

examples.target: 時代[じだい]の変化[へんか]とともに、人々[ひとびと]の価値観[かちかん]も変[か]わってきた。
examples.reading: じだいのへんかとともに、ひとびとのかちかんもかわってきた。
examples.translation_tr: As the times have changed, people's values have also changed.

examples.target: 台風[たいふう]の接近[せっきん]とともに、風[かぜ]が強[つよ]くなってきた。
examples.reading: たいふうのせっきんとともに、かぜがつよくなってきた。
examples.translation_tr: As the typhoon approached, the wind grew stronger.

examples.target: 卒業[そつぎょう]とともに、新[あたら]しい生活[せいかつ]が始[はじ]まる。
examples.reading: そつぎょうとともに、あたらしいせいかつがはじまる。
examples.translation_tr: With graduation, a new life begins.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は驚[おどろ]きとともに、喜[よろこ]びの声[こえ]を上[あ]げた。
examples.reading: かのじょはおどろきとともに、よろこびのこえをあげた。
examples.translation_tr: Along with surprise, she let out a cry of joy.
examples.note_tr: Here とともに links two simultaneous feelings/actions, similar to 'along with'.

to-ieba.title_tr: 〜といえば / 〜というと (Speaking of..., when it comes to...)
to-ieba.intro_tr: 〜といえば and 〜というと both mean "speaking of...", "when it comes to...", or "now that you mention...", introducing a topic that has just come up in conversation and linking it to a related idea, memory, example, or question. This is a topic-association usage of と, not the conditional "if/when" と, so it cannot be swapped with たら or ば. といえば tends to introduce whatever spontaneously comes to the speaker's mind, while というと is often used to restate or double-check what the listener just said, frequently ending in a question. The idiomatic opener そういえば ("come to think of it") is built from this exact same pattern used standalone. It's an extremely common, natural way to shift or expand a topic in everyday spoken Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: attaching といえば / というと
rows: N + といえば / というと
V(plain) + といえば / というと
Adj(plain) + といえば / というと
Na + だ + といえば / というと
元気[げんき]だといえば〜
そういえば〜 (come to think of it)

tables.caption_tr: Comparing といえば, というと, and related expressions
rows: Introduces whatever comes to mind when the topic is mentioned
Free association, giving a typical example
Restates the topic to check/confirm understanding, or draws an implication from it
Clarifying questions, logical deduction from what was said
Neutral, slightly more formal in questions
Adds strong emotional emphasis to the association (often surprise or admiration)
Introduces a topic with a critical or enthusiastic personal comment
Complaining about or praising a familiar person/topic

tables.caption_tr: Three core functions of といえば / というと
rows: Speaking of X, it reminds me of / makes me think of Y
X といえば/というと、Y (whatever comes to mind)
When you say/mention X, do you mean...? (restating to check)
X というと、〜ですか / 〜という意味[いみ]ですか
Come to think of it... (recalling something related just now)

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed associations with といえば
rows: 日本[にほん]といえば富士山[ふじさん]ですね。
夏[なつ]といえば花火[はなび]です。
冬[ふゆ]といえばこたつですね。
京都[きょうと]といえば紅葉[こうよう]です。
エッフェル塔[とう] (Eiffel Tower)
フランスといえばエッフェル塔[とう]です。

tables.caption_tr: Points to note / common mistakes
rows: This といえば/というと is a topic-association marker, unrelated to the conditional と ('if/when'); it cannot be replaced with たら or ば.
When というと is followed by a question, it usually signals the speaker is confirming or clarifying what was just said.
そういえば is a set idiomatic opener meaning 'come to think of it'; native speakers don't analyze it word-by-word.
といえば/というと naturally follows something already mentioned or clearly understood in context; introducing a totally unrelated topic with it sounds unnatural.

examples.target: 日本[にほん]といえば、富士山[ふじさん]を思[おも]い出[だ]します。
examples.reading: にほんといえば、ふじさんをおもいだします。
examples.translation_tr: Speaking of Japan, it makes me think of Mt. Fuji.
examples.note_tr: Function 1 (association): the topic 日本 triggers a typical mental image.

examples.target: すしというと、やっぱり新鮮[しんせん]なネタが一番[いちばん]ですね。
examples.reading: すしというと、やっぱりしんせんなネタがいちばんですね。
examples.translation_tr: Speaking of sushi, fresh ingredients really are the best, aren't they.

examples.target: A: 来週[らいしゅう]、京都[きょうと]に行[い]くんです。 B: 京都[きょうと]といえば、今[いま]は紅葉[こうよう]がきれいな季節[きせつ]ですね。
examples.reading: らいしゅう、きょうとにいくんです。きょうとといえば、いまはこうようがきれいなきせつですね。
examples.translation_tr: A: I'm going to Kyoto next week. B: Speaking of Kyoto, it's the season when the autumn leaves are beautiful, isn't it.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんというと、あの背[せ]の高[たか]い人[ひと]ですか。
examples.reading: たなかさんというと、あのせのたかいひとですか。
examples.translation_tr: When you say Tanaka, do you mean that tall person?
examples.note_tr: Function 2 (confirmation): the speaker checks the referent of the topic just mentioned.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]といえば、最近[さいきん]結婚[けっこん]したらしいですよ。
examples.reading: かれといえば、さいきんけっこんしたらしいですよ。
examples.translation_tr: Speaking of him, I heard he got married recently.

examples.target: そういえば、明日[あした]は休[やす]みでしたね。
examples.reading: そういえば、あしたはやすみでしたね。
examples.translation_tr: Come to think of it, tomorrow is a holiday, isn't it.
examples.note_tr: そういえば is the fixed idiomatic form built from the same pattern; it means 'come to think of it / now that you mention it'.

examples.target: 夏[なつ]といえば、花火[はなび]ですね。
examples.reading: なつといえば、はなびですね。
examples.translation_tr: Speaking of summer, fireworks come to mind, don't they.

examples.target: 「先生[せんせい]、来週[らいしゅう]のテストは何[なん]ページからですか。」「テストというと、まだ範囲[はんい]を発表[はっぴょう]していませんでしたね。」
examples.reading: 「せんせい、らいしゅうのテストはなんページからですか。」「テストというと、まだはんいをはっぴょうしていませんでしたね。」
examples.translation_tr: "Teacher, what page does next week's test start from?" "Speaking of the test, I haven't announced the range yet, have I."

to-iu-yori.intro_tr: 〜というより is used when the speaker feels that a word or description just mentioned isn't quite accurate, and offers a better-fitting one instead; similar to English "rather than X, it's more like Y" or "it's not so much X as Y." It attaches to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns, and is very often paired with むしろ (rather, on the contrary) for extra emphasis. Unlike より alone, which compares degree or quantity between two things, というより compares which label, word, or description more accurately fits a single situation. It's extremely common in everyday spoken Japanese for gently correcting yourself or softening a disagreement.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Rules: What Comes Before というより
rows: 行[い]くというより / 行[い]ったというより
rather than going / rather than having gone
学生[がくせい]というより
好[す]きじゃないというより
it's not so much that I don't like it
footnotes_tr: だ is always dropped before というより for nouns and な-adjectives; 学生だというより is incorrect; 学生というより is correct.
The clause after というより states the more accurate description and can end in plain form, です/ます, or だ.

tables.caption_tr: Common Patterns and Variations
rows: Neutral: B describes the situation better than A
犬[いぬ]というより狼[おおかみ]みたいだ。(More like a wolf than a dog.)

to-shite-mo.title_tr: 〜としても (Even if / Even Granting That ~)
to-shite-mo.intro_tr: 〜としても is an N2-level compound conjunction meaning "even if ~" or "even granting/assuming that ~". It sets up a hypothetical premise; real or imagined, possible or counterfactual; and then states that the conclusion or situation described afterward does not change because of it. It attaches to the PLAIN form of verbs and adjectives (and to nouns/な-adjectives followed by だ), so it can combine with present, past, and negative forms alike. Compared to plain 〜ても, 〜としても sounds a little more formal/written and more clearly frames the clause before it as a hypothesis being "granted" for the sake of argument, which is why it pairs naturally with たとえ ("even if"), 仮に ("hypothetically"), and 万が一 ("in the unlikely event"). Be careful not to confuse it with the unrelated 〜としては ("from the standpoint of ~", "as ~"), which expresses a viewpoint rather than a concession.

ni-shiro-ni-shiro.title_tr: 〜にしても / 〜にしろ〜にしろ (Even if...; Whether...or...)
ni-shiro-ni-shiro.intro_tr: 〜にしても expresses concession: you acknowledge a fact, assumption, or hypothetical situation as true or fair, but then state that it doesn't change your conclusion; roughly "even if/granting that ~, still...". 〜にしろ〜にしろ (and its more literary twin 〜にせよ〜にせよ) pairs up two contrasting options; an action vs. its opposite, or option A vs. option B; to say the same conclusion holds "whichever" one is actually the case. Both patterns come historically from にする ("to treat/suppose as ~"), which is why the imperative-derived しろ/せよ appear in the paired form. にしても is neutral and usable in speech and writing; にしろ leans formal/written, and にせよ is the most formal/literary of the three. These patterns are extremely common in argumentative writing, complaints, and reasoned concessions.

wa-betsu-toshite.title_tr: 〜は別として (Setting X Aside / Apart From X)
wa-betsu-toshite.intro_tr: 〜は別として means "setting X aside," "apart from X," or "regardless of X"; it takes a topic, a fact, or a condition and explicitly removes it from the current discussion so the speaker can focus on the remaining point. It attaches to nouns directly, or to a plain-form clause followed by かどうか or a か...か structure when the excluded element is uncertain or a yes/no matter. It is a fairly neutral, slightly formal expression that works in both spoken and written Japanese, and it is very close in meaning to 〜はさておき, though 〜は別として sounds a touch more objective and is common in explanatory or argumentative writing. Do not confuse it with the unrelated-looking 〜とは別に, which means "separately/in addition to," not "setting aside."

nashi-dewa.intro_tr: 〜なしで(は) and 〜ぬきで both express "without ~," but they differ in nuance and typical usage. なし comes from ない ("nonexistent") and expresses the plain absence or lack of something, often a necessary condition; なしでは commonly pairs with a negative predicate (できない, ならない, 生[い]きられない) to stress that without X, Y is impossible or unlikely. ぬき comes from the verb 抜[ぬ]く ("to pull out, omit") and expresses deliberately leaving something out that would normally be present; it is more conversational and is often used for social rituals, formalities, or topics being skipped (敬語[けいご]抜[ぬ]きで "without the polite language," 冗談[じょうだん]抜[ぬ]きで "joking aside"). Both attach directly to nouns and have several extended forms (〜なしに, 〜なくして, 〜抜[ぬ]きには, 〜抜[ぬ]きの) that shift the register from spoken to literary/formal. This page lays out all forms, their nuances, and common fixed expressions side by side.

tables.caption_tr: Common Pitfalls & Usage Notes
rows: なし never conjugates like an い-adjective directly before で
Treat なし as fixed; it does not become なかった or なくて in this pattern; use なかった/なくて only for the separate い-adjective ない.
抜き retains a link to the verb 抜[ぬ]く
This is why extended forms like 抜[ぬ]きにする, 抜[ぬ]きにして, 抜[ぬ]きにしても exist, unlike なし which has no verbal origin in this usage.
なしでは leans formal/written, 抜きでは leans conversational
Using 抜きでは in a formal essay, or なしでは in very casual chat, can sound mismatched in register.
Do not confuse with 〜なしに(は) / 〜なくして(は)
Those are more literary/formal variants covered on a separate grammar page; なしで(は) and 抜きで are the more everyday equivalents.
N抜きの + N requires a modifying noun after it
抜[ぬ]きの cannot end a sentence on its own the way 抜きで can; it must modify a following noun (e.g. 骨[ほね]抜[ぬ]きの魚[さかな] = deboned fish).

mono-to-shite.title_tr: 〜ものとして (treating/regarding as..., on the assumption that...)
mono-to-shite.intro_tr: 〜ものとして is a formal, written-register pattern meaning "treating X as..., regarding it as a given that..., on the assumption that...". The speaker deliberately sets up a fact, condition, or premise; whether confirmed or hypothetical; as the basis for an action, plan, or argument that follows. It attaches to the plain form of verbs/i-adjectives, or to であるものとして after nouns and na-adjectives. It is closely related to but distinct from 〜ものとする (used to state rules/definitions in contracts and regulations) and 〜ものと思われる/考えられる (used for formal inference). This pattern is common in reports, business writing, academic texts, and official announcements rather than casual conversation.

Noun + であるものとして

footnotes_tr: The plain-form connection works the same as for many other 〜もの constructions; the copula である is required after nouns and na-adjectives, not simple な or だ.

Sets up a hypothetical premise as the basis for a subsequent plan, calculation, or decision
彼[かれ]が来[く]るものとして準備[じゅんび]する (preparing on the assumption that he will come)
Frequent in business reports, contracts, academic papers, and official notices; rarely used in casual speech

footnotes_tr: 〜ものとする is often confused with 〜ものとして; the key difference is that とする fixes a rule/definition, while として treats something as a premise for an action.

causative-keigo.intro_tr: 〜させていただく is one of the most common humble (kenjōgo-style) expressions in Japanese, especially in business, customer service, and formal writing. It is built from the causative form of a verb (〜せる/〜させる) plus the humble verb いただく ("to receive," a humble form of もらう), literally meaning "to humbly receive the favor of being allowed to do something." Grammatically it still carries the nuance of asking or acknowledging permission, but in modern usage it is often just a very polite way of announcing that the speaker will do something, especially when that action concerns, affects, or requires the tacit approval of the listener. Because of its extreme politeness it appears constantly in emails, announcements, and workplace speech, but attaching it to every single verb regardless of context can sound unnatural or overused; a habit sometimes mocked as "part-timer keigo" (バイト敬語).

Natural mainly when the action affects, benefits, or needs the tacit approval of the listener; using it for unrelated facts sounds odd

te-aru.title_tr: 〜てある (Resulting State from a Deliberate Transitive Action)
te-aru.intro_tr: 〜てある is formed by attaching ある to the te-form of a TRANSITIVE verb. It describes a resulting state that exists because a person deliberately caused it; the emphasis is on the fact that someone did the action on purpose, often in preparation for something, and the effect is still visible or in effect now. Because ある (not いる) is used, the object of the original transitive verb typically switches from を to が. This is different from 〜ている, which can attach to either transitive or intransitive verbs and does not necessarily imply a deliberate human cause, and from 〜ておく, which focuses on the act of preparing in advance rather than on the resulting state itself. Since ある is a suppletive verb (its negative is ない, not あらない), 〜てある conjugates irregularly for negation.

uru-enai.intro_tr: 〜得る (attached as える or うる) attaches to the masu-stem of a verb to state that something is theoretically, logically, or generally possible; "can happen," "could conceivably occur." Its negative counterpart, 〜得ない (always read えない), means "cannot happen" or "is impossible." This is different from できる or the regular potential form (可能形, e.g. 読める), which describe a person's actual ability or skill to perform an action; 〜得る instead judges whether a situation or outcome is conceivable given logic, circumstances, or general knowledge. It appears mainly in written Japanese, news reports, essays, and formal speech, and pairs naturally with verbs of occurrence, cognition, and communication rather than everyday physical actions. The single most common word built on this pattern is あり得る／あり得ない ("that's possible" / "that's impossible, unbelievable"), which has also become a common casual exclamation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: masu-stem + 得る (possible) / 得ない (impossible)
rows: 起こり得る[おこりうる]
起こり得ない[おこりえない]
あり得ない[ありえない]
考える[かんがえる] (to think)
考え得る[かんがえうる]
考え得ない[かんがええない]
理解する[りかいする] (to understand)
理解し得る[りかいしうる]
理解し得ない[りかいしえない]
予測する[よそくする] (to predict)
予測し得る[よそくしうる]
予測し得ない[よそくしえない]
許し得ない[ゆるしえない]
犯す[おかす] (to commit, e.g. an error)
犯し得ない[おかしえない]
footnotes_tr: 得る attaches directly to the masu-stem with no て-form and no ます; it behaves as a separate ichidan-like ending: える/えない or うる/えない.

tables.caption_tr: Reading rules: える vs うる vs えない
rows: Natural in modern spoken and written Japanese; used freely in most sentences, especially when the verb ends the clause (predicative use).
More literary/formal tone; very common in set phrases (あり得る, 起こり得る) and almost always used when 得る comes directly before a noun (attributive use, e.g. 起こり得る事故[おこりうるじこ]).
The ONLY reading; うない does not exist. Never read the negative form as えない → うない.
footnotes_tr: Both える and うる are considered correct for the affirmative form; choice is largely stylistic, with うる leaning more formal/written.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions built on 〜得る / 〜得ない
rows: ありうる / ありえる
The most frequent word in this whole pattern; often modifies a noun directly: あり得る話[ありうるはなし] "a plausible story".
Also used casually as an exclamation of disbelief or outrage, similar to English "no way!" or "unbelievable!"
Common in news/science writing about risks, accidents, disasters.
Often used as 考え得る限り[かんがえうるかぎり] "as far as one can imagine".
Literary; from 為す[なす] "to accomplish".
Often in しか言い得ない[しかいいえない] "can only be described as...".

tables.caption_tr: 〜得る vs できる vs 可能形 (potential form): what each one expresses
rows: Whether an event or outcome is logically/theoretically possible, independent of any one person's skill
そのミスは誰にでも起こり得る[おこりうる]。 (That mistake could happen to anyone.)
General capability or possibility of doing something; neutral and very broad
彼は泳ぐことができる[およぐことができる]。 (He can swim.)
可能形[かのうけい] (e.g. 読める, 話せる)
A specific person's learned or physical ability to perform an action
漢字が読める[かんじがよめる]。 (I can read kanji.)
footnotes_tr: 〜得る cannot usually replace できる/可能形 for simple personal-ability statements like "I can swim" or "I can read kanji"; using 泳ぎ得る sounds unnatural.

tables.caption_tr: Verb types that combine naturally (and unnaturally) with 〜得る
rows: 起こる[おこる], ある, 生じる[しょうじる]
Excellent fit; the most natural and common use of the pattern.
考える[かんがえる], 理解する[りかいする], 想像する[そうぞうする]
Very common in essays, discussions, academic writing.
言う[いう], 断言する[だんげんする], 許す[ゆるす]
Common when hedging or qualifying a statement.
食べる[たべる], 走る[はしる], 泳ぐ[およぐ]
Rare and often sounds unnatural; use できる or 可能形 (食べられる, 走れる, 泳げる) instead.

examples.reading: かれがそんなことをいうなんてありえない！
examples.translation_tr: There's no way he'd say something like that!
examples.note_tr: あり得ない is the single most common word built from this pattern; it is often used casually to mean "unbelievable" or "no way."

examples.target: この問題[もんだい]は複雑[ふくざつ]すぎて、簡単[かんたん]には理解し[りかいし]得ない[えない]。
examples.reading: このもんだいはふくざつすぎて、かんたんにはりかいしえない。

examples.reading: しょうらい、AIがにんげんのしごとをうばうことはありえるはなしだ。
examples.translation_tr: It's a plausible story that AI will take over human jobs in the future.
examples.note_tr: 得る placed directly before a noun (attributive use) is often read うる rather than える.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]の罪[つみ]は到底[とうてい]許し[ゆるし]得ない[えない]ものだ。
examples.reading: かれのつみはとうていゆるしえないものだ。
examples.translation_tr: His crime is something that absolutely cannot be forgiven.

examples.translation_tr: This medicine can cause side effects, so caution is necessary.

gatai-zurai.title_tr: 〜がたい / 〜づらい (Hard to Do / Difficult to Do)
gatai-zurai.intro_tr: 〜がたい and 〜づらい both attach to the masu-stem of a verb to express that an action is "difficult to do," but they differ sharply in nuance and range. 〜がたい (from the kanji 難い) is a rather formal, literary expression used with a small, fixed set of verbs; mostly ones describing mental or emotional states like believing, forgiving, or forgetting; and it conveys that something is almost impossible to do for psychological or moral reasons. 〜づらい (from 辛い, "painful/hard") is a common, everyday expression that attaches freely to almost any verb and conveys a personal, physical, or situational difficulty or discomfort (awkwardness, inconvenience, physical strain). Both behave as い-adjectives once attached and are often compared with the more neutral, general-purpose 〜にくい, which can describe either objective or subjective difficulty and is the most broadly usable of the three.

tables.caption_tr: Formation and conjugation (both attach as い-adjectives to the masu-stem)
footnotes_tr: がたい is lexically restricted; it does not naturally attach to every verb; only certain (often mental/emotional) verbs form common がたい words.
Once attached, both conjugate exactly like an い-adjective: 〜がたい → 〜がたくない / 〜がたかった / 〜がたくて; 〜づらい → 〜づらくない / 〜づらかった / 〜づらくて.

tables.caption_tr: い-adjective conjugation pattern once attached (example: 言いづらい)
rows: 言[い]いづらくなかった
footnotes_tr: がたい follows the identical pattern (信じがたい → 信じがたくない → 信じがたかった...), though the negative and past forms of がたい are rare in natural speech since がたい already implies near-impossibility.

tables.caption_tr: Nuance comparison: 〜がたい vs 〜づらい vs 〜にくい
rows: narrow; a fixed set of mostly mental/emotional verbs
信[しん]じがたい (hard to believe)
personal / physical / situational discomfort or awkwardness
言[い]いづらい (awkward to say)
objective or general difficulty (design, nature of the thing)
使[つか]いにくい (inconvenient to use)
footnotes_tr: づらい tends to point to a difficulty felt by the speaker personally (physical strain, emotional awkwardness); にくい more often describes an inherent property of the object/situation itself, though the two overlap heavily in casual speech and are often interchangeable.
がたい almost never appears with physical-object difficulty (you would not normally say 読みがたい for 'hard-to-read handwriting'; that is 読みづらい/読みにくい).

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜がたい (limited, often idiomatic set)
rows: hard to put into words, indescribable
footnotes_tr: These combinations are essentially fixed vocabulary items and are best memorized as set phrases rather than freely generated.

tables.caption_tr: Common everyday verbs + 〜づらい
rows: hard to hear, or awkward to ask
hard to write (with, e.g. a bad pen)
footnotes_tr: Most of these can also take にくい (読みにくい, 使いにくい, etc.) with a slightly more neutral/objective nuance instead of personal discomfort.

examples.target: この話は少し信じ[しん]じがたいです。
examples.reading: kono hanashi wa sukoshi shinjigatai desu
examples.translation_tr: This story is a little hard to believe.

examples.reading: kare no koudou wa yurushigatai

examples.reading: ano hi no omoide wa wasuregatai
examples.translation_tr: The memory of that day is hard to forget (unforgettable).

examples.target: 先生[せんせい]にはちょっと聞[き]きづらいことがあります。
examples.reading: sensei ni wa chotto kikizurai koto ga arimasu
examples.translation_tr: There's something a little awkward to ask the teacher.

examples.target: この靴[くつ]は歩[ある]きづらいです。
examples.reading: kono kutsu wa arukizurai desu
examples.translation_tr: These shoes are hard to walk in.

examples.target: 小[ちい]さい字[じ]で書[か]かれていて、読[よ]みづらいです。
examples.reading: chiisai ji de kakarete ite, yomizurai desu
examples.translation_tr: It's written in small letters, so it's hard to read.

examples.target: 新[あたら]しいシステムはまだ使[つか]いづらい。
examples.reading: atarashii shisutemu wa mada tsukaizurai
examples.translation_tr: The new system is still hard to use.

examples.target: 証拠[しょうこ]は動[うご]かしがたい事実[じじつ]だ。
examples.reading: shouko wa ugokashigatai jijitsu da
examples.translation_tr: The evidence is an undeniable (hard-to-move) fact.

kake-kakeru.title_tr: 〜かける / 〜かけだ (halfway through …, about to …)
kake-kakeru.intro_tr: 〜かける attaches to the ます-stem of a verb and has two closely related core meanings: (1) an action was started but left unfinished or was interrupted midway (食[た]べかける "to start eating and leave it half-eaten"), and (2) a change of state is about to happen or is very close to occurring (死[し]にかける "to be on the verge of dying"). かける itself conjugates like a regular ichidan verb (かける/かけます/かけた/かけて), and it also has adjectival/nominal derivatives 〜かけの (noun-modifying: "half-done ...") and 〜かけだ (predicate: "is half-done"). This grammar point is very common with verbs describing physical/gradual processes (壊[こわ]れる, 崩[くず]れる, 消[き]える) and with verbs of communication or consumption (言[い]う, 食[た]べる, 読[よ]む, 書[か]く). Because かける implies the action stopped or hasn't reached completion, it is often paired with words like ところで, まま, or a following clause describing what interrupted it.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb ます-stem + かける
rows: to be on the verge of dying
to start to say (and trail off)
footnotes_tr: かける follows the same connection rule as other auxiliary verbs: it attaches directly to the ます-stem, with no て-form or particle involved.

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation of 〜かける and its derived forms
rows: 食[た]べかけて、席[せき]を立[た]った
このパンは食[た]べかけだ
is on the verge of dying
footnotes_tr: かける itself is a regular ichidan (る-verb), so all standard ichidan endings apply directly to it.

tables.caption_tr: The two core meanings of 〜かける
rows: volitional action verbs: 食べる, 読む, 書く, 言う
a book I'm partway through reading
About to happen / near-completion of a change
change-of-state / gradual process verbs: 死ぬ, 壊れる, 崩れる, 消える, 忘れる
消[き]えかけたろうそくの火[ひ]
a candle flame that is about to go out
footnotes_tr: Context and verb type usually disambiguate the two meanings; there is rarely genuine ambiguity in practice.

tables.caption_tr: 〜かける vs. similar 'start / about to' expressions
rows: started but interrupted, OR about to happen/near-complete
implies the action stopped short of completion or is about to reach a state
neutral 'to begin doing', no implication of stopping
just marks the starting point; the action is expected to continue
looked like it was about to happen (near miss)
describes appearance/perception of a near-event; the action need not have actually begun
adjectival/predicate: describes the resulting half-done state
食[た]べかけの弁当[べんとう]
grammatically a noun-modifier or predicate rather than a verb suffix

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜かける
rows: to be near death, almost die
to start to say something (then trail off/stop)
footnotes_tr: やりかけ, 読みかけ, and 書きかけ are frequently used on their own as nouns, e.g. やりかけのまま (left half-done).

examples.target: 本[ほん]を読[よ]みかけたところで電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]った。
examples.reading: ほんをよみかけたところででんわがなった。
examples.translation_tr: Just as I had started reading the book, the phone rang.
examples.note_tr: かける marks that the action of reading was begun and then interrupted.

examples.target: これは食[た]べかけのケーキです。
examples.reading: これはたべかけのケーキです。
examples.translation_tr: This is a half-eaten cake.
examples.note_tr: かけの + noun: an adjectival phrase describing an incomplete object.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]か言[い]いかけてやめた。
examples.reading: かれはなにかいいかけてやめた。
examples.translation_tr: He started to say something but stopped himself.
examples.note_tr: て-form of かける linking to another clause; classic 'trailed off' usage.

examples.target: その老人[ろうじん]は死[し]にかけている。
examples.reading: そのろうじんはしにかけている。
examples.translation_tr: That old man is on the verge of dying.
examples.note_tr: With change-of-state verbs like 死ぬ, かける means 'about to happen', not 'started and interrupted'.

examples.target: 日[ひ]が暮[く]れかけたころ、家[いえ]に帰[かえ]った。
examples.reading: ひがくれかけたころ、いえにかえった。
examples.translation_tr: I went home around the time the sun was about to set.

examples.target: やりかけの仕事[しごと]がまだたくさんある。
examples.reading: やりかけのしごとがまだたくさんある。
examples.translation_tr: There is still a lot of unfinished work left.
examples.note_tr: やりかけ used as a noun on its own, meaning 'something left half-done'.

examples.target: 橋[はし]が崩[くず]れかけていて危[あぶ]ない。
examples.reading: はしがくずれかけていてあぶない。
examples.translation_tr: The bridge is on the verge of collapsing, so it's dangerous.

examples.target: このレポートは書[か]きかけだから、あとで続[つづ]きを書[か]きます。
examples.reading: このレポートはかきかけだから、あとでつづきをかきます。
examples.translation_tr: This report is only half-written, so I'll write the rest later.
examples.note_tr: かけだ used as the predicate of the sentence (X は 〜かけだ).

nuku-kiru.title_tr: 〜ぬく / 〜きる (to do something all the way to the end)
nuku-kiru.intro_tr: 〜抜く[ぬく] and 〜きる[きる] are both compound-verb endings attached directly to the ます-stem of a verb (no て form needed), and both express that an action is carried through to its very end or to full completion. 抜く[ぬく] literally means "to pull through" and carries the nuance of pushing past hardship, resistance, or a long struggle; enduring and persevering all the way to the finish. きる[きる] literally means "to cut," and here it signals that an action reaches 100% completeness, exhaustiveness, or an extreme state, often used for physical/mental limits (疲[つか]れ切[き]る "to be utterly exhausted") or for using something up entirely. きる[きる] also forms the extremely common negative-potential pattern 〜きれない, meaning "cannot fully do X" (too much, impossible to finish). Both 抜く[ぬく] and きる[きる] conjugate as ordinary godan verbs once attached (抜く like a く-ending godan verb, きる like a る-ending godan verb), so all normal tense/negative/te-form rules apply to the compound.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb ます-stem + 抜く[ぬく] / きる[きる]
rows: 考える[かんがえる] (to think)
考え抜く[かんがえぬく]
考え切る[かんがえきる] (less common)
footnotes_tr: Not every verb naturally combines with both 抜く and きる; usage is largely fixed by convention; the most common combinations are listed in the tables below.
Attachment is always to the ます-stem directly, with no て form or particle in between.

tables.caption_tr: Nuance comparison: 〜抜く[ぬく] vs 〜きる[きる]
rows: Pushing through resistance, hardship, or a long struggle to the finish
Reaching 100% completeness or an extreme/final state
抜けない (rare, and means something different: 'cannot pull out')
〜きれない (very common: 'cannot fully do / too much to finish')
生きる, やる, 走る, 悩む, 苦しむ, 戦う, 考える
疲れる, 使う, 食べる, 言う, 信じる, 守る, 出す, 読む
Slightly literary/narrative, common in stories about struggle
困難[こんなん]を乗[の]り越[こ]えて生[い]き抜[ぬ]く (survive through hardship)
力[ちから]を出[だ]し切[き]る (give it all, use up all one's strength)

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜抜く[ぬく]
rows: to survive through, live through hardship
to carry something out to the end, see it through
to run all the way through (a race, difficulty)
to agonize thoroughly, think hard to the very end
to suffer through something to the end
to fight through to the very end

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜きる[きる]
rows: to defend/protect something all the way through
to give it all, put out everything (effort, strength)

tables.caption_tr: 〜きれない: expressing 'cannot fully / completely do'
rows: can manage to finish eating it all
cannot finish eating it all / it's too much to eat
couldn't finish eating it (in the end)
cannot say for certain / cannot state definitively
footnotes_tr: 抜く rarely forms this 'cannot fully do' negative-potential pattern; 〜きれない is the standard way to express 'too much/impossible to complete.'

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation of the compound verb (using 走[はし]り抜く and 疲[つか]れ切る as models)
column_headers: 走[はし]り抜く[はしりぬく] (run through)
疲[つか]れ切る[つかれきる] (be exhausted)
footnotes_tr: 抜く conjugates like a く-ending godan verb (い-onbin in the past/て forms: 抜いた, 抜いて).
きる conjugates like a る-ending godan verb (small っ onbin in the past/て forms: 切った, 切って); do not confuse with the ichidan verb 着る[きる] 'to wear.'

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は苦[くる]しいマラソンを走[はし]り抜[ぬ]いた。
examples.reading: かれはくるしいマラソンをはしりぬいた。

examples.reading: きのうはつかれきって、すぐにねてしまった。
examples.translation_tr: Yesterday I was completely exhausted and fell asleep right away.

you-ga-nai.intro_tr: 〜ようがない (also 〜ようもない) attaches to the ます-stem of a verb and literally means "there is no way/method by which one could do V." It expresses that an action is completely impossible to carry out; not because it's merely difficult, but because no means, method, or path to doing it exists at all, usually due to missing information, missing tools, or the sheer nature of the situation. It is stronger and more absolute than plain できない, and unlike 〜わけがない (which negates a fact/state), it specifically negates the existence of a *method*. This is a fixed, moderately literary pattern that shows up constantly in both spoken complaints ("どうしようもない") and written explanations.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: verb type + ます-stem + ようがない
rows: there's no way to explain/talk about it
there's no way to read it
there's no way to eat it
説明[せつめい]する (to explain)
説明[せつめい]しようがない
there's no way to explain it
there's nothing that can be done
there's no way (for someone) to come
footnotes_tr: Note: the -よう here attaches to the plain ます-stem (連用形) for every verb type, including godan verbs; it is NOT the true volitional form (話そう, 読もう). This is a fixed pattern specific to 〜ようがない/〜ようもない.

tables.caption_tr: Common set phrases with 〜ようがない / 〜ようもない
rows: it's absolutely hopeless / a lost cause
何[なん]とも言[い]いようがない
なんとも いいようがない
there's really no way to say
I honestly can't put it into words
手[て]の施[ほどこ]しようがない
てのほどこしようがない
no way to apply a hand (remedy)
beyond help, nothing can be done to fix it
比較[ひかく]しようがない
there's simply no basis for comparison
疑[うたが]いようがない

tables.caption_tr: 〜ようがない vs. similar-looking expressions
rows: no method/way exists to do V
absence of a means or path to act
資料[しりょう]がないから確認[かくにん]しようがない; 'I can't verify it, there's simply no way (no data to work with)'
言葉[ことば]で言[い]い表[あらわ]しようもない; 'there is truly no way to put it into words'
泳[およ]げないから泳[およ]げない; 'I can't swim' (simple fact, no implication of 'no method')
there's no way that X is true/the case
negates a fact or conclusion, not an action's method
彼[かれ]が犯人[はんにん]のわけがない; 'there's no way he's the culprit'
hard/emotionally difficult to do, though not impossible
信[しん]じがたい話[はなし]; 'a hard-to-believe story' (still conceivable)
utterly out of the question, no room to even consider
合格[ごうかく]は望[のぞ]むべくもない; 'passing is not even worth hoping for'

tables.caption_tr: Usage notes and common pitfalls
rows: 〜ようがない attaches to action verbs that could in principle be performed intentionally; it does not attach to stative verbs like ある or できる, or to adjectives directly.

To express 'there's no way it could be [adjective]', Japanese typically rephrases with a noun + のしようがない, or uses 〜としか言[い]いようがない ('I can only say it's...') rather than attaching ようがない straight to an い/な-adjective.
For する-verbs taking an object, you can front the noun with の instead of を: 料理[りょうり]をしようがない → 料理[りょうり]のしようがない ('there's no way to cook').

Unlike 〜がたい or 〜にくい (which mean 'hard to do' but still doable), 〜ようがない claims the action cannot be done AT ALL because no method exists; reserve it for genuinely impossible situations, not mere difficulty.
A common beginner mix-up: ようがない negates the *means* to perform an action (verb-focused), while わけがない negates the *plausibility* of a stated fact or conclusion (proposition-focused).

mai.title_tr: 〜まい (Negative Volitional / Negative Conjecture: "I will not..." / "probably won't...")
mai.intro_tr: 〜まい is a literary auxiliary that attaches directly to the dictionary form of a verb to express two related negative meanings: (1) the speaker's firm intention NOT to do something ("I will not... / I'm determined not to..."), and (2) a negative guess or conjecture about the future or about someone else ("probably won't... / I doubt that..."). It functions as the negative mirror image of the volitional 〜よう and the conjectural 〜だろう combined into a single old-fashioned form. Because it comes from classical Japanese, 〜まい sounds formal, literary, or slightly dramatic in modern speech; it appears often in novels, narration, proverbs, and set phrases rather than in everyday casual conversation, where 〜ないつもりだ and 〜ないだろう are used instead. Formation has some irregularity across verb groups, and する/来る have multiple accepted forms, so pay close attention to the conjugation table below.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of 〜まい by verb group
rows: 食[た]べまい / 食[た]べるまい
stem + まい (classical/formal) or dict. form + まい (also accepted)
見[み]まい / 見[み]るまい
both forms are used; stem+まい is slightly more literary
しまい / するまい / すまい
three variants exist; するまい is most common in modern writing
来[こ]まい / 来[く]るまい
こまい uses the mizenkei-like reading こ; くるまい uses dict. form
footnotes_tr: すまい (from する) is now mostly archaic/literary and rare outside fixed expressions.
For ichidan verbs, both the stem+まい and dictionary-form+まい patterns are considered standard in modern Japanese; choose either.

tables.caption_tr: Two core meanings of 〜まい
rows: 1. Negative volition; 'I will not / I'm determined not to'
もう酒[さけ]は飲[の]むまい。
もう酒[さけ]は飲[の]まないつもりだ。
Strong personal resolve, usually first-person, often about breaking a habit or vow
2. Negative conjecture; 'probably won't / I doubt that'
彼[かれ]は来[こ]ないだろう。
Speaker's guess about a third party, the weather, or a future event; not a promise
footnotes_tr: Context (subject and situation) usually disambiguates which of the two meanings is intended; first person subjects lean toward volition, third person/inanimate subjects lean toward conjecture.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜まい
rows: 'never again do X'; emphatic vow never to repeat an action
'to resolve/intend not to do X' (thinking of not doing)
'to try/resist not doing X'; actively struggling against doing something
'whether to do X or not'; expressing indecision/dilemma (volitional + まい paired)
footnotes_tr: In the 〜うか〜まいか pattern, the same verb is repeated: 行[い]こうか行[い]くまいか (whether to go or not).

tables.caption_tr: 〜まい vs. modern negative equivalents; register comparison
rows: 二度[にど]と忘[わす]れまい。
I don't intend to / I'm not planning to
二度[にど]と忘[わす]れないつもりだ。
彼[かれ]は忘[わす]れないだろう。
彼[かれ]は忘[わす]れないでしょう。
footnotes_tr: Native speakers rarely use 〜まい in casual daily conversation; it signals literary or somewhat dramatic/old-fashioned tone, similar to how 'shall not' sounds more formal than 'won't' in English.

beku.title_tr: 〜べく / 〜べからず (in order to; formal prohibition, literary)
beku.intro_tr: 〜べく and 〜べからず are both literary/formal descendants of the classical auxiliary べし ("must, should"). 〜べく is the adverbial (連用形) form and means "in order to / so as to," introducing the purpose behind the action in the main clause; a stiffer, more written alternative to 〜ために. 〜べからず is the classical negative form and means "must not / shall not," used for blunt, formal prohibitions such as signs, rules, mottos, and proverbs. Both attach directly to the dictionary form of most verbs, though a handful of verbs; notably ones that were historically nidan verbs (like 忘れる) and the irregulars する/来る; revert to an older classical stem. These forms appear mainly in written Japanese, official notices, mottos, news, and essay-style writing, and are rarely used in everyday conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb + べく / べからず
rows: す[す]べく / するべく
す[す]べからず / するべからず
footnotes_tr: The classical form す/来[く] is more literary; するべく/来[く]るべく forms with the modern dictionary form are also accepted today.

tables.caption_tr: 〜べく: expressing purpose "in order to / so as to"
rows: States the purpose behind the action in the main clause; more formal/literary than 〜ために
目標[もくひょう]を達成[たっせい]すべく (in order to achieve the goal)
"Bound to happen as expected"; stresses inevitability rather than plain purpose
起[お]こるべくして起[お]こった (it happened as it was bound to happen)
〜べく努[つと]める / 〜べく努力[どりょく]する

するべく is also accepted in modern usage
footnotes_tr: Most modern godan and ichidan verbs that were not historically nidan verbs attach べく/べからず directly to the plain dictionary form, e.g. 行[い]くべく, 見[み]るべく.

zaru-wo-enai.title_tr: 〜ざるを得ない (Have No Choice But To...)
zaru-wo-enai.intro_tr: 〜ざるを得ない is a formal N2 pattern meaning "have no choice but to...", "cannot help but...", or "am forced to...". It combines ざる, the classical attributive negative form of ず (the archaic ancestor of ない), with 得[え]ない ("cannot obtain/manage"), literally "cannot manage NOT to do X" → "must do X even against one's will." Unlike plain obligation expressions, it stresses that the speaker acts reluctantly because circumstances leave no real alternative; not because of a direct order. It appears frequently in news reports, business Japanese, and formal speech, and attaches to the negative (nai-form) stem of a verb, with する irregularly becoming せざるを得ない.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb (negative stem) + ざるを得ない
rows: 行[い]かざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to go
話[はな]さざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to speak
休[やす]まざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to rest
食[た]べざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to eat
認[みと]めざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to admit
せざるを得[え]ない (NOT しざる)
have no choice but to do
have no choice but to come
footnotes_tr: する uses the classical irregular negative stem せ instead of the modern し; this is the single most common mistake learners make with this pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Tense, Polarity, and Register Forms of ~ざるを得ない
rows: 行[い]かざるを得[え]ない
have no choice but to go
行[い]かざるを得[え]なかった
had no choice but to go
ない → なかった, standard i-adjective past
行[い]かざるを得[え]ません
have no choice but to go (polite)
行[い]かざるを得[え]ませんでした
had no choice but to go (polite)
ません → ませんでした
行[い]かざるを得[え]ない状況[じょうきょう]
a situation where one has no choice but to go
ない functions as an adjective before a noun
行[い]かざるを得[え]ないのだ
it's that I have no choice but to go
adds explanatory/emphatic nuance, common in speech

tables.caption_tr: ~ざるを得ない vs. Similar 'must / no choice' Expressions
rows: Forced by external circumstance; done reluctantly, no direct order implied
認[みと]めざるを得[え]ない (must admit, reluctantly)
行[い]かなければならない (must go)
Cannot avoid doing due to social norms, duty, or logic
行[い]かないわけにはいかない (can't not go)
Only option left; resignation, no external force implied
行[い]くしかない (nothing to do but go)
Cannot suppress an internal emotional urge, not external pressure
笑[わら]わないではいられない (can't help but laugh)
Forced into a state by circumstances; more passive/formal, often used for groups or institutions
撤退[てったい]を余儀[よぎ]なくされる (be forced to withdraw)
footnotes_tr: ~ざるを得ない focuses on the speaker's own reluctant judgment/action; ~を余儀なくされる is more passive and often used about being forced by an outside agent or situation, frequently in news reporting.

tables.caption_tr: Key Formation Notes and Common Pitfalls
rows: する becomes せざるを得[え]ない, using the classical irregular stem せ; しざるを得ない is incorrect.
ざる is the classical attributive form of the negative auxiliary ず (= modern ない); 得[え]ない means 'cannot obtain/manage'. Literally: 'cannot manage to not-do X' → 'have no choice but to do X'.
The pattern attaches to the affirmative negative-stem shape (e.g. 行か-), not to an already negative form like 行かなく-.
Common in formal writing, news, and business speech; in casual conversation, speakers often use しかない or なきゃいけない instead.
Most naturally used with the speaker's own actions/judgments (1st person) or in objective/reported statements about others; less natural as a direct command to the listener.

nai-koto-niwa.title_tr: 〜ないことには (Unless… / Without … it just won't happen)
nai-koto-niwa.intro_tr: 〜ないことには is an N2-level pattern built on the negative form of a verb/adjective plus ことには, meaning "unless X happens/is done, Y (which is stated in the second, usually negative clause) cannot happen." It always pairs with a negative or negative-nuance predicate in the main clause (わからない, できない, 始まらない, 治らない, etc.), because the whole point is that the first action is an indispensable precondition for the second. Compared with plain conditionals like 〜なければ or 〜ないと, 〜ないことには carries a stronger, more emphatic "there is absolutely no way forward without this" feel, and it is very commonly combined with 〜てみる ("try doing") to mean "unless you actually try/experience it, you won't know." Because of the double-negative structure (negative + には), it can feel tricky for beginners, so pay close attention to the formation rules and the fact that the second clause must be negative.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: how to attach 〜ないことには to each word type
rows: 高[たか]くないことには
unless it is expensive... (rare, but possible)
静[しず]かでないことには
学生[がくせい]だ (be a student)
学生[がくせい]でないことには

tables.caption_tr: Core sentence pattern and required elements
rows: Verb/adjective/noun in NEGATIVE form + ことには
States the missing action/state that must happen first
MUST be negative or carry a negative nuance
e.g., わからない, できない, 始[はじ]まらない, 治[なお]らない, 進[すす]まない
"Unless you try/experience X"; very frequent pattern, e.g., 食[た]べてみないことには味[あじ]がわからない
Neutral to slightly formal, common in speech and writing
Not overly stiff; usable in daily conversation and essays alike

tables.caption_tr: 〜ないことには vs. similar conditional patterns
rows: Strong emphasis: "there is absolutely no way forward without X"; second clause MUST be negative
練習[れんしゅう]しないことには上手[じょうず]にならない (Unless you practice, you simply won't get good)
Plain necessary condition, neutral tone, second clause can be positive or negative

"As long as X does not happen"; focuses on an ongoing negative condition/state continuing, not a one-time missing action
許可[きょか]が出[で]ないかぎり、外出[がいしゅつ]できない (As long as permission isn't granted, I can't go out)
Literary/formal: "without X"; no explicit prediction, more essay-like
努力[どりょく]なくして成功[せいこう]なし (Without effort, there is no success)

zuni-wa-irarenai.title_tr: 〜ずにはいられない; Can't Help But... / Can't Resist...
zuni-wa-irarenai.intro_tr: 〜ずにはいられない is an N2 pattern used to say that the speaker (or someone else) cannot control an emotional or instinctive reaction; "can't help but do X", "can't resist doing X". It is built from the negative stem of a verb + ず (a classical negative meaning the same as 〜ないで) + は (emphasis) + いられない (the negative potential of いる, "to be/stay"), literally "cannot stay/remain without doing X". It describes a natural, almost automatic response triggered by something (a movie, news, someone's kindness, etc.), not a logical obligation. It has a slightly literary/written flavor compared to its more colloquial twin 〜ないではいられない, and should not be confused with 〜ざるを得ない (forced necessity) or 〜ずにはすまない (social obligation).

zu-ni.intro_tr: 〜ずに and 〜ないで both mean "without doing ~" and attach to the negative stem of a verb to describe an action that happens (or should happen) in the absence of another action. 〜ずに is the more formal/literary equivalent of 〜ないで, commonly seen in writing, news, and set phrases, while 〜ないで is the everyday spoken form. Both are built from the same negative (nai-form) base, but they are NOT interchangeable in every context; for example, only 〜ないで can be followed by ください to make a polite negative request. There is also a classic beginner trap: 〜ないで (connective "without doing") must not be confused with 〜なくて (causal "because ~ not / and ~ not"). Note the one major irregularity: する becomes せずに, never しずに.

Often used with い-adjectives and な-adjectives too (e.g. 忙[いそが]しくて); ないで cannot replace it here.

kanenai-kaneru.title_tr: 〜かねない / 〜かねる (might do something bad / cannot bring myself to do)
kanenai-kaneru.intro_tr: 〜かねない and 〜かねる both attach to the ます-stem of a verb and both come from the old verb 兼[か]ねる ("to be unable to combine/reconcile"), but in modern Japanese they have split into two very different meanings. 〜かねる means "it is difficult/impossible for me to do X" and is a very polite, indirect way of refusing or expressing inability, heavily used in customer service, business e-mails, and official announcements. 〜かねない means "might well do X" or "there's a real risk that X will happen," and is almost always used to warn about a negative, undesirable, or dangerous outcome; never a good one. Because かねない looks exactly like the plain-negative (ない-form) of かねる, learners frequently confuse the two; this page lays out the trap clearly. Both forms belong to written/formal spoken Japanese (newspapers, reports, business speech) and are rarely used in casual conversation.

gachi.intro_tr: 〜がち attaches to the ます-stem of a verb or directly to certain nouns to express that something happens "often," "tends to," or "is prone to" happening; almost always describing an undesirable, unfortunate, or negative-leaning tendency rather than a neutral or positive habit. It behaves grammatically like a な-adjective, so it can be used predicatively (〜がちだ), to modify a noun (〜がちな N / 〜がちの N), or adverbially (〜がちに + verb). がち differs from simple frequency adverbs like よく because it implies an inherent tendency or weakness ("prone to X, whether one wants to or not") rather than a simple repeated action by choice. This is an N2-level pattern that appears constantly in both spoken and written Japanese, especially in health, weather, and personal-habit contexts.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: what attaches to がち
footnotes_tr: For verbs, always drop ます and attach がち directly to the stem: 忘れます → 忘れ + がち.
Not all nouns can take がち; it is limited to a fairly fixed set of nouns related to states/conditions (病気, 留守, 不足, 遠慮, 曇り, etc.).

a student who is often late

gimi.title_tr: 〜気味 (a little bit of..., showing signs of)
gimi.intro_tr: 〜気味 (ぎみ) is a suffix meaning "a slight tendency toward X" or "showing a bit of signs of X." It attaches directly to a noun or to the masu-stem of a verb to describe a mild, often physical or mental, state; like being a little tired, a little sick, or slightly delayed; without saying the state is fully established. It is a mild hedging expression: the speaker softens the claim, implying "not fully, but somewhat." 〜気味 can function as a predicate (〜気味だ), a noun modifier (〜気味の+N), or an adverb (〜気味に). Note that 気味 also appears in a handful of unrelated fixed idioms (like 気味が悪い "creepy") that have nothing to do with this "slight tendency" suffix pattern; these must be learned separately as vocabulary.

ppoi.intro_tr: 〜っぽい turns a noun, the masu-stem of a verb, or an adjective stem into a な-adjective meaning "-ish", "-like", or "tends to be/do...". It highlights a superficial resemblance or a repeated tendency, and it very often carries a mildly negative or critical nuance (cheap-looking, childish, forgetful, short-tempered) rather than a neutral or admiring one. Because it conjugates exactly like a な-adjective, tenses and negatives are formed the normal な-adjective way. It differs from みたい/らしい (which express appearance or hearsay about a whole situation) and from 気味 (which is limited to a slight tendency/symptom); っぽい focuses on surface qualities or habitual behavior of a person or thing. It is common in casual spoken Japanese and is considered N2-level vocabulary/grammar because of its many fixed combinations that must be learned individually.

darake.intro_tr: 〜だらけ attaches directly to a noun to mean "covered in ~" or "full of ~," and it almost always describes something negative or undesirable; dirt, mistakes, wounds, debt, holes, and the like. Think of it as expressing an excessive, messy, scattered abundance of something unwanted, unlike neutral expressions such as 〜だらけ's cousins まみれ (sticky/liquid substances) and ずくめ (a uniform, often positive "all-~" state). Grammatically だらけ behaves like a na-adjective: it can end a sentence with だ/です, take past and negative forms, and modify a following noun with だらけの. Because the noun it attaches to is always a countable or mass noun representing the "unwanted thing," だらけ cannot attach to verbs or i-adjectives directly. This is a very common, everyday expression despite being tagged N2; it shows up constantly in casual speech and writing.

mamire.intro_tr: 〜まみれ attaches directly to a noun to describe a person, object, or surface that is entirely covered with a substance; typically something liquid, powdery, or dirty such as mud, sweat, blood, dust, or grease. It grammatically behaves like a な-adjective/noun (まみれの for modifying a noun, まみれに for "become," まみれだ/です as a predicate). The image is always negative or unpleasant: something sticky, dirty, or messy clinging all over the surface. By extension, まみれ can also describe an overwhelming abstract burden, most commonly 借金まみれ ("buried in debt"). It contrasts with 〜だらけ, which is broader and can describe countable/abstract things "riddled with" flaws, and with 〜ずくめ, which means "entirely/exclusively made of one thing" without the negative, physical-covering nuance.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns of 〜まみれ
rows: Noun + まみれだ / まみれです
泥[どろ]まみれだ (is covered in mud)
汗[あせ]まみれの服[ふく] (sweat-covered clothes)
血[ち]まみれになる (become covered in blood)
泥[どろ]まみれで帰[かえ]ってきた (came home covered in mud)

tables.caption_tr: Common Noun + まみれ Collocations
rows: 借金[しゃっきん]まみれ

tables.caption_tr: 〜まみれ vs. 〜だらけ vs. 〜ずくめ
rows: Entire surface covered with a sticky/dirty substance; almost always negative and physical
泥[どろ]まみれの子供[こども] (a mud-covered child)
Scattered all over with something countable or abstract (mistakes, spots, holes); negative, broader scope
間違[まちが]い、しみ、ゴミ、穴
間違[まちが]いだらけの作文[さくぶん] (an essay full of mistakes)
Entirely made up of one single category, no exceptions; can be neutral or even positive
黒[くろ]、いいこと、規則[きそく]
黒[くろ]ずくめの服装[ふくそう] (an all-black outfit)

tables.caption_tr: Grammatical Notes & Restrictions
rows: まみれ behaves like a な-adjective/noun: attaches directly to a noun with no particle, and takes の before a modified noun, に for 'become,' だ/です as a plain predicate
Only nouns attach to まみれ (Noun + まみれ); it cannot attach directly to verbs or い-adjectives
The noun must denote a substance capable of physically covering a surface (liquid, powder, dust, blood, dirt), or by extension an overwhelming burden like debt
Always carries a negative, messy, or unpleasant connotation; never used for something desirable
〜まみれになる (to become covered), 〜まみれで + Verb (to do something while in a covered state)

keigo-full-system.title_tr: The Full Keigo System: 3 Axes (尊敬語[そんけいご] / 謙譲語[けんじょうご] / 丁寧語[ていねいご])
keigo-full-system.intro_tr: Keigo (敬語[けいご]) is the Japanese system of respectful language, built on three separate axes that work together: 尊敬語[そんけいご] (sonkeigo) raises the person you are talking about (never yourself), 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (kenjougo) lowers your own action to indirectly elevate the listener, and 丁寧語[ていねいご] (teineigo) is the neutral polite tone of です/ます that doesn't elevate or lower anyone. The single hardest part for learners is that these axes are chosen based on WHOSE action is being described, not on how polite you personally want to sound. Many verbs have entirely separate irregular forms for each axis (e.g. 行く becomes いらっしゃる in sonkeigo but 参る in kenjougo), while other verbs are built with productive patterns like お〜になる (sonkeigo) and お〜する (kenjougo). This page is a reference map of the whole system; for deep dives into each axis's special verbs, see the related topics below.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Axes of Keigo; Overview
rows: Shows respect for the other person's action or existence
The listener or a third party; never yourself
お〜になる, 〜れる/〜られる, special verbs (いらっしゃる, おっしゃる...)
Humbles your own (or your in-group's) action to indirectly raise the listener
Yourself / your in-group is lowered, so the listener appears higher
お〜する, お〜いたす, special verbs (伺う[うかがう], 申す[もうす]...)
General politeness marker; does not elevate or lower anyone
No one specifically; just sets a polite tone
です, ます, お/ご + noun
footnotes_tr: A related fourth category, 丁重語[ていちょうご] (teichougo, formal humble style like おる/いたす used regardless of listener), is covered separately.
二重敬語[にじゅうけいご] (double honorifics, e.g. おっしゃられる) is a common overcorrection error; see the mistakes table below.

tables.caption_tr: Sonkeigo (尊敬語[そんけいご]) Formation Patterns
rows: Attach お to the ます-stem of a verb, then add になる
Same conjugation shape as the passive form, attached to the verb's negative-stem base
読[よ]まれる, 来[こ]られる
"to read / to come" (mild respect, weaker than お〜になる)
The entire verb is replaced with a dedicated honorific verb
行[い]く → いらっしゃる
footnotes_tr: お〜になる cannot be used with already-irregular verbs (e.g. never おいらっしゃになる).

tables.caption_tr: Kenjougo (謙譲語[けんじょうご]) Formation Patterns
rows: Attach お to the ます-stem, then add する
More formal/humble variant of the する pattern, common in business
Frame the other person's action as a favor received by you (humble)
"to have (someone) kindly write it for me"
The entire verb is replaced with a dedicated humble verb
行[い]く → 参[まい]る / 伺[うかが]う
footnotes_tr: お〜する/いたす is generally not used with る-verb stems of one syllable (e.g. 見る, 寝る); special verbs are used instead.

tables.caption_tr: Special Irregular Verbs Across Sonkeigo and Kenjougo
rows: いらっしゃる / おいでになる
参[まい]る / 伺[うかが]う
申[もう]す / 申[もう]し上[あ]げる
存[ぞん]じておる / 存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げる
伺[うかが]う / 拝聴[はいちょう]する
footnotes_tr: These irregular verbs must be memorized individually; they do not follow the productive お〜になる/お〜する patterns.
Some verbs only have one honorific direction because the other direction rarely occurs in natural speech (e.g. you don't usually need a humble form of くれる).

tables.caption_tr: Teineigo (丁寧語[ていねいご]) Basic Forms
rows: e.g. お茶[おちゃ], ご飯[ごはん]; adds general refinement, not tied to elevating any specific person
footnotes_tr: Teineigo can be layered together with sonkeigo or kenjougo in the same sentence; e.g. いらっしゃいます combines the sonkeigo verb いらっしゃる with the teineigo ending ます.

tables.caption_tr: Choosing the Right Axis: Who Performs the Action?
rows: The listener or a respected third party (customer, boss, teacher)
先生[せんせい]がいらっしゃいます。
Yourself or your in-group, when the action involves or benefits a superior
私[わたし]が参[まい]ります。
Anyone at all, in neutral polite conversation with no elevation involved
明日[あした]、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ります。
footnotes_tr: A single sentence often needs both sonkeigo/kenjougo AND teineigo at the same time, since teineigo just controls the overall politeness of the sentence ending.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
rows: 二重敬語[にじゅうけいご] (double honorific): おっしゃる is already sonkeigo, adding られる over-elevates and sounds unnatural
Same issue; ご覧になる is already a complete sonkeigo form
お客様[きゃくさま]が申[もう]す
Using kenjougo (a humble form) for the customer's action wrongly lowers the customer instead of raising them
お客様[きゃくさま]がおっしゃる
伺[うかが]わせていただきます
Redundant stacking of humble forms; overused in business speech, though widely tolerated colloquially
伺[うかが]います / 参[まい]ります
先生[せんせい]、何[なん]を食[た]べますか
Plain teineigo used for a teacher's action instead of sonkeigo; sounds too flat/rude toward a superior
先生[せんせい]、何[なん]を召[め]し上[あ]がりますか
footnotes_tr: 二重敬語 is technically "incorrect" but some forms (like おっしゃられる) are so common they are becoming accepted in casual business speech; formal writing should still avoid them.

examples.reading: せんせいはもういらっしゃいました。
