keigo-business.title_tr: Business Japanese Set Phrases (敬語[けいご] in Practice)
keigo-business.intro_tr: Business Japanese is essentially keigo (sonkeigo, kenjōgo, teineigo) put into practice through fixed, ready-made phrases that office workers reuse every single day; in phone calls, emails, meetings, and simple greetings. Rather than introducing new grammar, this page is a chunk-based reference: memorize these expressions as whole units first, since native speakers rarely build them word by word. Because misusing keigo (especially stacking two honorifics into 二重敬語 "double keigo") is one of the most noticeable mistakes a learner can make, a dedicated table below lists the most common errors next to their corrected forms. For the underlying grammar behind these phrases (お〜になる／お〜する, 〜ていただく, kenjōgo-specific verbs), see the related topics listed at the bottom.

tables.caption_tr: Essential Business Set Phrases (定型表現[ていけいひょうげん])
rows: いつもお世話[せわ]になっております。
"Thank you always for your support."; used to open almost any business interaction
初[はじ]めまして、〇〇と申[もう]します。
"Nice to meet you, I'm called ___." (申す = humble form of 言う)
〜していただけますでしょうか。
"Could you possibly do ~ for me?"; very polite request form
誠[まこと]に申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません。
"I am truly sorry."; highest-register formal apology
ご多忙[たぼう]のところ、恐[おそ]れ入[い]ります。
"I appreciate it despite your busy schedule."
引[ひ]き続[つづ]きよろしくお願[ねが]いいたします。
"I look forward to your continued support."
"Certainly / Understood."; replaces casual 分[わ]かりました
確認[かくにん]いたします。
"I will confirm (it)."; kenjōgo いたす instead of する
少々[しょうしょう]お待[ま]ちください。
お先[さき]に失礼[しつれい]します。
"Excuse me for leaving before you."; fixed daily phrase

tables.caption_tr: Business Verb Conversion Chart: Plain → Respectful (尊敬語[そんけいご]) → Humble (謙譲語[けんじょうご])
rows: 申[もう]す／申[もう]し上[あ]げる
いらっしゃる／お越[こ]しになる
存[ぞん]じる／存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げる
伺[うかが]う／拝聴[はいちょう]する

tables.caption_tr: Phone Call Script (電話応対[でんわおうたい])
rows: お電話[でんわ]ありがとうございます。〇〇株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ]でございます。
"Thank you for calling. This is ___ Company."
いつもお世話[せわ]になっております。〇〇と申[もう]します。
"Thank you for your support. This is ___ speaking."
〇〇様[さま]はいらっしゃいますでしょうか。
少々[しょうしょう]お待[ま]ちくださいませ。
ただいまお繋[つな]ぎいたします。
あいにく〇〇は席[せき]を外[はず]しております。
よろしければご伝言[でんごん]を承[うけたまわ]ります。
"If you'd like, I can take a message."
失礼[しつれい]いたします。

tables.caption_tr: Business Email Phrases (メール表現[ひょうげん])
rows: 〇〇株式会社[かぶしきがいしゃ] 〇〇様[さま]
いつもお世話[せわ]になっております。
"Thank you always for your support."; near-universal email opener
〇〇会社[がいしゃ]の〇〇でございます。
〜の件[けん]についてご連絡[れんらく]いたしました。
ご確認[かくにん]のほど、よろしくお願[ねが]いいたします。
ご迷惑[めいわく]をおかけし、誠[まこと]に申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません。
"I sincerely apologize for the inconvenience caused."
何卒[なにとぞ]よろしくお願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
"I humbly ask for your kind understanding/support."
"Sincerely,"; pairs with the opening word 拝啓[はいけい]

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: Double Keigo (二重敬語[にじゅうけいご]) and Register Errors
rows: Double honorific: おっしゃる is already respectful; adding られる stacks a second honorific unnecessarily
Same issue: ご覧になる is already respectful; られる is redundant
了解[りょうかい]しました (to a superior/client)
了解 sounds flat/equal-status, too casual for hierarchy-sensitive business speech
かしこまりました／承知[しょうち]いたしました
すみません (in formal writing or serious apology)
Too casual/conversational for business email or formal apology
申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません
見[み]れる／食[た]べれる (ら抜[ぬ]き言葉[ことば])
Dropped-ら speech is casual and clashes with a polite/keigo register
見[み]られる／召[め]し上[あ]がる, 食[た]べられる／召[め]し上[あ]がる
ご苦労様[くろうさま]です (said to a superior)

お疲[つか]れ様[さま]です

keigo-humble-special.title_tr: Kenjōgo Special Verbs (伺う, 申す, いたす...)
keigo-humble-special.intro_tr: Kenjōgo (謙譲語) humble language lowers the speaker's own actions in order to show respect toward the listener or a third party of higher status. Unlike the productive お〜する / ご〜する pattern, a small closed set of verbs completely replaces the plain dictionary form with an entirely different word; these are the 謙譲語I "special verbs" (伺う, 申す, いたす, 参る, いただく, 拝見する, お目にかかる, 存じる, etc.). Because these verbs describe only the speaker's (or the speaker's in-group's) actions, they can NEVER be used to describe what the listener or a respected third party does; using them that way is a very common and embarrassing mistake, since that role belongs to sonkeigo (尊敬語) instead. Several of these verbs are irregular in meaning too: 伺う alone covers "ask," "hear," and "visit," while いただく covers both "eat/drink" and "receive." Mastering this fixed list is essential for business Japanese, job interviews, and any formal/polite register from N3–N2 level onward.

used when the speaker gives something to a superior

set-phrases-formal.title_tr: Formal Set Phrases (よろしく / 恐れ入りますが...)
set-phrases-formal.intro_tr: Formal set phrases are fixed, ritualized expressions used in Japanese business, service, and other formal contexts instead of freely constructed sentences. Because their wording and nuance are fixed by convention, they must be memorized as whole chunks rather than built on the fly from grammar rules. Two key families dominate this register: the よろしく family, used to close introductions, requests, and emails with an implicit "please treat me favorably," and cushion words (クッション言葉) such as 恐れ入りますが, which soften a request, interruption, or refusal before it is actually stated. Mastering these phrases; and knowing which politeness level fits which situation; is essential for sounding natural in Japanese business and service interactions.

proverbs-yoji.title_tr: Four-Character Idioms (四字熟語) and Proverbs (ことわざ); Introduction
proverbs-yoji.intro_tr: 四字熟語[よじじゅくご] (four-character idioms) and ことわざ (proverbs) are two of the most common ways Japanese speakers pack condensed wisdom, imagery, or moral advice into a fixed, memorable phrase. 四字熟語 are exactly four kanji long, are usually read with their Chinese-derived (on'yomi) readings, and many originate from classical Chinese literature (故事成語[こじせいご]); they are common in writing, speeches, and slightly formal speech. ことわざ are traditional folk sayings of varying length; often a full clause; that give practical life advice or observations about human nature, and they appear constantly in everyday conversation, usually introduced with と言う[という] or ということわざがある. This page is only an introduction: it shows how these expressions are built, how they differ from related terms like 慣用句[かんようく] (idioms), and lists the handful of yoji-jukugo and proverbs every learner meets first. Treat each expression as a fixed vocabulary chunk to memorize as a whole; the individual kanji meanings are a helpful mnemonic, but the phrase's real meaning is often figurative and cannot be guessed word-by-word.

a full phrase or short sentence, variable length
A traditional folk saying that states practical advice or an observation about life; often in native Japanese words, not just kanji
猿[さる]も木[き]から落[お]ちる
A fixed idiomatic expression (not necessarily kanji-only) whose meaning is figurative, e.g. body-part idioms

ni-hokanaranai.title_tr: 〜にほかならない (Nothing Other Than …; Precisely …)
ni-hokanaranai.intro_tr: 〜にほかならない ("nothing other than," "none other than," "precisely") is a formal, written-style expression used to assert emphatically that something is exactly X and could not be explained any other way. It literally combines に (target particle) + ほか (other, else) + ならない (negative of なる, "to become"), giving a literal sense of "it does not become anything other than X" → "it is nothing but X." It is most commonly used to state the true cause, identity, or nature of something with strong conviction, often in essays, editorials, speeches, and academic writing. Because of its formality and rhetorical weight, it is rarely used in everyday casual conversation; native speakers reserve it for making a decisive, almost dramatic claim.

Comments on the nature/definition of a situation; can sound preachy

Using で instead of に
The particle must be に, not で, matching the classical 〜に他[ほか]ならない structure
Always use 〜にほかならない, never 〜でほかならない
Because it's emphatic, repeating it too often makes writing sound melodramatic
Reserve it for the key claim or conclusion of a paragraph, not every sentence

ni-suginai.intro_tr: 〜にすぎない is an N1 expression meaning "nothing more than ~", "merely ~", or "just ~". It attaches to the plain form of nouns, adjectives, and verbs to assert that something does not exceed a certain limited degree, often carrying a nuance of downplaying, dismissing, or minimizing its importance; the speaker is implying "and that's all, nothing more significant." It is frequently reinforced with adverbs such as ただ, 単に, or ほんの to sharpen the "merely" feeling. Note that it is close in structure but nearly opposite in nuance to 〜にほかならない, which instead affirms "it is precisely X." This pattern appears often in written Japanese, essays, news commentary, and formal or argumentative speech.

tables.caption_tr: How 〜にすぎない attaches to different word types
rows: 学生[がくせい]にすぎない; 'is nothing more than a student'
小[ちい]さいにすぎない; 'is merely small'
Stem + である + にすぎない
便利[べんり]であるにすぎない; 'is merely convenient'
Plain form (non-past / past / negative) + にすぎない
知[し]っているにすぎない / 言[い]ったにすぎない / 知[し]らないにすぎない
footnotes_tr: Unlike many N1 patterns, nouns attach directly without だ; only な-adjectives require である (not simply な or だ) before にすぎない.

ni-katakunai.intro_tr: 〜に難くない is a formal, written-style N1 expression meaning "it is not difficult to..." or "one can easily...". Despite its negative grammatical form, it conveys a positive, natural conclusion; that something is easy or obvious to do. It attaches almost exclusively to a small, fixed set of verbal nouns related to mental activity, most commonly 想像 (imagine), 理解 (understand), and 察する (sense/guess). Because it derives from the classical/literary adjective 難い ("difficult"), the pattern is confined to formal writing such as news articles, essays, and business or legal documents, and rarely appears in casual speech. It should not be confused with the more productive, everyday "difficulty" suffixes 〜がたい, 〜づらい, and 〜にくい, which freely attach to the ます-stem of almost any verb.

tables.caption_tr: Usage notes and common mistakes
rows: Only used with a small closed set of words tied to mental/cognitive activity (想像, 理解, 察する, 推察, 察知). It cannot be freely attached to arbitrary nouns or verbs the way 〜がたい/〜にくい can.
The affirmative form 〜に難[かた]い is essentially obsolete in modern Japanese; the expression survives almost exclusively as 〜に難[かた]くない.
Grammatically negative ('not difficult'), but the overall nuance is 'it is easy/natural to...'; a formal litotes (understatement) common in written Japanese.
Confined to formal, written, or literary contexts (news reports, essays, legal/business documents). Very rare in everyday conversation.
Unlike 〜がたい/〜づらい/〜にくい, which attach to almost any verb stem, 〜に難くない is a fixed, semi-idiomatic phrase with only a handful of accepted collocations.

wo-yoginakusareru.title_tr: 〜を余儀なくされる (to be forced to / compelled to do)
wo-yoginakusareru.intro_tr: 〜を余儀[よぎ]なくされる is a very formal, written-style N1 expression meaning "to be forced/compelled to do something because there is no other option," due to circumstances entirely outside the subject's control (disasters, economic crisis, accidents, illness, etc.). It comes from the い-adjective 余儀[よぎ]ない ("having no alternative, unavoidable") combined with the causative-passive される. Because it inherently expresses passivity and helplessness, the grammatical subject is almost always the party who suffers the forced outcome (a person, company, organization, or event), while the cause is marked with で/により or as the subject of the related causative form 〜を余儀[よぎ]なくさせる. This pattern is extremely common in news reports, official announcements, and academic/business writing, but it sounds stiff and unnatural in casual conversation.

[Noun (action/result)] + を + 余儀[よぎ]なくされる

余儀[よぎ]ない = 'having no other way, unavoidable'
the literal root meaning underlying the whole pattern: 'no other option'
Noun + を余儀[よぎ]なくさせる (causative)
[Cause] + が + ([Target] + に) + [Noun] + を + 余儀[よぎ]なくさせる

wo-kinjienai.title_tr: 〜を禁じ得ない (cannot help feeling ~ / cannot suppress ~)
wo-kinjienai.intro_tr: 〜を禁じ得ない is a very formal, written-language (書き言葉) expression meaning "cannot suppress/hold back ~" or "cannot help feeling ~." It attaches to a noun denoting an emotion (tears, surprise, anger, sympathy, doubt, etc.) and describes an involuntary emotional reaction that the speaker/writer is powerless to control. 得ない here is the classical negative potential of the auxiliary 得る (える) "to be able to," so 禁じ得ない literally means "cannot manage to suppress." Because of its stiff, literary tone, it appears mainly in news reports, essays, speeches, editorials, and formal writing; almost never in casual conversation. It is essentially a fixed phrase; the affirmative form 禁じ得る is not used in practice, only the negative 禁じ得ない / past 禁じ得なかった.

to-aimatte.intro_tr: 〜と相[あい]まって (also spelled 〜とあいまって) is an N1-level written expression meaning "combined with ~" or "coupled with ~." It describes a situation in which two or more factors interact together and jointly produce a resulting effect; often one that is stronger, more notable, or somewhat unexpected compared to what either factor would produce alone. It attaches to nouns and is used almost exclusively in formal written Japanese such as news articles, business reports, and academic writing; it is rarely heard in casual spoken conversation. Because the expression inherently describes an interaction between multiple causes, it always requires at least two combining factors (stated or clearly implied); it cannot mark a single isolated reason. Grammatically, 相[あい]まって is the te-form of the verb 相[あい]まる ("to combine, to be mutual"), so it can also surface as 〜と相[あい]まっている (a resulting state) or 〜と相[あい]まった (past).

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns of 〜と相[あい]まって
rows: 才能[さいのう]と相[あい]まって成功[せいこう]した
Basic pattern: one stated factor combines with an already-mentioned or implied factor to produce result Y.
Noun + と + Noun + とが相[あい]まって
X と Y とが相[あい]まって、Z
味[あじ]と価格[かかく]とが相[あい]まって人気[にんき]だ
Both combining factors are explicitly listed, joined by と...とが, before 相[あい]まって.
Noun + と + Noun + が相[あい]まって
X と Y が相[あい]まって、Z
経験[けいけん]と知識[ちしき]が相[あい]まって
が is common when the two nouns joined by と function as one combined subject.
(既出[きしゅつ]の要因[よういん])に、X も相[あい]まって、Y
円安[えんやす]も相[あい]まって値上[ねあ]げされた
Used to add one more factor to a cause already mentioned earlier in the sentence or context.
同[おな]じ意味[いみ]、ひらがな表記[ひょうき]
努力[どりょく]とあいまって
相まって is very often written in hiragana (あいまって) even in formal writing; both spellings are equally correct and equally common.

tables.caption_tr: 〜と相[あい]まって vs. Similar Combining/Additive Expressions
rows: Two (or more) factors interact and jointly produce an effect, often stronger or more notable than expected
Simple co-occurrence or simultaneity; no implication that the factors interact to cause a result
Simply adds one more item/factor to a list; no strong implication of synergistic interaction
One change causes or accompanies another change over time
Marks a contrast/opposite between two things, not a combination

経験[けいけん]と知識[ちしき]が相[あい]まって

天候[てんこう]不順[ふじゅん] + 価格[かかく]高騰[こうとう]
天候[てんこう]不順[ふじゅん]も相[あい]まって

tables.caption_tr: Key Grammar Points and Restrictions
rows: Word class before と相まって
Attaches only to nouns or noun phrases; it does NOT attach directly to verbs or plain-form adjectives.
Requires at least two combining factors (explicitly stated or clearly implied from context); it cannot mark a single isolated cause.
Typically appears mid-sentence describing the combined cause, followed by a clause stating the resulting situation.
相[あい]まって is the te-form of the verb 相[あい]まる ('to combine, to be mutual'). It can also appear as 〜と相[あい]まっている (a static resulting state) or 〜と相[あい]まった (past tense, in narrative writing).
Almost exclusively written/formal Japanese; news reports, business documents, academic papers. It is essentially never used in casual spoken conversation.
Unlike plain addition (〜に加えて) or co-occurrence (〜とともに), と相まって implies the factors interact synergistically, producing an effect stronger or more notable than either factor alone would cause.

examples.target: 急激[きゅうげき]な円安[えんやす]は、原材料[げんざいりょう]価格[かかく]の高騰[こうとう]と相[あい]まって、企業[きぎょう]の経営[けいえい]を圧迫[あっぱく]している。

examples.target: 天候[てんこう]不順[ふじゅん]に加[くわ]え、原材料[げんざいりょう]価格[かかく]の高騰[こうとう]も相[あい]まって、商品[しょうひん]の値上[ねあ]げが決定[けってい]された。

examples.target: その曲[きょく]は美[うつく]しいメロディーと歌詞[かし]の力強[ちからづよ]いメッセージとが相[あい]まって、多[おお]くの人[ひと]の心[こころ]を打[う]った。

yue-ni.title_tr: 〜ゆえに / 〜がゆえに; Literary "Because of, Due to"
yue-ni.intro_tr: 〜ゆえに (故に) and its more emphatic variant 〜がゆえに are literary, written-register (文語) causal expressions meaning "because of, due to, on account of." ゆえ is itself a noun meaning "reason, cause," and ゆえに works as a causal connector attaching after nouns, な-adjectives, い-adjectives, and verbs in their plain forms. Inserting が before ゆえに (がゆえに) adds a classical subject-marking nuance and heightens the formality and emphasis, often implying "precisely because ~." These forms appear in essays, novels, legal documents, academic writing, and formal speeches; essentially never in casual conversation. Related forms include the noun-modifying 〜ゆえの, the sentence-initial connector それゆえ(に) "therefore," and fixed phrases like 故なく "without reason."

examples.target: それゆえに、彼女は誰からも信頼されている。
examples.reading: それゆえに、かのじょはだれからもしんらいされている。
examples.translation_tr: For that reason, she is trusted by everyone.

examples.target: 正直であるがゆえに、時に人を傷つけてしまう。

nagara-ni.title_tr: 〜ながらに (in the state of…, from birth, unchanged)
nagara-ni.intro_tr: 〜ながらに (also 〜ながらにして) is a literary N1 pattern that attaches to a small, fixed set of nouns to mean "in that very state," "while remaining as ~," often describing something that is true from birth or unchanged since long ago. It is NOT a productive grammar point; it only combines with a handful of nouns like 生まれ (birth), 涙 (tears), 昔 (the past), and 居 (staying put), each forming its own idiomatic expression. In its attributive form, Noun + ながらの + Noun, it modifies a following noun to mean "the same ~ as ever" (e.g. 昔ながらの町 "a town unchanged since the old days"). Do not confuse it with the concessive 〜ながらも ("even though") or the more general 〜まま ("as is, unchanged"); 〜ながらに is far more restricted in what it can attach to and belongs to written/formal register.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns
rows: Describes an action/state occurring in a fixed, unchanged condition, often from birth or origin
生[う]まれながらにして (from/by birth)
Modifies a following noun: '~ that remains as it originally was'
昔[むかし]ながらの町並[まちな]み (streets unchanged since the old days)
'Even in the state of being X...'; close to ながらも but only with certain nouns
子供[こども]ながらに (even as a mere child)

tables.caption_tr: Common Fixed Expressions with 〜ながらに
rows: 生[う]まれながらに(して)
Most common use; often before a verb like 持[も]つ, 備[そな]わる
生まれながらの天才[てんさい] = 'a born genius'
Common in narration of emotional speech/testimony
traditional, as it was long ago, old-fashioned
女性[じょせい]ながらに / 男性[だんせい]ながらに
じょせいながらに / だんせいながらに
despite being a woman/man (older, can sound dated)
Modern usage is decreasing; use with care

tables.caption_tr: 〜ながらに vs Similar Grammar
rows: Small fixed set of nouns only
'In that very unchanged state'; innate or original condition

い/な-adjective, verb ます-stem, some nouns

知[し]りつつも黙[だま]っていた

rows: Using ながらに freely with any noun (e.g. 学生ながらに)

examples.target: この町[まち]には昔[むかし]ながらの町並[まちな]みが残[のこ]っている。

examples.target: 子供[こども]ながらに、両親[りょうしん]の苦労[くろう]がよくわかっていた。

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は生[う]まれながらの指導者[しどうしゃ]だ。
examples.reading: かれはうまれながらのしどうしゃだ。

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は女性[じょせい]ながらに力強[ちからづよ]い意見[いけん]を述[の]べた。
examples.reading: かのじょはじょせいながらにちからづよいいけんをのべた。
examples.translation_tr: Despite being a woman (in a context where that was seen as unusual), she stated her opinion powerfully.
examples.note_tr: This older usage can sound outdated/biased today; used carefully in modern speech.

examples.target: 祖母[そぼ]は昔[むかし]ながらのやり方[かた]で味噌[みそ]を作[つく]っている。
examples.reading: そぼはむかしながらのやりかたでみそをつくっている。

koto-naku.intro_tr: 〜ことなく attaches to the dictionary (plain, non-past) form of a verb to mean "without doing ~" or "without ~ing ever happening." It is a literary, written-style equivalent of 〜ないで / 〜ずに, and is typically found in narrative prose, news reports, essays, and formal writing rather than everyday conversation. The clause it forms usually describes a state or action that continues or occurs while the event named by the verb never takes place (e.g., "he kept working without ever resting"). Because it already carries a built‑in negative meaning ("without"), it almost never attaches to an already-negative verb form, and it cannot attach to adjectives directly; only to verbs. As an N1-level item, mastering ことなく also means knowing how it differs in register and nuance from ないで, ずに, and its close cousin 〜ことなしに.

諦める[あきらめる]ことなく (without giving up)

心配する[しんぱいする] (to worry)
心配する[しんぱいする]ことなく (without worrying)

tables.caption_tr: Structural Rules and Cautions
rows: Only attaches to the plain dictionary (non-past, affirmative) form of a verb; never to い-adjectives or な-adjectives directly.
Because ことなく already means "without," it is not combined with a negative verb stem (avoid ×〜ないことなく).
[Verb-dict]ことなく、[main clause]; the main clause states what happens/continues while the first action never occurs.
Reserved for written/formal contexts (essays, news, novels, speeches); in daily conversation use 〜ないで or 〜ずに instead.
Frequently combines with passive forms to describe something that never happened to the subject: 忘れられることなく (without being forgotten).
〜ことなしに is near-synonymous but leans even more literary and pairs especially often with 〜はできない/〜はありえない for "impossible without ~ing."

to-wa-ie.intro_tr: 〜とはいえ is an N1-level concessive expression meaning "even though...", "that said...", or "although it is true that... (still)". It first acknowledges a stated fact as true, then immediately points out a contrasting or qualifying reality that the listener might not expect given that fact. It is more formal and literary than けれども or のに, and is common in essays, news reports, and formal speech rather than casual conversation. The pattern always attaches to the PLAIN form of the preceding clause, regardless of word type. A common spoken variant, とはいっても, softens the tone slightly and is more natural in everyday conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Connecting 〜とはいえ to different word types (always plain form)
rows: 病気[びょうき](だ)とはいえ、休[やす]めない。; Even though it's an illness, I can't take time off.
便利[べんり](だ)とはいえ、危険[きけん]も伴[ともな]う。; Although it's convenient, it also carries risk.
安[やす]いとはいえ、質[しつ]は悪[わる]くない。; Although it's cheap, the quality isn't bad.
合格[ごうかく]したとはいえ、油断[ゆだん]はできない。; Even though I passed, I can't be careless.

Similar concession, slightly softer, often used with achievements vs. remaining problems
Very close in meaning to とはいえ, often interchangeable
No special nuance of "admitting a surprising fact"
Strong contrast, "in spite of", often expresses surprise or criticism
Stronger and more emphatic than とはいえ
Carries more personal feeling than とはいえ
Spoken equivalent of とはいえ
Natural substitute for とはいえ in conversation

to-itte-mo-kagon-dewanai.title_tr: ~と言っても過言ではない; "It's No Exaggeration to Say..."
to-itte-mo-kagon-dewanai.intro_tr: 〜と言っても過言ではない literally means "even if (one) says [X], it is not an exaggeration (過言[かごん])," and is used to make a strong, confident assertion while softening it slightly with a rhetorical concession. It is a formal, written/speech-register pattern typical of essays, speeches, articles, and persuasive writing, often paired with superlatives (最も[もっとも], 一番[いちばん], 史上[しじょう]最高[さいこう]) or dramatic claims. Because it attaches to a full clause ending in the plain form (with だ for nouns/な-adjectives), it functions much like an emphatic "it's no exaggeration to say that..." in English. It is an N1-level fixed expression, so learners should focus on recognizing its structure and formal nuance rather than producing it casually in conversation.

rows: 変[か]えたと言[い]っても過言[かごん]ではない

made-mo-nai.title_tr: 〜までもない / 〜までのことだ (No Need to..., Not Worth Doing...)
made-mo-nai.intro_tr: 〜までもない attaches to the dictionary form of a verb and means "there is no need to go so far as to do X" or "it's not even worth doing X"; typically because the matter is obvious, trivial, or easily resolved without that action. Its adverbial cousin 〜までもなく means "without even needing to..." and is used mid-sentence. A close look-alike, 〜までのことだ, is often confused with までもない but actually means something quite different: "if X happens, I'll simply do Y"; expressing simple resolve rather than unnecessity. This page lays out both patterns side by side along with related expressions so you can tell them apart at a glance. All forms are common in formal writing, news commentary, and slightly formal speech, and 言うまでもない ("needless to say") is one of the most frequently used fixed expressions built on this pattern.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation and core meanings
rows: There's no need to go so far as to do ~; not worth doing ~
説明[せつめい]するまでもない (no need to explain)
Without even needing to ~ (adverbial, used mid-sentence)
言[い]うまでもなく、彼[かれ]は天才[てんさい]だ (needless to say, he's a genius)
Verb (dictionary form) + までもないことだ
A matter that doesn't need ~-ing (emphatic, noun-modifying form)
わざわざ聞[き]くまでもないことだ (something not even worth asking about)
Verb (dictionary form) + までもない話だ
It's a story/matter not worth mentioning ~
今更[いまさら]言[い]うまでもない話[はなし]だ (a matter not worth mentioning at this point)

tables.caption_tr: Don't confuse these! 〜までもない vs. 〜までのことだ vs. similar patterns
rows: No need to do X (because it's obvious, trivial, or minor)
Downplays the necessity of an action; often follows because reasoning is given
電話[でんわ]するまでもない、すぐ近[ちか]くだから (no need to call, it's right nearby)
If X happens, I'll simply do Y / that's all there is to it
Expresses calm resolve or resignation after a conditional; NOT about necessity
ダメなら、また挑戦[ちょうせん]するまでのことだ (if it fails, I'll simply try again)
Impossible to even hope for X
Much stronger than までもない; expresses flat impossibility, not mere unnecessity
合格[ごうかく]は望[のぞ]むべくもない (passing is not even something one can hope for)
Not to the extent of X; not a big deal
Similar softening effect to までもない but slightly more casual/conversational
心配[しんぱい]するほどのことではない (it's nothing worth worrying about)
Not worth doing X; insufficient to warrant X
Formal, often used with 論[ろん]じる, 恐[おそ]れる, etc.
恐[おそ]れるに足[た]りない (nothing to be afraid of)

made-da.title_tr: 〜まで(のこと)だ; "I'll simply...", "I only did... that's all"
made-da.intro_tr: 〜まで(のこと)だ is an N1 expression built on the same まで that means "until," but here it has drifted into a very different, idiomatic function. Attached to a verb's dictionary form, it expresses a calm, undramatic resolve or fallback plan: "if things go a certain way, I'll simply do X, that's all; no big deal." Attached to a verb's past (た) form, it instead downplays or justifies something the speaker already did, meaning "I only did X (for this simple reason), nothing more, no deeper motive." のこと adds a slightly more formal, emphatic "and that is all there is to it" flavor, while plain までだ is a touch more direct. This pattern signals composure, lack of worry about consequences, or modest self-justification, and is common in written Japanese, speeches, and dramatic dialogue.

tables.caption_tr: Two Core Usages of 〜まで(のこと)だ
rows: Verb dictionary form + までだ / までのことだ
"If X happens, I'll simply do Y"; a calm, undramatic backup option, no anxiety implied
雨[あめ]が降[ふ]れば、中止[ちゅうし]するまでだ。(If it rains, I'll simply cancel it.)
Verb た form + までだ / までのことだ
"I only did Y (for this simple reason), nothing more"; downplays or defends a past action, denies a deeper motive
ただ確認[かくにん]したまでだ。(I merely confirmed it, that's all.)

tables.caption_tr: Formation Pattern
rows: 行[い]くまでだ / 行[い]くまでのことだ
行[い]ったまでだ / 行[い]ったまでのことだ
Often preceded by a conditional clause
だめなら、断[ことわ]るまでだ
"If it's no good, I'll simply refuse"
Can follow ただ for extra emphasis on 'merely'

tables.caption_tr: 〜までだ vs 〜までのことだ vs Similar Expressions
rows: Slightly more direct, common in speech and writing
Just do X, simple as that
逃[に]げるなら追[お]うまでだ。(If you run, I'll simply chase you.)
Slightly more formal/emphatic, stresses 'that is all there is to it'
Just do X, and nothing more needs saying
逃[に]げるなら追[お]うまでのことだ。(If you run, I'll simply chase you; that's all.)
Different meaning: 'not even necessary to go that far'
No need to do X (it would be excessive)
聞[き]くまでもない。(There's no need to even ask.)
Neutral 'only/just', no implication of resolve or fallback
待[ま]つだけだ。(I'm just waiting.)
Implies no other option exists, more forced than までだ
Have no choice but to X
頼[たよ]るしかない。(I have no choice but to rely on it.)

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations and Fixed Patterns
rows: 断[ことわ]られれば、諦[あきら]めるまでだ。(If I'm refused, I'll simply give up.)
ただ〜V-たまでだ / までのことだ
"I merely did X, nothing special intended"
ただ思[おも]ったことを言[い]ったまでだ。(I just said what I thought, that's all.)
〜わけではない。ただ〜までのことだ
Used to correct a misunderstanding: 'It's not that ~; I simply ~'
怒[おこ]っているわけではない。ただ言[い]ったまでのことだ。(It's not that I'm angry; I simply said it, nothing more.)

examples.target: 負[ま]けたら、また挑戦[ちょうせん]するまでだ。
examples.reading: maketara, mata chousen suru made da.
examples.translation_tr: If I lose, I'll simply try again.

examples.target: 失敗[しっぱい]を恐[おそ]れているわけではない。ただ慎重[しんちょう]に行動[こうどう]しているまでのことだ。
examples.reading: shippai o osorete iru wake dewa nai. tada shinchou ni koudou shite iru made no koto da.
examples.translation_tr: It's not that I'm afraid of failing. I'm simply acting carefully, that's all.

examples.target: 規則[きそく]だから従[したが]ったまでで、納得[なっとく]しているわけではない。
examples.reading: kisoku dakara shitagatta made de, nattoku shite iru wake dewa nai.
examples.translation_tr: I only followed it because it's the rule; that doesn't mean I'm convinced by it.

nomi-narazu.title_tr: 〜のみならず (Not Only ~ But Also ~, Literary)
nomi-narazu.intro_tr: 〜のみならず is a formal, literary way of saying "not only ~ but also ~". It attaches to the plain form of nouns, adjectives, and verbs, and the second clause is typically emphasized with も, さえ, まで, or a subject marker like が. Because it belongs to written/formal register (newspapers, essays, speeches, business writing), it is rarely heard in casual conversation, where だけでなく or ばかりでなく would be used instead. As an N1-level pattern, mastering its connection rules and typical pairing words in the second clause is essential for reading formal Japanese texts.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Patterns (how to attach 〜のみならず)
rows: 学生[がくせい]のみならず (not only students)
Noun + であるのみならず
専門家[せんもんか]であるのみならず (not only being an expert)
Stem + であるのみならず
便利[べんり]であるのみならず (not only convenient)
美[うつく]しいのみならず (not only beautiful)
話[はな]せるのみならず (not only can speak)
知[し]らないのみならず (not only not knowing)
footnotes_tr: The た-form can also be used before のみならず to describe a completed state: 失敗[しっぱい]したのみならず (not only did [it] fail).

tables.caption_tr: Typical Pairing Words in the Second Clause
rows: even to the extent of / to the point of
used when the second clause introduces a new subject
footnotes_tr: Choosing さえ or まで in the second clause increases the sense of surprise or escalation compared to plain も.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Similar 'Not Only ~ But Also' Expressions
rows: Most bookish; common in essays, news, formal speeches; rarely spoken casually
Slightly less stiff than のみならず; often implies the second fact is more surprising
Usable in both writing and polite speech; very common in textbooks
Most common in daily conversation; safe default choice
Focuses on 'in addition to', weaker 'not only' nuance than のみならず
Old-fashioned, mostly found in classical or highly literary text
footnotes_tr: For spoken Japanese, prefer だけでなく or ばかりでなく; reserve のみならず for essays, reports, and formal writing/speeches.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Usage Notes
rows: Attaching のみならず directly to an い-adjective stem (e.g. 美しのみならず)
Use the full plain form: 美[うつく]しいのみならず
Using 〜のみならず in casual conversation with friends
Sounds unnaturally stiff; use だけでなく or ばかりでなく instead
Confusing のみならず with 〜のみ (only) + 〜ならず (is not)
Historically it comes from 'のみ + ならず [is not merely]', but today it functions as one fixed connector meaning 'not only ~'
Forgetting to mark the second clause with も/さえ/まで
Without a marker, the 'but also' contrast becomes unclear or ungrammatical
Using な-adjective/noun without である before のみならず
Noun and な-adjective normally require である: 便利[べんり]であるのみならず, not 便利のみならず alone (though noun+のみならず without である is also acceptable for simple nouns)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は英語[えいご]のみならず、フランス[ふらんす]語[ご]も話[はな]せる。
examples.reading: かれはえいごのみならず、ふらんすごもはなせる。
examples.translation_tr: Not only can he speak English, he can also speak French.
examples.note_tr: Noun + のみならず, second clause marked with も.

examples.target: この薬[くすり]は風邪[かぜ]のみならず、頭痛[ずつう]にも効[き]く。
examples.reading: このくすりはかぜのみならず、ずつうにもきく。
examples.translation_tr: This medicine is effective not only for colds but also for headaches.
examples.note_tr: Noun + のみならず, particle に retained before も.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は美[うつく]しいのみならず、賢[かしこ]くもある。
examples.reading: かのじょはうつくしいのみならず、かしこくもある。
examples.translation_tr: She is not only beautiful, but also intelligent.
examples.note_tr: い-adjective plain form + のみならず.

examples.target: 経済的[けいざいてき]な損失[そんしつ]のみならず、人的[じんてき]な被害[ひがい]も甚大[じんだい]だった。
examples.reading: けいざいてきなそんしつのみならず、じんてきなひがいもじんだいだった。
examples.translation_tr: Not only was there economic loss, but the human damage was also enormous.
examples.note_tr: な-adjective + な + Noun, then のみならず attaches to the noun phrase.

examples.target: その事故[じこ]は、本人[ほんにん]のみならず、家族[かぞく]の人生[じんせい]をも変[か]えてしまった。
examples.reading: そのじこは、ほんにんのみならず、かぞくのじんせいをもかえてしまった。
examples.translation_tr: That accident changed not only his own life, but his family's life as well.
examples.note_tr: をも emphasizes the object in the second clause.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は勉強[べんきょう]ができるのみならず、スポーツも万能[ばんのう]だ。
examples.reading: かれはべんきょうができるのみならず、すぽーつもばんのうだ。
examples.translation_tr: Not only is he good at studying, he's also excellent at every sport.
examples.note_tr: Verb (potential, plain form) + のみならず.

examples.target: この問題[もんだい]は日本[にほん]のみならず、世界中[せかいじゅう]で議論[ぎろん]されている。
examples.reading: このもんだいはにほんのみならず、せかいじゅうでぎろんされている。
examples.translation_tr: This issue is being discussed not only in Japan, but all over the world.
examples.note_tr: Common in news/formal writing to expand scope.

examples.target: 社長[しゃちょう]のみならず、社員[しゃいん]全員[ぜんいん]がそのプロジェクトに反対[はんたい]した。
examples.reading: しゃちょうのみならず、しゃいんぜんいんがそのぷろじぇくとにはんたいした。
examples.translation_tr: Not only the president, but all the employees opposed that project.
examples.note_tr: Noun + のみならず, second clause with subject marker が.

taru-mono.title_tr: 〜たるもの (As One Who Is..., One Should...)
taru-mono.intro_tr: 〜たるもの is a highly formal, literary N1 expression meaning "as one who holds the status/role of ~, one ought to...". It comes from the classical auxiliary たり (attributive form たる), the classical equivalent of である/という, and attaches to nouns denoting a role, profession, or social position (教師, リーダー, 親, 社会人, etc.). The phrase 〜たるもの generalizes that noun into "a person who is in that position," and is almost always followed by an expression of duty or expected behavior such as べきだ, ねばならない, or ものだ. Because of its classical, moralizing tone, it appears in speeches, editorials, ethics essays, and formal writing about responsibility; rarely in everyday conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Structure and formation of 〜たるもの
rows: Subject whose duty is being stated
Attributive form of classical auxiliary たり (= である)
Links the role-noun to もの, meaning 'who is N'
Generalizes to 'a person in that position'
教師[きょうし]たるもの
べきだ / ねばならない / ものだ, etc.
States the duty or expected behavior that follows from the status
教師[きょうし]たるもの、生徒[せいと]を愛[あい]すべきだ

tables.caption_tr: Common role/status nouns used with 〜たるもの
rows: 教師[きょうし]たるもの
社会人[しゃかいじん]たるもの
政治家[せいじか]たるもの
経営者[けいえいしゃ]たるもの
人間[にんげん]たるもの

tables.caption_tr: 〜たるもの compared with similar 'as X' expressions
rows: 'Being in status X obliges one to...'; moral duty tied to a role
教師[きょうし]たるもの、模範[もはん]を示[しめ]すべきだ
'In the capacity of / as'; neutral statement of role, no built-in moral push
教師[きょうし]として働[はたら]く
Defines the general nature or essence of a category
教師[きょうし]というものは大変[たいへん]な仕事[しごと]だ
'Unbefitting one who is X'; used for criticizing behavior that violates the status
教師[きょうし]にあるまじき行為[こうい]だ
'Should be X'; states a required quality, without the role-duty link
リーダーであるべき人物[じんぶつ]

tables.caption_tr: Predicates that typically follow 〜たるもの
rows: that is simply how it should be (general truth/norm)

tables.caption_tr: Usage notes and common pitfalls
rows: Cannot attach to ordinary objects or events; only nouns denoting a person's position, profession, or social role (親, 教師, リーダー), not things like 天気 or 問題.
In writing, a comma typically separates 〜たるもの from the rest of the sentence: 'N たるもの、 [duty statement]'.
Almost always paired with an obligation expression
〜たるもの rarely ends a sentence by itself; it sets up a claim about duty that is completed by べきだ, ねばならない, ものだ, etc.
Never used in casual conversation; typical of editorials, moral essays, ceremonial speeches, and classical-flavored writing.
Not the same as 〜である body register
〜たるもの is a fixed idiomatic phrase, distinct from general である/だ formal writing style, and carries a moralizing, prescriptive nuance.

examples.target: 教師[きょうし]たるもの、生徒[せいと]の手本[てほん]とならなければならない。
examples.reading: きょうしたるもの、せいとのてほんとならなければならない。
examples.translation_tr: As a teacher, one must become a model for one's students.

examples.target: リーダーたるもの、常[つね]に冷静[れいせい]でなければならない。
examples.reading: リーダーたるもの、つねにれいせいでなければならない。
examples.translation_tr: As a leader, one must always remain calm.

examples.target: 政治家[せいじか]たるもの、国民[こくみん]のために尽[つ]くすべきだ。
examples.reading: せいじかたるもの、こくみんのためにつくすべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: As a politician, one should devote oneself to the people.

examples.target: 親[おや]たるもの、子供[こども]の安全[あんぜん]を第一[だいいち]に考[かんが]えるべきだ。
examples.reading: おやたるもの、こどものあんぜんをだいいちにかんがえるべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: As a parent, one should put the child's safety first.

examples.target: 社会人[しゃかいじん]たるもの、時間[じかん]を守[まも]るのは当然[とうぜん]のことだ。
examples.reading: しゃかいじんたるもの、じかんをまもるのはとうぜんのことだ。
examples.translation_tr: As a member of society, keeping one's appointments is only natural.

examples.target: 武士[ぶし]たるもの、卑怯[ひきょう]な真似[まね]をしてはならない。
examples.reading: ぶしたるもの、ひきょうなまねをしてはならない。
examples.translation_tr: As a samurai, one must never act in a cowardly manner.

examples.target: 経営者[けいえいしゃ]たるもの、社員[しゃいん]の生活[せいかつ]に責任[せきにん]を持[も]つべきだ。
examples.reading: けいえいしゃたるもの、しゃいんのせいかつにせきにんをもつべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: As a business owner, one should take responsibility for employees' livelihoods.

examples.target: 人[ひと]の親[おや]たるもの、子[こ]の将来[しょうらい]を思[おも]わないはずがない。
examples.reading: ひとのおやたるもの、このしょうらいをおもわないはずがない。
examples.translation_tr: As anyone's parent, there is no way one would not think about their child's future.

to-shite-nai.title_tr: 〜として〜ない (Not a Single One... / None Whatsoever)
to-shite-nai.intro_tr: 〜として〜ない is an emphatic total-negation pattern built by attaching として to the smallest possible unit of something; usually 一 + a counter (一つ, 一人, 一度, 一日); and following it with a negative predicate. It literally frames that minimal unit 'as' the standard, then denies even that, producing the meaning 'not a single one, not even one.' This is a formal, literary (書き言葉) construction typical of essays, speeches, and written argument, and it is intensified further when combined with question words such as 誰, 何, or どれ (誰一人として, 何一つとして, どれ一つとして). It is rarely used in casual spoken Japanese, where 一つも〜ない or 誰も〜ない are the everyday equivalents.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Formation
rows: [Minimal quantity noun] (一つ, 一人, 一度, 一日...)
names the smallest conceivable single unit of the set
一つ / 一人 / 一度
marks that unit as 'counting as / serving as' the standard example
+ negative predicate (〜ない / 〜なかった / 〜ません)
denies even that single unit, so the negation covers the entire set
Question word + counter + として (誰一人として, 何一つとして, どれ一つとして)
adds extra emphasis, often translated 'not a single... at all'

tables.caption_tr: Common 〜として〜ない Combinations
rows: だれひとり[として]〜ない
なにひとつ[として]〜ない
どれひとつ[として]〜ない
not a single one (among a known set of choices)

tables.caption_tr: Predicate Forms Used with 〜として
rows: 一人として来[こ]なかった
一人[として]いませんでした
説明[せつめい]として納得[なっとく]できるものは一つとしてなかった

tables.caption_tr: 〜として〜ない vs. Similar Total-Negation Patterns
rows: emphatic: 'not a single one out of the whole set'
一つとして間違[まちが]いはない
'not even X' with an extreme/surprising example
子供[こども]ですら分[わ]かる
'not even X', slightly less formal than すら

examples.target: 彼の話には一つとして真実がない。
examples.reading: かれ[の]はなし[に][は]ひとつ[として]しんじつ[が]ない。
examples.translation_tr: There isn't a single truthful thing in what he says.
examples.note_tr: 一つとして emphasizes that out of everything he said, not even one part is true.

examples.target: このクラスには彼に勝てる人は誰一人としていない。
examples.reading: この[クラス][に][は]かれ[に]かてる[ひと][は]だれひとり[として]いない。
examples.translation_tr: In this class, there is not a single person who can beat him.
examples.note_tr: 誰一人として is the emphatic 'not a single person' version of 誰も.

examples.target: 私はこれまで彼を疑ったことは一度としてない。
examples.reading: わたし[は]これまで[かれ][を]うたがった[こと][は]いちど[として]ない。
examples.translation_tr: I have never once doubted him, not even a single time.

examples.target: 世界に同じ人間は一人としていない。
examples.reading: せかい[に]おなじ[にんげん][は]ひとり[として]いない。
examples.translation_tr: There is not a single identical person in the world.

examples.target: どれ一つとして完璧な作品はなかった。
examples.reading: どれひとつ[として]かんぺき[な][さくひん][は]なかった。
examples.translation_tr: Not a single one of the works was perfect.
examples.note_tr: どれ一つ is used when choosing from a specific, limited set of items.

examples.target: あの日以来、彼女のことを一日として忘れたことはない。
examples.reading: あの[ひ][いらい]、かのじょ[の][こと][を]いちにち[として]わすれた[こと][は]ない。
examples.translation_tr: Since that day, I have not forgotten about her for even a single day.

examples.target: この事件について何一つとして納得できる説明はなかった。
examples.reading: この[じけん][について]なにひとつ[として]なっとく[できる][せつめい][は]なかった。
examples.translation_tr: There was not a single explanation about this incident that I could accept.
examples.note_tr: 何一つとして is a stronger, more emphatic version of 何も, often used in writing.

ni-taru.title_tr: 〜に足る / 〜に足りない (worthy of ~ / not worth ~)
ni-taru.intro_tr: 〜に足る (にたる) attaches after a noun or a verb in dictionary form to mean "worthy of ~", "sufficient to ~", or "deserving enough to warrant ~". It is a survival of the classical verb 足る "to be sufficient" and is almost always used in formal, written, or literary Japanese; news articles, essays, formal speeches, and literature. Its negative counterpart, 〜に足りない (or the more classical 〜に足らない), means "not worth ~ing", "insufficient to justify ~", and is very often used to dismiss something as trivial, negligible, or unworthy of concern (e.g. 取るに足りない "not worth mentioning"). Both forms most commonly modify a noun that follows (attributive use, "a person/thing worth ~ing") or stand as a predicate at the end of a clause. This is a stiff, bookish pattern; it is rarely heard in casual conversation and belongs to the same register as other classical-verb remnants like 〜に堪える/たえる or 〜に値する/あたいする.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation patterns
rows: 信頼[しんらい]に足[た]る人物[じんぶつ]; a person worthy of trust
尊敬[そんけい]するに足[た]る人[ひと]; a person worth respecting
Noun + に足りない / 足らない
恐[おそ]れるに足[た]りない; nothing to fear
Verb (dictionary form) + に足りない / 足らない
取[と]るに足[た]らない; not worth mentioning, trivial
footnotes_tr: The verb before に足る/足りない is almost always in the plain dictionary (present) form, never ます-form.
When modifying a following noun, the whole phrase acts like a relative clause: [Vる/Nに足る] + Noun.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations (high-frequency for N1 reading/listening)
rows: 信頼[しんらい]するに足[た]る友人[ゆうじん]; a trustworthy friend
尊敬[そんけい]するに足[た]る人物[じんぶつ]
満足[まんぞく]するに足[た]る結果[けっか]
語[かた]るに足[た]る経歴[けいれき]
一読[いちどく]に足[た]る内容[ないよう]
取るに足りない/足らない
とるにたりない/たらない
取[と]るに足[た]らない失敗[しっぱい]
nothing to fear, not worth fearing
敵[てき]は恐[おそ]れるに足[た]りない
この結果[けっか]は驚[おどろ]くに足[た]りない
言[い]うに足[た]りない小事[しょうじ]

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation of the classical verb 足る behind these fixed expressions
rows: 足[た]らない / 足[た]らず
used in fixed phrases like 一年[いちねん]足[た]らず 'less than a year'
the far more common negative in 〜に足りない today
appears in older compounds; rarely used alone in modern text
the form used directly in 〜に足る
very rare, mostly found in classical/literary text
footnotes_tr: In modern Japanese, 足る survives almost exclusively in fixed expressions like 〜に足る, 〜足らず, and 二十歳[はたち]足[た]らず 'not quite twenty years old'.
足りる (いる-ichidan, everyday word for 'to be enough') is the modern replacement of 足る in ordinary speech.

tables.caption_tr: 〜に足る vs. similar N1 'worthy of' expressions
rows: broadly 'worthy/sufficient enough' for a person, thing, or action; formal, literary
信頼[しんらい]するに足[た]る人物[じんぶつ]
'deserving of' a specific value/reward/punishment; often praise or blame
称賛[しょうさん]に値[あたい]する行為[こうい]; an act deserving of praise
'able to withstand' / 'worth doing despite scrutiny' (e.g. viewing, reading, criticism)
鑑賞[かんしょう]にたえる作品[さくひん]; a work worth appreciating
footnotes_tr: 〜に足る and 〜に値する overlap heavily and are often interchangeable in the 'worthy of' sense, but 〜に値する leans toward concrete reward/praise/blame, while 〜に足る leans toward general sufficiency/qualification.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は信頼[しんらい]するに足[た]る人物[じんぶつ]だ。
examples.reading: かれはしんらいするにたるじんぶつだ。
examples.translation_tr: He is a person worthy of trust.

examples.target: この結果[けっか]は満足[まんぞく]するに足[た]るものではない。
examples.reading: このけっかはまんぞくするにたるものではない。
examples.translation_tr: This result is not something worthy of satisfaction.

examples.target: その提案[ていあん]は検討[けんとう]するに足[た]る価値[かち]がある。
examples.reading: そのていあんはけんとうするにたるかちがある。
examples.translation_tr: That proposal has value worth considering.

examples.target: 取[と]るに足[た]らない小[ちい]さな問題[もんだい]だ。
examples.reading: とるにたらないちいさなもんだいだ。
examples.translation_tr: It's a trivial little problem, not worth bothering about.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]の意見[いけん]は聞[き]くに足[た]りない。
examples.reading: かれのいけんはきくにたりない。
examples.translation_tr: His opinion isn't worth listening to.

examples.target: そんな噂[うわさ]は恐[おそ]れるに足[た]りない。
examples.reading: そんなうわさはおそれるにたりない。
examples.translation_tr: There's no need to fear rumors like that.

examples.target: 彼女[かのじょ]は尊敬[そんけい]するに足[た]る先生[せんせい]だった。
examples.reading: かのじょはそんけいするにたるせんせいだった。
examples.translation_tr: She was a teacher worthy of respect.

examples.target: この本[ほん]は一読[いちどく]に足[た]る内容[ないよう]だ。
examples.reading: このほんはいちどくにたるないようだ。
examples.translation_tr: This book's content is worth reading at least once.

beku-mo-nai.title_tr: 〜べくもない; "There's No Way to...," "Impossible to Even..." (N1)
beku-mo-nai.intro_tr: 〜べくもない is a formal, literary N1 expression built on the classical auxiliary べし, meaning "there is no way to..." or "it is completely impossible to even...". It attaches to the dictionary form of a verb (with する irregularly becoming the classical す before べく) and ends in the negative もない, literally "not even something one could do." Unlike a plain negative, it carries a nuance of resignation: the circumstances make the action so obviously out of reach that it is not even worth hoping for or attempting. It appears almost exclusively in written Japanese; news articles, essays, formal speeches, novels; and typically pairs with verbs of cognition or comparison such as 望む, 知る, 比べる, 及ぶ, and 想像する. Because it derives directly from classical grammar, it belongs to the same literary family as べからず, べからざる, and べき.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb (dictionary form) + べくもない
rows: there is no way to know
比[くら]べるべくもない
及[およ]ぶ → treated as godan (reach)
想像[そうぞう]すべくもない (classical す-stem; not 想像するべくもない in strict usage)
impossible to come (very rare, mostly classical texts)
footnotes_tr: With する-verbs, the traditional form drops する and attaches べく directly to the classical stem す: 期待すべくもない, 予測すべくもない. Modern casual writing sometimes uses 〜するべくもない, but the す form is considered the correct literary form.
This is a fixed, non-conjugating written pattern; the negative part is 〜もない, whose past tense is 〜もなかった.

tables.caption_tr: Core meaning and usage notes
rows: 'There is no way to...', 'It is completely impossible to even...'; the action lies so far outside reality that it is not even a realistic possibility
Stronger than a plain negative; conveys resignation; the speaker acknowledges the gap between hope/expectation and reality
Formal, literary written language (書[か]き言葉[ことば]); found in essays, news reports, novels, formal speeches; essentially never in casual conversation

wo-mono-tomo-sezu.intro_tr: 〜をものともせず (or the fuller 〜をものともせずに) is an N1-level written-style expression meaning "without being daunted by ~," "undeterred by ~," or "defying ~." It attaches to a noun that represents a difficulty, hardship, danger, or obstacle, and describes the subject heroically pushing forward as if that obstacle were nothing. Unlike more neutral expressions such as 〜にもかかわらず, this pattern always carries an admiring, positive nuance about the subject's courage; it is essentially the opposite in tone of 〜をよそに, which criticizes someone for coldly ignoring something. It shows up constantly in news reports, biographies, sports commentary, and formal narrative writing, but almost never in casual conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation patterns
rows: Noun + をものともせず + (comma), main clause
困難[こんなん]をものともせず、彼[かれ]は挑戦[ちょうせん]した。
Most common written form; often followed by a comma before the main clause
Noun + をものともせずに + verb phrase
病気[びょうき]をものともせずに、働[はたら]き続[つづ]けた。
Adds に, functioning like an adverbial phrase modifying the verb
Noun + をものともしない + Noun (modifies a following noun)
逆境[ぎゃっきょう]をものともしない選手[せんしゅ]
Dictionary-form negative, used attributively right before a noun
Noun + をものともせぬ + Noun (literary)
危険[きけん]をものともせぬ勇気[ゆうき]
Classical negative ぬ instead of ず; very literary/old-fashioned flavor

tables.caption_tr: Typical nouns that combine with 〜をものともせず
rows: the eyes/judgment of those around one

tables.caption_tr: 〜をものともせず compared to similar N1 expressions
rows: 台風[たいふう]をものともせず出航[しゅっこう]した。
Ignores something one should be concerned about
周囲[しゅうい]の心配[しんぱい]をよそに、彼[かれ]は旅立[たびだ]った。
雨[あめ]にもかかわらず、試合[しあい]は行[おこな]われた。
Pushes through despite one's own poor condition

tables.caption_tr: Key grammatical and usage notes
rows: Written, formal, literary style; found in news, biographies, essays; almost never in casual speech
Only a noun (or noun phrase); never a verb or adjective directly; verbs must first be nominalized if needed
An active, positive achievement verb: 成功[せいこう]する, 乗[の]り越[こ]える, 進[すす]む, やり遂[と]げる, 出場[しゅつじょう]する, etc.
Almost always an animate, willful subject (a person, team, company) displaying courage or resolve
What NOT to use it for
Neutral facts with no admirable struggle involved; use 〜にもかかわらず instead in those cases
〜をものともしない; same meaning, used adjectivally directly before a noun instead of adverbially before a clause
Literally 'not even treating ~ as a thing (もの)'; i.e., not regarding the obstacle as worth worrying about

wo-yoso-ni.title_tr: 〜をよそに (paying no heed to…, disregarding…)
wo-yoso-ni.intro_tr: 〜をよそに attaches to a noun (usually one expressing worry, opposition, expectation, criticism, or a surrounding situation) to mean "paying no heed to N," "ignoring N," or "in disregard of N." It describes a subject who acts without caring about, or seemingly oblivious to, feelings or circumstances that would normally be expected to influence their behavior. The tone is literary and often carries a nuance of criticism or surprise toward the subject's indifference. It is commonly found in news reports, essays, and narrative writing rather than casual speech. Unlike neutral contrast markers such as 〜にもかかわらず, をよそに almost always implies that someone else's feelings, warnings, or a notable situation are being brushed aside.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure
rows: paying no heed to N / ignoring N / in disregard of N
Noun + をよそに + して
N + をよそにして、[main clause]
same meaning, slightly more formal/emphatic variant
footnotes_tr: The noun before をよそに is almost always someone else's feeling, warning, or a notable surrounding circumstance; not the speaker's own effort or hardship.

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocation Nouns
Comparison: をよそに vs. Similar Grammar
rows: usually someone else's feeling or a surrounding situation
家族[かぞく]の心配[しんぱい]をよそに、彼[かれ]は旅[たび]に出[で]た。
overcoming a difficulty without being stopped by it, admirable tone
病気[びょうき]をものともせず、彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]を続[つづ]けた。
any fact or condition, no emotional coloring
雨[あめ]にもかかわらず、試合[しあい]は行[おこな]われた。
everyday 'even though', can express disappointment/surprise, casual register
頑張[がんば]ったのに、失敗[しっぱい]した。
footnotes_tr: をものともせず frames the subject as brave/persevering; をよそに frames the subject as indifferent/uncaring; they are not interchangeable even though both translate roughly as 'in spite of'.

tables.caption_tr: Usage Restrictions & Notes
rows: Literary and written; typical of news reports, essays, novels; rarely used in casual conversation
The noun usually expresses feelings/warnings belonging to people OTHER than the main-clause subject, or a general situation surrounding the subject
Cannot naturally replace をものともせず: avoid using をよそに with one's own illness, pain, or personal struggle as the noun
Typically describes an action, especially one that seems bold, reckless, calm, or surprising given the disregarded circumstance
The main clause is descriptive/narrative; it does not naturally end with commands like 〜てください or 〜ましょう
Psychological nouns (心配, 不安, 期待, 反対, 批判) or situational nouns (不況, 混乱, 台風)

nai-mademo.title_tr: 〜ないまでも (Even If Not... At Least...)
nai-mademo.intro_tr: 〜ないまでも is an N1-level written/formal expression meaning "even if (something) doesn't go as far as ~" or "though not quite ~, at least...". It sets up a high or ideal benchmark in the first clause that the speaker admits is NOT being reached or is not necessary, and then presents a lower, more realistic or minimum expectation in the second clause. It literally builds on 〜ない (negative) + まで (to the extent of) + も (even), so the core image is "even without reaching the extent of X". This pattern is common in essays, speeches, and formal writing to soften a demand or admit a limitation while still asserting a meaningful minimum. The second clause very often contains words like せめて (at least), 少なくとも (at the very least), or a modal like 〜たい/〜べきだ/〜ほうがいい, reinforcing the "minimum acceptable line" nuance.

tables.caption_tr: Formation patterns
rows: Negative plain form (〜ない) + までも
話[はな]す → 話[はな]さない
話[はな]さないまでも (even without going so far as to speak)
Negative plain form (〜くない) + までも
高[たか]い → 高[たか]くない
高[たか]くないまでも (even if not [that] expensive)
〜でないまでも / 〜ではないまでも
上手[じょうず]だ → 上手[じょうず]でない
上手[じょうず]でないまでも (even if not skillful)
〜でないまでも / 〜ではないまでも
プロではないまでも (even if not a professional)
普通形[ふつうけい] + とは言[い]わないまでも
行[い]く → 行[い]くとは言[い]わない
行[い]くとは言[い]わないまでも (I wouldn't go so far as to say 'go', but...)

tables.caption_tr: Internal logic of the sentence (Clause A ないまでも, Clause B)
rows: States an ideal / high / extreme benchmark that is explicitly NOT required or NOT being met
毎日, 完璧, 合格, プロ並み, 感謝される, etc. (a high standard)
States the realistic minimum that IS expected, hoped for, or asserted
Often paired with せめて, 少なくとも, 最低限, or ends in 〜たい/〜べきだ/〜ほしい/〜ほうがいい
"Even if we don't reach A, B should still hold"
Softens a request while still setting a firm minimum line

tables.caption_tr: 〜ないまでも vs. similar N1 grammar
rows: Even if not reaching X, at least Y (minimum standard asserted)
Always implies a MINIMUM that must still be met in clause B
There's no need to go as far as ~ (unnecessary action)
No comparison to a lesser alternative; just says the action is unnecessary
Neutral, no implication of 'a lesser but still meaningful degree'; lacks the formal register
It doesn't quite reach the level of ~, but...
Nearly synonymous, slightly more colloquial than 〜ないまでも
Concedes a point rather than setting an unmet high bar with a required minimum
States something that DID happen/is true, not a hypothetical unmet standard

wa-oroka.title_tr: 〜はおろか (let alone…, not to mention…)
wa-oroka.intro_tr: 〜はおろか is an N1-level emphatic pattern meaning "let alone ~, not even ~" or "far from ~, not even ~." It takes an extreme or higher-level item (X), states it as obviously out of the question, and then adds an even more basic or lower-level item (Y) that turns out to be impossible or untrue as well; almost always followed by a negative predicate marked with も, さえ, or すら. It is stronger and more formal than どころか, and is commonly found in written Japanese, news reports, and formal speech to stress how bad, extreme, or unexpected a situation is. Because the sentence structure builds from "big/hard thing" down to "small/easy thing," getting the order of X and Y right is essential; reversing them produces an illogical sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation of 〜はおろか
rows: Noun / Noun phrase / Verb (dictionary form) + こと
はおろか connects directly after a noun; verbs must first be nominalized with こと
States the obviously-impossible or clearly-true extreme case first
[basic/lower item] + も・さえ・すら + ない/なかった/できない, etc.
The second, more basic item is negated to emphasize the whole situation is bad
A rare positive use exists (Y is also true, emphasizing how impressive X is), but negative is by far the standard pattern
More literary and forceful than どころか; common in news, essays, complaints, narration

tables.caption_tr: Core sentence pattern and logical structure
rows: X はおろか、Y も〜ない
Not only is X impossible/not the case, even Y (something easier/more basic) is not the case
Can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji
X はおろか、Y さえ〜ない
Same as above, さえ adds slightly stronger emphasis on Y
Can't even stand, let alone walk
X はおろか、Y すら〜ない
Most formal/literary variant, often in written narration
Wasn't even allowed a phone call, let alone visitors
Verb こと はおろか、Verb こと も〜ない
Used when comparing two actions rather than two nouns
Can't even stand, let alone walk

tables.caption_tr: はおろか vs. similar 'let alone / not even' expressions
rows: Strong, decisive 'needless to say X, not even Y'; X is treated as self-evidently impossible
Emphasizing severity of a bad situation
'Far from X, actually Y'; often contrasts X with an opposite or unexpected reality; can be positive or negative
No; can be positive or negative
Neutral, common in speech and writing
Correcting an assumption; showing an unexpected reverse situation
'Even Y'; marks a single extreme example, no explicit first item X required
Usually negative, but can be positive
General emphasis on a minimum case
Literary equivalent of さえ, more formal and forceful
'X is impressive enough, but Y as well'; normally positive, opposite polarity focus from はおろか
Praising two things, with the second being equally or more notable

tables.caption_tr: Typical words and situations used before はおろか
column_headers: Example words before はおろか
rows: 漢字[かんじ], 英語[えいご], 運転[うんてん]
漢字[かんじ]はおろか、ひらがなも読[よ]めない

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes with 〜はおろか
rows: Using a positive predicate after Y
はおろか almost always requires a negative predicate on the second clause; a bare positive breaks the 'not even' logic
漢字[かんじ]はおろか、ひらがなも読[よ]めない (not 読[よ]める)
はおろか must present the harder/more extreme item first, then the easier/more basic item second; reversing makes the sentence illogical

Omitting も／さえ／すら on Y

...ひらがなも読[よ]めない, not ...ひらがなは読[よ]めない
Using it in casual daily conversation
はおろか is bookish/formal; native speakers rarely use it in casual chat, preferring どころか or さえ
Prefer どころか/さえ in casual speech; keep はおろか for writing or formal speech

sura.intro_tr: 〜すら is a literary/formal equivalent of さえ, meaning "even." It presents an extreme, minimal, or unexpected example to emphasize that if even THIS is true, then everything else is naturally true (or false) too; the classic "even X, let alone Y" logic. It appears mostly in written Japanese, formal speech, essays, and news, and pairs very strongly with negative predicates (〜すら〜ない) for maximum emotional or rhetorical force. Because it belongs to N1-level literary register, casual conversation almost always uses さえ or でも instead.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns of 〜すら
rows: 彼[かれ][の]なまえ[すら]しらない。
せんもんか[ですら]わからない。
More formal / polite variant, common in speeches and writing
Noun + すら + ない form
かんがえること[すら]なかった。
Used to nominalize a verb before すら
しにたい[と][すら]おもった。
'There is even the case that...'; extreme positive/negative claim
を/が/は dropped, other particles kept (に, で, と remain)
かれ[に][すら]はなさなかった。
When the noun already takes に, で, と, すら attaches after that particle instead of replacing it

tables.caption_tr: 〜すら vs さえ vs でも vs まで; Comparing 'Even'
rows: Cites an extreme minimal example; rhetorical, often dramatic
かれ[は]なまえ[すら]かけない。
Same core meaning as すら but usable in everyday speech
かれ[は]なまえ[さえ]かけない。
Emphasizes reaching a surprising extra extreme ('even to the point of')
かれ[は]わたし[の][ぶん][まで]たべた。

tables.caption_tr: Common Collocations with 〜すら
rows: かんがえ[すら]しなかった

すら clause + まして/いわんや + comparison

dani.intro_tr: 〜だに is a classical/literary particle that survives in modern written Japanese as an extreme-case minimizer, similar in spirit to さえ or すら but carrying a much stronger literary, almost archaic flavor. It attaches to a noun or the dictionary form of a verb; very often verbs of thinking or imagining such as 想像[そうぞう]する, 考[かんが]える, 思[おも]う, 予想[よそう]する; and is nearly always paired with a negative predicate, giving the meaning "not even X" or "X is unthinkable." Less commonly, it appears without negation in emotional, exclamatory statements, meaning "the mere act of X-ing is enough to cause [some strong feeling]." In practice, 〜だに is largely fossilized into a small set of fixed expressions (想像だにしない, 夢にだに思わない, 微動だにしない, 一顧だに値しない) and is mainly important for reading comprehension of formal writing, news reports, and literature rather than for everyday speech production.

tables.caption_tr: Two Core Patterns of 〜だに
rows: Noun / Verb(dictionary form) + だに + …ない (negative predicate)
想像[そうぞう]だにしなかった (never even imagined it)
Verb(dictionary form) + だに + emotional adjective (no negation)
"the mere act/thought of ~ing is enough to be [feeling]"
聞[き]くだに恐[おそ]ろしい (frightening just to hear)
footnotes_tr: Pattern A is by far the more common of the two in modern written Japanese.
Pattern B is largely restricted to fixed literary phrases (考えるだに, 思い出すだに, 聞くだに + emotion word).

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Fixed Expressions with 〜だに
rows: cannot even imagine / never even imagined
ゆめにだにおもわない
かんがえるだにおそろしい
いっこだにあたいしない
いっしゅんだにゆだんしない
doesn't let their guard down even for a moment

tables.caption_tr: 〜だに vs. Similar "Even" Expressions (すら, さえ, でも)
rows: Almost always negative, or exclamatory without negation
Limited to a small set of fixed phrases; strongest literary flavor of the four; not used to form new sentences freely
More productive than だに; still clearly formal/written register
Most common and productive of the group; usable in both writing and careful speech
Everyday spoken equivalent; the default choice in conversation
footnotes_tr: All four can be glossed as "even ~" but differ sharply in register; だに should be recognized in reading, not necessarily produced in speech.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Rules for 〜だに
rows: 想像[そうぞう] + だに → 想像だに(しない)
聞[き]く + だに → 聞くだに(恐ろしい)
夢[ゆめ] + にだに → 夢にだに(思わない)
footnotes_tr: The にだに variant adds extra emphasis and is common in the fixed phrase 夢にだに思わない.

koso-sure.title_tr: 〜こそすれ (Emphatic Contrast: "If Anything A, Never B")
koso-sure.intro_tr: 〜こそすれ is a formal, literary (bungo-derived) N1 pattern used to emphatically affirm one side of a contrast while flatly denying the other: "If anything, S is/does A; and certainly NOT B." It descends from the classical kakari-musubi construction, in which the particle こそ forces the sentence-final verb into its izenkei (realis) form; here すれ, the izenkei of classical する; before the sentence continues into a strongly negative second clause. It is not a conditional ("even if... never"); rather, it is a rhetorical device for rejecting a possible misunderstanding by first conceding/asserting the true (positive) state of affairs. You will meet it in speeches, editorials, business writing, and formal essays, almost always paired with a clear negative predicate later in the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Patterns
rows: 感謝[かんしゃ]こそすれ、批判[ひはん]はしない
I only feel gratitude, never criticism
Ordinary verb (ます-stem used as noun)
Vます-stem + こそすれ、〜ない
手伝[てつだ]いこそすれ、邪魔[じゃま]はしない
I'll help, I'll never get in the way
Noun+する stem + こそすれ
尊敬[そんけい]こそすれ、軽蔑[けいべつ]などしない
I respect them, I never look down on them
重[おも]んじこそすれ、軽視[けいし]はしない
I hold it in high regard, I never dismiss it
footnotes_tr: こそすれ is always followed, later in the same sentence, by a clause with a negative predicate (〜ない, 〜はしない, 〜わけではない, 〜まい, 〜ものではない, etc.) that expresses the rejected/denied idea.

tables.caption_tr: Grammatical Structure: Why すれ, Not する?
rows: Adds strong emphatic focus to the preceding word/phrase ('indeed', 'precisely')
已然形 (izenkei) of classical する
The 'realis' conjugation form; classical Japanese required こそ to trigger izenkei instead of the plain 終止形 (shūshikei) する; this is 'kakari-musubi' agreement
Survives in modern formal Japanese as a set pattern meaning 'indeed does X (as opposed to Y)'
The sentence pivots into a negative clause that denies the alternative interpretation implied by X

tables.caption_tr: Common Negative Predicates Following 〜こそすれ
rows: 感謝[かんしゃ]こそすれ、恨[うら]みはない
There is gratitude, but definitely no resentment
尊敬[そんけい]こそすれ、軽蔑[けいべつ]はしない
I respect them; I certainly do not despise them
尊敬[そんけい]こそすれ、恨[うら]んだことはない
I've always respected him, never once resented him
重[おも]んじこそすれ、軽視[けいし]しているわけではない
It's not that they disregard it, if anything they value it
感謝[かんしゃ]こそすれ、忘[わす]れはすまい
I am grateful, and will surely never forget it
〜ものではない (it is not the kind of thing that...)
招[まね]きこそすれ、解決[かいけつ]するものではない
It invites (trouble), it is not the sort of thing that solves it

tables.caption_tr: 〜こそすれ vs. Similar Advanced Contrastive Patterns
rows: N/Vます-stem + こそすれ, then negative clause
'If anything A, definitely not B'; emphatic assertion of A while denying B; literary register
感謝[かんしゃ]こそすれ、非難[ひなん]はしない
'Precisely BECAUSE of X'; emphasizes a reason, not a contrast with a denial
親[おや]であればこそ、厳[きび]しく言[い]う
N/Adj + こそあれ, then contrast
Older sibling pattern using classical ある; 'there IS X, but...'; broader use with states rather than actions
多少[たしょう]の違[ちが]いこそあれ、本質[ほんしつ]は同[おな]じだ
'Even though/granted that X'; concedes a fact then adds a qualifying remark; no requirement for negative predicate
初心者[しょしんしゃ]とはいえ、ミスは許[ゆる]されない
'Although X'; plain concession, weaker emphasis, no kakari-musubi origin
合格[ごうかく]したものの、油断[ゆだん]はできない
'It's not that X'; a simple partial denial, often used as the closing half of こそすれ sentences
反対[はんたい]しているわけではない
footnotes_tr: 〜こそすれ is the most literary/formal of this group and is essentially restricted to written or highly formal spoken Japanese (speeches, essays, business documents).

examples.target: 新しい制度は問題を解決こそすれ、悪化させることはないだろう。

ba-koso.intro_tr: 〜ばこそ is a formal, literary N1 pattern built from the conditional ば-form plus the emphatic particle こそ. It means "precisely/only because..." and is used to single out one reason as the true, exclusive cause of something; rejecting the idea that any other reason could explain it. It is stronger and more literary than 〜からこそ, and unlike a normal 〜ば conditional, it does NOT express a hypothetical "if"; the reason clause is understood to be real and true. Sentences with 〜ばこそ very often end in 〜のだ/〜のです or simply 〜ばこそだ to explain or justify something. Because of its stiff, written-language feel, it is rare in casual conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: how to attach 〜ばこそ to each word type
rows: あなたを思[おも]えばこそ (precisely because I care about you)
彼[かれ]を信[しん]じればこそ (precisely because I believe in him)
努力[どりょく]する (to make an effort)
努力[どりょく]すればこそ
努力[どりょく]すればこそ (precisely because one makes an effort)
彼[かれ]が来[く]ればこそ (precisely because he comes)
若[わか]ければこそ (precisely because one is young)
健康[けんこう]であればこそ
健康[けんこう]であればこそ (precisely because one is healthy)
親[おや]であればこそ (precisely because one is a parent)
footnotes_tr: For na-adjectives and nouns, こそ never attaches directly (❌なばこそ); the copula である (or だ→であれば) must appear first: Xであればこそ.
Negative forms rarely take ばこそ directly; speakers normally switch to 〜ないからこそ instead of 〜なければこそ.

tables.caption_tr: 〜ばこそ vs. other reason-expressing grammar
rows: Singles out ONE reason as the true, exclusive cause; strongly emphatic
Essays, speeches, formal writing; ends in 〜のだ/〜ばこそだ
Emphasizes the reason but with less rhetorical weight; still clearly emphatic
Common in both speech and writing
General emphatic reason, everyday and formal contexts
Neutral, slightly more polite than から

tables.caption_tr: Typical sentence-final patterns used with 〜ばこそ
rows: Presents the emphasized reason as the explanation for the main clause
心配[しんぱい]すればこそ、注意[ちゅうい]するのです。(It is precisely because I worry that I warn you.)
Ends the sentence right after こそ + だ, meaning "it is precisely because..."
成功[せいこう]したのは努力[どりょく]すればこそだ。(His success is precisely because of his effort.)
Reason clause followed directly by the main clause, no のだ; more literary/terse
愛[あい]すればこそ、叱[しか]ることもある。(Precisely because I love them, I sometimes scold them.)

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and restrictions
rows: こそ cannot attach directly to a bare noun/na-adjective without である/だ
❌ 忙[いそが]しくないばこそ
Direct negative + ばこそ is very rare and sounds unnatural
✅ 忙[いそが]しくないからこそ
❌ Using 〜ばこそ in casual chat with friends
Too stiff and literary for everyday spoken Japanese
❌ Treating ばこそ as a hypothetical "if"
〜ばこそ marks a reason that IS true, not a hypothetical condition like normal 〜ば
✅ Understand it as "precisely because (this real fact is true)..."

examples.target: あなたのことを思[おも]えばこそ、厳[きび]しいことを言[い]うのです。
examples.reading: あなたのことをおもえばこそ、きびしいことをいうのです。

to-omoikiya.title_tr: 〜と思いきや (I thought that..., but contrary to expectations...)
to-omoikiya.intro_tr: 〜と思いきや means "I thought/assumed that..., but contrary to that..."; it introduces an expectation that turns out to be wrong, often with a dramatic, ironic, or humorous twist. It comes from the classical rhetorical expression 思わんや ("would one think so?; of course not!"), so the sense of surprise and reversal is built into the grammar point itself, unlike more neutral time-sequence patterns such as かと思うと. It attaches to the plain form of the assumed situation and is always followed by a clause stating the actual, unexpected outcome; it can never end a sentence on its own. This is an N1-level pattern common in essays, novels, news commentary, and lively spoken narration (storytelling, recounting surprising events).

tables.caption_tr: Formation: How to Attach と思いきや to Different Word Types
rows: Plain dictionary form + と思いきや
Plain た-form + と思いきや
難[むずか]しいと思いきや
Stem + だ + と思いきや
簡単[かんたん]だと思いきや
Noun + だ + と思いきや
学生[がくせい]だと思いきや
Plain form + かと思いきや
怒[おこ]るかと思いきや
footnotes_tr: The clause before と思いきや is always in the plain/short form. だ before と思いきや can be dropped in very casual speech, but is standard in writing.
Adding か (かと思いきや) softens the assumption into 'I thought maybe...'; extremely common in spoken narration.

tables.caption_tr: と思いきや vs. Similar 'Contrary to Expectation' Patterns
rows: I assumed X, but reality turned out opposite/different; often with a dramatic or ironic twist
Written and spoken narration; literary flavor
Just as X happened, Y happened right after (can be surprising, but can also be simple quick succession)
Even though one might say X, ... (concession with reasoning)
However, contrary to expectation... (starts a new sentence rather than joining a clause)
footnotes_tr: と思いきや is the only one of these that inherently guarantees a surprise; its meaning comes from classical 思わんや ('would one think so?; no!').

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Structure Pattern
rows: [Assumed situation] (plain form + だ if noun/な-adjective)
What the speaker believed or expected to be true
'I thought that...'; carries a built-in 'but actually no!' nuance
The reality that contradicts the assumption; this clause is mandatory
footnotes_tr: Example mapped to the pattern: 簡単[かんたん]だ(①) + と思いきや(②) + 意外[いがい]と難[むずか]しかった(③)。

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Usage Notes
rows: Must be followed by a contrasting clause
と思いきや cannot end a sentence; the actual, unexpected outcome must always follow.
✕ 簡単[かんたん]だと思いきや。 → ○ 簡単[かんたん]だと思いきや、意外[いがい]と難[むずか]しかった。
If the actual result matches the expectation (no surprise), と思いきや is unnatural; use 案[あん]の定[じょう] ('as expected') instead.
✕ 難[むずか]しいと思いきや、本当[ほんとう]に難[むずか]しかった。
Common in essays, novels, news commentary, and lively spoken storytelling; sounds more vivid/witty than plain かと思ったら.
Derived from classical 思わんや, a rhetorical question meaning 'would one think so?; of course not!' This is why the reversal meaning is built into the grammar point itself.

ya-ina-ya.intro_tr: 〜や否や is a highly formal, literary N1 pattern meaning "no sooner had ... than ..." or "the very instant ... happened...". It attaches to the dictionary (plain, non-past) form of a verb and links two events that follow each other with almost no gap in time. It appears almost exclusively in written narrative, news reports, novels, and formal essays to depict a vivid, sudden chain of events; it is never used in everyday spoken conversation. Both clauses must describe actual, uncontrollable events (not requests, invitations, or the speaker's own future plans), and the whole sentence is normally understood as a completed past event even though the verb right before や否や stays in the dictionary (non-past) form. Literally, 否[いな] means "or not," so や否や preserves a classical Japanese structure roughly meaning "whether [X] or not [X], [Y] happened"; hence the strong sense of "the exact instant."

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb (dictionary/plain non-past form) + や否や
rows: 会う[あう]や否や[やいなや]
鳴る[なる]や否や[やいなや]
見る[みる]や否や[やいなや]
開く[あく]/開く[ひらく] (to open)
開く[ひらく]や否や[やいなや]
到着する[とうちゃくする] (to arrive)
到着する[とうちゃくする]や否や[やいなや]
来る[くる]や否や[やいなや]

tables.caption_tr: Key grammatical points and restrictions
rows: Dictionary (plain non-past) form of a verb only; never ます-form, ない-form, or た-form.
The two events happen essentially simultaneously; the gap between clause 1 and clause 2 is extremely short, often instantaneous.
Even though the verb before や否や is in dictionary form, the overall sentence is normally in the past (the second clause usually ends in 〜た).
Must describe an actual, already-occurred event. Cannot be a command (〜てください), invitation (〜ましょう), request, or the speaker's own volitional plan (〜つもりだ / 〜よう).
Subjects of clause 1 and clause 2 are often different (someone/something triggers, another party reacts), which heightens the sense of an unexpected chain reaction.
Extremely formal and literary; found in novels, newspapers, formal reports. Not used in daily conversation; use 〜たとたん(に) instead in speech.
Often implies surprise, drama, or a vivid, almost cinematic sequence of events.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with similar 'as soon as / no sooner than' patterns
rows: Emphasizes an almost simultaneous, dramatic chain of events
Must be a real, non-volitional past event
Vividly stresses the speed; 'as fast as / no sooner than'
Same restriction as や否や; no volition or command
First action is immediately followed by a second, often surprising action by the same subject
2nd clause = an actual, usually unexpected action, not the speaker's own will
The most natural, common way to say 'the instant ~'
2nd clause is usually unexpected or uncontrollable, but slightly more flexible than や否や
'As soon as ~, (I) will do ~'; used for future plans/requests
2nd clause is typically the speaker's own future action; opposite restriction from や否や

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes to avoid
rows: 使う[つかう]ます-form + や否や
や否や only attaches to the dictionary form, never ます-form
使う[つかう]や否や[やいなや] (not 使います[つかいます]や否や[やいなや])
Using や否や in casual conversation
It is a bookish, literary pattern; sounds unnatural or overly stiff in speech
Use 〜たとたん(に) or 〜てすぐ in daily conversation instead
や否や requires a completed, actual event in both clauses
Rewrite with a plain declarative past-tense clause, e.g. 〜た/〜だ, not 〜てください
や否や cannot describe intentional future action
Use 〜次第[しだい] for 'as soon as ~, I will ~' instead
Treating や否や as habitual/repeated action
や否や almost always describes a single, specific instance, not a repeated habit
For habitual immediacy use 〜と (e.g. 朝[あさ]起[お]きると顔[かお]を洗[あら]う)
