tari-tomo.intro_tr: 〜たりとも is a very formal, literary N1 pattern meaning "not even a single..." It attaches to a number + counter (typically 一, "one") and is almost always followed by a negative predicate, creating an emphatic, absolute denial that allows no exceptions whatsoever; stronger than everyday "even" expressions like さえ or でも. It commonly appears in solemn speeches, legal or official writing, formal announcements, and dramatic narration, but essentially never in casual conversation. A related form, 何人[なんぴと]たりとも, means "no one at all, whoever they may be," and is frequently used in legal or rule-like statements. Because the pattern is archaic in flavor, it often pairs with たとえ ("even if") for extra rhetorical weight.

rows: Number + Counter + たりとも + Negative predicate
一瞬[いっしゅん]たりとも〜ない
not even a single moment (do/is not)
何人[なんぴと]たりとも〜ない
no matter who it is, not a single person
たとえ + Number/Counter + たりとも

even if it's just a single day, ... not

rows: 一瞬[いっしゅん]たりとも
very common; paired with 気[き]を抜[ぬ]く, 油断[ゆだん]する
一日[いちにち]たりとも
一円[いちえん]たりとも
何人[なんぴと]たりとも

rows: A number + counter (一瞬, 一日, 一円, 一歩, 一人...) or 何 + counter (何人, 何事)

Written/literary, formal speeches, legal texts, solemn narration; not used in casual speech
Expresses total, uncompromising negation with zero exceptions; stronger than でも/さえ

narade-wa.title_tr: 〜ならではの (uniquely characteristic of..., something only X could do)
narade-wa.intro_tr: 〜ならではの is an N1-level expression used to praise something as being uniquely possible, achievable, or characteristic because of a specific person, place, or thing; and impossible to find or replicate anywhere else. It always carries a strongly positive, admiring nuance ("this could only exist thanks to X"), which sets it apart from more neutral expressions like 特有の or にしかない. Structurally, it attaches to nouns: N + ならでは + の + Noun when modifying a following noun, or N + ならでは + だ/です when ending a sentence. Historically ならでは came from a classical negative construction meaning "unless it is N," and that "nothing else could do this except N" logic is still the core of its modern positive meaning. This grammar point is common in tourism writing, product advertising, reviews, and speeches praising a person's unique talent.

tables.caption_tr: Core Meaning and Structure
rows: N1 ならでは の N2
N2 is something special that exists only because of N1; praises N1's uniqueness (most common form)
Noun + ならでは + だ/です
Sentence-final version; declares 'this is precisely what only N could produce/achieve'
Noun + ならではの + もの/こと
N ならでは の もの
Refers abstractly to 'a thing/quality that is unique to N'
N ならでは〜ない・まい
Archaic root meaning: 'unless it is N, ~not' → 'only N can do this' (rarely used in modern speech, mostly in old texts)

tables.caption_tr: Connection Rules
rows: Verb stem/noun form + ならでは
手作[てづく]り (from 手作[てづく]りする) + ならでは
Not used directly; needs a noun equivalent
× 美[うつく]しいならでは → use 美[うつく]しさならでは

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Similar Expressions
rows: Positive/admiring: something uniquely possible only because of X
職人[しょくにん]ならではの技[わざ] (a craftsman's own special skill)
Limited to the extent/qualification of X, not necessarily praise
大人[おとな]だけの特権[とっけん] (a privilege limited to adults)
Objective fact: physically only exists at/in X
ここにしかない味[あじ] (a taste that exists nowhere but here)
Characteristic/peculiar to X; neutral, often academic tone
日本[にほん]特有[とくゆう]の習慣[しゅうかん] (a custom peculiar to Japan)
Typical of, fitting the expected image of X
男[おとこ]らしい態度[たいど] (a manly attitude)

tables.caption_tr: Common Set Phrases with ならでは
rows: This too is something only possible because of ○○
a taste that only ○○ can offer

tables.caption_tr: Nuance Notes and Common Mistakes
rows: ならでは carries admiration or praise; it cannot be used to point out a negative unique trait (use 特有の instead for neutral/negative cases)
It cannot attach directly to a plain verb or い-adjective form; nominalize first (e.g., 作[つく]る → 手作[てづく]り, 美[うつく]しい → 美[うつく]しさ)
の is required before a following noun
When modifying a noun, dropping の (× Nならでは Noun) is ungrammatical; you must say N ならでは の Noun
だ/です replaces の at sentence end
When ending a sentence rather than modifying a noun, drop の and attach だ/です directly: N ならでは だ

ga-gotoshi.title_tr: 〜がごとし (as if..., classical literary simile)
ga-gotoshi.intro_tr: 〜がごとし (from Classical Japanese 如し gotoshi, "to be like/resemble") is a literary auxiliary meaning "as if...", "like...", "as though..."; the classical ancestor of the modern ようだ/みたいだ. It survives today only in formal writing, academic/legal prose, speeches, proverbs (ことわざ), and famous quotations, giving sentences a solemn, old-fashioned, or elevated tone. Like a classical adjective, ごとし has three key forms depending on its grammatical role: ごとし (sentence-final), ごとく (adverbial, modifies a verb/clause), and ごとき (attributive, modifies a noun). It attaches to nouns with の, and to verbs (often in old/negative forms) with が. You will almost never hear it in casual speech; it belongs to written, ceremonial, or quotation-style Japanese, and is closely related to 〜ごとき / 〜ごとく and 〜かのごとし.

tables.caption_tr: Basic formation: what attaches to ごとし
rows: N + の + ごとし/ごとく/ごとき
V(plain) + が + ごとし/ごとく/ごとき
V-ざる + が + ごとし
及[およ]ばざるがごとし
as if not reaching, i.e. as bad as falling short
V-たる + が + ごとし/ごとく
〜かの + ごとし/ごとく/ごとき
知[し]らないかのごとく
footnotes_tr: The が here is a classical subject/attributive particle, not the modern contrastive が.
たる is the classical attributive form of the copula たり, common in formal written register.

tables.caption_tr: The three forms of ごとし and their grammatical function
rows: Ends the sentence, like a predicate 'is like ~'
光陰[こういん]矢[や]の如[ごと]し。(Time is like an arrow.)
Modifies a following verb or clause: 'like ~, ...'
風[かぜ]の如[ごと]く走[はし]る (run like the wind)
女神[めがみ]の如[ごと]き美[うつく]しさ (beauty like a goddess')
footnotes_tr: This three-way split mirrors classical adjective conjugation (cf. 高し/高く/高き) and is the same pattern seen in 〜べし/べく/べき.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions and proverbs using ごとし
rows: 光陰[こういん]矢[や]の如[ごと]し
こういん やのごとし
過[す]ぎたるは猶[なお]及[およ]ばざるが如[ごと]し
すぎたるはなお およばざるがごとし
Excess is as bad as insufficiency
百聞[ひゃくぶん]は一見[いっけん]に如[し]かず
ひゃくぶんは いっけんにしかず
Seeing once beats hearing a hundred times
Note: 如かず here is a related but different verb (to be equal to), not ごとし itself
疾[と]きこと風[かぜ]の如[ごと]く
ときこと かぜのごとく
Part of Takeda Shingen's famous 風林火山 banner motto
前述[ぜんじゅつ]の如[ごと]く
ぜんじゅつの ごとく
Extremely common in formal reports/academic writing
かのごとし / かのごとく
かのごとし / かのごとく
Attaches after plain-form clauses to mean 'as though'

tables.caption_tr: Register comparison: がごとし vs modern equivalents
rows: Proverbs, classical quotations, ceremonial speech, legal/academic prose
述[の]べたるがごとく (as stated)
知[し]らないかのようだ (as if not knowing)
知[し]らないらしい (apparently doesn't know)
footnotes_tr: がごとし is a stylistic/literary choice, not a difference in core meaning from ようだ; native speakers reach for it to sound solemn, archaic, or academic.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and pitfalls
rows: Using 〜がごとし in casual conversation
It sounds unnaturally archaic/pompous in daily speech; native speakers will find it odd or comical outside formal/literary contexts
Use 〜かのようだ or 〜みたいだ instead in casual speech
Attaching が directly to a noun
が connects to verbs (plain/classical forms); nouns need の
Say 矢[や]の如[ごと]し, not 矢[や]がごとし
Confusing ごとし with 如[し]かず
如[し]かず (as in 百聞は一見に如かず) means 'is not as good as / doesn't compare to', a different classical verb, not a form of ごとし
Keep the two separate; they look similar but differ in meaning
Forgetting to switch forms (ごとし/ごとく/ごとき) based on position
Using ごとし mid-sentence before a noun or verb is grammatically wrong
Use ごとく before verbs, ごとき before nouns, ごとし only to end a clause/sentence

n-ga-tame.title_tr: 〜んがため(に); "in order to ~" (literary, classical-derived purpose expression)
n-ga-tame.intro_tr: 〜んがため(に) is a highly literary, classical-derived expression meaning "in order to ~" or "for the purpose of ~." It comes from Classical Japanese: the negative/volitional stem of a verb (未然形) + the archaic auxiliary ん (from む, expressing intention) + が (subordinating particle) + ため(に) ("for the sake of"). Unlike the neutral, everyday 〜ために, 〜んがため(に) carries a strong, often dramatic nuance of deliberate will, determination, effort, or even sacrifice; it is typically found in written narrative, speeches, historical/biographical writing, and formal or rhetorical prose, almost never in casual speech. It attaches only to verbs (not adjectives or nouns), and its attributive form 〜んがための is used directly before a noun.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb negative stem (未然形) + んがため(に)
Attributive use: 〜んがための + Noun
rows: Adverbial: expresses purpose within a sentence
生[い]きんがために働[はたら]く (work in order to live)
Attributive: directly modifies a following noun, meaning "N that exists/is done for the purpose of Ving"
勝[か]たんがための戦略[せんりゃく] (a strategy meant purely for winning)
Often included but can be dropped, especially before a comma/pause
生[い]きんがため、彼[かれ]は働[はたら]いた = 生[い]きんがために、彼[かれ]は働[はたら]いた

tables.caption_tr: 〜んがため(に) vs. similar purpose expressions
rows: Strong, deliberate intention; often implies effort, hardship, or sacrifice to achieve the goal; used in narrative/formal writing
General purpose or benefit; can be used with volitional or non-volitional verbs, and with nouns (Nのために)
Similar dramatic/formal purpose nuance, often paired with an action described as necessary or resolute; commonly seen with せんべく-type patterns is wrong; べく attaches to dictionary form, e.g. 勝つべく
Purpose with potential, non-volitional, or state verbs (e.g. わかるように, 忘れないように); cannot be used with plain volitional action verbs in the same way

tables.caption_tr: Key irregularities and things to watch for
rows: する → せんがため(に), never しんがため(に); this せ- comes from the classical negative form せず
来る → 来[こ]んがため(に), using the classical stem こ-, same as in 来[こ]ない
Cannot attach to い-adjectives, な-adjectives, or nouns directly; there is no adjective/noun equivalent of んがため(に)
んがため and んがために are both acceptable; に is more common before a following clause
Essentially confined to written/literary Japanese (speeches, novels, historical accounts, formal essays); would sound unnatural in everyday conversation

te-mae.title_tr: 〜てまえ / 〜手前 (Because of appearances/one's position, one has no choice but to…)
te-mae.intro_tr: 〜手前[てまえ] literally means "in front of" (its original, concrete meaning is the space just before/in front of something, as in 駅[えき]の手前[てまえ] "just before the station"). As a grammar pattern, it is grammaticalized to mean "given that X is a known fact (to other people, or because of my own words/position), I am now obliged to do Y / I cannot possibly do the opposite of Y." It always carries the nuance of social face, reputation, or self-consistency: because someone is watching, or because I already said/did something, backing down would be embarrassing or inconsistent, so the second clause almost always expresses restraint, obligation, or the impossibility of an action (〜ざるを得ない, 〜わけにはいかない, 〜ない, etc.). It is a fairly formal/written N1 pattern, close in meaning to 〜以上[いじょう] but with a stronger "can't lose face" flavor, and it is not used to describe someone else's psychological obligation in a neutral way; it's about self-imposed pressure from circumstances or one's own prior words.

tables.caption_tr: Connection patterns: how to attach 手前[てまえ]
rows: Verb, plain form (present, describing a habitual/ongoing fact)
客[きゃく]に出[だ]す手前[てまえ]、味見[あじみ]はしておく
Since I'm about to serve it to the customer, I taste it beforehand
Verb, plain past form (an action/statement already done; the most common case)
Verb (た form) + 手前[てまえ]
言[い]った手前[てまえ]、やめられない
Since I already said it (that I would do it), I can't back out
Noun (a person or group who is 'watching' / in front of whom face must be kept)
Noun + の + 手前[てまえ]
先生[せんせい]の手前[てまえ]、うそはつけない
In front of the teacher, I can't tell a lie
な-adjective + な + 手前[てまえ]
真面目[まじめ]な手前[てまえ]、遅刻[ちこく]はできない
Being (known as) a serious person, I can't be late
忙[いそが]しい手前[てまえ]、断[ことわ]るしかなかった
Given that I was busy, I had no choice but to refuse

tables.caption_tr: 〜手前[てまえ] vs. similar reason/circumstance patterns
rows: Because of appearances/face in front of someone, or because of my own prior words; I can't act otherwise
obligation / restraint (〜わけにはいかない, 〜ざるを得ない, 〜ない)
Given that a certain situation/fact holds; logically I must/should
obligation (〜べきだ, 〜なければならない)
Emphasizes the reason as THE precise reason (positive emphasis)

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations with 手前[てまえ]
rows: in front of the children (must set a good example)
in front of one's subordinates (must maintain authority)
in front of the teacher (must keep up appearances)
in front of the customer(s) (professional face)
約束[やくそく]した手前
since I already agreed to take it on
立場[たちば]上[じょう]の手前
たちばじょうのてまえ

tables.caption_tr: Typical clause-final patterns paired with 〜手前[てまえ]
rows: 'cannot possibly / there's no way I can'
やめるわけにはいかない (can't quit)
認[みと]めざるを得ない (have no choice but to admit it)
弱音[よわね]は吐[は]けない (can't show weakness)
obligation that follows from the 'face' situation
笑顔[えがお]でいなければならない (must keep smiling)
admitting something is hard to do
言[い]いにくい (hard to say)

examples.target: 子供[こども]の手前[てまえ]、弱音[よわね]は吐[は]けない。

examples.translation_tr: Given my position in front of my subordinates, I can't admit that I failed.

examples.reading: ひきうけたてまえ、とちゅうでやめるわけにはいかない。
examples.translation_tr: Since I already agreed to take it on, there's no way I can quit halfway through.

examples.translation_tr: Having made such big claims, I can't turn around now and say I can't do it.

examples.translation_tr: Because customers are watching, staff must always keep a smiling face.

examples.target: 約束[やくそく]した手前[てまえ]、行[い]かないわけにはいかない。
examples.reading: やくそくしたてまえ、いかないわけにはいかない。
examples.translation_tr: Since I promised, I have no choice but to go.

examples.target: 一度[いちど]引[ひ]き受[う]けた手前[てまえ]、今更[いまさら]断[ことわ]れない。
examples.reading: いちどひきうけたてまえ、いまさらことわれない。
examples.translation_tr: Having accepted the job once, I can't very well refuse it now.

to-atte.intro_tr: 〜とあって means "since it is [a special/noteworthy circumstance], naturally/understandably...". It introduces a notable, unusual, or special situation and then states the natural, expected consequence that follows from it; the nuance is "given that this special thing is the case, it's only to be expected that...". It is common in news reports, narration, and descriptive writing, and almost always describes an observable fact or state, never a command, request, or the speaker's own will. It attaches to nouns, na-adjectives, i-adjectives, and verbs in their plain form, and the clause that follows must be a description of a resulting fact or state; this is a purely written/narrative, formal (N1) pattern, distinct from casual conversational connectors like から or ので.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: what 〜とあって attaches to
rows: Stem (+である optional) + とあって
有名[ゆうめい](である)とあって
珍[めずら]しいとあって
Plain form (often 〜ている/〜た) + とあって
増[ふ]えているとあって

tables.caption_tr: 〜とあって vs. similar reason/circumstance patterns
rows: No; result clause only, no imperative/volitional
If it is the case that... (hypothetical, 'if that's so')
Subjective/direct reason given by the speaker
Yes; freely used with commands, invitations, will
Objective, polite reason, softer than から
Reason tied to social obligation/face, 'because of the position I'm in'

tables.caption_tr: Typical clause-final patterns after 〜とあって (result must be descriptive, not a command)
rows: 列[れつ]ができた (a line formed)
〜がなかった/〜が尽[つ]きなかった (negative state)
Describes an unending or absent state as a natural result
話[はなし]が尽[つ]きなかった (the talk never ran out)
Describes a natural change resulting from the circumstance
厳重[げんじゅう]になった (became tightened)

tables.caption_tr: Restrictions and common mistakes
rows: No commands/requests after とあって
The following clause must state a fact/result, not tell someone to do something
*祭[まつ]りとあって、来[き]てください
Cannot end with a request (〜てください)
No speaker's own volition after とあって
Cannot express the speaker's own intention/決意 with 〜よう/〜つもり
*休[やす]みとあって、旅行[りょこう]しようと思う (as main reasoning) is unnatural for this pattern's descriptive use
とあって describes external/observed natural consequences, not the speaker's personal plan
Ordinary, unremarkable facts sound odd with とあって compared to から/ので
?ご飯[はん]を食[た]べたとあって、お腹[なか]がいっぱいだ
Eating and being full is too mundane; とあって suits noteworthy situations (festivals, rare events, famous people, etc.)
Rare in casual daily conversation; sounds like a news report or formal narration
(casual chat) 今日[きょう]、雨[あめ]とあって、傘[かさ]持[も]った
In casual speech, から/ので is far more natural; とあって feels overly formal here

to-areba.title_tr: 〜とあれば (Given That... / If It's the Case That...)
to-areba.intro_tr: 〜とあれば is a formal, literary N1 pattern meaning "if it turns out to be the case that...", "given that...", or "supposing that...". It sets up a condition and then states that, given that condition, the speaker (or a strongly implied subject) is willing to take extreme, unusual, or resolute action. Unlike neutral conditionals like なら or ば, とあれば carries a nuance of "no matter how difficult, if this is the situation, I will act"; it almost always pairs with statements of strong resolve, sacrifice, or willingness. It attaches directly to nouns, quoted clauses, and plain-form verbs/adjectives, and is common in speeches, narration, news reports, and dramatic/emphatic written or spoken register; rarely used in casual daily conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: what can precede とあれば
rows: 必要[ひつよう]とあれば
忙[いそが]しいとあれば
必要[ひつよう]だとあれば
だ is often dropped: 必要とあれば
行[い]けということとあれば
Noun/Clause + のため + とあれば
子供[こども]のためとあれば
Very common set pattern: 'if it's for the sake of X'
footnotes_tr: とあれば comes historically from と + あれば (the classical conditional of ある), literally 'if it is the case that...'.

tables.caption_tr: とあれば vs. similar conditional patterns
rows: If it's the case that X, [I am willing to do something extreme/resolute]
必要[ひつよう]とあれば手伝[てつだ]います
Neutral hypothetical/known condition, 'if it's the case'
必要[ひつよう]ならば手伝[てつだ]います
Purely hypothetical assumption, no resolve implied
必要[ひつよう]だとすれば、どうする？
Formal equivalent of なら, states a condition plainly
必要[ひつよう]であれば、ご連絡[れんらく]ください
Similar to とあれば but focuses on a situation arising/becoming true, less resolve-heavy
戦争[せんそう]となれば、大変[たいへん]なことになる
'given that...' with a negative/troublesome result implied
そこまで言[い]われたとあっては黙[だま]っていられない
footnotes_tr: とすれば and であれば are more neutral; とあれば almost always implies the speaker will go to great lengths as a result.

tables.caption_tr: Typical follow-up expressions after 〜とあれば (expressing extreme willingness)
rows: どんな苦労[くろう]も惜[お]しまない
いつでも駆[か]けつける
命[いのち]をかけても守[まも]る
行[い]かないわけにはいかない
行[い]かないわけにはいかない
footnotes_tr: These strong-resolve phrases are what typically complete a とあれば sentence, reinforcing its dramatic, all-in nuance.

tables.caption_tr: Common learner mistakes
rows: Using とあれば in casual daily speech
とあれば is a formal/literary pattern; sounds unnatural in casual chat
Use なら or だったら instead in casual speech
Adding ば again: 〜とあればば
あれば already contains the conditional ば; no further ば needed
必要[ひつよう]とあれば (not 必要とあればば)
Treating とあれば as purely neutral like とすれば
とあれば usually implies a strong, resolute reaction will follow
Reserve とあれば for contexts with a resolve/sacrifice statement afterward
Forgetting だ before とあれば with な-adjectives/nouns in some formal contexts
Both 必要とあれば and 必要だとあれば are acceptable; but adjective stems without だ sound incomplete in careful writing
必要[ひつよう](だ)とあれば; either is fine, だ optional

mo-sarukoto-nagara.title_tr: 〜もさることながら (Not to mention A, but B even more so)
mo-sarukoto-nagara.intro_tr: 〜もさることながら is a formal, written-register N1 expression meaning roughly "A is certainly true/notable, but B is even more so" or "not to mention A, but also B." It always attaches to a NOUN (or a nominalized phrase), and its core function is to acknowledge the first point (A) as valid or impressive, then shift the spotlight to a second point (B) that is presented as equally or more significant. Unlike negating patterns such as 〜どころか, it does NOT deny or dismiss A; both A and B remain true and positive (or both negative, in critical contexts). It is common in reviews, formal speeches, essays, and business writing, but rare in casual conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Formation Patterns
rows: Noun A + もさることながら、Noun B + も〜
味[あじ]もさることながら、見[み]た目[め]も〜
Direct attachment; the most common pattern
stem (as noun) + もさることながら
静[しず]かさもさることながら〜
Use the noun-stem form, often via 〜さ
stem+さ / 〜いこと + もさることながら
美[うつく]しさもさることながら〜 / 美[うつく]しいこともさることながら〜
Must be nominalized first; cannot attach directly to 〜い
dictionary form + こと + もさることながら
努力[どりょく]することもさることながら〜
footnotes_tr: The clause after もさることながら almost always contains a corresponding も, explicitly marking the second element as an addition to the first.

tables.caption_tr: Core Meaning Structure: A もさることながら、B も〜
rows: A (before もさることながら)
Presented as true, valid, and worth mentioning; NOT denied or dismissed
Literally 'being a matter of course,' i.e. 'that goes without saying, but...'
Presented as equally important or even MORE significant than A
'Not only A, but B as well (and B stands out even more)'
Both A and B are affirmed; the sentence highlights B without erasing A

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Similar N1 Patterns
rows: A is true, but B is even more notable
味[あじ]もさることながら、盛[も]り付[つ]けも見事[みごと]だ。
A is not just insufficient; reality is the opposite/extreme of A
Yes; often reverses or negates A
安[やす]いどころか、むしろ高[たか]い。
Not even A, let alone B (usually negative context)
Yes; A is dismissed as too basic/obvious
漢字[かんじ]はおろか、ひらがなも読[よ]めない。
Not only A, but also B (neutral addition)
No; but does not emphasize B over A specifically
彼[かれ]は語学[ごがく]のみならず、数学[すうがく]にも優[すぐ]れている。
In addition to A, also B (simple additive)
No; purely additive, no emphasis shift
経験[けいけん]に加[くわ]えて、資格[しかく]も必要[ひつよう]だ。
footnotes_tr: Key distinction: only 〜もさることながら keeps A fully valid while shifting emphasis to B; 〜どころか and 〜はおろか involve negation or dismissal of A.

い-adjectives must be nominalized via さ or こと
美[うつく]しさもさることながら / 美[うつく]しいこともさることながら
Using it to mean 'A is false, B is true' (like どころか)
もさることながら never negates A; both A and B stay valid
Use 〜どころか or 〜はおろか instead if A must be denied

This is a formal, written-register expression, rarely heard in everyday chat
In casual speech, prefer 〜も〜けど、それより〜 or similar plain patterns
Omitting the second も after B
The pairing も...も is what creates the 'both, but B more so' meaning
Always include も (or an equivalent) marking B: Bも〜

bekarazaru.intro_tr: 〜べからざる is the pre-noun (attributive) form of the classical auxiliary べし combined with the classical negative ざる, literally meaning "that must not / cannot be ~ed." It always attaches directly in front of a noun, turning the whole phrase into a formal, literary modifier; unlike its sentence-final cousin 〜べからず, which appears on public notices like 立入るべからず ("No Entry"). 〜べからざる survives almost exclusively in fixed, high-register collocations (許すべからざる, 欠くべからざる, 侵すべからざる) found in formal writing, speeches, legal/moral statements, and idiomatic set phrases; it is not freely productive with any verb. As an N1 item, the priority is recognizing the pattern and memorizing the handful of common fixed expressions rather than generating new ones freely.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Verb (dictionary form) + べからざる + Noun
rows: 許すべからざる行為[こうい]
欠くべからざる存在[そんざい]
侵すべからざる権利[けんり]
語るべからざる秘密[ひみつ]
a secret that must not be told
触れるべからざる領域[りょういき]
a domain that must not be touched
すべからざる行動[こうどう]
conduct that must not be done
footnotes_tr: Attaches to the plain dictionary (終止形/しゅうしけい) form of the verb, exactly like べし/べからず.
する is irregular: it becomes すべからざる (not するべからざる), a classical remnant, mirroring すべき/すべからず.
Ichidan and godan verbs both simply take the bare dictionary form + べからざる; there is no euphonic change.

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed collocations (memorize these as set phrases)
rows: secret that must not be spoken
a secret that must never be told
触れるべからざる領域
area that must not be touched
軽視すべからざる事実
fact that must not be lightly regarded
a fact that cannot be taken lightly
見過ごすべからざる問題
problem that must not be overlooked
a problem that cannot be ignored

tables.caption_tr: べからざる vs. related classical/literary forms
rows: "that must not/cannot be ~ed"; modifies the following noun
許すべからざる行為[こうい] (an unforgivable act)
立入[たちい]るべからず (No Entry)
力[ちから]を尽[つ]くすべし (One must exert all effort)
modern attributive form of べし: "that should be ~ed"
すべき行動[こうどう] (action that should be taken)
"unbecoming of / that should never be done", used with こと/行為/態度
許すまじき行為[こうい] (an inexcusable act; near-synonym of 許すべからざる)
footnotes_tr: べからざる and べき are structurally parallel (attributive), but べき expresses positive obligation while べからざる expresses prohibition/impossibility.
べからざる and まじき are near-synonyms in modern literary style; まじき tends to pair with a narrower set of nouns (こと, 行為, 態度, 言葉).

tables.caption_tr: Nuance and register notes
rows: Expresses that something is prohibited, impossible, or unacceptable; a strong negative judgment placed directly on the noun it modifies.
Very formal/literary (文語); used in speeches, legal or moral pronouncements, editorials, and set idiomatic phrases; essentially never in casual speech.
Modern usage is largely limited to a closed set of fixed expressions (許すべからざる, 欠くべからざる, etc.); coining new combinations sounds unnatural except in intentionally archaic/formal writing.
Do not confuse with 〜べからず (sentence-final, used for prohibition notices); べからざる can NEVER end a sentence; it must be followed by a noun.
Do not attach べからざる to the ます-stem or て-form; it takes the plain dictionary form, just like べし/べからず.

gatera.title_tr: 〜しな / 〜がてら; "while doing / on the way, combining two purposes"
gatera.intro_tr: 〜しな and 〜がてら are two related but distinct N1-level patterns that describe an action happening "in the course of" or "on the occasion of" another action. 〜しな attaches to the masu-stem of a verb and appears mostly in a small set of fixed, slightly old-fashioned or literary expressions meaning "just as one is doing X" (e.g. 行きしな "on the way there"). 〜がてら also attaches to the masu-stem of a verb (or directly to certain nouns) but has a broader, still-productive use meaning "while doing A, also doing B"; the two actions are accomplished together in a single trip or occasion, with A being the ostensible main purpose and B a convenient add-on. Neither pattern is common in casual speech; both belong to written or slightly formal registers and are frequently tested for reading comprehension rather than active production. Because 〜しな's vocabulary is largely fixed, it is best learned as a short list of set phrases, while 〜がてら behaves more like a productive grammar pattern that can combine with many verbs of movement or activity.

tables.caption_tr: Formation rules
rows: 動詞[どうし]ます形[けい] + しな
just as/while doing A (fixed expressions only)

動詞[どうし]ます形[けい] + がてら
Name[めいし] + がてら
while doing A, also doing B (two purposes, one occasion)

tables.caption_tr: Common fixed expressions with 〜しな (this list is essentially closed; new coinages are rare)
rows: on the way there / just as one is leaving
on the way back / just as one is returning
just as one is going out / leaving
just as one is standing up
just as one is passing by

tables.caption_tr: がてら vs. similar 'while / on the occasion of' patterns

Two actions performed simultaneously by the same subject, ongoing and parallel (no purpose combining)

Doing B by taking convenient advantage of already doing A; more casual, everyday

Very formal/business version of がてら, often in written greetings and letters
ご挨拶[あいさつ]かたがたお伺[うかが]いします
Marks the occasion/timing of a formal event, not two combined purposes
開会[かいかい]に際して一言[ひとこと]申[もう]し上[あ]げます

koto-to-natte-iru.title_tr: 〜こととなっている (It Is Established/Provided That..., as a Rule)
koto-to-natte-iru.intro_tr: 〜こととなっている is a stiff, written-register pattern that states something has been officially established as a rule, regulation, custom, or fixed arrangement; roughly "it is provided that..." or "as a rule, it is the case that...". Structurally it is 〜こととなる (the formal counterpart of 〜ことになる, "it has been decided/turns out that...") combined with the resultant-state 〜ている, so it describes a decision or regulation that is currently in force, not the moment of deciding. It shows up constantly in laws, contracts, official manuals, bylaws, and news reports, but almost never in casual conversation, where 〜ことになっている is used instead. Because the subject of the "deciding" is left vague (nobody says who decided), the sentence sounds objective, impersonal, and authoritative; perfect for describing systems and rules rather than personal plans.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Formation: How 〜こととなっている Attaches
rows: V-る + こととなっている
会議[かいぎ]は毎週[まいしゅう]開[ひら]くこととなっている
It is established that the meeting is held every week
V-ない + こととなっている
館内[かんない]では撮影[さつえい]しないこととなっている
It is a rule that photography is not permitted inside
V-られる + こととなっている
違反者[いはんしゃ]は処罰[しょばつ]されることとなっている
It is provided that violators shall be penalized
N+する + こととなっている
毎年[まいとし]健康診断[けんこうしんだん]を実施[じっし]することとなっている
It is established practice to conduct a health checkup every year

tables.caption_tr: Tense and Polarity Variations
rows: States a rule currently in effect: "it is (currently) provided/established that..."
The rule was in effect at a past point in time, often implying it later changed: "it used to be established that..."
Announces a new decision or outcome as it is fixed, without the ongoing-state nuance: "it has been decided that..."
States that something is ruled OUT / prohibited by regulation: "it is provided that... not..."
A prohibition/rule that used to hold in the past

tables.caption_tr: 〜こととなっている vs. Similar Expressions
rows: Objective, impersonal statement of an established rule or system
規約[きやく]により、会費[かいひ]は年[ねん]に一度[いちど]徴収[ちょうしゅう]することとなっている
Same core meaning, but usable in everyday conversation; far more common overall
明日[あした]は9時[くじ]に集合[しゅうごう]することになっている
Emphasizes something is fixed by custom, convention, or common sense rather than explicit regulation
挨拶[あいさつ]は基本[きほん]と決まっている
Explicitly references a stipulated clause or article of a regulation/law
本件[ほんけん]は第[だい]三条[さんじょう]に規定されている
Used in the text of laws/contracts themselves to define a rule ("shall be deemed/treated as")
甲[こう]は乙[おつ]に通知[つうち]するものとする

tables.caption_tr: Typical Contexts Where 〜こととなっている Appears
rows: 制服[せいふく]を着用[ちゃくよう]することとなっている
It is the rule to wear the uniform
契約[けいやく]満了後[まんりょうご]は自動更新[じどうこうしん]することとなっている
Upon expiration, the contract is provided to renew automatically
未成年者[みせいねんしゃ]の飲酒[いんしゅ]は禁止[きんし]されることとなっている
Alcohol consumption by minors is prohibited by law
申請書[しんせいしょ]は本人[ほんにん]が提出[ていしゅつ]することとなっている
It is procedure that the application be submitted by the person in question

ni-tarinai.title_tr: 〜に足りない (Not Worth ~ing, Insignificant, Insufficient to Warrant)
ni-tarinai.intro_tr: 〜に足りない is a formal/literary N1 expression built from the negative form of the classical verb 足る (modern 足りる, "to be sufficient"). Attached after a verb's dictionary form (or a noun via する), it means the action or thing described does not reach the threshold of being "worth doing," "worth mentioning," or "sufficient to warrant" a reaction; in short, "not worth ~ing," "insignificant," or "not enough to." It pairs almost exclusively with a small set of verbs of speech, emotion, and evaluation (恐れる, 驚く, 信じる, 言う, 語る, 論じる, 取る, 心配する). Its affirmative counterpart 〜に足る means the opposite ("worthy of / sufficient to"). The expression is common in written, formal, or slightly literary registers rather than casual speech, and the fixed phrase 取るに足りない ("trivial, insignificant, not worth mentioning") is by far its most frequent everyday use.

tote.intro_tr: 〜とて is a literary/classical concessive particle meaning "even if," "even though," or "although one says/thinks that." It attaches to nouns, quoted clauses, and the plain form of verbs and adjectives to express that even granting the preceding circumstance, the expected conclusion still doesn't follow. It survives in modern Japanese mainly in fixed expressions like さりとて ("even so") and 〜からとて ("just because ~"), and otherwise appears chiefly in novels, essays, historical dramas, and formal or old-fashioned speech. In everyday conversation, its meaning is normally expressed instead by 〜としても, 〜といっても, or 〜でも.

de-are-darouto.title_tr: 〜(で)あれ / 〜であろうと (whatever/whoever it may be, no matter what)
de-are-darouto.intro_tr: 〜(で)あれ and 〜であろうと are formal, literary N1 concessive patterns meaning "whatever/whoever/wherever it may be" or "even if it is ~, no matter ~." Grammatically, あれ is the classical imperative form of ある (via である), and であろう is the volitional form of である, both frozen into fixed concessive expressions. They typically attach to nouns, な-adjectives, or question words (何, 誰, どこ, いつ, どちら) to state that the following clause holds true regardless of the value that fills in the blank. These patterns appear almost exclusively in written, formal, or rhetorical speech (essays, speeches, legal/business text) and rarely in casual conversation, where 〜ても or 〜にしても are used instead.

te-shikarubeki.title_tr: 〜てしかるべき (it should rightly be ~ / it would only be proper for ~)
te-shikarubeki.intro_tr: 〜てしかるべき is a formal, written N1 expression built from the て-form of a verb (or adjective) plus しかるべき, a fossilized classical form meaning "as it should rightly be." It expresses the speaker's judgment that a certain state is the natural, fitting, or deserved outcome; "X should rightly/naturally be ~," "it is only proper that ~." Unlike 〜べきだ, which attaches to a plain dictionary-form verb and urges an action ("you should do X"), 〜てしかるべき attaches to a て-form and evaluates a resulting state or condition, so it is extremely common with passive verbs (認められる, 評価される, 罰せられる, 保障される). It is frequently used with a contrastive が/のに clause to criticize a gap between how things ought to be and how they actually are. Because しかるべき itself derives from classical 然り(しかり)+べき, this pattern belongs to a family of stiff, written/argumentative-register expressions typical of editorials, essays, and formal opinion pieces.

iza-shirazu.title_tr: 〜いざ知らず; "Setting X aside...", "I wouldn't know about X, but..."
iza-shirazu.intro_tr: 〜いざ知らず (lit. "I would/might not know") is a formal, literary N1 expression used to set up a contrast between two cases: "Granting/Setting aside X (which might be acceptable, understandable, or simply unknown), Y is a completely different, more extreme matter." It almost always attaches to a noun with は or なら (NはいざしらずY / NならいざしらずY) and is followed by a clause that states the real, more surprising or more serious point. It carries a slightly old-fashioned, bookish tone and is common in essays, speeches, and formal criticism rather than casual conversation. Because 知らず is the classical negative form of 知る (= 知らない), the phrase literally means "as for X, I wouldn't know (so I won't comment on it), but as for Y..."

Make sure M presents a fact that stands out as more serious, extreme, or unexpected than X

examples.target: 素人[しろうと]ならいざ知[し]らず、プロがこんな初歩[しょほ]的[てき]なミスをするなんて信[しん]じられない。
examples.reading: しろうとならいざしらず、プロがこんなしょほてきなミスをするなんてしんじられない。
examples.translation_tr: An amateur, maybe I could understand; but I can't believe a professional would make such a basic mistake.
examples.note_tr: N + ならいざ知らず sets up an extreme, unbelievable contrast: 'if it were X, fine, but Y is unacceptable.'

examples.target: 昔[むかし]はいざ知[し]らず、今[いま]の若者[わかもの]はスマホがないと生活[せいかつ]できない。
examples.reading: むかしはいざしらず、いまのわかものはスマホがないとせいかつできない。
examples.translation_tr: I don't know about the old days, but today's young people can't live without a smartphone.
examples.note_tr: Time noun + はいざ知らず contrasts a past situation (irrelevant/unknown) with the present reality.

examples.target: 子供[こども]ならいざ知[し]らず、いい大人[おとな]がそんなことも分[わ]からないのか。
examples.reading: こどもならいざしらず、いいおとながそんなこともわからないのか。
examples.translation_tr: If you were a child, I could understand; but you're a grown adult; how can you not understand something like that?
examples.note_tr: Common pattern criticizing an adult by contrasting with the excusable case of a child.

examples.target: 一日[いちにち]や二日[ふつか]ならいざ知[し]らず、一週間[いっしゅうかん]も休[やす]むのは困[こま]る。
examples.reading: いちにちやふつかならいざしらず、いっしゅうかんもやすむのはこまる。
examples.translation_tr: A day or two would be one thing, but taking a whole week off is a problem.
examples.note_tr: いざ知らず often follows two small/acceptable examples joined by や to set the excusable baseline.

examples.target: 田舎[いなか]ならいざ知[し]らず、都会[とかい]でそんなことをすれば大[だい]問題[もんだい]になる。
examples.reading: いなかならいざしらず、とかいでそんなことをすればだいもんだいになる。
examples.translation_tr: In the countryside maybe, but doing that in the city would cause a huge problem.
examples.note_tr: Contrasts locations: countryside (tolerated) vs. city (not tolerated).

examples.target: 神[かみ]ならいざ知[し]らず、人間[にんげん]に未来[みらい]のことなど分[わ]かるはずがない。
examples.reading: かみならいざしらず、にんげんにみらいのことなどわかるはずがない。
examples.translation_tr: If you were a god, perhaps; but there's no way a human could know the future.
examples.note_tr: A classic rhetorical use: contrasting an impossible/idealized subject (god) with the realistic one (human).

examples.target: 冗談[じょうだん]ならいざ知[し]らず、本気[ほんき]でそう思[おも]っているなら問題[もんだい]だ。
examples.reading: じょうだんならいざしらず、ほんきでそうおもっているならもんだいだ。
examples.translation_tr: If it were a joke, fine; but if you seriously think that, it's a problem.
examples.note_tr: Used to distinguish a harmless interpretation from a serious, problematic one.

examples.target: 少額[しょうがく]ならいざ知[し]らず、百万円[ひゃくまんえん]も貸[か]すことはできない。
examples.reading: しょうがくならいざしらず、ひゃくまんえんもかすことはできない。
examples.translation_tr: A small amount might be fine, but I can't lend as much as a million yen.
examples.note_tr: Formal/written register typical of business or financial contexts.

de-are-de-are.intro_tr: 〜であれ〜であれ is a formal, written-style N1 pattern built on the classical imperative-like form of だ/である (あれ). By pairing two contrasting nouns or na-adjective stems, each followed by であれ, the speaker lists two (or more) possible cases and states that the conclusion that follows holds true regardless of which one applies; equivalent to English "whether ... or ...". It is close in meaning to 〜にしろ〜にしろ and 〜にせよ〜にせよ, but carries a slightly more literary, formal tone typically found in essays, speeches, and written argumentation rather than casual conversation. The clause that follows usually expresses an obligation, a fact that doesn't change, or a judgment that applies uniformly to both alternatives (often with 〜なければならない, 〜べきだ, 〜に変わりはない, etc.). A related but distinct single form, 〜であれ (not doubled), attaches to a question word (誰であれ, 何であれ) or stands alone with a concessive meaning of "even if it is ...".

whether it's expensive or cheap (alternative pattern)
footnotes_tr: であれ comes from the classical imperative-conditional of だ/である, so it grammatically behaves like a fixed connective rather than a conjugating verb.
い-adjectives and verbs cannot take であれ directly; use 〜うと〜うと, 〜であろうと〜であろうと, or 〜にしろ〜にしろ instead.

nu-zu-negation.title_tr: 〜ぬ / 〜ず; Classical Negation and Its Modern Remnants
nu-zu-negation.intro_tr: 〜ぬ and 〜ず are classical (bungo) negative auxiliary verbs that attach to the imperfective (mizenkei) stem of a verb; the same stem used before ない in modern Japanese. They are the historical ancestors of modern ない: ぬ corresponds to the plain negative form (ends a sentence or modifies a noun), while ず corresponds to the "without doing" connective form (ないで/ずに). Although replaced by ない in everyday conversation, both survive heavily in modern Japanese: ぬ shows up in proverbs, literary narration, period-drama/samurai speech, and fixed set phrases, while ず is the productive base of many advanced grammar points you already know, such as 〜ずに, 〜ざるを得ない, and 〜のみならず. Learning this pair unlocks proverbs, classical/literary texts, and N1-level idioms built on this old negative system.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of ぬ / ず by verb type (attach to the negative/imperfective stem, i.e. the same stem used before ない)
rows: ある (special, no negative stem in modern grammar)
footnotes_tr: *あらぬ is not used as a plain modern negative; it survives mainly in fixed attributive phrases like あらぬ疑[うたが]い (an unfounded/groundless suspicion) and あらぬ方向[ほうこう] (the wrong/unexpected direction).
する takes せ (not し) before ぬ/ず; this is a classical irregularity: せぬ・せず, not しぬ・しず.

tables.caption_tr: ぬ vs ず; grammatical function and role

Connects to the next clause or verb, meaning "without doing ~"
何[なに]も食[た]べず、寝[ね]た。(Went to bed without eating anything.)
footnotes_tr: Because ぬ can end a sentence, it is the form you meet in proverbs and dramatic dialogue (知らぬ、行かぬ, etc.).
Because ず connects clauses, it is the form that survives as the productive grammatical base of modern N1 patterns (〜ずに, 〜ざるを得ない, 〜のみならず, 〜ずにはいられない).

beshi-relics.title_tr: 〜べし / 〜べからず (Classical Relics of Obligation and Prohibition)
beshi-relics.intro_tr: べし and べからず are classical (bungo) auxiliary verbs that expressed obligation, natural conclusion, or strong prohibition in Old Japanese; roughly the classical ancestors of modern 〜なければならない and 〜てはいけない. Modern Japanese handles everyday obligation with べきだ and prohibition with 〜てはいけない/禁止, but べし and べからず survive as fixed "relics" in proverbs, dojo mottos, old signage, legal/formal writing, and famous quotations. This is mainly a passive-reading skill: you rarely need to produce these forms yourself, but you will meet them on shrine plaques, training-hall walls, historical signs, and literary text. べし attaches directly to the dictionary (終止形) form of a verb and means "should / must / is bound to," while べからず is its classical negative counterpart meaning "must not / shall not." Their conjugated relatives; べき (attributive) and べく (adverbial); remain fully alive and productive in modern Japanese, most visibly in words like なるべく.

mu-volitional.intro_tr: In Classical Japanese, the auxiliary 〜む attached to the negative base (未然形) of a verb expressed volition or conjecture, roughly corresponding to modern 〜う/〜よう ("will / shall / let's"). Through a common sound change (音便), む shifted to ん; especially right before the particle と; giving the fixed literary pattern 〜んとする "to be about to do / on the verge of doing something." This 〜んとする form survives into modern Japanese as a formal, literary way of saying 〜ようとする, and is a staple of N1-level reading passages, news writing, and dramatic narration. Irregular verbs behave specially: する becomes せん (not すん), and 来る becomes こん. Recognizing 〜んとする lets you read classical remnants embedded in otherwise modern, formal Japanese text.

来る never becomes くん; the correct irregular form is こん (written 来ん).

ki-keri-tari.title_tr: Classical Past-Tense Auxiliaries き / けり / たり; For Reading Classical Texts
ki-keri-tari.intro_tr: This entry covers three classical Japanese (文語[ぶんご], "bungo") past-tense auxiliary verbs; き, けり, and たり; which you will encounter constantly in classical literature (monogatari, waka, diaries), in quoted classical language, in fixed idiomatic phrases, and in formal/literary modern Japanese (especially at N1 level). Unlike modern 〜た, which flattens all past nuance into one form, classical Japanese distinguishes the *source* and *feel* of the pastness: き marks something the speaker personally witnessed or experienced directly; けり marks something learned by hearsay/tradition, or expresses a sudden realization or emotional exclamation (詠嘆[えいたん]); and たり (from て + あり) marks completion or a resulting state, and is the direct grammatical ancestor of modern 〜た. This is a receptive, reading-oriented topic: the goal is to recognize these forms in text and understand their nuance, not to actively produce them in speech. Pay special attention to their attributive (連体形[れんたいけい]) forms; し, ける, たる; since these often survive as fossilized patterns in modern formal/literary Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Classical Past Auxiliaries at a Glance
rows: Simple past; a fact the speaker personally witnessed or experienced
'I did / it happened, and I was there for it'
連用形[れんようけい] of the preceding verb/adjective (irregular attachment with カ変[かへん]・サ変[さへん] verbs)
Past learned by hearsay/tradition, OR sudden realization / emotional exclamation (詠嘆[えいたん])
'I heard that...' / 'Oh, it turns out that...!'
連用形[れんようけい] of the preceding verb/adjective
Completion of an action, or the resulting state after it
連用形[れんようけい] of the preceding verb
Same completion/state meaning as たり, but a different historical origin
四段[よだん] verbs' 已然形[いぜんけい]; サ変[さへん] verbs' 未然形[みぜんけい]

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation Table (all six classical bases)
footnotes_tr: き has no 連用形[れんようけい] or 命令形[めいれいけい]; けり likewise has no 連用形[れんようけい] or 命令形[めいれいけい], and けら is only used before ば (けらば, rare).

終止形[しゅうしけい] is the plain 'dictionary' ending form used at the end of a sentence; 連体形[れんたいけい] is used right before a noun; 已然形[いぜんけい] is used with かかり-particles (こそ) or before ば/ど for 'because/although' meaning.

tables.caption_tr: How to Spot Each Form When Reading
rows: 終止形[しゅうしけい] of き
Ends a sentence: states a fact the speaker witnessed directly
Diary literature (日記[にっき]), first-person classical narration
連体形[れんたいけい] of き
Fixed literary phrases, e.g. 若[わか]かりし日[ひ] 'the days when [I] was young'
已然形[いぜんけい] of き
Emphatic or interrogative past, triggered by a preceding かかり-particle
Classical poetry and prose with こそ...しか constructions
終止形[しゅうしけい] of けり
Ends a sentence: hearsay past, or sudden realization
Closing lines of waka; narrative openings like ...ありけり
連体形[れんたいけい] of けり
Modifies a noun, or resolves a kakari-musubi triggered by ぞ・なむ・や・か
終止形[しゅうしけい] of たり (完了)
Ends a sentence: 'has done / is in the resulting state'
Classical prose; direct ancestor of modern 〜た
連体形[れんたいけい] of たり
Adjectival use before a noun: 'that has become...'
Survives today in set phrases like 堂々[どうどう]たる態度[たいど] 'a dignified attitude'; compare the 〜たる sıfat kullanımı pattern in 文語[ぶんご] remnants

tables.caption_tr: き vs. けり; Telling the Two Apart (a common source of confusion)
rows: Speaker's own direct experience or eyewitness account
Hearsay, tradition, or a fact the speaker suddenly realizes
'I heard that...' or 'Oh! It turns out that...!'
Personal diaries (日記[にっき]), autobiographical writing
Monogatari narration; waka poem endings (詠嘆[えいたん] use)

tables.caption_tr: Fossilized Traces of These Auxiliaries in Modern Japanese
rows: Contraction/descendant of たり's forms over time
The standard modern past tense, having absorbed the completion nuance of たり
名残[なごり]惜[お]しき, 若[わか]かりし日[ひ]
連体形[れんたいけい] し of き
Literary/poetic 'the [x] that was...', still used for stylistic effect
堂々[どうどう]たる, 断固[だんこ]たる, 確固[かっこ]たる
連体形[れんたいけい] たる of たり
Formal written Japanese: '[noun]たる[noun]' = 'a [noun] that is emphatically...'
昔々[むかしむかし]…ありけり (storytelling openings)
終止形[しゅうしけい] けり
Still imitated in modern retellings of old tales for a 'once upon a time' flavor

examples.target: 今[いま]は昔[むかし]、竹取[たけとり]の翁[おきな]という者[もの]ありけり。
examples.reading: いまはむかし、たけとりのおきなというものありけり。
examples.translation_tr: Long, long ago, there lived an old bamboo cutter. (opening line of the Taketori Monogatari; けり sets the tone of a traditional tale being retold, not witnessed firsthand)

examples.target: 春[はる]は来[き]にけり。
examples.reading: はるはきにけり。
examples.translation_tr: Spring has come! (the speaker suddenly realizes/exclaims this; the 詠嘆[えいたん] use of けり, common at the end of waka poems)

examples.target: 昔[むかし]、男[おとこ]ありけり。
examples.reading: むかし、おとこありけり。
examples.translation_tr: Once upon a time, there was a man. (opening formula of the Ise Monogatari, using narrative けり)

examples.target: 若[わか]かりし日[ひ]を思[おも]い出[い]づ。
examples.reading: わかかりしひをおもいいづ。
examples.translation_tr: I recall the days when I was young. (し is the attributive form of き, marking a fact the speaker personally lived through)

examples.target: われ、この目[め]にて見[み]き。
examples.reading: われ、このめにてみき。
examples.translation_tr: I saw it with my own eyes. (き = simple past of direct personal witness, typical of diary literature)

examples.target: 花[はな]は散[ち]りたり。
examples.reading: はなはちりたり。
examples.translation_tr: The flowers have scattered (and remain so). (たり expresses completion with a resulting state; the direct ancestor of modern 〜た)

examples.target: 堂々[どうどう]たる態度[たいど]で語[かた]った。
examples.reading: どうどうたるたいどでかたった。
examples.translation_tr: He/she spoke with a dignified attitude. (たる is the attributive form of たり, still surviving today as a fossilized adjectival pattern before nouns)

examples.target: 桜[さくら]の花[はな]は今[いま]や盛[さか]りなりけり。
examples.reading: さくらのはなはいまやさかりなりけり。
examples.translation_tr: The cherry blossoms are now at their very peak! (けり here again marks the speaker's sudden realization, not something merely reported)

bungo-relic-forms.title_tr: 文語 Relic Conjugations: 〜ざる / 〜べき / 〜たる as Adjectival Forms
bungo-relic-forms.intro_tr: Classical Japanese (文語/bungo) had a different conjugation system from modern spoken Japanese (口語/kōgo), and a handful of its forms survive today as frozen, mostly written-register fossils rather than living conjugation patterns. The three most important survivors are ざる (the classical attributive negative, from the auxiliary ず), べき (the classical attributive form of べし, "should/must"), and たる (the classical attributive form of the copula たり, "to be ~"). All three share one key trait: they are attributive (連体形) forms, meaning their natural job is to sit directly in front of a noun and modify it; 知らざる人 ("a person who does not know"), 行くべき道 ("the path one should take"), 堂々たる態度 ("a dignified manner"). In modern Japanese they no longer conjugate through the full six-stage classical paradigm; they appear almost exclusively as fixed set phrases, proverbs, formal writing, legal/regulatory text, and literary style (である体). This page maps each form back to its classical parent auxiliary, shows the full historical conjugation for reference, and lists the everyday fossilized expressions a learner will actually encounter.

tables.caption_tr: Overview: the three relic forms and their classical origin
rows: negative attributive: 'which does not ~', modifies a noun
知[し]らざる人[ひと]; 'a person who does not know'
行[い]くべき道[みち]; 'the path one should take'
責任者[せきにんしゃ]たる者[もの]; 'one who is the responsible party'

tables.caption_tr: Classical ず (negation auxiliary); full six-form conjugation and modern survival
rows: stem before volitional む: ざらむ
literary 'without ~ing': 言[い]わず語[かた]らず
fixed proverbs/mottos: 為[な]せば成[な]る、為[な]さねば成[な]らず
ざる is the productive relic form: 知[し]らざる者[もの]
rare, only in set phrases: 知[し]らねば
footnotes_tr: The modern negative suffix 〜ない has no direct classical ancestor in this paradigm; ぬ/ざる/ず are the true classical negators. Modern ん (as in すみません) is actually a sound-shift of ぬ, not ない.

tables.caption_tr: Classical べし ('should/must'); full six-form conjugation and modern survival
rows: 行[い]くべく努力[どりょく]する; 'strive so as to go'
mottos, regulations, classical quotations: 初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず
the most productive relic today: 行[い]くべき道[みち]
footnotes_tr: Attaching べき to する is irregular: classical grammar requires the classical shūshikei す, giving すべき, though modern usage widely accepts するべき as well; すべき is considered the more traditionally 'correct' written form.

tables.caption_tr: Classical たり (copula 'to be ~'); full six-form conjugation and modern survival
rows: と is fully alive: 堂々[どうどう]と話[はな]す; 'to speak in a dignified way'
almost never used alone in modern text
modifies the following noun directly, like a な-adjective
alive in written style: 堂々[どうどう]たる態度[たいど]
survives in fixed mottos: 紳士[しんし]たれ; 'Be a gentleman!'

tables.caption_tr: Common たる-adjectives (タリ活用 words) still used in formal/written Japanese
footnotes_tr: These words cannot take な before a noun the way ordinary な-adjectives do; they only use たる (before nouns) or と (before verbs), never plain だ/である conjugation in casual speech; they belong almost exclusively to formal writing (news reports, essays, literary narration).

tables.caption_tr: Frozen idioms and set phrases built from ざる / べき / たる
rows: 見[み]ざる言[い]わざる聞[き]かざる
みざる・いわざる・きかざる
'see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil' (the three wise monkeys)
許[ゆる]されざる罪[つみ]
初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず
しょしんわするべからず
the way things ought to be
one who is a leader (as a leader, one should...)
教師[きょうし]たる自覚[じかく]
the self-awareness of being a teacher

tables.caption_tr: Usage notes: how these relic forms differ from their modern equivalents
rows: ざる is written/literary register only, and normally cannot end a sentence by itself in modern Japanese (unlike ない); it survives mainly attached directly before a noun or in 〜ざるを得[え]ない type constructions
べき modifying a noun directly (べき道, べき姿) is attributive use; べきだ as a sentence-ending predicate is the modern extension of the same classical form
〜な / 〜という (modern な-adjective or explanatory clause)
たる is confined to formal/literary register and a closed set of onomatopoeic-origin words (堂々たる, 確固たる, etc.) plus the '⟨role⟩たる者' pattern; it cannot be freely created with new adjectives the way な can

examples.target: 見[み]ざる言[い]わざる聞[き]かざる。
examples.reading: みざる、いわざる、きかざる。
examples.translation_tr: See no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil. (the classic 'three wise monkeys' proverb; ざる is the classical negative attributive form modifying an implied noun, 'monkey')

examples.target: 許[ゆる]されざる過[あやま]ちを犯[おか]してしまった。
examples.reading: ゆるされざるあやまちをおかしてしまった。
examples.translation_tr: I committed an unforgivable mistake. (許されざる = 'that cannot be forgiven', modifying 過ち directly, in place of modern 許されない)

examples.target: これが本来[ほんらい]あるべき姿[すがた]だ。
examples.reading: これがほんらいあるべきすがただ。
examples.translation_tr: This is the way things ought to originally be. (べき from classical べし, attributive form modifying 姿)

examples.target: 指導者[しどうしゃ]たる者[もの]、常[つね]に責任[せきにん]を持[も]つべきだ。
examples.reading: しどうしゃたるもの、つねにせきにんをもつべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: One who is a leader should always bear responsibility. (指導者たる者 = 'one who is [in the position of] a leader', formal/written register)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は堂々[どうどう]たる態度[たいど]で質問[しつもん]に答[こた]えた。
examples.reading: かれはどうどうたるたいどでしつもんにこたえた。
examples.translation_tr: He answered the question with a dignified, composed manner. (堂々たる functions like a な-adjective before 態度, from classical タリ活用)

examples.target: 確固[かっこ]たる決意[けつい]を持[も]って挑[いど]んだ。
examples.reading: かっこたるけついをもっていどんだ。
examples.translation_tr: He took on the challenge with firm resolve. (確固たる = 'firm, unshakeable', a common written-style フル tる-adjective)

examples.target: 初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず、と先生[せんせい]は言[い]った。
examples.reading: しょしんわするべからず、とせんせいはいった。
examples.translation_tr: 'Never forget your beginner's spirit,' the teacher said. (a fixed proverb combining べし's negative form べからず)

examples.target: 紳士[しんし]たれ、と父[ちち]に教[おし]えられた。
examples.reading: しんしたれ、とちちにおしえられた。
examples.translation_tr: I was taught by my father to 'be a gentleman.' (たれ is the classical imperative of たり, surviving only in fixed mottos and quotations)

kanbun-kakikudashi.title_tr: Kanbun Kundoku Remnants in Formal Writing (〜べく / 〜ざる)
kanbun-kakikudashi.intro_tr: Kanbun kundoku (漢文訓読) was the traditional method of reading classical Chinese texts by reordering and inflecting them according to Japanese grammar, using a fixed set of auxiliary verbs and connectors to render Chinese logical structure in Japanese. Although this reading style is over a thousand years old, many of its grammatical fossils survive intact in modern formal, legal, academic, and official written Japanese (公文書, 法律文, 論文, 規則, 掲示). The most visible remnants are the classical auxiliary べし (giving べく, べからず, べからざる, べき) and the classical negative ず (giving ざる, ざれば, ざるを得ない), plus a family of stiff kanbun-style connectors (及び, 並びに, 且つ, 若しくは, 即ち, 故に). Recognizing these forms is essential for reading laws, regulations, official notices, and formal essays, even though they are never used in everyday speech. This page gathers the core kanbun-kundoku remnants in one reference so you can identify them quickly wherever they appear."

tables.caption_tr: Core べし-family remnants (obligation / prohibition, classical→modern formal)
rows: adverbial: in order to / so as to
attributive: that must not be ~ / that cannot be ~
before a noun in formal writing
an act that cannot be forgiven
attributive: that should be ~ (fully modern, very common)
a problem that should be considered

tables.caption_tr: Classical negative ず conjugation and its modern formal remnants
column_headers: Still used in modern Japanese as
rows: fixed adverbial phrases, formal predicate endings
許さず (does not permit / permits not)
知らざる世界 (a world one does not know)
為さざれば成らず (if one does not do, nothing is achieved)
'cannot help but ~', 'have no choice but to ~'
fully productive in modern formal speech/writing
認めざるを得ない (cannot help but admit)
literary variant of 〜ざるを得ない (ends in ず instead of ない)
従わざるを得ず (has no choice but to comply)

tables.caption_tr: Kanbun-kundoku connectors still standard in legal and official documents
rows: and also (connects larger groups when 及び is used for smaller ones)
or (used for the smaller-level 'or' when 又は marks the larger)
and moreover, and at the same time

tables.caption_tr: Other frozen kanbun-kundoku forms you will meet in formal text
rows: classical attributive of たり (copula 'to be')
責任者たる者 (a person who is the person in charge)
classical written for これ/この
formal pointer word in legal/old text
違反せる者 (one who has violated)
記載せる事項 (matters that have been recorded)
去らんとする (about to leave)

examples.target: 新規則を制定するに当たり、全職員は之[これ]を遵守すべく努めるものとする。
examples.reading: しんきそくをせいていするにあたり、ぜんしょくいんはこれをじゅんしゅすべくつとめるものとする。
examples.translation_tr: In establishing the new regulations, all staff members shall make efforts so as to comply with them.
examples.note_tr: べく = classical purpose/manner form of べし, still standard in formal regulations and legal writing.

examples.target: 未成年者は本契約を締結すべからず。
examples.reading: みせいねんしゃはほんけいやくをていけつすべからず。
examples.translation_tr: Minors shall not conclude this contract.
examples.note_tr: べからず = classical prohibitive, frozen ending common on official notices and legal texts.

examples.target: 看過すべからざる問題が発見された。
examples.reading: かんかすべからざるもんだいがはっけんされた。
examples.translation_tr: A problem that cannot be overlooked was discovered.
examples.note_tr: べからざる = attributive form of べからず, used directly before a noun.

examples.target: 彼の功績は少なからざるものがある。
examples.reading: かれのこうせきはすくなからざるものがある。
examples.translation_tr: His achievements are by no means small (lit. are not few).
examples.note_tr: ざる = classical attributive negative, from ず; here modifying もの as a noun-modifying clause.

examples.target: 規則に従わざる者は処分される。
examples.reading: きそくにしたがわざるものはしょぶんされる。
examples.translation_tr: Those who do not comply with the rules will be disciplined.
examples.note_tr: Verb + ざる + noun is a fixed kanbun-kundoku pattern meaning 'one who does not ~'.

examples.target: 事態は予断を許さざる状況にある。
examples.reading: じたいはよだんをゆるさざるじょうきょうにある。
examples.translation_tr: The situation is one that does not allow for premature judgment.
examples.note_tr: 許さざる = 許す(negative attributive), a very common formal-writing collocation.

examples.target: 本会議は関係者及び有識者をもって構成する。
examples.reading: ほんかいぎはかんけいしゃおよびゆうしきしゃをもってこうせいする。
examples.translation_tr: This committee shall be composed of related parties and experts.
examples.note_tr: 及び = 'and', a kanbun-derived formal connector still standard in laws and official documents.

examples.target: 提出期限に遅れたる者は受理せざるものとする。
examples.reading: ていしゅつきげんにおくれたるものはじゅりせざるものとする。
examples.translation_tr: Those who are late for the submission deadline shall not be accepted.
examples.note_tr: 遅れたる = classical たり attributive ('who is/has become late'), paired with せざる (negative of する).

keigo-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Keigo: Double Honorifics and 二重敬語 (Nijū Keigo) Errors
keigo-advanced.intro_tr: 二重敬語 (nijū keigo, "double honorifics") is a classic N1-level error where two honorific markers are stacked onto a single verb that is already fully honorific by itself. This most often happens when a learner (or even a native speaker being overly cautious) adds られる or an お/ご~になる/する pattern on top of a special irregular keigo verb like おっしゃる, いらっしゃる, 伺う, or 拝見する; verbs that are already complete sonkeigo or kenjōgo forms and need no further marking. While standard style guides (文化庁 敬語の指針) label these forms as incorrect, a handful of double-structured phrases; such as お召し上がりください and お伺いする; have become so conventionalized through repeated business/service use that they are now accepted as correct despite technically violating the rule. This page catalogs the most common double-honorific mistakes, shows the correct alternatives, and separates true errors from accepted lexicalized exceptions.

tables.caption_tr: Quick Reference: Basic Honorific Formulas (context for the errors below)
column_headers: Special irregular verb (already complete; add NOTHING more)
rows: お読みになる、ご利用になる
おっしゃる・いらっしゃる・なさる・召し上がる・ご覧になる・くださる
(do NOT apply られる to the special verbs on the left)
お/ご + stem + する/いたす
お読みする、ご利用いたす
伺う・申す・いたす・存じる・拝見する・参る・頂く・差し上げる

tables.caption_tr: Type 1 Error: Special Sonkeigo Verb + られる (most common 二重敬語)
rows: おっしゃる already = honorific 'say'; られる adds a second honorific layer
おっしゃる / おっしゃいます
いらっしゃる / いらっしゃいます
なさる / なさいます
召し上がる / 召し上がります
くださる / くださいます
ご覧になる is already a full お/ご~になる sonkeigo phrase; られる is redundant
ご覧になる / ご覧になります

tables.caption_tr: Type 2 Error: お/ご~になる Pattern Stacked onto an Already-Honorific Verb
rows: おっしゃりになる / お + おっしゃりになる
adds お~になる on top of a verb that is already sonkeigo
adds お~になる on top of an already sonkeigo verb
召し上がる (note: お召し上がりください is a separate, accepted set phrase; see exceptions table)
ご存知でいらっしゃる / ご存知になられる
stacks いらっしゃる/になられる onto the already-honorific ご存知
ご存知だ / ご存知でいらっしゃいます (single layer only)

tables.caption_tr: Type 3 Error: Special Kenjōgo Verb + させていただく / お~する (over-humbling)
rows: very common in business speech; grammar purists call it double, but widely tolerated
extremely common; borderline-accepted in business register
true error; also a malformed conjugation
申します / 申し上げます
存じます / 存じております

tables.caption_tr: Lexicalized Exceptions: Historically Double but Now Accepted as Standard
column_headers: Why it looks like 二重敬語
rows: お召し上がりください
お + 召し上がる (already sonkeigo) + ください
adds お prefix to an already-honorific verb
Fully accepted; standard in hospitality/service Japanese
お伺いする / お伺いいたす
お + 伺う (already kenjōgo) + する/いたす
adds お~する to an already-humble verb
Fully accepted; extremely common in business Japanese
お + 見える (semi-polite 'to arrive/appear') + になる
見える itself carries a polite nuance before becoming a full お~になる phrase
ご + 覧 + に入れる (kenjōgo 'show')
layered kenjōgo structure fixed by convention
Accepted as a set kenjōgo phrase meaning 'humbly show'

tables.caption_tr: Diagnostic Checklist: How to Spot and Avoid 二重敬語
rows: Is the verb one of the special sonkeigo verbs? (いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, 召し上がる, ご覧になる, くださる)
Never add られる or お/ご~になる on top; the verb alone is already complete.
Is the verb one of the special kenjōgo verbs? (伺う, 申す, いたす, 存じる, 拝見する, 参る, 頂く, 差し上げる)
Never add お/ご~する・いたす or させていただく unless the result is a recognized lexicalized exception.
Are two honorific markers attached to the same verb stem (e.g., られる + お~になる, or お~ + already-honorific verb)?
This is the structural red flag for 二重敬語; simplify to a single marker.
Is the combination one of the conventional fixed phrases (お召し上がりください, お伺いする, お見えになる, ご覧に入れる)?
If yes, treat it as a correct, accepted exception; do not 'fix' it.
When unsure in business writing, which form is safer?
Prefer the single, non-doubled special verb form (e.g., 伺います over 伺わせていただきます) unless the doubled form is the established convention in that context.

examples.target: 社長がおっしゃられた内容を確認します。

keigo-written.title_tr: Formal Written Language (拝啓[はいけい]/敬具[けいぐ], Letter Formulas)
keigo-written.intro_tr: Formal written Japanese letters follow a rigid, almost ritualistic structure inherited from classical epistolary style (候文/書簡文). Every proper letter opens with a 頭語[とうご] ("opening word" such as 拝啓[はいけい]) and must close with a matching 結語[けいご] ("closing word" such as 敬具[けいぐ]); these two always come as fixed pairs, never mixed at random. Between them, the letter follows a set sequence: seasonal greeting → well-wishing greeting → main body → closing wish → date/signature/addressee. This register is used for business correspondence, formal invitations, condolence/congratulation letters, and official documents, and is almost never used in everyday speech or casual email. Mastering the fixed phrase inventory (時候の挨拶, 結びの言葉) matters more than grammar creativity; native writers largely select from a known repertoire of set phrases rather than composing freely.

written-vs-spoken.title_tr: Written vs Spoken Register (である体 vs だ・である)
written-vs-spoken.intro_tr: Japanese has two broad stylistic registers built on the copula: the spoken/plain style using だ (and its polite counterpart です), and the written/literary style using である, often called である体. である体 is the default register for newspapers, academic papers, essays, reports, and encyclopedic writing; it sounds objective, impersonal, and authoritative, and is never used in face-to-face conversation. だ体 is the plain form used among friends and family, while です/ます体 is the polite spoken form used with strangers or in polite conversation. A key rule of written Japanese is register consistency: a single text must not mix である with です/ます endings. This page maps out how だ, です, and である relate to each other across all conjugations, which vocabulary and grammar items shift between spoken and written style, and where each register is expected.

tables.caption_tr: Core Copula Conjugation: だ (spoken) vs である (written)

じゃない / ではない
じゃありません / ではありません
じゃない is casual-only; ではない works in both plain and written style
じゃなかった / ではなかった
じゃありませんでした / ではありませんでした
である体 uses であって to link clauses formally
であろう is common in essays/news commentary
; (cannot attach directly; needs という + noun)
e.g. 学生である彼 = 'he, who is a student'; plain だ cannot precede a noun this way
であるならば / であれば
であれば is the formal written conditional

そのため / それゆえ
非常[ひじょう]に / きわめて
progressive/state aspect (full form required in writing)
directional aspect (full form required in writing)
わたし / ぼく / おれ
私[わたくし] / 筆者[ひっしゃ]
first person (formal writing often avoids pronouns or uses 筆者 'the author')
し得[え]ない / しかねる

Business emails, service interactions, textbooks aimed at learners
Conversation with friends/family, casual diaries, informal texts/chat

Choose one register: either 彼は学生である。(written) or 彼は学生です。(spoken polite)

Spoken contractions look unpolished in written registers
Always write the full form: 〜ている / 〜ていく

de-aru-tai.intro_tr: である体 is the formal written register built on the copula である, the literary/written counterpart of だ. It is used in academic papers, newspaper articles, reports, encyclopedia entries, and other objective, impersonal writing; never in conversation. である behaves like だ but conjugates more like a linking verb, giving it extra forms (であり, であった, であろう, であれば) that だ lacks. Because である体 signals distance and objectivity, first-person opinions are usually softened with hedging patterns like 〜と考えられる or 〜のではないだろうか rather than stated bluntly. This page maps out the full conjugation, compares it side-by-side with です/ます and だ, and lists the vocabulary and sentence-final patterns typical of academic Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation of である compared with だ
rows: ではない / じゃない
ではなかった / じゃなかった
な (as in 学生[がくせい]な → rare) / の
である (as in 学生[がくせい]である〜)
であるか / であろうか (formal rhetorical question)
footnotes_tr: である itself never takes ます; it has no polite counterpart; that role is filled by です in the polite register.
The negative of である is not であらない; ではない / でない is used instead.

行[い]く。 (verbs are identical in だ体 and である体)
footnotes_tr: である only replaces the copula (だ/です); it does not change how verbs or i-adjectives conjugate.
です/ます is used in polite speech and polite writing (letters, blogs, business emails); だ体 is casual speech/diaries; である体 is reserved for objective, impersonal written text.

nominalization-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Nominalization: こと vs の vs ところ vs 次第 Compared
nominalization-advanced.intro_tr: こと, の, ところ, and 次第 can all turn a clause into a noun-like unit, but at the N1 level the real challenge is knowing exactly which one native speakers choose and why. こと nominalizes an abstract fact, content, or idea that is reported, decided, or referred to conceptually. の nominalizes a concrete scene or moment that is directly perceived with the senses (or used for emphatic/explanatory のだ). ところ does not nominalize an action itself so much as a specific temporal phase of it; about to happen, in progress, or just finished. 次第 nominalizes a condition that determines an outcome, or marks strict immediacy ('the moment X happens'), and belongs mainly to formal/written register. This page compares all four side by side so you can choose correctly instead of guessing.

tables.caption_tr: Core functions at a glance
rows: facts, ideas, reported content, activities as labels
a concrete scene directly perceived; explanatory emphasis (のだ)
moments witnessed with the senses; explanations
a specific point/phase within an ongoing event
the 'about to / mid-way / just finished' moment of an action
a condition that determines the outcome; strict immediacy

tables.caption_tr: こと vs の: which verbs require which
rows: 見[み]る, 聞[き]こえる, 感[かん]じる, 眺[なが]める
Describes a scene unfolding physically before the speaker; こと sounds unnatural or wrong here.
伝[つた]える, 命[めい]じる, 決[き]める, 約束[やくそく]する, 祈[いの]る, 望[のぞ]む
The content is conceptual, not something witnessed with the eyes/ears.
やめる, 始[はじ]める
Both exist, but こと is preferred in writing; のをやめる is common in casual speech.
泳[およ]ぐことができる is correct; 泳[およ]ぐのができる is ungrammatical.
Not true nominalization of an action; it explains or emphasizes a situation.
好[す]きだ, 嫌[きら]いだ
こと feels slightly more formal/general; の feels more immediate/personal, e.g. 音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]くのが好[す]きだ.

tables.caption_tr: ところ: marking the phase of an action
rows: 出[で]かけるところです (I'm about to head out)
right in the middle of doing something
食[た]べているところです (I'm in the middle of eating)
着[つ]いたところです (I've just arrived)
遊[あそ]んでいるところを見[み]られた (I was seen while playing)
Vる/Vている + ところに/ところへ
出[で]かけるところに電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]った (the phone rang just as I was about to leave)
走[はし]ったところで間[ま]に合[あ]わない (even if I run, I won't make it)

tables.caption_tr: 次第: dependency and immediacy
rows: the outcome depends entirely on this
結果[けっか]は運[うん]次第[しだい]だ (the result depends entirely on luck)
天気[てんき]次第[しだい]で中止[ちゅうし]になる (it may be cancelled depending on the weather)
as soon as… (formal 'the moment X happens')
着[つ]き次第[しだい]、電話[でんわ]します (I'll call as soon as I arrive)
(formal) that is the situation/reason; used to close an explanation
こういう次第[しだい]でございます (that is how the situation came to be)
